s1.text: human knowledge of truth is limited by mortality, for now

biblical.text: For we know in part, and we prophesy in part. But when that which is perfect is come, then that which is in part shall be done away... For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known.
biblical.comment: Paul's foundational statement on mortal epistemic limits.

biblical.text: For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, saith the Lord. For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways, and my thoughts than your thoughts.
The secret things belong unto the Lord our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever, that we may do all the words of this law.
biblical.comment: The revealed / unrevealed distinction that governs this article.

restoration.text: Behold, great and marvelous are the works of the Lord. How unsearchable are the depths of the mysteries of him; and it is impossible that man should find out all his ways.
restoration.comment: Confirms the biblical posture: God's depths exceed mortal search.

restoration.text: Yea, verily I say unto you, in that day when the Lord shall come, he shall reveal all things—things which have passed, and hidden things which no man knew, things of the earth, by which it was made, and the purpose and the end thereof.
restoration.comment: Full revelation is reserved for the day of the Lord's coming.

s2.text: we neither reject nor disrespect religious institutions, traditions, or their formalized creeds and theologies

biblical.text: Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations.
biblical.comment: The posture of fellowship without forcing agreement.

biblical.text: Let us not therefore judge one another any more: but judge this rather, that no man put a stumblingblock or an occasion to fall in his brother's way.
But take heed lest by any means this liberty of yours become a stumblingblock to them that are weak.

restoration.text: We claim the privilege of worshiping Almighty God according to the dictates of our own conscience, and allow all men the same privilege, let them worship how, where, or what they may.
restoration.comment: Restoration witness to the biblical principle of conscience in worship.

restoration.text: We believe that religion is instituted of God; and that men are amenable to him, and to him only, for the exercise of it, unless their religious opinions prompt them to infringe upon the rights and liberties of others.

s3.text: no one among us has walked the full ranges of heaven to measure and catalog its glories, to count and classify its inhabitants, or to chart the order and hierarchy of its councils

biblical.text: And no man hath ascended up to heaven, but he that came down from heaven, even the Son of man which is in heaven.
biblical.comment: The direct biblical anchor — only Christ has ascended.

biblical.text: Who hath ascended up into heaven, or descended? who hath gathered the wind in his fists? who hath bound the waters in a garment? who hath established all the ends of the earth? what is his name, and what is his son's name, if thou canst tell?
biblical.comment: The rhetorical question Agur answers with silence.

biblical.text: Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth? declare, if thou hast understanding. Who hath laid the measures thereof, if thou knowest? or who hath stretched the line upon it?
biblical.comment: God's response to speculative claims about His works.

restoration.text: For it came to pass after I had desired to know the things that my father had seen... I was caught away in the Spirit of the Lord, yea, into an exceedingly high mountain, which I never had before seen, and upon which I never had before set my foot.
restoration.comment: Even in the Restoration record, heaven is not walked by mortal initiative — it is shown in vision by the Spirit. Consistent with the biblical posture of this phrase.

s4.text: speculating beyond the bounds of wisdom God has set

biblical.text: The secret things belong unto the Lord our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever.
Trust in the Lord with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding. In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths. Be not wise in thine own eyes.
I say... to every man that is among you, not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think soberly, according as God hath dealt to every man the measure of faith.
biblical.comment: Sober thinking as the biblical antidote to speculation.

restoration.text: But behold, the Jews were a stiffnecked people; and they despised the words of plainness... and sought for things that they could not understand. Wherefore, because of their blindness, which blindness came by looking beyond the mark, they must needs fall.
restoration.comment: “Looking beyond the mark” — the Restoration's own diagnosis of the same disease Proverbs names.

restoration.text: And as all have not faith, seek ye diligently and teach one another words of wisdom; yea, seek ye out of the best books words of wisdom; seek learning, even by study and also by faith.
restoration.comment: Study remains the disciple's duty; speculation is the distortion of that duty.

s5.text: Secret things belong unto the Lord our God

biblical.text: The secret things belong unto the Lord our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever, that we may do all the words of this law.
biblical.comment: Moses' closing address to Israel. The verse carries the full principle: what is hidden is God's; what is revealed is ours to obey. This is the Plainness article in miniature.

restoration.text: Yea, verily I say unto you, in that day when the Lord shall come, he shall reveal all things—things which have passed, and hidden things which no man knew.
restoration.comment: Witnesses that the “secret things” of Deuteronomy will eventually be opened — in God's time, not man's.

s6.text: weightier matters” of which Christ spoke: justice, mercy, and faithfulness

biblical.text: Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye pay tithe of mint and anise and cummin, and have omitted the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy, and faith: these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone.
biblical.comment: Christ's own hierarchy. The specific terms — judgment, mercy, faith — govern this ministry's self-limitation.

biblical.text: But woe unto you, Pharisees! for ye tithe mint and rue and all manner of herbs, and pass over judgment, and the love of God: these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone.
biblical.comment: Luke's parallel, emphasizing judgment and the love of God.

biblical.text: He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the Lord require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?
biblical.comment: The prophetic summary Christ echoes in Matthew 23.

restoration.text: And now, for the sake of these things which I have spoken unto you—that is, for the sake of retaining a remission of your sins from day to day... I would that ye should impart of your substance to the poor, every man according to that which he hath, such as feeding the hungry, clothing the naked, visiting the sick, and administering to their relief, both spiritually and temporally.
restoration.comment: King Benjamin's practical articulation of what justice and mercy look like when walked out.

s7.definition: Coined from the Greek ek merous (“out of a part”) — Paul’s own words in 1 Corinthians 13:9, “we know in part.” Merognosis names the honest epistemic posture of this ministry: our knowing is real but partial, until the day we shall know as we are known. Distinct from gnostic overreach (claiming full knowledge of divine things) and agnostic underreach (claiming they are unknowable), to walk in merognosis is to affirm what God has revealed, confess freely what He has not, and decline to bind another’s conscience with what cannot be known.

biblical.text: For we know in part (ἐκ μέρους, ek merous), and we prophesy in part... For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known.
biblical.comment: The Greek phrase ek merous — “out of a part” — is the etymological root of merognosis. Paul's own confession of partial knowing is the posture the coined term names.

biblical.text: Canst thou by searching find out God? canst thou find out the Almighty unto perfection?
And if any man think that he knoweth any thing, he knoweth nothing yet as he ought to know.

restoration.text: Whose wisdom is great, whose understanding reacheth to heaven... which he will make known unto all who serve him in righteousness and in truth.
restoration.comment: Revelation is promised to the faithful — but always as gift, never as mortal achievement.

restoration.text: It is given unto many to know the mysteries of God; nevertheless they are laid under a strict command that they shall not impart... save according to the portion of his word which he doth grant unto the children of men.
restoration.comment: Mysteries are portioned, not possessed — a Restoration parallel to Paul's “in part.”

crossref.label: Companion Essay
crossref.title: Merognosticism — A Plain Confession of Partial Knowing

s8.text: sophistries of gnosticism, agnosticism, skepticism, atheism, and any ‘-ism’ that divides faith in Christ

biblical.text: Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.
biblical.comment: Paul's warning against intellectual systems that displace Christ.

biblical.text: O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science falsely so called: which some professing have erred concerning the faith.
biblical.comment: Pauline pattern: guard the trust; avoid contentions that divide faith.

biblical.text: But foolish and unlearned questions avoid, knowing that they do gender strifes.

restoration.text: O the vainness, and the frailties, and the foolishness of men! When they are learned they think they are wise, and they hearken not unto the counsel of God... But to be learned is good if they hearken unto the counsels of God.
restoration.comment: Jacob's diagnosis of learning that divorces from faith.

restoration.text: They shall contend one with another; and their priests shall contend one with another, and they shall teach with their learning, and deny the Holy Ghost, which giveth utterance.
restoration.comment: A warning against contending sects — precisely the dynamic the Articles refuse.

s9.text: We know in part, and we prophesy in part

biblical.text: For we know in part, and we prophesy in part. But when that which is perfect is come, then that which is in part shall be done away.
biblical.comment: Paul's direct language. The merognosis posture named by the biblical Greek itself (ek merous).

restoration.text: If thou shalt ask, thou shalt receive revelation upon revelation, knowledge upon knowledge, that thou mayest know the mysteries and peaceable things—that which bringeth joy, that which bringeth life eternal.
restoration.comment: Line-upon-line is the Restoration's cadence of partial knowing becoming fuller in time.

restoration.text: He that will harden his heart, the same receiveth the lesser portion of the word; and he that will not harden his heart, to him is given the greater portion of the word.
restoration.comment: Knowledge is always portioned — even under the new covenant of the Restoration.

s10.text: when we shall know as we are known

biblical.text: For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known.
biblical.comment: The paraphrase draws directly from Paul's closing line of the hymn to charity.

restoration.text: They who dwell in his presence are the church of the Firstborn... and they see as they are seen, and know as they are known, having received of his fulness and of his grace.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's direct echo of 1 Corinthians 13:12, applied to those who dwell in God's presence.

s11.text: we will not bind the conscience of any fellow believer with doctrines built from our own speculation or from the theologies of others

biblical.text: Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations.
biblical.comment: Paul's governing rule for fellowship across differing convictions.

biblical.text: Let us not therefore judge one another any more: but judge this rather, that no man put a stumblingblock or an occasion to fall in his brother's way.
Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage.
biblical.comment: Conscience-binding without divine warrant is the very yoke Paul warns against.

restoration.text: We claim the privilege of worshiping Almighty God according to the dictates of our own conscience, and allow all men the same privilege, let them worship how, where, or what they may.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's explicit confession of conscience-freedom — one of its clearest interfaith affirmations.

restoration.text: We believe that religion is instituted of God; and that men are amenable to him, and to him only, for the exercise of it, unless their religious opinions prompt them to infringe upon the rights and liberties of others.

s12.text: no soul is barred from Christ or from salvation for lacking a perfect understanding

biblical.text: And he said unto Jesus, Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom. And Jesus said unto him, Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.
biblical.comment: The thief on the cross: no creedal competency, no catechesis — only faith in Christ. Christ's answer is decisive for the doctrine of this phrase.

biblical.text: For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.

If thou shalt confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus, and shalt believe in thine heart that God hath raised him from the dead, thou shalt be saved... For whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.
biblical.comment: Paul's universal offer. The test is calling on the Lord, not passing a doctrinal exam.

restoration.text: He denieth none that come unto him, black and white, bond and free, male and female... all are alike unto God.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's most sweeping affirmation of Christ's unconditional welcome.

restoration.text: And I am filled with charity, which is everlasting love; wherefore, all children are alike unto me; wherefore, I love little children with a perfect love; and they are all alike and partakers of salvation.

s13.text: You believe in God; believe also in me

biblical.text: Let not your heart be troubled: ye believe in God, believe also in me.
biblical.comment: Christ's Upper Room discourse. The simplicity of the invitation is the weight of the phrase.

restoration.text: And this is my doctrine, and it is the doctrine which the Father hath given unto me; and I bear record of the Father, and the Father beareth record of me, and the Holy Ghost beareth record of the Father and me; and I bear record that the Father commandeth all men, everywhere, to repent and believe in me.
restoration.comment: The risen Christ in Bountiful restating the same invitation: believe in Him.

s14.text: If you love me, keep my commandments

biblical.text: If ye love me, keep my commandments.
biblical.comment: Christ's own summary of discipleship: love expressed as obedience.

biblical.text: He that hath my commandments, and keepeth them, he it is that loveth me: and he that loveth me shall be loved of my Father, and I will love him, and will manifest myself to him.
biblical.comment: Seven verses later, Christ returns to the same principle with a deeper promise — He manifests Himself to those who keep His word.

biblical.text: For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments: and his commandments are not grievous.

restoration.text: If thou lovest me thou shalt serve me and keep all my commandments.
restoration.comment: Christ's own word through Joseph Smith, identical in substance to John 14:15.

restoration.text: And he said unto the children of men: Follow thou me. Wherefore, my beloved brethren, can we follow Jesus save we shall be willing to keep the commandments of the Father?
restoration.comment: Nephi's pastoral restatement: following Jesus is keeping commandments, not sentiment alone.

s15.text: what the Spirit whispers to the humble conscience

biblical.text: But the Comforter, which is the Holy Ghost, whom the Father will send in my name, he shall teach you all things, and bring all things to your remembrance, whatsoever I have said unto you.
biblical.comment: The Spirit's office is instruction aligned with what Christ has said — never departing from Him.

biblical.text: And after the earthquake a fire; but the Lord was not in the fire: and after the fire a still small voice.
biblical.comment: Elijah on Horeb. The “whisper” register named by scripture itself.

biblical.text: For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, they are the sons of God... The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God.
biblical.comment: The Spirit's witness to the honest conscience is universal Christian territory — Paul's own language.

restoration.text: Yea, behold, I will tell you in your mind and in your heart, by the Holy Ghost, which shall come upon you and which shall dwell in your heart.
restoration.comment: Revelation given to Oliver Cowdery, describing the same Spirit-to-conscience witness Paul names in Romans 8.

restoration.text: And by the power of the Holy Ghost ye may know the truth of all things.
restoration.comment: Moroni's closing promise — echoing the biblical pattern that the Spirit confirms truth to the honest seeker.

s16.text: Mysteries and judgment we leave to God

biblical.text: But why dost thou judge thy brother?... we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ... So then every one of us shall give account of himself to God.
biblical.comment: Paul places final judgment firmly with God, not with fellow believers.

biblical.text: Therefore judge nothing before the time, until the Lord come, who both will bring to light the hidden things of darkness, and will make manifest the counsels of the hearts: and then shall every man have praise of God.
biblical.comment: The “hidden things” are disclosed by God in His time — not by us in ours.

biblical.text: Judge not, that ye be not judged. For with what judgment ye judge, ye shall be judged: and with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again.
biblical.comment: Christ's own instruction. The article's closing posture flows directly from the Sermon on the Mount.

restoration.text: Wherefore I show unto you the way to judge; for every thing which inviteth to do good, and to persuade to believe in Christ, is sent forth by the power and gift of Christ... Wherefore, I beseech of you, brethren, that ye should search diligently in the light of Christ that ye may know good from evil.
restoration.comment: Mormon's guidance: we may judge between good and evil by the Light of Christ, but the judgment of souls remains the Lord's alone.

s17.text: The “weighty” things of God are plain. They exist in plainness for our salvation.
s17.panel_comment: The article's positive thesis on plainness in miniature. Where Span 5 ('Secret things belong unto the Lord our God') names what is hidden, this span names what is given — and gives it a teleological frame: plainness for our salvation. The biblical anchors register the apostolic and Mosaic witness to plain saving speech. The Restoration anchors form a Book-of-Mormon-anchored cluster — 2 Nephi 31:3 (the verse from which this ministry takes its name), Jacob 4:13 (the most thematically exact match — 'manifested unto us plainly, for the salvation of our souls'), and Alma 13:23 (plainness yields understanding that does not err). Cross-references Span 5 as the sibling claim — the Plainness article in two halves; what God has revealed is plain, and what He has not revealed remains His.

biblical.text: But I fear, lest by any means, as the serpent beguiled Eve through his subtilty, so your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ.
biblical.comment: Paul's foundational concern — that minds may be led away from 'the simplicity that is in Christ.' The most direct biblical anchor for plainness-as-the-nature-of-saving-truth. Where the article distinguishes the 'weighty things' from the speculative, Paul names the same principle from the apostolic side — devotion to Christ is meant to be simple and pure, not burdened by complex additions.

biblical.text: Seeing then that we have such hope, we use great plainness of speech.
biblical.comment: Paul's apostolic method named in his own words. The proclamation of the new covenant is bold and open, not veiled. The biblical model the article's whole architecture honors — saving truth is to be communicated plainly, not held in mysteries reserved for elites.

biblical.text: For this commandment which I command thee this day, it is not hidden from thee, neither is it far off. It is not in heaven, that thou shouldest say, Who shall go up for us to heaven, and bring it unto us, that we may hear it, and do it?... But the word is very nigh unto thee, in thy mouth, and in thy heart, that thou mayest do it.
biblical.comment: Moses on the nature of God's commandment — not hidden, not far off, but very nigh unto the heart. The OT's most direct statement that saving truth is accessible — near to the heart, not concealed in the heavens. Paul quotes this same passage in Romans 10:6–8 and applies it directly to the gospel — 'the word is nigh thee, even in thy mouth, and in thy heart... the word of faith, which we preach.' The plain-and-near principle threads from Moses through Paul into the article's claim.

restoration.text: For my soul delighteth in plainness; for after this manner doth the Lord God work among the children of men. For the Lord God giveth light unto the understanding; for he speaketh unto men according to their language, unto their understanding.
restoration.comment: Nephi's signature confession — and the source of this ministry's name. The Restoration anchor for plainness is not incidental; it is foundational. The Lord's manner of working among His children is plainness itself, and He speaks to each soul in the language of their own understanding. The verse the entire ministry rests on, surfaced here for the first time in the apparatus.

restoration.text: Behold, my brethren, he that prophesieth, let him prophesy to the understanding of men; for the Spirit speaketh the truth and lieth not. Wherefore, it speaketh of things as they really are, and of things as they really will be; wherefore, these things are manifested unto us plainly, for the salvation of our souls.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's most thematically exact anchor for this span — the phrase 'plainly, for the salvation of our souls' matches the article's claim almost verbatim. The Spirit speaks in plainness for the salvation of the soul. The two clauses of the article's span (plainness; for our salvation) are held together in a single Restoration verse. The strongest single anchor in either column.

restoration.text: And they are made known unto us in plain terms, that we may understand, that we cannot err; and this because of our being wanderers in a strange land; therefore, we are thus highly favored, for we have these glad tidings declared unto us in all parts of our vineyard.
restoration.comment: Alma's pastoral confidence — plainness yields the kind of understanding that does not err. The article's whole epistemic posture in miniature — what is plainly given is sufficient for salvation, and what is not plainly given is not required for salvation. The 'highly favored' language frames plainness as gift rather than constraint.

s18.text: He never said “be sure to sort out every theological question before you love and accept one another.”
s18.panel_comment: The negative-form pair to Span 12 (no soul barred from Christ for lacking perfect understanding). Where Span 12 names what Christ does not require for salvation, this span names what He does not require for fellowship — and grounds the claim in Christ's own pastoral practice rather than in a bare argument from silence. The rhetorical form 'He never said X' carries known exposure when pressed beyond legitimate use; here it is bounded by what Christ in fact did say and do. The biblical anchors witness Christ's own response to fellowship-by-doctrinal-credential questions: Mark 9:38–40 / Luke 9:49–50 records Christ rebuking the disciples for refusing to acknowledge a stranger casting out devils in His name; Acts 15 records the apostolic refusal to require full doctrinal alignment between Jewish and Gentile believers as a condition of fellowship; John 13:34–35 names the mark of discipleship Christ Himself identified — love, not doctrinal alignment. The plain-center protectors (3 Nephi 11:28–30 and D&C 10:67–68) close the door this phrasing would otherwise leave open: the article refuses doctrinal completionism without sliding into pluralism. Articles of Faith 1:13 supplies the Restoration's broadest fellowship-ethic confession — the disposition the negation reaches toward. Forms a structural pair with Span 19 (positive ground of fellowship); together they mirror the Span 5 / Span 17 sibling architecture (negative + positive ground for epistemology) applied to fellowship ethics.

biblical.text: And John answered him, saying, Master, we saw one casting out devils in thy name, and he followeth not us: and we forbad him, because he followeth not us. But Jesus said, Forbid him not: for there is no man which shall do a miracle in my name, that can lightly speak evil of me. For he that is not against us is on our part.
biblical.comment: The most direct biblical anchor — Christ's own response to a fellowship-by-doctrinal-credential question. The disciples refused fellowship to a stranger because 'he followeth not us'; Christ rebuked them. The grammar is exact: not 'he is fully credentialed' but 'he is not against us.' The threshold Christ Himself set is lower than the threshold the article's rhetorical contrast denies.

biblical.text: And John answered and said, Master, we saw one casting out devils in thy name; and we forbad him, because he followeth not with us. And Jesus said unto him, Forbid him not: for he that is not against us is for us.
biblical.comment: Luke's parallel to the Mark passage. The same scene with the same rebuke. Two-witness biblical confirmation of Christ's pattern.

biblical.text: A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another; as I have loved you, that ye also love one another. By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another.
biblical.comment: The mark of discipleship Christ Himself named — love, not doctrinal completeness. The phrase 'all men' specifies that the recognition Christ envisioned operates across boundaries; the badge the world reads is mutual love among His followers, not their agreement on every point.

biblical.text: And God, which knoweth the hearts, bare them witness, giving them the Holy Ghost, even as he did unto us; And put no difference between us and them, purifying their hearts by faith. Now therefore why tempt ye God, to put a yoke upon the neck of the disciples, which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear? But we believe that through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ we shall be saved, even as they.
biblical.comment: Peter at the Jerusalem Council. The apostolic precedent for refusing to make doctrinal completeness a condition of fellowship — God Himself 'put no difference' between Jewish and Gentile believers, and required only what was necessary. The closing line is decisive: salvation is by grace, not by alignment on every disputed point.

restoration.text: And there shall be no disputations among you, as there have hitherto been; neither shall there be disputations among you concerning the points of my doctrine, as there have hitherto been. For verily, verily I say unto you, he that hath the spirit of contention is not of me, but is of the devil, who is the father of contention, and he stirreth up the hearts of men to contend with anger, one with another. Behold, this is not my doctrine, to stir up the hearts of men with anger, one against another; but this is my doctrine, that such things should be done away.
restoration.comment: The risen Christ in Bountiful naming contention itself — not doctrinal disagreement, but the spirit that turns disagreement into anger — as not of Him. Reasserted from Article 2 Span 7 and Article 3 Span 6, where the same anchor governs doctrinal restraint; here it does different work. There the function is to limit what we dogmatize about cosmology; here the function is to refuse the contentious spirit that makes fellowship contingent on doctrinal alignment. Same anchor, distinct rhetorical movement.

restoration.text: Behold, this is my doctrine—whosoever repenteth and cometh unto me, the same is my church. Whosoever declareth more or less than this, the same is not of me, but is against me; therefore he is not of my church.
restoration.comment: The plain-center protector. Christ Himself names the minimal doctrine as the boundary of His church — repentance and coming unto Him. Doctrinal additions and subtractions are alike rejected. The verse closes the door against pluralist over-reach (no plain center) on one side and fundamentalist over-reach (more than the plain center required) on the other. Holds the article's claim against both misreadings.

restoration.text: We believe in being honest, true, chaste, benevolent, virtuous, and in doing good to all men; indeed, we may say that we follow the admonition of Paul—We believe all things, we hope all things, we have endured many things, and hope to be able to endure all things. If there is anything virtuous, lovely, or of good report or praiseworthy, we seek after these things.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's broadest fellowship-ethic confession — the disposition the article's negation reaches toward. The closing phrase 'if there is anything virtuous, lovely, or of good report or praiseworthy, we seek after these things' is one of the most generous interfaith dispositions in the Restoration canon. Where the span states what Christ never required, this anchor states what the disciples affirmatively pursue.

s19.text: Interfaith fellowship is governed by what Christ taught, what the prophets witnessed
s19.panel_comment: The positive-ground pair to Span 18 (what fellowship is not built on). Where Span 18 names what Christ never required, this span names the framework He did identify — and traces it back through the prophets He confirmed. The two clauses of the span demand distinct anchor work. The 'what Christ taught' clause is anchored in the Great Commandments (Matthew 22:36–40 / Mark 12:29–31), Christ's own naming of the hermeneutic key — and crucially, His closing claim that 'on these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets.' That single line does double duty: it anchors what Christ taught, AND it tells us how Christ Himself read what the prophets witnessed. The 'what the prophets witnessed' clause is then anchored in the OT roots Christ cites — Deuteronomy 6:4–5 (the Shema, Moses witnessing the first commandment) and Leviticus 19:18 (the Holiness Code, Moses witnessing the second commandment). John 13:34–35 carries Christ's own application of the framework to discipleship recognition; cross-referenced rather than reasserted with full text since it appears in Span 18 in its full discipleship-mark function. The Restoration anchors confirm the same architecture in modern revelation: 2 Nephi 26:30 names charity as the governing law, D&C 59:5–6 has Christ Himself reaffirm both commandments in modern revelation in the same order, and Moroni 7:45–48 supplies the Restoration's most sustained meditation on what love-of-neighbor concretely is. Forms the second half of the structural pair with Span 18; together they mirror the Span 5 / Span 17 sibling architecture applied to fellowship ethics.

biblical.text: Master, which is the great commandment in the law? Jesus said unto him, Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind. This is the first and great commandment. And the second is like unto it, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets.
biblical.comment: The lead anchor for the entire span. Christ's own naming of the hermeneutic key — the two commandments on which everything else hangs. The closing line ('on these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets') does double duty: it tells us what Christ taught, AND how Christ Himself read what the prophets witnessed. The single biblical text the article's claim turns on.

biblical.text: And Jesus answered him, The first of all the commandments is, Hear, O Israel; The Lord our God is one Lord: And thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind, and with all thy strength: this is the first commandment. And the second is like, namely this, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. There is none other commandment greater than these.
biblical.comment: Mark's parallel adds the Shema preamble ('Hear, O Israel; The Lord our God is one Lord') that Matthew omits, anchoring Christ's teaching explicitly in the prophet Moses's own confession. The closing line — 'there is none other commandment greater than these' — is the strongest biblical statement of governing primacy and load-bearing for the article's claim that fellowship is governed by these and not by accumulated doctrinal positions.

biblical.text: Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God is one Lord: And thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thine heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might.
biblical.comment: The Shema. Moses witnessing the first commandment Christ identifies in Matthew 22 and Mark 12. The OT root of half of the framework Christ named — direct evidence of what the prophet witnessed before Christ's ministry confirmed it. Anchors 'what the prophets witnessed' with the prophetic source-text Christ Himself quotes.

biblical.text: Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the Lord.
biblical.comment: The Holiness Code. Moses witnessing the second commandment Christ identifies. The OT root of the second half of the framework — and notable for its embedded grammar ('not avenge, nor bear any grudge') which preempts the very contention Christ later forbids in 3 Nephi 11. The prophet's witness supplies the affirmative content Christ confirms.

restoration.text: Behold, the Lord hath forbidden this thing; wherefore, the Lord God hath given a commandment that all men should have charity, which charity is love. And except they should have charity they were nothing. Wherefore, if they should have charity they would not suffer the laborer in Zion to perish.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's most concentrated charity-as-foundation statement. The structure — 'commandment that all men should have charity, which charity is love' — places the second great commandment at the load-bearing center of Restoration ethics, with the consequence that without charity the disciple is 'nothing.' Pairs with the Pauline charity hymn (1 Corinthians 13, cited at Span 7) but does distinct rhetorical work: Paul names what charity is; Nephi names that it is commanded.

restoration.text: Wherefore, I give unto them a commandment, saying thus: Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, with all thy might, mind, and strength; and in the name of Jesus Christ thou shalt serve him. Thou shalt love thy neighbor as thyself. Thou shalt not steal; neither commit adultery, nor kill, nor do anything like unto it.
restoration.comment: Christ Himself in modern revelation reaffirming both commandments in the same order Matthew records — the first with the addition 'in the name of Jesus Christ thou shalt serve him,' the second exactly as Leviticus and Matthew carry it. The Restoration's explicit confirmation that the framework Christ named in mortality remains the governing law in His ongoing word.

restoration.text: And charity suffereth long, and is kind, and envieth not, and is not puffed up, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil, and rejoiceth not in iniquity but rejoiceth in the truth, beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things. Wherefore, my beloved brethren, if ye have not charity, ye are nothing, for charity never faileth. Wherefore, cleave unto charity, which is the greatest of all... Wherefore, my beloved brethren, pray unto the Father with all the energy of heart, that ye may be filled with this love, which he hath bestowed upon all who are true followers of his Son, Jesus Christ; that ye may become the sons of God.
restoration.comment: Moroni quoting Mormon — the Restoration's most sustained meditation on what love-of-neighbor concretely is. Translates Paul's charity hymn (1 Corinthians 13) into the Restoration's pastoral mantle. Where the Matthew anchors name the commandment, this anchor names the texture of obedience to it. Pairs with 1 Corinthians 13 (cited at Span 7 as the merognosis ek-merous source) while doing distinct rhetorical work — there the partial-knowing anchor; here the charity-as-fellowship-substance anchor.

crossref.title: Span 18: He never said sort out every theological question...

crossref.label: Within this article
crossref.title: Span 17: The 'weighty' things of God are plain

s1.text: the Eternal Father of our spirits
s1.panel_comment: Aaron's locked editorial choice. Receiving traditions fill “Father of our spirits” with God-as-creator-and-sustainer-of-souls (Trinitarian, Catholic, Orthodox); Latter-day Saint readers fill it with literal eternal Fatherhood. Container-word discipline operating on a tight margin. Anchor cluster matches Manuscript Ch 4.

biblical.text: Furthermore we have had fathers of our flesh which corrected us, and we gave them reverence: shall we not much rather be in subjection unto the Father of spirits, and live?
biblical.comment: 'The Father of spirits' is Scripture's own phrase — set here against the 'fathers of our flesh.' God is the origin of the human spirit as our earthly fathers are of our bodies. The same witness runs through Numbers 16:22, Zechariah 12:1, Ecclesiastes 12:7, and Job 33:4, and Christian readers across the centuries have received Hebrews 12:9 this way. How each tradition understands the manner of that fatherhood it works out in its own house; this Article confesses only what the verse confesses.

biblical.text: And they fell upon their faces, and said, O God, the God of the spirits of all flesh, shall one man sin, and wilt thou be wroth with all the congregation?
biblical.comment: Moses' own appeal to the “God of the spirits of all flesh” — the OT antecedent to Hebrews 12:9.

biblical.text: Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it.
biblical.comment: The spirit returning to God who gave it — the bookend of mortal life that confirms its origin in Him.

biblical.text: For in him we live, and move, and have our being; as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring. Forasmuch then as we are the offspring of God, we ought not to think that the Godhead is like unto gold, or silver, or stone, graven by art and man's device.
biblical.comment: Paul on Mars Hill, citing Greek poets to affirm divine offspring. The interfaith voice in scripture itself.

restoration.text: Man was also in the beginning with God. Intelligence, or the light of truth, was not created or made, neither indeed can be. All truth is independent in that sphere in which God has placed it, to act for itself, as all intelligence also; otherwise there is no existence.
restoration.comment: Aaron's existing canonical citation pairing in Manuscript Ch 4 (Spiritual Knowledge). The Restoration's anchor for eternal intelligence and personal agency. Restoration amplification — witness only; not required to receive the Article.

restoration.text: That by him, and through him, and of him, the worlds are and were created, and the inhabitants thereof are begotten sons and daughters unto God.
restoration.comment: The most explicit Restoration affirmation: “the inhabitants thereof are begotten sons and daughters unto God.” Restoration amplification — witness only; not required to receive the Article.

s2.text: whose love for His children is without limit

biblical.text: Behold, what manner of love the Father hath bestowed upon us, that we should be called the sons of God.
biblical.comment: John's astonishment at Fatherly love. The benchmark text for divine paternal affection.

biblical.text: For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.
biblical.comment: Paul's exhaustive list of what cannot separate us from God's love. The “without limit” clause finds its biblical scope here.

biblical.text: Like as a father pitieth his children, so the Lord pitieth them that fear him.
biblical.comment: The OT image of God as father in pity — earlier than Christ's teaching, receiving the same testimony.

restoration.text: And I said unto him: I know that he loveth his children; nevertheless, I do not know the meaning of all things.
restoration.comment: Nephi pairs love-confidence with merognosis. Mirrors this article's posture exactly: confident in God's love, restrained about what we cannot know.

restoration.text: And again I say unto you as I have said before, that as ye have come to the knowledge of the glory of God... ye shall always rejoice, and be filled with the love of God, and always retain a remission of your sins.
restoration.comment: King Benjamin's promise: those who taste God's goodness will be “filled with the love of God.” Practical witness.

biblical.text: Who being the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person, and upholding all things by the word of his power, when he had by himself purged our sins, sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high.
biblical.comment: Christ “upholding all things by the word of his power.” The biblical anchor for divine sustenance.

biblical.text: And he is before all things, and by him all things consist.
biblical.comment: Paul's most concentrated statement: by Christ all things consist.

biblical.text: For in him we live, and move, and have our being.
biblical.comment: Universal, not denominational. The most quoted phrase across Christian traditions for this truth.

restoration.text: I say unto you that if ye should serve him who has created you from the beginning, and is preserving you from day to day, by lending you breath, that ye may live and move and do according to your own will... ye would still be unprofitable servants.
restoration.comment: King Benjamin's pastoral version: God preserves us “from day to day, by lending you breath.”

restoration.text: The light which is in all things, which giveth life to all things, which is the law by which all things are governed, even the power of God who sitteth upon his throne, who is in the bosom of eternity, who is in the midst of all things.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's full theological articulation: the light, the law, and the power of God present in all things.

s4.text: Nothing exists apart from His knowledge

biblical.text: O Lord, thou hast searched me, and known me. Thou knowest my downsitting and mine uprising, thou understandest my thought afar off. Thou compassest my path and my lying down, and art acquainted with all my ways. For there is not a word in my tongue, but, lo, O Lord, thou knowest it altogether.
biblical.comment: The classic biblical psalm of God's exhaustive knowledge of the individual soul.

biblical.text: Neither is there any creature that is not manifest in his sight: but all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do.
biblical.comment: The epistemic claim made explicit: nothing escapes His knowledge.

biblical.text: Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing? and one of them shall not fall on the ground without your Father. But the very hairs of your head are all numbered.
biblical.comment: Christ's own teaching: God's knowledge extends to sparrows and to numbered hairs. Pastoral, intimate, comprehensive.

restoration.text: O how great the holiness of our God! For he knoweth all things, and there is not anything save he knows it.
restoration.comment: Jacob's most direct affirmation of divine omniscience.

restoration.text: He comprehendeth all things, and all things are before him, and all things are round about him; and he is above all things, and in all things, and is through all things, and is round about all things; and all things are by him, and of him, even God, forever and ever.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's most cosmic statement: God comprehends, surrounds, and is in all things.

biblical.text: Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you.
biblical.comment: The simplest biblical anchor for the second of the parallel pair (knowledge → care).

biblical.text: Therefore I say unto you, Take no thought for your life, what ye shall eat, or what ye shall drink; nor yet for your body, what ye shall put on... Behold the fowls of the air: for they sow not, neither do they reap, nor gather into barns; yet your heavenly Father feedeth them. Are ye not much better than they?
biblical.comment: Christ's Sermon on the Mount: God's care extends to lilies, sparrows, and us. Provident divine attention.

biblical.text: The Lord shall preserve thee from all evil: he shall preserve thy soul. The Lord shall preserve thy going out and thy coming in from this time forth, and even for evermore.
biblical.comment: OT pastoral assurance — the Lord preserves the soul, the going out, the coming in.

restoration.text: Now my brethren, we see that God is mindful of every people, whatsoever land they may be in; yea, he numbereth his people, and his bowels of mercy are over all the earth.
restoration.comment: Ammon: God is mindful of every people, in every land. Universal scope.

restoration.text: And whoso receiveth you, there I will be also, for I will go before your face. I will be on your right hand and on your left, and my Spirit shall be in your hearts, and mine angels round about you, to bear you up.
restoration.comment: Christ's promise to His disciples: His Spirit in their hearts, His angels round about them. Personal care made operational.

biblical.text: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men.
biblical.comment: The angels' announcement at Christ's birth — the original biblical doxology this phrase quotes directly.

biblical.text: And the multitudes that went before, and that followed, cried, saying, Hosanna to the Son of David: Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord; Hosanna in the highest.
biblical.comment: The triumphal entry: “Hosanna in the highest.” The same phrase echoed in praise.

restoration.text: And they did all cry out with one voice, saying: May the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob protect this people in righteousness, so long as they shall call on the name of their God for protection. And it came to pass that they did break forth, all as one, in singing, and praising their God for the great thing which he had done for them, in preserving them from falling into the hands of their enemies.
restoration.comment: The Nephite people's deliverance song. The doxological pattern — “the God of Abraham, of Isaac, of Jacob” — echoes the biblical exaltation of God in the highest.

s7.text: Of the eternal functions and hierarchy of heavenly populations we remain carefully neutral and avoid speculation for the sake of interfaith unity
s7.panel_comment: The doctrinal-restraint move — Plainness operating inside the God article. Cross-references Article 1's merognosis principle. The neutrality covers Trinity formulations, Elohim councils, angelic orders, and any other contested cosmology.

biblical.text: The secret things belong unto the Lord our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever, that we may do all the words of this law.
biblical.comment: The same verse anchoring Article 1. The doctrinal-restraint principle stays consistent across articles.

biblical.text: Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations.
biblical.comment: Paul's governing rule: receive the brother of differing conviction without forcing disputation.

biblical.text: Now I beseech you, brethren, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you; but that ye be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment.
biblical.comment: Paul's plea against schism. The article applies it to speculative cosmology, where divisions are most easily multiplied.

biblical.text: Let us therefore, as many as be perfect, be thus minded: and if in any thing ye be otherwise minded, God shall reveal even this unto you. Nevertheless, whereto we have already attained, let us walk by the same rule, let us mind the same thing.
biblical.comment: Paul allows for differing conviction and trusts God to reveal further. The mature posture for matters not yet plain.

restoration.text: And there shall be no disputations among you, as there have hitherto been; neither shall there be disputations among you concerning the points of my doctrine, as there have hitherto been. For verily, verily I say unto you, he that hath the spirit of contention is not of me, but is of the devil, who is the father of contention, and he stirreth up the hearts of men to contend with anger, one with another.
restoration.comment: The risen Christ in Bountiful: the most explicit Restoration anchor for this article's restraint.

restoration.text: But behold, the Jews were a stiffnecked people; and they despised the words of plainness... and sought for things that they could not understand. Wherefore, because of their blindness, which blindness came by looking beyond the mark, they must needs fall.
restoration.comment: “Looking beyond the mark” — the Restoration's diagnosis of the same disease. (Cited also in Article 1, Span 4.)

crossref.label: See Article 1
crossref.title: Plainness

s8.text: no mortal human can claim to know the full nature of God

biblical.text: Canst thou by searching find out God? canst thou find out the Almighty unto perfection? It is as high as heaven; what canst thou do? deeper than hell; what canst thou know?
biblical.comment: The OT's foundational rhetorical question. (Verse 7 also cited in Article 1, Span 7; reasserted here as the positive doctrinal version.)

biblical.text: O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out! For who hath known the mind of the Lord? or who hath been his counsellor?
biblical.comment: Paul's doxology of unsearchability — the Pauline summit of this confession.

biblical.text: Who only hath immortality, dwelling in the light which no man can approach unto; whom no man hath seen, nor can see: to whom be honour and power everlasting. Amen.
biblical.comment: God dwelling “in the light which no man can approach unto.” The strongest Pauline statement of God's incommunicability.

restoration.text: Behold, great and marvelous are the works of the Lord. How unsearchable are the depths of the mysteries of him; and it is impossible that man should find out all his ways.
restoration.comment: Already cited in Article 1, Span 1. Re-cited here as the most direct Restoration support for the same epistemic limit — stated positively as a confession of God.

crossref.label: See Article 1
crossref.title: Plainness

s9.text: We only know as much as He chooses to reveal plainly
s9.panel_comment: Paraphrase of Deuteronomy 29:29 — the same verse quoted in Article 1 (“Secret things belong unto the Lord our God”). Cross-reference acknowledges the same-source pairing rather than concealing it.

biblical.text: The secret things belong unto the Lord our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever, that we may do all the words of this law.
biblical.comment: Same anchor as Article 1, Span 5. The qualifier “as He chooses to reveal plainly” makes the revealed/unrevealed distinction explicit.

biblical.text: Surely the Lord God will do nothing, but he revealeth his secret unto his servants the prophets.
biblical.comment: The biblical pattern of revelation: God discloses through chosen channels in His own time.

biblical.text: He revealeth the deep and secret things: he knoweth what is in the darkness, and the light dwelleth with him.
biblical.comment: The complement to Deuteronomy 29:29 — what God chooses to disclose, He discloses fully.

biblical.text: I thank thee, O Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them unto babes... All things are delivered unto me of my Father: and no man knoweth the Son, but the Father; neither knoweth any man the Father, save the Son, and he to whomsoever the Son will reveal him.
biblical.comment: Christ's prayer: revelation given to babes, hidden from the wise. The pastoral subversion of human gatekeeping.

restoration.text: For behold, thus saith the Lord God: I will give unto the children of men line upon line, precept upon precept, here a little and there a little; and blessed are those who hearken unto my precepts, and lend an ear unto my counsel, for they shall learn wisdom.
restoration.comment: The Restoration cadence: knowledge given as the soul is ready, not all at once.

restoration.text: For he will give unto the faithful line upon line, precept upon precept; and I will try you and prove you herewith.
restoration.comment: The covenantal echo: “line upon line, precept upon precept” to the faithful, in His timing.

crossref.label: See Article 1
crossref.title: Plainness

s10.text: As the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways and my thoughts than your thoughts

biblical.text: For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, saith the Lord. For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways, and my thoughts than your thoughts.
biblical.comment: The original. The phrase quoted directly from the prophet's invitation “Seek ye the Lord while he may be found.” (Also cited in Article 1, Span 1, as a supporting witness; here it is the article's own closing voice.)

s11.panel_comment: The natural-revelation anchor for the act of belief itself. Where Span 1 carries the *content* of belief (the Father of our spirits), this span carries the *grounds* of belief (creation as witness). Fourfold witness: Job's pastoral invitation to ask creation (OT), Paul's doctrinal capstone of natural revelation (NT), Alma's direct confrontation with denial (Restoration), and Moses 6:63's Christological declaration that all things bear record of Him. The pattern moves from gentle to doctrinal to confrontational to Christ-centered.

biblical.text:
7 But ask now the beasts, and they shall teach thee; and the fowls of the air, and they shall tell thee:
8 Or speak to the earth, and it shall teach thee: and the fishes of the sea shall declare unto thee.
9 Who knoweth not in all these that the hand of the Lord hath wrought this?
10 In whose hand is the soul of every living thing, and the breath of all mankind.
biblical.comment: Job's invitation to ask creation itself: the beasts, the air, the earth, the sea — all teach the hand of the Lord. The OT's most pastoral creation-witness passage.

biblical.text:
19 Because that which may be known of God is manifest in them; for God hath shewed it unto them.
20 For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead; so that they are without excuse.
biblical.comment: Paul's doctrinal capstone of natural revelation: the invisible things of God are clearly seen by the things that are made, leaving humanity 'without excuse.' The most-cited NT anchor in the Christian natural-theology tradition; here completing the OT–NT witness arc.

restoration.text: 44 But Alma said unto him: Thou hast had signs enough; will ye tempt your God? Will ye say, Show unto me a sign, when ye have the testimony of all these thy brethren, and also all the holy prophets? The scriptures are laid before thee, yea, and all things denote there is a God; yea, even the earth, and all things that are upon the face of it, yea, and its motion, yea, and also all the planets which move in their regular form do witness that there is a Supreme Creator.
restoration.comment: Alma's response to Korihor's atheism: 'all things denote there is a God... do witness that there is a Supreme Creator.' The Restoration's directly parallel argument made in the face of explicit denial. Where Job invites, Alma confronts — both grounded in the same creation-witness logic.

restoration.text: And behold, all things have their likeness, and all things are created and made to bear record of me, both things which are temporal, and things which are spiritual; things which are in the heavens above, and things which are on the earth, and things which are in the earth, and things which are under the earth, both above and beneath: all things bear record of me.
restoration.comment: Adam's instruction to his posterity in the Pearl of Great Price: 'all things bear record of me' — Christ Himself naming the testimony creation carries. Adds Christological weight: it is not God-in-general whom creation witnesses, but the One who upholds all things by the word of His power.

s12.panel_comment: The phrase claims the moral character of God's intent toward His children. Bible and Restoration witnesses converge on the same affirmation: God's purposes flow from His goodness. Genesis 1:31 grounds this in creation — what God purposes, He sees as good. Exodus 34:6 names goodness as essential to God's revealed name. Jeremiah 29:11 makes the claim direct: God's thoughts toward His people are thoughts of peace. James 1:17 anchors the goodness in God's unchanging character — the Father of lights with whom there is no shadow of turning. The Restoration intensifies the claim: God's work and glory is the immortality and eternal life of man (Moses 1:39); He does nothing save it be for the benefit of the world (2 Nephi 26:24). The reader who can hold no other claim about God can still rest in this one — the will behind their existence is benevolent, not capricious.

biblical.text: For I know the thoughts that I think toward you, saith the Lord, thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you an expected end.
biblical.comment: The most direct biblical statement of God's *thoughts* — His intentional designs — being good toward His children. The Hebrew (machashabot) names purposes deliberately formed; the verse names them as peace, not evil. Load-bearing for the entire span.

biblical.text: The Lord is good to all: and his tender mercies are over all his works.
biblical.comment: The broadest scope statement available: God's goodness extends to all His works without exception. The Psalm 145 cluster is already pastorally familiar in this ministry (verse 18 cited in the Sincere Prayer chapter); verse 9 supplies the universal-character claim that grounds the article's restraint posture in a Father whose goodness is not selective.

biblical.text: Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning.
biblical.comment: Joseph Smith assembled this verse with Exodus 34:6 in Lectures on Faith as the foundation for understanding God's character of goodness. Pairs structurally with Span 1 (the Father of our spirits) — the Father's purposes are good because He is the Father of lights. The 'no variableness, neither shadow of turning' clause closes off any reading that would make God's goodness contingent or fluctuating.

biblical.text: And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good.
biblical.comment: The original projection of goodness onto God's purposes — what He purposes, He sees as good. The creation grammar both Bible-readers and Restoration readers share. Anchors the span at the most universally affirmed point in the canon: the goodness of what God deliberately brings forth.

biblical.text: And the Lord passed by before him, and proclaimed, The Lord, The Lord God, merciful and gracious, longsuffering, and abundant in goodness and truth.
biblical.comment: God's own self-naming to Moses — His character revelation. The 'abundant in goodness' clause is the Old Testament's most direct statement that goodness is essential to God's name. Joseph Smith opens Lecture 3 of the Lectures on Faith with this verse as the foundation for understanding God's character. The OT anchor for goodness as constitutive, not incidental, to who God is.

restoration.text: For behold, this is my work and my glory — to bring to pass the immortality and eternal life of man.
restoration.comment: The single most explicit statement in Restoration scripture of what God's purposes are — and the answer is unambiguously good. Talmage cites this exact verse to argue 'It was not His design that the souls of mankind be lost.' The canonical Restoration answer to the question this span asks. First deployment of Moses 1:39 in the apparatus.

restoration.text: He doeth not anything save it be for the benefit of the world; for he loveth the world, even that he layeth down his own life that he may draw all men unto him.
restoration.comment: Nephi's most direct claim about the moral character of God's purposes — every divine action is for the benefit of the world. The Christological grounding ('that he may draw all men unto him') anticipates Article 5 without dogmatizing here; the span itself stays at the Father's-purposes register.

restoration.text: My son, peace be unto thy soul; thine adversity and thine afflictions shall be but a small moment; And then, if thou endure it well, God shall exalt thee on high; thou shalt triumph over all thy foes.
restoration.comment: The Liberty Jail revelation — God's purposes hold even through suffering. The pastoral form of the claim: not 'suffering is good,' but 'thy God shall stand by thee forever and ever.' The reader can rest in the goodness of intent even when the particulars of providence remain opaque. Light theodicy register honored — the heavier theodicy work belongs in Article 3.

restoration.text: And now behold, my brethren, since it has been all that we could do (as we were the most lost of all mankind) to repent of all our sins and the many murders which we have committed, and to get God to take them away from our hearts, for it was all we could do to repent sufficiently before God that he would take away our stain — Now, my best beloved brethren, since God hath taken away our stains, and our swords have become bright, then let us stain our swords no more with the blood of our brethren.
restoration.comment: The anti-Nephi-Lehies' confession: God's purposes toward them — even toward those they had once persecuted — were goodness and mercy. The narrative anchor for 'whose purposes are good' as experienced witness, not abstract claim. The most concrete Restoration story of receiving God's good purposes after having been on the receiving end of judgment.

s1.panel_comment: The foundational creation claim that grounds the entire article — that the world has a Creator, and that the creation is purposive. Universal Christian territory; no container-word discipline required. The biblical anchors emphasize habitation (Isaiah 45:18), deeding (Psalm 115:16), vocation (Genesis 2:15), and ordered relationship (Acts 17:24–28). The Restoration witnesses confirm and deepen with explicit purpose-statements naming what the biblical anchors imply. This span is the structural predecessor to spans 2–5, which together unfold what kind of place God created the world to be.

biblical.text: For thus saith the LORD that created the heavens; God himself that formed the earth and made it; he hath established it, he created it not in vain, he formed it to be inhabited: I am the LORD; and there is none else.
biblical.comment: This is the strongest single biblical witness that habitation was the purpose of the creation, not an afterthought. The negative ("not in vain") and the positive ("to be inhabited") are placed side by side. Worth opening any chapter on this theme.

biblical.text: The heaven, even the heavens, are the LORD's: but the earth hath he given to the children of men.
biblical.comment: A direct deeding of the earth to humanity. The two spheres are distinguished and the earth is named as gift.

biblical.text: And the LORD God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it.
biblical.comment: The first vocation is the keeping of a home.

biblical.text: God that made the world and all things therein... hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation; That they should seek the Lord.
biblical.comment: This is the New Testament's most explicit statement that the earth's habitability and the human family are deliberately ordered together by God for the purpose of relationship with Him.

restoration.text: Believe in God; believe that he is, and that he created all things, both in heaven and in earth; believe that he has all wisdom, and all power, both in heaven and in earth.
restoration.comment: King Benjamin's catechetical confession — the most direct Restoration statement of God-as-Creator in plain confessional voice. Matches the foundational register of the biblical anchors.

restoration.text: And worlds without number have I created; and I also created them for mine own purpose... For behold, this is my work and my glory—to bring to pass the immortality and eternal life of man.
restoration.comment: God Himself naming both the cosmic scope of creation (1:33) and its purpose (1:39). Where Isaiah 45:18 declares the earth was formed 'to be inhabited,' Moses 1:39 names what that habitation is for — the immortality and eternal life of man. The most concentrated Restoration statement of creation's teleology.

restoration.text: Behold, I am Jesus Christ the Son of God. I created the heavens and the earth, and all things that in them are. I was with the Father from the beginning.
restoration.comment: The risen Christ identifying Himself as Creator — the Christological dimension Acts 17:24–28 implies and Colossians 1:16 makes explicit elsewhere. Pairs with D&C 76:24 (Article 2 Span 1) to establish the Restoration's consistent witness that creation is the work of Christ.

s2.text: His spirit children live within bodies of mortal flesh
s2.panel_comment: Container word, multi-tradition fill. Origenist and Latter-day Saint readers receive 'spirit children' as conscious pre-mortal offspring of God now incarnate; Reformed and Catholic readers receive it within their own anthropologies (foreknowledge, hylomorphic union, soul-as-given). The biblical anthropology floor is high enough — Hebrews 12:9 'Father of spirits,' Genesis 2:7 spirit-into-flesh, Ecclesiastes 12:7 spirit-returns-to-God — that no tradition is forced into pre-mortalism by this phrase. See Article 2 Span 1 for the parallel container-word treatment of 'Father of our spirits.'

biblical.text: Furthermore we have had fathers of our flesh which corrected us, and we gave them reverence: shall we not much rather be in subjection unto the Father of spirits, and live?
biblical.comment: The biblical 'Father of spirits' phrase — also the lead anchor for Article 2 Span 1. Each tradition fills it from its own understanding.

biblical.text: And they fell upon their faces, and said, O God, the God of the spirits of all flesh, shall one man sin, and wilt thou be wroth with all the congregation?
biblical.comment: Moses' appeal to the 'God of the spirits of all flesh' — the OT anchor for divine sovereignty over the spirits indwelling mortal bodies.

biblical.text: The burden of the word of the Lord for Israel, saith the Lord, which stretcheth forth the heavens, and layeth the foundation of the earth, and formeth the spirit of man within him.
biblical.comment: God 'formeth the spirit of man within him.' The clearest OT statement that the human spirit is divinely formed and resides in the person.

biblical.text: And the Lord God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
biblical.comment: The foundational creation passage — spirit and body united into a living soul. Affirmed across all Christian traditions regardless of position on pre-mortal existence.

biblical.text: Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it.
biblical.comment: The bookend of mortal life: spirit returns to God who gave it. The Hebrew verb shuv (return) carries directional weight — the spirit goes back where it belongs.

biblical.text: For as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead also.
biblical.comment: The NT explicit statement: spirit indwells body and gives it life. James as the practical witness to the anthropology Genesis 2:7 establishes.

restoration.text: Man was also in the beginning with God. Intelligence, or the light of truth, was not created or made, neither indeed can be. All truth is independent in that sphere in which God has placed it, to act for itself, as all intelligence also; otherwise there is no existence.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's eternal-intelligence doctrine. Aaron's canonical anchor (Manuscript Ch 4). Names what the biblical texts allow but do not demand.

restoration.text: Now the Lord had shewn unto me, Abraham, the intelligences that were organized before the world was; and among all these there were many of the noble and great ones; And God saw these souls that they were good, and he stood in the midst of them, and he said: These I will make my rulers; for he stood among them, and he was Abraham.
restoration.comment: Abraham's vision of pre-mortal intelligences — the Restoration's most explicit pre-mortal-existence text. Adds the directness the biblical anchors honor without forcing.

crossref.label: See Article 2
crossref.title: God

biblical.text: And if it seem evil unto you to serve the Lord, choose you this day whom ye will serve... but as for me and my house, we will serve the Lord.
biblical.comment: Joshua's covenant address to Israel — the OT's most explicit invitation to choose. Agency invoked as the response God Himself authorizes.

biblical.text: I call heaven and earth to record this day against you, that I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life, that both thou and thy seed may live.
biblical.comment: Moses places life and death before Israel and commands the choice. The covenantal frame for divinely-endowed agency.

biblical.text: And the Lord God commanded the man, saying, Of every tree of the garden thou mayest freely eat: But of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, thou shalt not eat of it.
biblical.comment: The original endowment of choice in the Garden — commandment given to a creature capable of obedience or disobedience.

restoration.text: Wherefore, men are free according to the flesh; and all things are given them which are expedient unto man. And they are free to choose liberty and eternal life, through the great Mediator of all men, or to choose captivity and death, according to the captivity and power of the devil.
restoration.comment: Lehi's most direct articulation. The Restoration's foundational agency text — free to choose liberty and eternal life through Christ, or captivity through the devil.

restoration.text: That every man may act in doctrine and principle pertaining to futurity, according to the moral agency which I have given unto him, that every man may be accountable for his own sins in the day of judgment.
restoration.comment: Christ's own naming of moral agency as His gift, with accountability as the necessary corollary.

s4.text: encounter opposition of good and evil
s4.panel_comment: Biblical witness names the moral binary (Genesis 2:17 in Eden, Paul's divided self, James on the human encounter with desire); the Lehi opposition doctrine (2 Nephi 2:11–12) extends this into a metaphysical claim that moral contrast is necessary for moral existence. Aaron's canonical pairing in Manuscript Ch 41.

biblical.text: But of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, thou shalt not eat of it: for in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die.
biblical.comment: The Edenic introduction of the moral binary. Knowledge of good and evil enters human experience by command and by transgression.

biblical.text: Let no man say when he is tempted, I am tempted of God: for God cannot be tempted with evil, neither tempteth he any man: But every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed.
biblical.comment: James locates temptation in the human encounter with desire — not in God. The pastoral grammar of moral struggle.

biblical.text: For I know that in me (that is, in my flesh,) dwelleth no good thing: for to will is present with me; but how to perform that which is good I find not. For the good that I will I do not: but the evil which I will not, that I do.
biblical.comment: Paul's confession of the divided self — the universal Christian witness to moral struggle in the flesh.

restoration.text: For it must needs be, that there is an opposition in all things. If not so... righteousness could not be brought to pass, neither wickedness, neither holiness nor misery, neither good nor bad. Wherefore, all things must needs be a compound in one.
restoration.comment: Lehi's opposition doctrine — the Restoration's most distinctive metaphysical claim about the necessity of moral contrast for moral existence. Aaron's canonical pairing in Manuscript Ch 41.

s5.panel_comment: First mention of the soul-formation theme; reasserted explicitly in Span 10. Mortal experience produces growth — not as accident but as design.

biblical.text: And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience; And patience, experience; and experience, hope: And hope maketh not ashamed; because the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us.
biblical.comment: Paul's chain of growth: tribulation → patience → experience → hope. The most concentrated NT statement of formation through mortal trial.

biblical.text: My brethren, count it all joy when ye fall into divers temptations; Knowing this, that the trying of your faith worketh patience. But let patience have her perfect work, that ye may be perfect and entire, wanting nothing.
biblical.comment: James echoes Paul — trial yields patience, patience yields completeness. 'Perfect and entire' (teleios) is the formation-toward-fullness language.

biblical.text: My son, despise not thou the chastening of the Lord, nor faint when thou art rebuked of him: For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth... Now no chastening for the present seemeth to be joyous, but grievous: nevertheless afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness unto them which are exercised thereby.
biblical.comment: Hebrews on chastening as Fatherly formation — the affirmation that hardship in mortal life serves character.

restoration.text: And if thou shouldst be cast into the pit, or into the hands of murderers... if the very jaws of hell shall gape open the mouth wide after thee, know thou, my son, that all these things shall give thee experience, and shall be for thy good.
restoration.comment: Christ's word to Joseph Smith in Liberty Jail. The Restoration's most pastoral statement that mortal extremity yields experience that is 'for thy good.'

restoration.text: They were in a preparation to hear the word; therefore I said unto you, Behold, I behold that they were in a preparation to hear the word.
restoration.comment: Alma observes that humbling experience prepared the Zoramite poor to receive the word. Mortal affliction as preparation for spiritual reception.

s6.text: More than these general statements of faith we will not dogmatize within an interfaith fellowship
s6.panel_comment: Sibling to Article 2 Span 7 — merognosis-in-context. The same doctrinal-restraint move, here applied to creation and anthropology. The neutrality covers: the mechanics of creation (six-day vs. evolutionary), the timing of the soul's formation, the precise mode of pre-mortal existence (if any), and contested cosmologies of fallenness. Cross-references Article 1's foundational statement and Article 2's parallel restraint.

biblical.text: The secret things belong unto the Lord our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever, that we may do all the words of this law.
biblical.comment: The same anchor governing Article 1 and Article 2. The doctrinal-restraint principle stays consistent across all articles.

biblical.text: Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations.
biblical.comment: Paul's governing rule for fellowship across differing convictions. Reasserted in each merognosis-in-context article.

biblical.text: Now I beseech you, brethren, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you; but that ye be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment.
biblical.comment: Paul's plea against schism. Applied here to speculative cosmology, where divisions are most easily multiplied.

biblical.text: Let us therefore, as many as be perfect, be thus minded: and if in any thing ye be otherwise minded, God shall reveal even this unto you. Nevertheless, whereto we have already attained, let us walk by the same rule, let us mind the same thing.
biblical.comment: Paul allows for differing conviction and trusts God to reveal further. The mature posture for matters not yet plain.

restoration.text: And there shall be no disputations among you, as there have hitherto been; neither shall there be disputations among you concerning the points of my doctrine, as there have hitherto been. For verily, verily I say unto you, he that hath the spirit of contention is not of me, but is of the devil.
