restoration.comment: The risen Christ in Bountiful: the most explicit Restoration anchor for doctrinal restraint and the refusal of contention. Reasserted in each merognosis-in-context article.

restoration.text: But behold, the Jews were a stiffnecked people; and they despised the words of plainness... and sought for things that they could not understand. Wherefore, because of their blindness, which blindness came by looking beyond the mark, they must needs fall.
restoration.comment: 'Looking beyond the mark' — the Restoration's diagnosis of the disease this restraint resists. (Cited also in Article 1 Span 4 and Article 2 Span 7.)

crossref.label: See Article 1
crossref.title: Plainness

crossref.label: See Article 2
crossref.title: God

s7.text: this life is not an accident. It is not a punishment
s7.panel_comment: Twofold negation kept as one span. Negates the two most common reductive readings of mortal life — secular accident and theological punishment — to clear the way for the providential reading that follows.

biblical.text: And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good. And the evening and the morning were the sixth day.
biblical.comment: The original divine evaluation: creation 'very good.' The biblical refusal of any view that mortal existence is intrinsically accidental or punitive.

biblical.text: And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose.
biblical.comment: Paul's most quoted assurance — 'all things work together for good.' The pastoral statement of providence over the chaos of mortal experience.

biblical.text: For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them.
biblical.comment: Humanity as God's intentional workmanship, with works prepared in advance. The opposite of accident.

restoration.text: Adam fell that men might be; and men are, that they might have joy.
restoration.comment: Lehi's affirmation of providential intent — mortal life ordered toward joy, not punishment. Aaron's canonical anchor in Manuscript Ch 43.

restoration.text: Now behold, it was not expedient that man should be reclaimed from this temporal death, for that would destroy the great plan of happiness.
restoration.comment: Alma names the providential frame: the 'great plan of happiness.' Mortal existence designed for purpose, not accident.

s8.text: The fall of humankind from paradise — the thorns, thistles, and sweat of mortality — were not beyond God’s plans
s8.panel_comment: The genuinely Restoration-distinctive line of Article 3. Major Christian traditions read the fall differently: Augustinian Catholicism sees it as catastrophe — redemption restores what was lost rather than fulfills what was begun. Eastern Orthodoxy holds the fall as real rupture and yet within the divine economy of theosis — death entering as both consequence of sin and as God's mercy, preventing eternal entrenchment in it (St. Athanasius); the trajectory the fall interrupted is humanity's growth toward divine likeness, which the Incarnation reopens. The Orthodox vantage shares more with the Restoration's affirmative reading than either shares with Augustinian catastrophe-doctrine. Reformed theology frames it as covenantal breach under decretal sovereignty; the felix culpa affirmation lives in Easter Vigil liturgy ('O happy fault, O necessary sin of Adam') but is rarely stated as confident structural assertion. The Restoration affirms it directly: the fall was foreknown, foreordained, and necessary for human becoming. 2 Nephi 2:25 carries the affirmative reading. The container holds for traditions that affirm any version of felix culpa, but the directness is the editorial signature here.

biblical.text: Cursed is the ground for thy sake; in sorrow shalt thou eat of it all the days of thy life; Thorns also and thistles shall it bring forth to thee... In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread, till thou return unto the ground.
biblical.comment: The biblical source of 'thorns, thistles, and sweat' — the article quotes Genesis 3 directly. The language of the curse is, in the Restoration reading, the language of the providential condition.

biblical.text: Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned.
biblical.comment: Paul's foundational fall theology. Read by Augustinian and Reformed traditions as catastrophe-doctrine; read by the Restoration as the necessary architecture of redemption.

biblical.text: For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive.
biblical.comment: Paul's Adam-Christ parallel. The fall makes the Atonement possible — the redemption is greater than the catastrophe.

restoration.text: And now, behold, if Adam had not transgressed he would not have fallen, but he would have remained in the garden of Eden... And they would have had no children; wherefore they would have remained in a state of innocence, having no joy, for they knew no misery; doing no good, for they knew no sin... Adam fell that men might be; and men are, that they might have joy.
restoration.comment: Lehi's complete teaching — the fall as the precondition of human becoming, joy, and posterity. Aaron's canonical anchor in Manuscript Ch 43.

restoration.text: And Eve, his wife, heard all these things and was glad, saying: Were it not for our transgression we never should have had seed, and never should have known good and evil, and the joy of our redemption, and the eternal life which God giveth unto all the obedient.
restoration.comment: Eve's witness in the Pearl of Great Price — the most pastoral and personal Restoration statement of the affirmative reading. Eve names the fall as the gateway to seed, knowledge, joy, and eternal life.

s9.text: every soul has room to choose, to fall, to rise, and to be made new through His grace
s9.panel_comment: Fourfold movement kept as one span: choose, fall, rise, be made new. The full mortal arc compressed into a single sentence — agency exercised, agency failing, agency restored, agency transformed by grace. Splitting would fragment the integrated motion.

biblical.text: Choose you this day whom ye will serve... but as for me and my house, we will serve the Lord.
biblical.comment: The choosing. (Also cited in Span 3; here the foundational verb of the fourfold motion.)

biblical.text: For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.
biblical.comment: The falling. The universal Pauline confession of moral failure.

biblical.text: Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted.
biblical.comment: The rising. Paul's pastoral theology of restoration after fall — with the warning that any of us may also fall.

biblical.text: Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.
biblical.comment: The being-made-new. The Pauline anchor for transformation in Christ — not improvement but new creation.

restoration.text: Behold, he who has repented of his sins, the same is forgiven, and I, the Lord, remember them no more. By this ye may know if a man repenteth of his sins—behold, he will confess them and forsake them.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's pastoral grace statement — the rising, with the operational marks of confession and forsaking.

restoration.text: And the Lord said unto me: Marvel not that all mankind, yea, men and women, all nations, kindreds, tongues and people, must be born again; yea, born of God, changed from their carnal and fallen state, to a state of righteousness, being redeemed of God, becoming his sons and daughters.
restoration.comment: Alma the Younger's revelation — the most direct Restoration statement of being-made-new. 'Changed from carnal and fallen state to a state of righteousness.'

s10.text: Mortal experiences provide the developmental conditions under which our character is being shaped
s10.panel_comment: The soul-formation flag. Mortal life is part of an eternal educational experience — not just a testing-for-judgment court. Has Irenaean theodicy roots — second-century Eastern reading that humanity was created immature and matures through encounter with mortality. Augustinian frameworks more often treat mortal life as forensic probation; the formation-language register here is closer to the Eastern Christian inheritance and to Restoration theosis. The biblical anchors (Romans 5, James 1, Hebrews 12, 2 Corinthians 4) carry the reading without forcing the choice.

biblical.text: And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience; And patience, experience; and experience, hope.
biblical.comment: Reasserted from Span 5 here as the explicit positive doctrine — mortal experience yields character formation. Same anchor, different rhetorical function.

biblical.text: My brethren, count it all joy when ye fall into divers temptations; Knowing this, that the trying of your faith worketh patience. But let patience have her perfect work, that ye may be perfect and entire, wanting nothing.
biblical.comment: James's teleios language — 'perfect and entire' — names the developmental endpoint toward which mortal trial moves the soul.

biblical.text: For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth... Now no chastening for the present seemeth to be joyous, but grievous: nevertheless afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness unto them which are exercised thereby.
biblical.comment: Hebrews on chastening: the explicit New Testament statement that hardship in mortal life is Fatherly training, not punitive sentence.

biblical.text: For our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory.
biblical.comment: Paul's eschatological economy: mortal affliction itself produces eternal glory. Formation language at its most explicit.

restoration.text: All these things shall give thee experience, and shall be for thy good.
restoration.comment: Christ to Joseph Smith in Liberty Jail. The Restoration's pastoral declaration that mortal extremity yields experience that is for the disciple's good. Reasserted from Span 5 here as the doctrine made explicit.

restoration.text: They were in a preparation to hear the word.
restoration.comment: Alma's observation that humbling mortal experience prepares the soul to receive God's word. Reasserted from Span 5 as the operational mechanism.

s11.text: The pains and pleasures of this existence are not evidence that God has abandoned us
s11.panel_comment: Pastoral anchor against the most common doubt: that suffering means abandonment. The article negates the inference rather than explaining suffering — the right pastoral move. Both pains and pleasures are named because either can be misread as evidence of God's absence (suffering as abandonment, ease as license).

biblical.text: Let your conversation be without covetousness; and be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.
biblical.comment: The promise that anchors the negation. God Himself declares He will not abandon — the grounds for the article's confidence.

biblical.text: Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?... Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him that loved us.
biblical.comment: Paul's exhaustive list of what cannot separate us from Christ's love — explicitly including the pains the article names. (Cited also in Article 2 Span 2.)

biblical.text: My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?... But thou art holy, O thou that inhabitest the praises of Israel... For he hath not despised nor abhorred the affliction of the afflicted; neither hath he hid his face from him; but when he cried unto him, he heard.
biblical.comment: The psalm Christ quoted from the cross. The cry of abandonment given divine voice — and answered. Pastoral acknowledgment that the feeling of abandonment is honest, the conclusion is wrong.

restoration.text: My son, peace be unto thy soul; thine adversity and thine afflictions shall be but a small moment; And then, if thou endure it well, God shall exalt thee on high.
restoration.comment: Christ's word to Joseph Smith in Liberty Jail — the same context as D&C 122:7. Affliction acknowledged as real; abandonment denied; promise affirmed.

restoration.text: And whoso receiveth you, there I will be also, for I will go before your face. I will be on your right hand and on your left, and my Spirit shall be in your hearts, and mine angels round about you, to bear you up.
restoration.comment: Christ's promise of His own ongoing presence. (Reused from Article 2 Span 5; the cross-Article reuse is honest — the same promise carries multiple articles' pastoral weight.)

s12.text: We now live in a sphere of existence God designed for our benefit
s12.panel_comment: The positive teleological claim. Where Span 7 negates the false readings (accident, punishment), this span asserts the affirmative — mortal existence is providentially designed for the disciple's benefit. The Abraham 3 anchor makes the design explicit ('we will prove them herewith') in a way the biblical anchors honor without naming.

biblical.text: And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good.
biblical.comment: The original divine evaluation — creation declared 'very good' before the fall. Reasserted from Span 7 as the foundation for design-for-benefit.

biblical.text: And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose.
biblical.comment: Paul's pastoral capstone of providence. Reasserted from Span 7 as the explicit theology of benefit through all things.

biblical.text: There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it.
biblical.comment: The operational guarantee — mortal trials are calibrated to capacity. The benefit-design is not abstract; it is bounded by faithfulness.

restoration.text: And again, verily I say unto you, the earth abideth the law of a celestial kingdom, for it filleth the measure of its creation, and transgresseth not the law— Wherefore, it shall be sanctified.
restoration.comment: The earth itself participates in the providential design — 'filleth the measure of its creation.' The cosmic frame for benefit-design.

restoration.text: And there stood one among them that was like unto God, and he said unto those who were with him: We will go down, for there is space there, and we will take of these materials, and we will make an earth whereon these may dwell; And we will prove them herewith, to see if they will do all things whatsoever the Lord their God shall command them.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's most explicit statement of mortal probation as design — 'we will prove them herewith.' Names what the biblical anchors imply.

crossref.label: Within this article
crossref.title: grow from within the experience

s13.text: We are free to either deny the Creator or to see the blessings inherent in this existence
s13.panel_comment: The epistemic dimension of agency. Where Span 3 names moral choice (good vs. evil), this span names interpretive choice (denial vs. perception). Romans 1:18–22 is the load-bearing anchor: humanity is capable of suppressing the truth that creation discloses. Cross-references Article 2 Span 11 — the same creation-witness logic, here applied to volitional response.

biblical.text: For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who hold the truth in unrighteousness; Because that which may be known of God is manifest in them; for God hath shewed it unto them... Because that, when they knew God, they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful... Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools.
biblical.comment: Paul's diagnosis of the deniers' choice — not ignorance but suppression. The biblical foundation for the interpretive-agency claim.

biblical.text: The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork. Day unto day uttereth speech, and night unto night sheweth knowledge. There is no speech nor language, where their voice is not heard.
biblical.comment: The blessings inherent in creation — the universal voice God's works speak to every soul under heaven.

biblical.text: Nevertheless he left not himself without witness, in that he did good, and gave us rain from heaven, and fruitful seasons, filling our hearts with food and gladness.
biblical.comment: Paul to the Lystrans — even outside covenant Israel, God's blessings are observable to those who will see.

biblical.text: 15 And if it seem evil unto you to serve the Lord, choose you this day whom ye will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were on the other side of the flood, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land ye dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve the Lord.
biblical.comment: Joshua's covenant address to Israel — the OT's most direct invitation to choose, here paralleled with Romans 1's negative case as the affirmative side of the same volitional choice. (Also cited in Span 3 and Span 9 within this article; reasserted here as the anchor for interpretive agency.)

restoration.text: But behold, if ye will awake and arouse your faculties, even to an experiment upon my words, and exercise a particle of faith, yea, even if ye can no more than desire to believe, let this desire work in you, even until ye believe in a manner that ye can give place for a portion of my words.
restoration.comment: Alma's invitation to interpretive choice — the Restoration's pastoral statement that the soul can choose to give place for faith. Pairs with Romans 1's negative case as the affirmative invitation.

restoration.text: And any man who hath seen any or the least of these hath seen God moving in his majesty and power... Behold, all these are kingdoms, and any man who hath seen any or the least of these hath seen God moving in his majesty and power.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's expansion of Psalm 19's claim — to see any work of God truly is to see God Himself moving. Frames the choice to see as a choice to encounter.

crossref.label: See Article 2
crossref.title: God

s14.text: these conditions remain, and the shaping takes place
s14.panel_comment: The article's thesis closure. The conditions of mortal pressure remain regardless of the soul's cooperation — Romans 5:3 affirms that tribulation works patience whether welcomed or not, and the formative weight of mortal life operates on every soul. But the prose's gentler claim is the right one: where the soul does cooperate with that pressure is where agency operates and where Christ's redemptive work meets human response. This carries Augustinian resonance (sovereign providence working in all conditions) and Restoration resonance (D&C 122:7's promise to Joseph in Liberty Jail) without collapsing into monergist determinism. The pastoral weight is in the assurance: the providential frame holds; what the disciple does within it is where sanctification proceeds.

biblical.text: For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth... Now no chastening for the present seemeth to be joyous, but grievous: nevertheless afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness unto them which are exercised thereby.
biblical.comment: The shaping declared as Fatherly love operating regardless of the soul's immediate experience. (Reasserted from Spans 5 and 10 as the closing affirmation.)

biblical.text: Tribulation worketh patience; And patience, experience; and experience, hope.
biblical.comment: The fixed sequence Paul names — mortal trial yields formation. Reasserted as the article's closing structural claim.

biblical.text: And he shall sit as a refiner and purifier of silver: and he shall purify the sons of Levi, and purge them as gold and silver, that they may offer unto the Lord an offering in righteousness.
biblical.comment: The OT image of God as refiner. The shaping is precise, patient, and purposive — not abandonment to chance.

biblical.text: Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ.
biblical.comment: Paul's confidence statement — the work God begins, He completes. The closing pastoral assurance for Article 3.

restoration.text: All these things shall give thee experience, and shall be for thy good.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's most concentrated statement of fixed providential shaping. Reasserted from Spans 5 and 10 as the article's closing word — the shaping happens, and it is for the disciple's good.

restoration.text: Yea, come unto Christ, and be perfected in him... and if ye shall deny yourselves of all ungodliness, and love God with all your might, mind and strength, then is his grace sufficient for you, that by his grace ye may be perfect in Christ.
restoration.comment: Moroni's closing invitation — the perfecting takes place by grace, in Christ, as the soul yields. The shaping is real; the soul's part is to receive.

s1.text: the witnesses of prophets, mortal men and women
s1.panel_comment: Container word, gender-inclusive prophetic ministry. Complementarian receiving traditions (Reformed, Catholic, conservative Anglican) fill 'prophets' with male office-holders; egalitarian traditions (most Protestant, charismatic, and Latter-day Saint via Relief Society and women's prophetic witness) include women's prophetic ministry. The biblical floor — Miriam, Deborah, Huldah, Anna, Philip's daughters, and Joel 2:28's sons-and-daughters prophecy — is high enough to hold the inclusive reading without forcing it on traditions that read the prophetic office as male-only. Cross-references Article 1 (merognosis posture: each tradition fills the container from its own understanding).

biblical.text: And it shall come to pass afterward, that I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, your young men shall see visions.
biblical.comment: The OT prophecy of universally-distributed prophetic gifting — explicitly naming sons and daughters. The biblical anchor for gender-inclusive prophetic witness, fulfilled in Acts 2 at Pentecost.

biblical.text: And Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lapidoth, she judged Israel at that time.
biblical.comment: Deborah — named prophetess and judge of Israel. The Old Testament's most direct narrative witness that the prophetic office has never been male-only in practice.

biblical.text: So Hilkiah the priest, and Ahikam, and Achbor, and Shaphan, and Asahiah, went unto Huldah the prophetess... and they communed with her.
biblical.comment: Huldah — the prophetess King Josiah's officials consulted to authenticate the rediscovered Book of the Law. Her prophetic word governed the Josianic reform. Female prophetic authority operating at the highest level of national religious life.

biblical.text: And the same man had four daughters, virgins, which did prophesy.
biblical.comment: Philip the evangelist's four daughters — named in Acts as prophesying. The New Testament's confirmation that the Joel 2:28 prophecy was understood as fulfilled in continuing female prophetic ministry.

restoration.text: And thou shalt be ordained under his hand to expound scriptures, and to exhort the church, according as it shall be given thee by my Spirit.
restoration.comment: Christ's word to Emma Smith — explicit Restoration witness to women's authorized teaching ministry under the Spirit. The Restoration confirms the biblical pattern without resolving every tradition's question about ordination.

restoration.text: For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost.
restoration.comment: Paul's principle preserved in Peter — prophecy originates in God, not in human selection. (Cross-cited because the article's substantive claim about prophetic authority is grounded here regardless of how the prophet's gender is read.)

crossref.label: See Article 1
crossref.title: Plainness

s2.text: testimonies survive despite their own human imperfections
s2.panel_comment: The textual-transmission claim. Anchors why prophetic witness retains authority across centuries despite the imperfections of those who carry it: the source is God, not the messenger. Pairs with Span 3 (revelations of God, not mortal origin) and Span 7 (broken vessels) as a triadic structure on prophetic authority.

biblical.text: Knowing this first, that no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation. For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost.
biblical.comment: The foundational New Testament statement: prophecy comes by the Holy Ghost, not by human will. The biblical anchor for the survival-through-imperfection claim.

biblical.text: All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness: That the man of God may be perfect, throughly furnished unto all good works.
biblical.comment: Paul to Timothy — scripture's profitability rests on its inspired source, not on the perfection of its human channels. The basis for the article's confidence in transmitted prophetic witness.

biblical.text: For who maketh thee to differ from another? and what hast thou that thou didst not receive? now if thou didst receive it, why dost thou glory, as if thou hadst not received it?
biblical.comment: Paul's reminder that what prophets carry is received, not generated. The imperfect vessel is not the source of the gift.

restoration.text: Nevertheless, I do not write anything upon plates save it be that I think it be sacred. And now, if I do err, even did they err of old; not that I would excuse myself because of other men, but because of the weakness which is in me, according to the flesh, I would excuse myself.
restoration.comment: Nephi's own confession of authorial weakness — a prophet writing scripture while acknowledging he writes through fallible flesh. The Restoration's most pastoral statement of the imperfection that the inspired witness survives.

restoration.text: And whoso receiveth this record, and shall not condemn it because of the imperfections which are in it, the same shall know of greater things than these... And if there be faults they be the faults of a man. But behold, we know no fault; nevertheless God knoweth all things.
restoration.comment: Moroni's plea — the Book of Mormon's own self-witness about imperfections in its mortal vessels. The transmission acknowledges weakness yet claims divine origin for what survives.

s3.text: the revelations were of God and not of mortal origin
s3.panel_comment: Direct paraphrase of 2 Peter 1:21. The most concentrated NT statement of revelation's source. Pairs with Span 2 (testimonies survive despite imperfections) as the affirmative grounds for that survival: imperfection of the vessel does not corrupt the divine source. Reasserts the same anchor as Span 2 in declarative voice.

biblical.text: For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost.
biblical.comment: The article paraphrases this verse directly. Reasserted from Span 2 here as the explicit positive doctrine: revelation originates in God, not in human will.

biblical.text: But I certify you, brethren, that the gospel which was preached of me is not after man. For I neither received it of man, neither was I taught it, but by the revelation of Jesus Christ.
biblical.comment: Paul's own apostolic claim — the gospel he preached was 'not after man.' The strongest first-person Pauline witness to non-mortal origin of revelation.

biblical.text: God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets, Hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son.
biblical.comment: The opening of Hebrews — God speaking in past ages through prophets and now through His Son. Names God as the consistent subject of the speaking, regardless of which mortal vessel He chose.

restoration.text: And whatsoever they shall speak when moved upon by the Holy Ghost shall be scripture, shall be the will of the Lord, shall be the mind of the Lord, shall be the word of the Lord, shall be the voice of the Lord, and the power of God unto salvation.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's most concentrated statement of inspired speech — what is spoken under the Holy Ghost is, by that fact, the Lord's word. Names the principle the article restates in plain terms: source determines status.

restoration.text: For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost.
restoration.comment: Reasserted from the biblical column above as the article's directly paraphrased anchor. The plainness of the principle is what gives the article its confidence.

s4.panel_comment: The first commandment in distilled form. Sets up Span 5's negation — worship belongs to God alone, which is why prophets and scriptures (however venerable) must not be worshiped as idols. The article moves immediately from positive affirmation to the corrective claim it warrants.

biblical.text: Thou shalt have no other gods before me.
biblical.comment: The first commandment. The foundational OT anchor for exclusive worship of God.

biblical.text: Then saith Jesus unto him, Get thee hence, Satan: for it is written, Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve.
biblical.comment: Christ's own words rebuking Satan in the wilderness — quoting Deuteronomy 6:13. Christ Himself names exclusive worship as the standard.

biblical.text: And when I had heard and seen, I fell down to worship before the feet of the angel which shewed me these things. Then saith he unto me, See thou do it not: for I am thy fellowservant, and of thy brethren the prophets... worship God.
biblical.comment: John, even at the climax of Revelation, is rebuked for offering worship to a fellow servant. The closing instruction of the New Testament canon: worship God.

restoration.text: That you shall fall down and worship the Father in my name.
restoration.comment: Christ's instruction — worship the Father in His (Christ's) name. The Restoration confirms the biblical pattern.

restoration.text: And again I say unto you as I have said before, that as ye have come to the knowledge of the glory of God, or if ye have known of his goodness and have tasted of his love... I would that ye should remember, and always retain in remembrance, the greatness of God, and your own nothingness.
restoration.comment: King Benjamin's call to worship rooted in remembrance of God's greatness and our dependence. Worship grounded in posture, not proximity to particular vessels.

s5.text: We respect but do not worship prophets or their scriptures as idols
s5.panel_comment: The corrective claim Span 4 warrants. The article affirms respect for prophetic witness while refusing the elevation of prophets or scriptures to objects of worship. John 5:39 is the load-bearing anchor — Christ's own naming of scripture as testifying witness, not terminus. The Restoration's anti-bibliolatry text is 2 Nephi 29:3–4, the rebuke of 'A Bible! A Bible! We have got a Bible!' — the most direct Restoration scripture rebuking the use of Bible-completeness as ground for rejecting further scriptural witness. Cross-references Article 1 (Plainness, refusal to bind conscience).

biblical.text: And when I had heard and seen, I fell down to worship before the feet of the angel which shewed me these things. Then saith he unto me, See thou do it not: for I am thy fellowservant, and of thy brethren the prophets... worship God.
biblical.comment: To honor the messenger or the page above the One they reveal is the very error John was forbidden — when he fell to worship the angel he was told, 'See thou do it not… worship God' (Revelation 22:8–9). We hold Scripture in the highest reverence precisely because it testifies of Christ (John 5:39); we will not turn that reverence into idolatry of the vessel. The Word points beyond itself to the living Word.

biblical.text: Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me. And ye will not come to me, that ye might have life.
biblical.comment: Christ's own diagnosis: the scriptures testify of Him, but searching them while refusing Him misses their purpose. The anchor for treating scripture as witness, not terminus. Pairs with Span 13 (search for what brings them to Christ) as the article's hermeneutical bookends.

biblical.text: And I fell at his feet to worship him. And he said unto me, See thou do it not: I am thy fellowservant, and of thy brethren that have the testimony of Jesus: worship God: for the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.
biblical.comment: The angel's correction of John — worship God, not the messenger; and the closing line names the heart of all prophecy: the testimony of Jesus. Prophecy that does not point to Christ has lost its purpose.

biblical.text: Who also hath made us able ministers of the new testament; not of the letter, but of the spirit: for the letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life.
biblical.comment: Paul's distinction — the letter and the Spirit. Scripture worshiped as letter without the Spirit that gives it life becomes idolatrous. The Pauline warning against bibliolatry as such.

restoration.text: And because my words shall hiss forth—many of the Gentiles shall say: A Bible! A Bible! We have got a Bible, and there cannot be any more Bible. But thus saith the Lord God: O fools, they shall have a Bible; and it shall proceed forth from the Jews, mine ancient covenant people. And what thank they the Jews for the Bible which they receive from them?
restoration.comment: The Restoration's most direct anti-bibliolatry text. The Lord rebukes the elevation of any single canonical witness to ultimate status. The very Restoration scripture that some traditions reject is itself a witness against scripture-as-idol. Restoration amplification — witness only; not required to receive the Article.

restoration.text: What I the Lord have spoken, I have spoken, and I excuse not myself; and though the heavens and the earth pass away, my word shall not pass away, but shall all be fulfilled, whether by mine own voice or by the voice of my servants, it is the same.
restoration.comment: Christ naming the source of authority: it is His word that endures, whether spoken directly or through chosen servants. Honor belongs to the Word; the servants are vessels through whom it passes. Restoration amplification — witness only; not required to receive the Article.

crossref.label: See Article 1
crossref.title: Plainness

s6.text: God spoke in ages past. God speaks today. God will yet speak in generations to come.
s6.panel_comment: The open-canon affirmation, in triadic form. Three coordinated claims kept as one span: God has spoken, speaks, and will yet speak. The biblical anchors (Hebrews 1:1–2, Amos 3:7) and the Restoration anchors (the same-yesterday-today-forever cluster from Manuscript Ch 8) carry the affirmation across both columns. Articles of Faith 1:9 is the canonical Restoration triadic statement and matches the article's own structure exactly. The 'line upon line' anchor (2 Nephi 28:30, D&C 98:12) reasserted from Articles 1 and 2 to ground continuing revelation in the Restoration's pastoral cadence rather than in dramatic claim alone.

biblical.text: And it shall come to pass in the last days, saith God, I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh: and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, and your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams: And on my servants and on my handmaidens I will pour out in those days of my Spirit; and they shall prophesy.
biblical.comment: To say God still speaks is not to add to anyone's Bible — it is to take the Bible at its word. Scripture promises the Spirit poured out 'in the last days' for prophecy, visions, and dreams (Acts 2:17–18, citing Joel), two witnesses who yet prophesy (Revelation 11:3–6), an angel proclaiming the everlasting gospel (Revelation 14:6–7), and the coming of Elijah (Malachi 4:5–6) — for 'the Lord God does nothing without revealing His secret to His servants the prophets' (Amos 3:7). Believers from Pentecostal to Presbyterian confess that God has not fallen silent. Whether His continuing voice ever becomes Scripture, each tradition answers in its own canon; this Article does not decide it.

biblical.text: God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets, Hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son, whom he hath appointed heir of all things, by whom also he made the worlds.
biblical.comment: The opening of Hebrews — God's speaking spans ages: 'in time past' through prophets, 'in these last days' through His Son. The biblical foundation for the article's triadic claim about prophetic speech across generations.

biblical.text: Surely the Lord God will do nothing, but he revealeth his secret unto his servants the prophets.
biblical.comment: Aaron's locked manuscript epigraph for Manuscript Chapter 8 (Prophets of God). The biblical principle: God's pattern is to disclose through chosen channels in His own time. Anchors the whole article's claim about prophetic ministry as God's chosen mode of speech.

biblical.text: And Moses said unto him, Enviest thou for my sake? would God that all the Lord's people were prophets, and that the Lord would put his spirit upon them!
biblical.comment: Moses's own desire — that all the Lord's people might be prophets. The biblical posture that anticipates and welcomes ongoing revelation rather than restricting it.

biblical.text: And I will give power unto my two witnesses, and they shall prophesy a thousand two hundred and threescore days, clothed in sackcloth... These have power to shut heaven, that it rain not in the days of their prophecy: and have power over waters to turn them to blood, and to smite the earth with all plagues, as often as they will.
biblical.comment: The two witnesses who yet prophesy — the New Testament's own future-tense prophetic ministry, promised within the biblical horizon itself.

biblical.text: And I saw another angel fly in the midst of heaven, having the everlasting gospel to preach unto them that dwell on the earth, and to every nation, and kindred, and tongue, and people, Saying with a loud voice, Fear God, and give glory to him; for the hour of his judgment is come: and worship him that made heaven, and earth, and the sea, and the fountains of waters.
biblical.comment: An angel proclaiming the everlasting gospel to every nation — continuing heavenly proclamation within the New Testament's own forward witness.

biblical.text: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and dreadful day of the Lord: And he shall turn the heart of the fathers to the children, and the heart of the children to their fathers, lest I come and smite the earth with a curse.
biblical.comment: The promised coming of Elijah — the Old Testament's closing word is itself a promise of future prophetic ministry.

biblical.text: Howbeit when he, the Spirit of truth, is come, he will guide you into all truth: for he shall not speak of himself; but whatsoever he shall hear, that shall he speak: and he will shew you things to come.
biblical.comment: Christ's promise of the Spirit of truth who 'will shew you things to come' — continuing divine speech grounded in Christ's own word. (Cited also at Span 14.)

restoration.text: We believe all that God has revealed, all that He does now reveal, and we believe that He will yet reveal many great and important things pertaining to the Kingdom of God.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's most direct triadic statement of open canon — past, present, future revelation — in exactly the structure the article follows. The canonical Restoration anchor for this span. Restoration amplification — witness only; not required to receive the Article.

restoration.text: Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever.
restoration.comment: Aaron's locked manuscript pairing in Chapter 8: God is the same yesterday, today, and forever. Reasserted here from the biblical canon (it functions as both biblical witness and Restoration-claimed witness because of its cross-canonical resonance with 1 Nephi 10:18, 2 Nephi 27:23, and Moroni 10:19). Restoration amplification — witness only; not required to receive the Article.

restoration.text: For behold, thus saith the Lord God: I will give unto the children of men line upon line, precept upon precept, here a little and there a little; and blessed are those who hearken unto my precepts, and lend an ear unto my counsel, for they shall learn wisdom.
restoration.comment: The Restoration cadence of progressive revelation: line upon line, precept upon precept. Reasserted from Article 1 Span 9 and Article 2 Span 9 as the structural thread of continuing-revelation theology across the article cluster. Same anchor, same principle, applied here to the open canon claim. Restoration amplification — witness only; not required to receive the Article.

restoration.text: For he will give unto the faithful line upon line, precept upon precept; and I will try you and prove you herewith.
restoration.comment: The covenantal echo — line-upon-line revelation given to the faithful, in the Lord's timing. (Reasserted from Article 2 Span 9.) The pairing makes continuing revelation a relational covenant, not a triumphalist claim. Restoration amplification — witness only; not required to receive the Article.

crossref.label: See Article 1
crossref.title: Plainness

crossref.label: See Article 2
crossref.title: God

s7.text: God chooses imperfect servants, broken vessels, for His own reasons that we often cannot understand
s7.panel_comment: The broken-vessel signature line of the article. The appositive 'imperfect servants, broken vessels' does deliberate work — 'imperfect servants' is the universal Christian frame; 'broken vessels' is the ministry's own vocabulary, drawing directly on 2 Corinthians 4:7. Introducing the signature phrase through a universally receivable one is the right order. The closing clause is a merognosis-shaped move: refusing to speculate about why God chooses particular vessels keeps the article's restraint consistent with Article 1.

biblical.text: But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us.
biblical.comment: The Pauline source of the 'broken vessels' framework. The structural claim: the imperfection of the vessel highlights the divine power of what it carries. Foundational to the ministry's own vocabulary on this theme.

biblical.text: But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty; And base things of the world, and things which are despised, hath God chosen, yea, and things which are not, to bring to nought things that are: That no flesh should glory in his presence.
biblical.comment: Paul's most extended treatment of God's pattern in choosing weak and despised vessels. The doctrinal anchor for why imperfect servants are the rule, not the exception.

biblical.text: Then said I, Ah, Lord God! behold, I cannot speak: for I am a child. But the Lord said unto me, Say not, I am a child: for thou shalt go to all that I shall send thee, and whatsoever I shall command thee thou shalt speak.
biblical.comment: Jeremiah's own protest — the prophet calling himself unfit, and God overriding the protest. The OT pattern of God commissioning vessels who themselves doubt their adequacy.

restoration.text: And if men come unto me I will show unto them their weakness. I give unto men weakness that they may be humble; and my grace is sufficient for all men that humble themselves before me; for if they humble themselves before me, and have faith in me, then will I make weak things become strong unto them.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's most pastoral statement of the broken-vessel principle: weakness is given on purpose, that grace might make weak things strong. Names the why of the broken-vessel pattern in covenantal language.

restoration.text: The weak things of the world shall come forth and break down the mighty and strong ones, that man should not counsel his fellow man, neither trust in the arm of flesh— But that every man might speak in the name of God the Lord, even the Savior of the world... that faith also might increase in the earth.
restoration.comment: Christ's own naming of the Restoration pattern: weak things break down the mighty so that no one trusts in the arm of flesh. The Restoration interprets its own emergence through the broken-vessel framework.

s8.text: study scriptural teachings while avoiding the mistake of leaning to our own understanding alone
s8.panel_comment: The interpretive humility claim. Two coordinate elements held in tension: study is required (not optional), but private interpretation alone is the trap. Proverbs 3:5–7 is the foundational anchor; 2 Peter 1:20 makes the claim explicit for scripture itself. Cross-references Article 1 Span 4 (speculation beyond the bounds of wisdom) — the same interpretive discipline applied to scripture rather than to cosmology.

biblical.text: Trust in the Lord with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding. In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths. Be not wise in thine own eyes: fear the Lord, and depart from evil.
biblical.comment: The article paraphrases this verse directly. The OT foundation for interpretive humility — study with trust, not with autonomous reason as the standard. (Cited also in Article 1 Span 4.)

biblical.text: Knowing this first, that no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation.
biblical.comment: The explicit New Testament claim about scripture itself: it does not yield to private interpretation alone. The biblical warrant for the article's claim.

biblical.text: These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
biblical.comment: The Bereans — Luke's praise for those who received the apostolic word with eagerness and tested it against scripture. The biblical model of study that holds Spirit-witness and scriptural verification together.

restoration.text: And as all have not faith, seek ye diligently and teach one another words of wisdom; yea, seek ye out of the best books words of wisdom; seek learning, even by study and also by faith.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's signature pairing: study and faith, together. Reasserted from Article 1 Span 4 here as the affirmative discipline that prevents both speculation and intellectual neglect.

restoration.text: And now I, Nephi, cannot say more; the Spirit stoppeth mine utterance, and I am left to mourn because of the unbelief, and the wickedness, and the ignorance, and the stiffneckedness of men; for they will not search knowledge, nor understand great knowledge, when it is given unto them in plainness, even as plain as word can be.
restoration.comment: Nephi's lament — even when truth is given plainly, those who refuse to search remain ignorant. The Restoration witness that study is not optional; the article preserves Nephi's diagnosis without the lament.

crossref.label: See Article 1
crossref.title: Plainness

s9.panel_comment: “God’s word” is the article’s opening container. Each receiving tradition fills it from its own canon and rule of faith — Protestants and Reformed readers fill it from the Bible alone, Catholic readers from Scripture and Sacred Tradition, Orthodox readers from Scripture in the living memory of the Church, Restoration readers from the open canon that A4 Span 6 confesses. The biblical anchors hold the floor every tradition affirms: scripture is God-breathed (2 Timothy 3:16), the disciple receives the engrafted word with meekness (James 1:21), and the standard for that reception is Christ Himself — quoting Moses to His tempter, declaring that man lives by every word that proceeds from God’s mouth (Matthew 4:4). The article does not adjudicate between the traditions’ fuller accounts of how Christ-as-Word, scripture-as-Word, and Spirit-borne-speaking-as-Word relate; those accounts exceed what this span articulates. What follows in the article — the prophetic channel (Spans 1–3), the anti-bibliolatry pair (Spans 4–5), the open canon (Span 6), and the Christological hermeneutic (Span 13) — develops the substance of what is received. This span only marks the door.

biblical.text: Wherefore lay apart all filthiness and superfluity of naughtiness, and receive with meekness the engrafted word, which is able to save your souls.
biblical.comment: The article’s opening verb in compressed apostolic form — “receive with meekness the engrafted word.” Names the disciple’s posture (meekness), the substance of what is received (the engrafted word), and its saving purpose. The most direct biblical anchor for “receive God’s word” in the article’s opening clause.

biblical.text: But he answered and said, It is written, Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God.
biblical.comment: Christ Himself, in the wilderness, modeling what receiving God’s word looks like — quoting Deuteronomy 8:3 to His tempter. The phrase “every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God” holds across all four traditions without forcing any specific layer or channel — receivable as scripture, as the Logos, as Spirit-borne speaking, as continuing revelation. The strongest single biblical anchor in the cluster because the receiving disciple is Christ Himself.

biblical.text: All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness: That the man of God may be perfect, throughly furnished unto all good works.
biblical.comment: The universal Christian anchor for scripture as God-breathed and saving. (Reasserted from Article 4 Span 2 in different rhetorical direction: at s2 verses 16–17 ground the survival-through-imperfection claim — transmission integrity despite mortal vessels; here verse 16 anchors the substance of what is received at the article’s opening. Same passage, opening container vs. transmission claim.)

restoration.text: Angels speak by the power of the Holy Ghost; wherefore, they speak the words of Christ. Wherefore, I said unto you, feast upon the words of Christ; for behold, the words of Christ will tell you all things what ye should do.
restoration.comment: Nephi’s signature reception-of-God’s-word passage. The verb “feast upon” names the disciple’s active reception, and the claim that “the words of Christ will tell you all things what ye should do” names the sufficiency of what is received for the disciple’s path. (Reasserted from Article 4 Span 14 in different rhetorical direction: at s14 verses 3–5 together ground the integration of receiving-truth with right-living through the Spirit’s comprehensive guidance; here verse 3 alone grounds the disciple’s reception-posture at the article’s opening. Same passage, integration claim vs. reception-at-opening.)

crossref.label: Within this article
crossref.title: Span 6: God spoke in ages past. God speaks today. God will yet speak in generations to come.

crossref.label: See Article 1
crossref.title: Plainness

crossref.label: See Article 2
crossref.title: God

s10.text: What God has spoken plainly through these channels has been preserved for us
s10.panel_comment: The bounded preservation claim. The article carefully says 'what God has spoken plainly through these channels has been preserved for us' — not 'every word of every transmission perfectly intact.' The biblical anchors (Psalm 12:6–7, Isaiah 40:8, Matthew 24:35) testify to God's preservation of His word in substance and across generations. The Restoration witness via 1 Nephi 13:34–40 is included not as a polemical claim about historic Christian transmission, but as the Restoration's own hermeneutic of preservation: God preserves what is plainly necessary for salvation, and where transmission has obscured the plain things, God restores them by His Spirit through chosen channels. This reading frames the Restoration as participation in God's ongoing preservation rather than as critique of others' canon. The 'plainly' qualifier governs both columns — what God has made plain He preserves; what is contested across traditions belongs to the merognosis territory of Article 1.

biblical.text: The words of the Lord are pure words: as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times. Thou shalt keep them, O Lord, thou shalt preserve them from this generation for ever.
biblical.comment: The OT's most direct claim about divine preservation of God's words — the words are pure, and the Lord Himself preserves them across generations.

biblical.text: The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.
biblical.comment: Isaiah's enduring word: human transience contrasted with the abiding word of God. The biblical anchor for confidence that what God has spoken does not pass away.

biblical.text: Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away.
biblical.comment: Christ's own claim about His words: they outlast the cosmos. The strongest possible NT statement of divine preservation. The article's confidence rests directly here.

restoration.text: ...wherefore, thou seest that after the book hath gone forth through the hands of the great and abominable church, that there are many plain and precious things taken away from the book, which is the book of the Lamb of God... Wherefore, these things go forth from the Jews in purity unto the Gentiles, according to the truth which is in God... And the angel spake unto me, saying: These last records, which thou hast seen among the Gentiles, shall establish the truth of the first, which are of the twelve apostles of the Lamb, and shall make known the plain and precious things which have been taken away from them.
restoration.comment: Nephi's vision of plain and precious truths lost and restored. The Restoration's foundational witness that preservation operates dynamically — God speaks, history strains transmission, and God speaks again to restore what was obscured. Cited here not to indict particular traditions' canons, but to ground the article's bounded claim that what is plainly necessary for salvation is preserved by divine faithfulness, not by human achievement.

restoration.text: And also those to whom these commandments were given, might have power to lay the foundation of this church, and to bring it forth out of obscurity and out of darkness, the only true and living church upon the face of the whole earth, with which I, the Lord, am well pleased, speaking unto the church collectively and not individually.
restoration.comment: Christ's own framing of the Restoration's role: bringing forth what had been in obscurity. The Restoration's self-understanding is participation in God's preservation work, not displacement of others' canons.

s11.text: what He continues to speak, He confirms by His Spirit
s11.panel_comment: The Spirit-confirmation principle for ongoing revelation. Pairs with Span 6 (open canon) and Span 14 (Spirit guidance for receiving and living truth) as the article's structure on continuing revelation: God speaks, the Spirit confirms what He speaks, the Spirit guides the soul that receives. 1 Thessalonians 5:19–21 names the disciple's responsibility: don't quench the Spirit, don't despise prophesyings, but prove all things and hold fast to what is good. The article's confidence in continuing revelation is bounded by this same testing-discipline.

biblical.text: Quench not the Spirit. Despise not prophesyings. Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
biblical.comment: Paul's discipline of receiving continuing prophetic word: don't quench the Spirit, don't dismiss prophecy, but test everything against what is good. The biblical pattern of openness with discernment. The most concentrated NT anchor for the article's claim.

biblical.text: This is he that came by water and blood, even Jesus Christ; not by water only, but by water and blood. And it is the Spirit that beareth witness, because the Spirit is truth.
biblical.comment: John's principle: the Spirit bears witness because the Spirit is truth. The biblical foundation for the Spirit's confirming office.

biblical.text: Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world.
biblical.comment: The companion to 1 Thessalonians 5:21: openness to ongoing revelation requires the discipline of trying the spirits. Confirmation by the Spirit is itself the testing standard.

restoration.text: Yea, behold, I will tell you in your mind and in your heart, by the Holy Ghost, which shall come upon you and which shall dwell in your heart. Now, behold, this is the spirit of revelation; behold, this is the spirit by which Moses brought the children of Israel through the Red sea on dry ground.
restoration.comment: Christ's instruction to Oliver Cowdery on the operation of the Spirit of revelation: in the mind and the heart, the same Spirit that operated in Moses. The Restoration's pastoral and operational anchor for Spirit-confirmed continuing revelation. (Reasserted from Article 1 Span 15.)

restoration.text: And by the power of the Holy Ghost ye may know the truth of all things.
restoration.comment: Moroni's closing promise reasserted (cited in Article 1 Span 15 and Article 4 Span 9). The Spirit's confirming witness is the disciple's standard for all truth-claims, including claims of ongoing revelation.

restoration.text: But, behold, I say unto you, that you must study it out in your mind; then you must ask me if it be right, and if it be right I will cause that your bosom shall burn within you; therefore, you shall feel that it is right. But if it be not right you shall have no such feelings, but you shall have a stupor of thought that shall cause you to forget the thing which is wrong.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's operational discipline of Spirit-confirmation: study, ask, and receive the Spirit's witness. The Restoration provides the most concrete pastoral process for what 1 Thessalonians 5:21 commands.

s12.text: recognizes its own canon of scripture
s12.panel_comment: Honest historical-theological observation. Canon dispute is universal across Christian traditions, not a Restoration peculiarity. Established Christian faiths have argued for centuries about which books to include in the Bible, which translations are acceptable, and what to do with the Apocrypha and deuterocanonical writings. The Dead Sea Scrolls have unsettled denominational convictions across the spectrum. The Restoration scriptures add another body of inspired writing to a conversation that was already in motion — they neither created the question nor uniquely answer it. The article's pastoral move is to refuse the dichotomy of 'divine clarification vs. sectarian chaos' and to apply Christ's own pearl-of-great-price standard: any plainly-understood truth, wherever found, is a rare treasure to hold close. Cross-references Article 1 Span 11 (refusal to bind conscience).

biblical.text: Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me.
biblical.comment: This is description, not doctrine. The communions of Christ already differ over which books they receive and which translation they read — a plain fact that needs no defending. We name it not to rank canons or to pry open anyone's, but to set the matter beneath Christ rather than beside Him. Whatever scripture a soul holds, our exhortation is one: search it diligently, for the Scriptures testify of Him (John 5:39).

biblical.text: Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto a merchant man, seeking goodly pearls: Who, when he had found one pearl of great price, went and sold all that he had, and bought it.
biblical.comment: The pearl-of-great-price parable, applied here not as soteriological metaphor (its more common reading) but as the disciple's posture toward truth wherever it surfaces. Christ's own standard: when plain truth is found, it is held close at any cost.

biblical.text: These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
biblical.comment: The Bereans — the original biblical model for testing all teachings against scripture and Spirit. The same eagerness Luke praises is the posture the article commends. (Cited also in Span 8.)

biblical.text: Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
biblical.comment: Paul's standing rule, applicable across the canon question: prove all things, and hold fast to what is plainly good. The biblical principle that allows the disciple to honor all sources without absolutizing any single one. (Reasserted from Span 11.)

restoration.text: Verily, thus saith the Lord unto you concerning the Apocrypha—There are many things contained therein that are true, and it is mostly translated correctly; There are many things contained therein that are not true, which are interpolations by the hands of men. Verily, I say unto you, that it is not needful that the Apocrypha should be translated. Therefore, whoso readeth it, let him understand, for the Spirit manifesteth truth; And whoso is enlightened by the Spirit shall obtain benefit therefrom; And whoso receiveth not by the Spirit, cannot be benefited.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's own model for navigating disputed canon: the Spirit, not imposed uniformity, is the discerning principle. Christ's own counsel about the Apocrypha applies the article's own approach — the Restoration's hermeneutic is consistent with the Berean model rather than with creedal exclusion. The most direct Restoration anchor for the multi-canon claim. Restoration amplification — witness only; not required to receive the Article.

restoration.text: Condemn me not because of mine imperfection, neither my father, because of his imperfection, neither them who have written before him; but rather give thanks unto God that he hath made manifest unto you our imperfections, that ye may learn to be more wise than we have been.
restoration.comment: Moroni's pastoral plea, applicable across the canon question: receive the witness without condemning the imperfection of its vessels. The Restoration's own request for charitable reading is the standard the article extends to all canonical witnesses. Restoration amplification — witness only; not required to receive the Article.

crossref.label: See Article 1
crossref.title: Plainness

s13.text: search their scriptures diligently for what brings them to Christ
s13.panel_comment: The Christological hermeneutic as governing standard — the article's closing pastoral move. Pairs with Span 5 (John 5:39–40, scripture testifies of Christ) as the article's hermeneutical bookends: scripture's witness terminates in Christ, and the disciple's reading must be governed by what brings them to Him. The article's whole posture toward prophets, scripture, canon, Spirit, and tradition resolves in this one Christological standard.

biblical.text: Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me.
biblical.comment: Christ's own naming of scripture's purpose: testimony of Him. (Cited also at Span 5; here as the affirmative invitation that closes the article.) Christ Himself authorizes the searching the article commends.

biblical.text: And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself.
biblical.comment: Christ on the road to Emmaus, opening all the scriptures concerning Himself. The biblical pattern of Christological hermeneutic, performed by Christ Himself: from Moses through the prophets, every scripture testifies of Him.

biblical.text: Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith.
biblical.comment: The disciple's standing posture: look to Jesus. The closing biblical anchor for the article's exhortation.

restoration.text: And we talk of Christ, we rejoice in Christ, we preach of Christ, we prophesy of Christ, and we write according to our prophecies, that our children may know to what source they may look for a remission of their sins.
restoration.comment: Nephi's signature passage — the Christ-saturated voice of the Book of Mormon's own self-witness. The Restoration's most concentrated statement of why scripture exists: that souls may know to what source they may look. Aaron's canonical anchor for the Christological hermeneutic.

restoration.text: And this is my doctrine, and it is the doctrine which the Father hath given unto me; and I bear record of the Father, and the Father beareth record of me, and the Holy Ghost beareth record of the Father and me; and I bear record that the Father commandeth all men, everywhere, to repent and believe in me.
restoration.comment: The risen Christ in Bountiful naming His doctrine: come unto Him. (Cited also in Article 1 Span 13.) The standard the article applies to all canonical searching: does it bring the soul to Christ?

s14.text: We require the guidance of God’s Spirit to receive His saving truths and to live our lives as He intends
s14.panel_comment: The article's pastoral integration claim. This span carries the full clause: receiving truth AND living rightly are the inseparable fruits of the Spirit's guidance. The biblical anchors (John 16:13, 1 Corinthians 2:12–14, Romans 8:14) name the Spirit's office; the Restoration anchors deepen the operational specifics — particularly 2 Nephi 32:3–5 ('the words of Christ will tell you all things... the Holy Ghost will show unto you all things what ye should do') and D&C 11:12–14 ('the Spirit which leadeth to do good — to do justly, to walk humbly, to judge righteously'). Together these complete the article's claim: the Spirit's role is not only to disclose what is true but to form how the disciple walks.

biblical.text: Howbeit when he, the Spirit of truth, is come, he will guide you into all truth: for he shall not speak of himself; but whatsoever he shall hear, that shall he speak: and he will shew you things to come.
biblical.comment: Christ's promise of the Spirit's office: guidance into all truth. The New Testament's most direct Christological grounding of the Spirit's interpretive ministry. The 'saving truths' half of the article's claim is grounded most plainly here.

biblical.text: Now we have received, not the spirit of the world, but the spirit which is of God; that we might know the things that are freely given to us of God. Which things also we speak, not in the words which man's wisdom teacheth, but which the Holy Ghost teacheth; comparing spiritual things with spiritual. But the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned.
biblical.comment: Paul's foundational statement: divine truths are spiritually discerned, not naturally accessed. The believer receives 'the spirit which is of God' precisely so that the things God has freely given may be understood. Paul's epistemology of grace.

biblical.text: For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, they are the sons of God.
biblical.comment: Paul's plainest summary: the Spirit-led life and divine sonship are inseparable. The Spirit who guides into truth is the same Spirit who shapes how the disciple lives. Bridges the article's two claims (receive truths / live as He intends) in a single verse.

restoration.text: And when ye shall receive these things, I would exhort you that ye would ask God, the Eternal Father, in the name of Christ, if these things are not true; and if ye shall ask with a sincere heart, with real intent, having faith in Christ, he will manifest the truth of it unto you, by the power of the Holy Ghost. And by the power of the Holy Ghost ye may know the truth of all things.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's pastoral capstone — sincere heart, real intent, faith in Christ, the Holy Ghost as the truth-confirming witness. Names the disciple's posture and the Spirit's response together. (Reasserted from Article 1 Span 15.)

restoration.text: Angels speak by the power of the Holy Ghost; wherefore, they speak the words of Christ. Wherefore, I said unto you, feast upon the words of Christ; for behold, the words of Christ will tell you all things what ye should do. … For behold, again I say unto you that if ye will enter in by the way, and receive the Holy Ghost, it will show unto you all things what ye should do.
restoration.comment: Nephi's signature pairing: feast upon the words of Christ, and the Holy Ghost will show unto you all things what ye should do. The single most direct Restoration anchor for the article's claim — uniting reception of truth ('the words of Christ will tell you all things') and right living ('the Holy Ghost... will show unto you all things what ye should do').

restoration.text: Yea, behold, I will tell you in your mind and in your heart, by the Holy Ghost, which shall come upon you and which shall dwell in your heart. Now, behold, this is the spirit of revelation; behold, this is the spirit by which Moses brought the children of Israel through the Red Sea on dry ground.
restoration.comment: Christ's instruction to Oliver Cowdery on the operation of the Spirit of revelation: in the mind and the heart, the same Spirit that operated in Moses. (Reasserted from Article 1 Span 15 and Article 4 Span 11.) The pattern is consistent — the Spirit confirms truth and shapes life by indwelling both the disciple's intellect and affections.

restoration.text: And now, verily, verily, I say unto thee, put your trust in that Spirit which leadeth to do good—yea, to do justly, to walk humbly, to judge righteously; and this is my Spirit. Verily, verily, I say unto you, I will impart unto you of my Spirit, which shall enlighten your mind, which shall fill your soul with joy; And then shall ye know, or by this shall you know, all things whatsoever you desire of me, which are pertaining unto things of righteousness, in faith believing in me that you shall receive.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's most direct statement uniting Spirit-led knowing with Spirit-led living: 'put your trust in that Spirit which leadeth to do good — to do justly, to walk humbly, to judge righteously.' Names the operational fruits ('enlighten your mind, fill your soul with joy') that the disciple may know are the Spirit's work. The strongest single anchor for the 'live our lives as He intends' half of the span text.

restoration.text: But, behold, I say unto you, that you must study it out in your mind; then you must ask me if it be right, and if it is right I will cause that your bosom shall burn within you; therefore, you shall feel that it is right. But if it be not right you shall have no such feelings, but you shall have a stupor of thought…
restoration.comment: The Restoration's operational discipline of Spirit-confirmation: study, ask, and receive the Spirit's witness. (Reasserted from Article 4 Span 11.) Names the process by which a disciple receives saving truth — not by passive waiting, but by the marriage of effort and the Spirit's confirming testimony.

s15.text: we contend for none of these boundaries
s15.panel_comment: Structural rhyme with Article 8 — the refusal to defend man-made walls, applied to canon boundaries. The same posture; a different fence.

crossref.label: See Article 8
crossref.title: Span 10: We refuse to defend them

s16.panel_comment: The norma-normans span — the divine-self-consistency reassurance that answers the override fear surfaced in the Common-Ground re-test (Voss, Marcus, Wendell). It does not adjudicate canon scope (the firewall keeps that in Volume 2); it grounds s11 (what He continues to speak, He confirms by His Spirit) in the deeper claim that God cannot contradict Himself — so continuing speech harmonizes with, never overturns, what He has already given. Bible-first non-contradiction anchors lead (1 Corinthians 14:33, John 10:35, Numbers 23:19); Alma 7:20 confirms. Deliberately distinguished from the immutability cluster at A9 s3 (Malachi 3:6 / James 1:17 / Mormon 9:9, Christ's personal changelessness): this span anchors non-contradiction of His word, not changelessness of His person. The reader-facing note rides on John 10:35.

biblical.text: For God is not the author of confusion, but of peace, as in all churches of the saints.
biblical.comment: Paul's principle stated as a divine attribute: what proceeds from God is orderly and self-consistent. He does not speak against Himself. The biblical floor for the article's claim that God does not contradict Himself.

biblical.text: If he called them gods, unto whom the word of God came, and the scripture cannot be broken;
biblical.comment: We never set what God still speaks above what He has already spoken. Because God does not contradict Himself, His continuing voice confirms His earlier word and never overturns it — for as the Lord Jesus said, 'the scripture cannot be broken' (John 10:35). What He gives by His Spirit today will always accord with what He has given before; we weigh the one by the other and find no quarrel between them.

biblical.text: God is not a man, that he should lie; neither the son of man, that he should repent: hath he said, and shall he not do it? or hath he spoken, and shall he not make it good?
biblical.comment: The Old Testament's plainest statement of divine truthfulness and constancy of word — what God has said, He performs. The ground of confidence that His later word will not betray His earlier word.

restoration.text: I perceive that it has been made known unto you, by the testimony of his word, that he cannot walk in crooked paths; neither doth he vary from that which he hath said; neither hath he a shadow of turning from the right to the left, or from that which is right to that which is wrong; therefore, his course is one eternal round.
restoration.comment: Alma's testimony that God 'cannot walk in crooked paths; neither doth he vary from that which he hath said' — the Restoration's direct confirmation of divine self-consistency. Restoration amplification — witness only; not required to receive the Article.

s17.text: prayerfully weigh beliefs, doubts, and personal conscience against the Scriptures God has given
s17.panel_comment: The disciple's-responsibility span — the line that warmed Marcus and Wendell inline in the Common-Ground re-test (weigh beliefs carefully, in the spirit of our tradition), lifting felt-welcome without conceding doctrine. Isaiah 8:20 leads as the first-time canonical anchor for measuring every claim against the given word. 1 Thessalonians 5:21 reused from A4 s12 and A8 s8; D&C 9:8–9 reused from A4 s11 and s14 — both pointed inward here (see reuse annotations). "The Scriptures God has given" is canon-agnostic (firewall): each tradition fills it from its own canon.

biblical.text: To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
biblical.comment: The prophet's standard for testing every voice: to the law and to the testimony. What does not accord with the given word has no light in it. The biblical anchor for weighing beliefs and doubts against the Scriptures God has given.

biblical.text: Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
biblical.comment: Paul's standing rule, here pointed at the disciple's own convictions: prove all things, hold fast what is good. (Reasserted from A4 s12 and A8 s8 in different rhetorical direction: at s12 'prove all things' governs the canon-question posture; at A8 s8 the testing of teachings within fellowship; here it governs the soul's prayerful weighing of its own beliefs, doubts, and conscience.)

restoration.text: But, behold, I say unto you, that you must study it out in your mind; then you must ask me if it be right, and if it be right I will cause that your bosom shall burn within you; therefore, you shall feel that it is right. But if it be not right you shall have no such feelings, but you shall have a stupor of thought that shall cause you to forget the thing which is wrong.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's process for prayerful weighing: study it out, ask, and receive the Spirit's witness or its withholding. (Reasserted from A4 s11 and s14 in different rhetorical direction: at s11/s14 the study-ask-confirm process governs receiving God's continuing speech and saving truths from Him; here the same process is turned inward — the disciple proving her own beliefs and doubts against the given word.) Restoration amplification — witness only; not required to receive the Article.

s18.text: tempts us to contend with one another
s18.panel_comment: Structural-rhyme xref — the merognosis-root of contention. "Our imperfect knowledge tempts us to contend with one another" is Article 1's posture applied to inter-tradition discord: partial knowing is what tempts disciples to quarrel. Mirrors s15's contend-idiom — s18 "contend with" (quarrel among ourselves) against s15 "contend for" (defend the walls), the two faces of the one anti-contention motif threaded through the clause. Thematic companion to the Contention and the Reach of Christ study (the cluster's ‡ study); no prose symbol is added — the locked clause carries no marker, and the connection lives in the apparatus, not the declaration text. No scripture anchors (xref type, as s15).

crossref.label: See Article 1
crossref.title: Plainness

crossref.label: Within this article
crossref.title: Span 15: we contend for none of these boundaries

s1.text: in a generation of His own choosing
s1.panel_comment: Divine sovereignty over Messianic timing. Galatians 4:4 ('the fulness of the time') and Mark 1:15 ('the time is fulfilled') name the same temporal claim from two angles — Paul's retrospective theology of the Incarnation's timing and Christ's own announcement that the appointed hour had arrived. The Restoration anchors deepen the specificity: 1 Nephi 10:4 records Lehi's prophetic naming of the timing six hundred years out, and Mosiah 3:5 frames the advent in covenant time. The article's restraint is intentional — 'a generation of His own choosing' affirms the divine sovereignty without importing dispensational architecture.

biblical.text: But when the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law.
biblical.comment: Paul's foundational claim on the divine sovereignty of Messianic timing — the most direct biblical anchor for 'a generation of His own choosing.'
