biblical.text: The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe the gospel.
biblical.comment: Christ's own announcement that the appointed hour had arrived — the temporal claim from Christ's own lips.

restoration.text: Yea, even six hundred years from the time that my father left Jerusalem, a prophet would the Lord God raise up among the Jews—even a Messiah, or, in other words, a Savior of the world.
restoration.comment: Lehi's specific prophetic naming of the timing — the Restoration's most direct anchor for the divine sovereignty of Messianic timing.

restoration.text: For behold, the time cometh, and is not far distant, that with power, the Lord Omnipotent who reigneth, who was, and is from all eternity to all eternity, shall come down from heaven among the children of men, and shall dwell in a tabernacle of clay.
restoration.comment: King Benjamin's prophetic framing of the advent in covenant time, naming the descent of the Lord Omnipotent into mortal flesh.

s2.panel_comment: The Messianic-promise claim. The biblical anchors carry the prophetic backbone — Isaiah 9:6–7 as the most concentrated OT Messianic prophecy, and Acts 10:43 as the NT summary that 'all the prophets' witness Christ. The Restoration anchors carry the multi-prophet witness pattern that the Book of Mormon foregrounds: 1 Nephi 19:13–14 names the Messianic suffering specifically, and Helaman 8:13–16 lists the chain of prophets who testified of the coming Messiah. 'Promised Messiah' is the universally Christian floor — every tradition fills the prophetic backbone from its own canon.

biblical.text: For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given: and the government shall be upon his shoulder: and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace.
biblical.comment: The most concentrated OT Messianic prophecy — names the Messiah's titles and the eternal scope of His government.

biblical.text: To him give all the prophets witness, that through his name whosoever believeth in him shall receive remission of sins.
biblical.comment: Peter's apostolic summary that the entire prophetic tradition converges on Christ as Messiah.

restoration.text: And as for those who are at Jerusalem, saith the prophet, they shall be scourged by all people, because they crucify the God of Israel, and turn their hearts aside, rejecting signs and wonders, and the power and glory of the God of Israel.
restoration.comment: Nephi's Messianic prophecy naming Christ as 'the God of Israel' who would suffer at the hands of His own people.

restoration.text: Yea, did he not bear record that the Son of God should come? And as he lifted up the brazen serpent in the wilderness, even so shall he be lifted up who should come. And as many as should look upon that serpent should live, even so as many as should look upon the Son of God with faith, having a contrite spirit, might live.
restoration.comment: Nephi the son of Helaman naming Moses, Abraham, and 'all the holy prophets' as the chain of Messianic witness — the multi-prophet pattern in compressed form.

s3.panel_comment: The Article's confession of 'the true Christ' is fidelity to Christ's own self-disclosure. Christ Himself warned that His name would be claimed by counterfeits — that false christs and false prophets would arise to deceive even the elect. The apostolic witness preserved this warning in two registers: John's pastoral letters identifying antichrist as the denial of the Son's relationship to the Father, and Paul's concern that 'another Jesus' could be preached and received in place of the Christ the apostles had borne witness to. The Restoration confirms and extends this witness: Joseph Smith—Matthew renders Christ's olivet warning with sharpened detail for the latter days (naming the elect according to the covenant as those at risk); Moroni teaches the Spirit of Christ as the discerning power by which counterfeits are recognized; D&C 49 refuses specific Christological forms claimed in the present age. The Article does not adjudicate which of any reader's beliefs about Christ are accurate — that work belongs to Christ Himself, by His Spirit, in each conscience. The confession of 'the true Christ' commits the Article to Jesus of Nazareth as Christ disclosed Himself, the Christ the apostles preached, the Christ to whom the Restoration witnessed — and to that Christ alone as the reference for every other claim made in His name.

biblical.text: Then if any man shall say unto you, Lo, here is Christ, or there; believe it not. For there shall arise false Christs, and false prophets, and shall shew great signs and wonders; insomuch that, if it were possible, they shall deceive the very elect.
biblical.comment: Christ's own warning, in the Olivet discourse, that His name would be claimed by deceivers — including with great signs and wonders — and that the elect themselves could be at risk. The first and central warrant for distinguishing the true Christ from counterfeits.

biblical.text: Who is a liar but he that denieth that Jesus is the Christ? He is antichrist, that denieth the Father and the Son. Whosoever denieth the Son, the same hath not the Father: he that acknowledgeth the Son hath the Father also.
biblical.comment: John's apostolic articulation of antichrist as the denial of the Son's relationship to the Father. The criterion is Christological: confession of the Son carries the Father with it; denial of the Son severs both.

biblical.text: But I fear, lest by any means, as the serpent beguiled Eve through his subtilty, so your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ. For if he that cometh preacheth another Jesus, whom we have not preached, or if ye receive another spirit, which ye have not received, or another gospel, which ye have not accepted, ye might well bear with him.
biblical.comment: Paul's pastoral alarm at how easily 'another Jesus' could be received in place of the Christ the apostles preached. Names the danger as substitution rather than outright denial — a quieter form of the same loss.

biblical.text: Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world. Hereby know ye the Spirit of God: Every spirit that confesseth that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh is of God: And every spirit that confesseth not that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh is not of God: and this is that spirit of antichrist.
biblical.comment: The apostolic test for the spirits: confession that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh distinguishes the Spirit of God from the spirit of antichrist. Anchors the discernment in the historical incarnation, not in mystical or speculative Christologies.

restoration.text: For in those days there shall also arise false Christs, and false prophets, and shall shew great signs and wonders, insomuch, that, if possible, they shall deceive the very elect, who are the elect according to the covenant. Behold, I speak these things unto you for the elect's sake.
restoration.comment: Joseph Smith's translation expands Christ's olivet warning, identifying 'the elect according to the covenant' as the population specifically at risk in the last days. Sharpens the Restoration's reading: covenant disciples are not exempt from being deceived by counterfeit christs.

restoration.text: For behold, the Spirit of Christ is given to every man, that he may know good from evil; wherefore, I show unto you the way to judge; for every thing which inviteth to do good, and to persuade to believe in Christ, is sent forth by the power and gift of Christ; wherefore ye may know with a perfect knowledge it is of God. But whatsoever thing persuadeth men to do evil, and believe not in Christ, and deny him, and serve not God, then ye may know with a perfect knowledge it is of the devil.
restoration.comment: The Spirit of Christ given to every soul as the discerning faculty by which counterfeits are recognized — what invites belief in Christ is of Christ; what dissuades from belief in Christ is not. Frames discernment as Christocentric rather than denominational.

restoration.text: And again, verily I say unto you, that the Son of Man cometh not in the form of a woman, neither of a man traveling on the earth. Wherefore, be not deceived, but continue in steadfastness, looking forth for the heavens to be shaken, and the earth to tremble and to reel to and fro as a drunken man, and for the valleys to be exalted, and for the mountains to be made low, and for the rough places to become smooth — and all this when the angel shall sound his trumpet.
restoration.comment: The Lord's specific refusal of certain Christological forms — He does not come as a woman, nor as a mortal traveler in the present age. Anchors the Restoration's witness against latter-day claims that Christ has already returned in some local or embodied form. His coming will be cosmic and unmistakable.

s4.text: Jesus of Nazareth, Divinity made flesh
s4.panel_comment: The universal Christological claim. 'Divinity made flesh' is John 1:14 in plain English, and every Christian tradition affirms it. The biblical anchors cluster the Incarnation: John 1:14 is the foundational Word-made-flesh statement; Philippians 2:6–8 carries the kenotic hymn (emptying, taking the form of a servant); Colossians 2:9 names the fullness of the Godhead bodily in Christ. The Restoration anchors deepen with characteristic specificity: Mosiah 3:5–7 names the 'tabernacle of clay' framing, and 1 Nephi 11:18–21 records Nephi's vision of Mary and the condescension of God. This claim carries the universal-affirmation floor — the Incarnation as Christian tradition affirms it — before any more specific claim is made.

biblical.text: And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.
biblical.comment: The foundational Word-made-flesh statement — the universal Christian claim of the Incarnation that every tradition affirms.

biblical.text: Who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God: but made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men: And being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.
biblical.comment: The kenotic hymn — early Christian liturgy naming the Incarnation as divine self-emptying into human form.

biblical.text: For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily.
biblical.comment: Paul's most concentrated Incarnation claim: the totality of divine being indwelling the bodily Christ.

restoration.text: For behold, the time cometh, and is not far distant, that with power, the Lord Omnipotent who reigneth, who was, and is from all eternity to all eternity, shall come down from heaven among the children of men, and shall dwell in a tabernacle of clay, and shall go forth amongst men, working mighty miracles.
restoration.comment: King Benjamin's 'tabernacle of clay' framing — the Restoration's signature Incarnation language. (Reasserted from Article 5 span 1 in different rhetorical direction: at s1 Mosiah 3:5 anchors the divine-sovereignty-over-timing claim; here Mosiah 3:5–7 anchors the Incarnation/tabernacle-of-clay claim.)

restoration.text: And he said unto me: Behold, the virgin whom thou seest is the mother of the Son of God, after the manner of the flesh. And it came to pass that I beheld that she was carried away in the Spirit; and after she had been carried away in the Spirit for the space of a time the angel spake unto me, saying: Look! And I looked and beheld the virgin again, bearing a child in her arms. And the angel said unto me: Behold the Lamb of God, yea, even the Son of the Eternal Father!
restoration.comment: Nephi's vision of Mary and the condescension of God — the Restoration's Christological vision of the Incarnation in narrative form.

s5.text: the living image of the Father’s heart
s5.panel_comment: Christ as the revelation of the Father's character — both how the Father looks and how the Father feels. The pastoral phrasing 'the Father's heart' carries two claims that the biblical anchors hold together. The first is the representation claim: Hebrews 1:3 names Christ as 'the express image of his person' and 'the brightness of his glory'; John 14:9 records Christ's own claim that 'he that hath seen me hath seen the Father'; 2 Corinthians 4:6 names 'the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ'; Colossians 1:15 names Christ as 'the image of the invisible God.' The second is the emotional-revelation claim: the Gospels' compassion verbs reveal what the Father feels toward His children. Matthew 9:36 records Christ 'moved with compassion' at the sight of the scattered multitudes — sheep without a shepherd. Mark 1:41 (the leper), Luke 7:13 (the widow's son), and the foundational instance at John 11:35 ('Jesus wept') name a divine heart that is moved by human suffering, not detached from it. Matthew 23:37 — Christ's lament over Jerusalem under the figure of a hen gathering her chickens — names the Father's heart as one that longs for His children's gathering and grieves their refusal without overriding their freedom. Hebrews 1:3 is reasserted from Article 2 span 3, where it grounded the claim about God's unseen character; here it surfaces in its Christological direction (Christ as the visible image of that unseen character). The Restoration anchors confirm the unity and deepen it: 3 Nephi 11:7 records the Father's voice introducing the Son; D&C 93:11–17 records John's witness of Christ as the Only Begotten in whom the Father's fulness dwelt; 3 Nephi 10:4–6 records the resurrected Christ expanding the gathering lament across past faithfulness, present grief, and future invitation. Moses 7:28–33 records the Weeping God of Enoch's vision: when Enoch beheld God weep over the wickedness of His children, his astonished question — 'how is it that thou canst weep?' — drew from God the answer that He weeps because His children have rejected love. The pastoral phrasing 'the living image of the Father's heart' carries that revelation: the Father's heart is a heart that weeps with His children, longs for their return, and sent His Son to show them His face.

biblical.text: Who being the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person, and upholding all things by the word of his power, when he had by himself purged our sins, sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high.
biblical.comment: Christ as 'the express image' of the Father — the biblical anchor for Christological revelation. (Reasserted from Article 2 span 3, where it grounded God's unseen character; here surfaces in its Christological direction as the visible image of that character.)

biblical.text: Jesus saith unto him, Have I been so long time with you, and yet hast thou not known me, Philip? he that hath seen me hath seen the Father; and how sayest thou then, Shew us the Father?
biblical.comment: Christ's own claim that to see Him is to see the Father — the Christological-revelation claim from Christ's own lips.

biblical.text: For God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, hath shined in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.
biblical.comment: Paul's claim that the knowledge of God's glory is given 'in the face of Jesus Christ' — the Father's character known through the Son's countenance.

biblical.text: Who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature.
biblical.comment: Christ as 'the image of the invisible God' — the visibility of the invisible Father in the person of the Son.

biblical.text: But when he saw the multitudes, he was moved with compassion on them, because they fainted, and were scattered abroad, as sheep having no shepherd.
biblical.comment: Christ moved with compassion at the sight of the scattered multitudes — the most frequently recorded emotional response of His ministry. The Father's heart toward His children is a heart that is moved by their suffering, not detached from it.

biblical.text: Jesus wept.
biblical.comment: The shortest verse in scripture, and one of the densest. At the tomb of Lazarus, the divine Son weeps with the grieving — the Father's heart revealed as a heart that weeps with His children rather than standing above their tears.

biblical.text: O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee, how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not!
biblical.comment: Christ's lament over Jerusalem — the Father's heart revealed as one that longs for the gathering of His children and grieves their refusal, while honoring the freedom He gave them. The maternal figure of the gathering hen carries the tenderness that 'Father's heart' names.

restoration.text: Behold my Beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased, in whom I have glorified my name—hear ye him.
restoration.comment: The Father's own voice introducing the Son to the Nephites — the Restoration's most direct testimony of Christ as the Father's chosen revelation.

restoration.text: And I, John, bear record that I beheld his glory, as the glory of the Only Begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth, even the Spirit of truth, which came and dwelt in the flesh, and dwelt among us. And I, John, saw that he received not of the fulness at the first, but received grace for grace; And he received not of the fulness at first, but continued from grace to grace, until he received a fulness.
restoration.comment: John's witness as preserved through Joseph Smith — Christ as the Only Begotten in whom the Father's fulness dwells, made flesh and dwelling among us.

restoration.text: O ye people of these great cities which have fallen, who are descendants of Jacob, yea, who are of the house of Israel, how oft have I gathered you as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and have nourished you. And again, how oft would I have gathered you as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, yea, O ye people of the house of Israel, who have fallen; yea, O ye people of the house of Israel, ye that dwell at Jerusalem, as ye that have fallen; yea, how oft would I have gathered you as a hen gathereth her chickens, and ye would not.
restoration.comment: The resurrected Christ expanding the Matthew 23:37 lament across past faithfulness ('how oft have I gathered'), conditional grief ('how oft would I have gathered'), and future invitation in the surrounding context ('how oft will I gather you'). The Father's heart revealed as covenant faithfulness reaching across the whole arc of history.

restoration.text: And it came to pass that the God of heaven looked upon the residue of the people, and he wept; and Enoch bore record of it, saying: How is it that the heavens weep, and shed forth their tears as the rain upon the mountains? And Enoch said unto the Lord: How is it that thou canst weep, seeing thou art holy, and from all eternity to all eternity? ... The Lord said unto Enoch: Behold these thy brethren; they are the workmanship of mine own hands, and I gave unto them their knowledge, in the day I created them; and in the Garden of Eden, gave I unto man his agency; And unto thy brethren have I said, and also given commandment, that they should love one another, and that they should choose me, their Father; but behold, they are without affection, and they hate their own blood.
restoration.comment: The Weeping God of Enoch's vision. When Enoch beheld God weep, his astonishment — that the holy God, eternal and self-existent, could weep at all — drew from God the answer that He weeps because His children have rejected the love He extended to them. This is the Restoration's most direct testimony that the Father has a heart, and that the heart is one that grieves when His children refuse the love He has given. Christ revealed in flesh what Enoch beheld in vision.

s6.text: What the prophets spoke imperfectly and only in part, Christ embodied in whole and in perfection
s6.panel_comment: The merognostic move applied to Christology. The article's claim — that what the prophets spoke 'imperfectly and only in part,' Christ 'embodied in whole and in perfection' — paraphrases Hebrews 1:1–2 directly, where the contrast between God's prophetic speech 'in time past' and His speech 'in these last days' through 'his Son' carries the same theological weight. John 1:18 supplies the complementary claim: where prophets pointed, the only-begotten Son 'declared' the Father. The Restoration anchors land the same point with characteristic specificity: 3 Nephi 15:5 records Christ's own claim that 'the law in me is fulfilled,' and 1 Nephi 10:5 names the chain of prophets who 'testified of these things, concerning this Messiah.' Hebrews 1:1–2 is reasserted from Article 4 spans 3 and 6 — Article 4 establishes the prophet-vs-Son contrast as the architecture of revelation; this span is the Christological landing point of that contrast.

biblical.text: God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets, hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son, whom he hath appointed heir of all things, by whom also he made the worlds.
biblical.comment: The direct paraphrase source — the prophet-vs-Son contrast that names Christ as the Father's complete word. (Reasserted from Article 4 spans 3 and 6; this span is the Christological landing point of that pairing.)

biblical.text: No man hath seen God at any time; the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him.
biblical.comment: John's complementary claim: where prophets pointed toward an unseen God, the only-begotten Son hath declared Him.

restoration.text: Behold, I am he that gave the law, and I am he who covenanted with my people Israel; therefore, the law in me is fulfilled, for I have come to fulfil the law; therefore it hath an end.
restoration.comment: Christ's own claim that He is the fulfillment of what the prophets received in part — the law spoken through Moses now embodied in His person.

restoration.text: And he also spake concerning the prophets, how great a number had testified of these things, concerning this Messiah, of whom he had spoken, or this Redeemer of the world.
restoration.comment: Lehi's witness that the prophets, however many, all testified of the same Messiah — the prophetic witness as cumulative and converging on Christ.

s7.text: Jesus Christ is the Savior and Redeemer of the world
s7.panel_comment: The titles cluster — 'Savior and Redeemer of the world.' The biblical anchors carry both terms: John 4:42 and 1 John 4:14 name Christ explicitly as 'Saviour of the world'; Job 19:25 carries the OT Redeemer language ('I know that my redeemer liveth'); Galatians 3:13 names the redemptive act ('Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law'). The Restoration anchors confirm the universal scope: Mosiah 3:8 names Christ as Savior in cosmic-creator language, and Helaman 5:9 names Him as 'the only way and means whereby man can be saved.' Declined: 2 Nephi 25:26, already cited in Article 4 span 13 — cross-article hygiene.

biblical.text: And said unto the woman, Now we believe, not because of thy saying: for we have heard him ourselves, and know that this is indeed the Christ, the Saviour of the world.
biblical.comment: The Samaritan villagers' witness — 'the Christ, the Saviour of the world' — naming the title that the article carries.

biblical.text: And we have seen and do testify that the Father sent the Son to be the Saviour of the world.
biblical.comment: John's apostolic confirmation that the Father's sending establishes Christ's office as Savior of the world.

biblical.text: For I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth.
biblical.comment: The OT's most concentrated Redeemer-confession, anchoring the title in the canonical witness from before the Incarnation.

biblical.text: Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us: for it is written, Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree.
biblical.comment: Paul's redemption-claim, naming the legal exchange by which Christ accomplished redemption.

restoration.text: And he shall be called Jesus Christ, the Son of God, the Father of heaven and earth, the Creator of all things from the beginning; and his mother shall be called Mary.
restoration.comment: King Benjamin's naming of Christ in cosmic-creator language as the Savior who would be born — the universal scope of His office.

restoration.text: O remember, remember, my sons, the words which king Benjamin spake unto his people; yea, remember that there is no other way nor means whereby man can be saved, only through the atoning blood of Jesus Christ, who shall come; yea, remember that he cometh to redeem the world.
restoration.comment: Helaman's instruction to his sons — Christ as 'the only way and means' of salvation, fulfilling the Savior-Redeemer titles in unified scope.

s8.text: the divine Son sent from the Father
s8.panel_comment: The divine-sonship + sending claim. Aaron's deliberate phrasing — 'the divine Son sent from the Father' — was chosen for the broadest interfaith floor: Trinitarians recognize their own doctrine in 'the divine Son'; Restoration readers recognize theirs; Oneness Pentecostals (who affirm Jesus as the Son of God and as divine but reject the three-persons framework that 'God the Son' presupposes) can receive the confession without friction; Messianic Jews, whose vocabulary around divine sonship often avoids the Latin-derived 'God the Son' formula, can also receive it. The biblical anchors honor that breadth: John 3:16–17 names the foundational sending; John 6:38 records Christ's own sending claim; 1 John 4:9–10 names the Father's love expressed through the sending. The Restoration anchors carry the same claim: 3 Nephi 11:11 records Christ's own self-introduction as the Son glorifying the Father, and D&C 76:23–24 records the visionary witness of Christ as the means by whom 'the inhabitants thereof are begotten sons and daughters unto God.' Declined: 3 Nephi 9:15, already cited in Article 3 span 1.

biblical.text: For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life. For God sent not his Son into the world to condemn the world; but that the world through him might be saved.
biblical.comment: The foundational sending — God's love expressed through the Son sent into the world for its salvation.

biblical.text: For I came down from heaven, not to do mine own will, but the will of him that sent me.
biblical.comment: Christ's own sending claim — His descent and mission framed as obedient submission to the Father's will.

biblical.text: In this was manifested the love of God toward us, because that God sent his only begotten Son into the world, that we might live through him. Herein is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins.
biblical.comment: John's apostolic claim that the Father's sending of the Son is the manifestation of divine love and the means of propitiation.

restoration.text: And behold, I am the light and the life of the world; and I have drunk out of that bitter cup which the Father hath given me, and have glorified the Father in taking upon me the sins of the world, in the which I have suffered the will of the Father in all things from the beginning.
restoration.comment: Christ's own self-introduction to the Nephites — the Son glorifying the Father by suffering His will from the beginning.

restoration.text: For we saw him, even on the right hand of God; and we heard the voice bearing record that he is the Only Begotten of the Father—That by him, and through him, and of him, the worlds are and were created, and the inhabitants thereof are begotten sons and daughters unto God.
restoration.comment: The Joseph Smith and Sidney Rigdon vision — Christ as the Only Begotten by whom others are begotten of God, the divine-sonship claim in cosmic scope.

s9.text: He was born of Mary, lived a sinless life
s9.panel_comment: Two doctrinal claims compressed into one span: the Incarnation-via-Mary and the sinless life. The biblical anchors split accordingly. Born of Mary: Luke 1:26–35 (the Annunciation), Matthew 1:18–25 (Joseph's witness), and Isaiah 7:14 ('Behold, a virgin shall conceive') — the last carrying the OT prophetic anchor that the NT narratives explicitly fulfill. Sinless life: Hebrews 4:15 (the foundational 'tempted like as we are, yet without sin') and 1 Peter 2:22 ('Who did no sin'). The Restoration anchors match Aaron's Manuscript Chapter 9 blueprint pairings: Alma 7:10 names Mary by name (a precision the Bible itself does not reach in this register) and Alma 7:11–12 names the sinlessness within the suffering. Five biblical anchors is heavier than typical density; the weight is appropriate for the dual claim being carried.

biblical.text: And the angel said unto her, Fear not, Mary: for thou hast found favour with God. And, behold, thou shalt conceive in thy womb, and bring forth a son, and shalt call his name JESUS. He shall be great, and shall be called the Son of the Highest... The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God.
biblical.comment: The Annunciation — the angel's naming of Christ as the Son of the Highest and the conception by the power of the Spirit. The most direct biblical narrative anchor for 'born of Mary.'

biblical.text: Now the birth of Jesus Christ was on this wise: When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost. Then Joseph her husband, being a just man... the angel of the Lord appeared unto him in a dream, saying, Joseph, thou son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost. And she shall bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins.
biblical.comment: Joseph's witness — the angelic confirmation that the conception was of the Holy Ghost and the naming of Jesus as the one who saves from sin.

biblical.text: Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.
biblical.comment: The OT prophetic anchor for the virgin conception — the prophecy that Matthew 1:23 explicitly names as fulfilled in Christ's birth.

biblical.text: For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin.
biblical.comment: The foundational sinlessness claim — Christ tempted as we are, yet without sin. Anchors the moral perfection without distancing Christ from human experience.

biblical.text: Who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth.
biblical.comment: Peter's apostolic affirmation of Christ's sinlessness — sin neither in act nor in speech.

restoration.text: And behold, he shall be born of Mary, at Jerusalem which is the land of our forefathers, she being a virgin, a precious and chosen vessel, who shall be overshadowed and conceive by the power of the Holy Ghost, and bring forth a son, yea, even the Son of God.
restoration.comment: Alma's prophetic naming of Mary by name — the Restoration's specific anchor for 'born of Mary,' confirming the biblical narrative with explicit prophetic preview.

restoration.text: And he shall go forth, suffering pains and afflictions and temptations of every kind; and this that the word might be fulfilled which saith he will take upon him the pains and the sicknesses of his people. And he will take upon him death, that he may loose the bands of death which bind his people; and he will take upon him their infirmities, that his bowels may be filled with mercy, according to the flesh, that he may know according to the flesh how to succor his people according to the infirmities.
restoration.comment: Alma's witness of Christ's sinless suffering — the Manuscript Chapter 9 anchor for the moral perfection that holds within the full weight of human affliction.

s10.text: taught the way of the Kingdom, healed the sick, forgave the broken, rebuked the proud, and loved without measure
s10.panel_comment: The compressed ministry summary — five verbs naming five distinct theological moves in Christ's mortal ministry. The structure is creedal but the texture is pastoral: 'forgave the broken' is softer than the conventional 'forgave sinners,' and 'rebuked the proud' pairs with it to establish that love and rebuke are not opposites in Christ's ministry. The biblical anchors track the verbs: Matthew 4:23 carries the kingdom-teaching + healing combined; Luke 7:48 names the forgiving moment; Matthew 23:13 names the rebuking pattern in the woes against the scribes and Pharisees; John 13:1 names the love that 'loved them unto the end.' The Restoration anchors confirm the pattern: 3 Nephi 17:7–9 records the resurrected Christ's healing ministry, and 3 Nephi 12 carries the kingdom-teaching at the temple.

biblical.text: And Jesus went about all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues, and preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing all manner of sickness and all manner of disease among the people.
biblical.comment: The integrated ministry summary in Matthew's Gospel — kingdom-teaching and healing combined as Christ's characteristic action.

biblical.text: And he said unto her, Thy sins are forgiven.
biblical.comment: The pardon spoken to the woman who anointed His feet — the most direct biblical anchor for 'forgave the broken.'

biblical.text: But woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye shut up the kingdom of heaven against men: for ye neither go in yourselves, neither suffer ye them that are entering to go in.
biblical.comment: The opening woe against the religious gatekeepers — the most direct biblical anchor for 'rebuked the proud.'

biblical.text: Now before the feast of the passover, when Jesus knew that his hour was come that he should depart out of this world unto the Father, having loved his own which were in the world, he loved them unto the end.
biblical.comment: John's framing of the upper-room sequence — Christ's love that 'loved them unto the end,' the rhythmic-close anchor for 'loved without measure.'

restoration.text: Have ye any that are sick among you? Bring them hither. Have ye any that are lame, or blind, or halt, or maimed, or leprous, or that are withered, or that are deaf, or that are afflicted in any manner? Bring them hither and I will heal them, for I have compassion upon you; my bowels are filled with mercy.
restoration.comment: The resurrected Christ's healing ministry to the Nephites — the Restoration's most direct echo of Christ's mortal pattern of healing the sick.

restoration.text: And it came to pass that when Jesus had spoken these words unto Nephi, and to those who had been called, (now the number of them who had been called, and received power and authority to baptize, was twelve)... [Christ proceeds to teach the Beatitudes and the higher law].
restoration.comment: The Sermon at the Temple — the Restoration's record of Christ teaching the way of the Kingdom in the New World.

s11.panel_comment: Direct quote from Acts 10:38 placed as a standalone sentence — Aaron's deliberate choice to give the verbatim apostolic phrasing its full force in this Christological position. This is the CCC-slide signature line surfacing at the right moment in the right document. The Restoration anchor (3 Nephi 17:7–9) confirms the pattern in the resurrected Christ's healing ministry. Direct-quote span; minimal anchor count is appropriate — the verse is the source.

biblical.text: How God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Ghost and with power: who went about doing good, and healing all that were oppressed of the devil; for God was with him.
biblical.comment: The verbatim source — Peter's apostolic summary of Christ's ministry, naming Him as the one who 'went about doing good' under the Father's anointing.

restoration.text: Have ye any that are sick among you? Bring them hither. Have ye any that are lame, or blind, or halt, or maimed, or leprous, or that are withered, or that are deaf, or that are afflicted in any manner? Bring them hither and I will heal them, for I have compassion upon you.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's confirming witness — the resurrected Christ continuing the 'doing good' pattern in the New World.

s12.text: He suffered beyond our understanding for our sins
s12.panel_comment: The merognostic move applied to atonement. The qualifier 'beyond our understanding' is the restraint discipline operating at exactly the boundary where Christian traditions diverge most sharply on mechanism — substitutionary, Christus Victor, satisfaction, moral exemplar, governmental. The article affirms the universal claim that Christ 'suffered for our sins' (1 Corinthians 15:3, the apostolic minimum every tradition affirms) and then declares the mechanism opaque to creaturely knowing. The biblical anchors hold the universal floor: 1 Corinthians 15:3 (the creedal minimum), Isaiah 53:4–6 (the OT suffering-servant prophecy from which every atonement theory draws), 2 Corinthians 5:21 ('him to be sin for us'), and 1 Peter 2:24 ('bare our sins in his own body on the tree'). Each carries language that substitution-readers, Christus-Victor-readers, and moral-exemplar-readers can fill from their own theology. The Restoration anchors deepen the suffering's interior: D&C 19:16–19 records Christ's first-person account ('which suffering caused myself, even God, the greatest of all, to tremble'); Mosiah 3:7 names the bloody sweat. Alma 7:11–12 also serves at Article 5 span 9 — different rhetorical functions (Christ-as-pastoral-companion at s9; Christ-as-suffering-redeemer at s12).

biblical.text: For I delivered unto you first of all that which I also received, how that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures.
biblical.comment: The apostolic creedal minimum — 'Christ died for our sins,' the universal claim every Christian tradition affirms without agreeing on mechanism.

biblical.text: Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows: yet we did esteem him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted. But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed. All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the Lord hath laid on him the iniquity of us all.
biblical.comment: The OT suffering-servant prophecy — the canonical anchor that every atonement theory draws from. Substitution-readers, Christus-Victor-readers, and moral-exemplar-readers each find their tradition's framing here.

biblical.text: For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.
biblical.comment: Paul's most concentrated atonement claim — the great exchange of Christ becoming sin so that we might become righteousness.

biblical.text: Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness: by whose stripes ye were healed.
biblical.comment: Peter's apostolic claim that Christ 'bare our sins' bodily on the cross — the suffering's redemptive direction without specifying mechanism.

restoration.text: For behold, I, God, have suffered these things for all, that they might not suffer if they would repent; But if they would not repent they must suffer even as I; Which suffering caused myself, even God, the greatest of all, to tremble because of pain, and to bleed at every pore, and to suffer both body and spirit—and would that I might not drink the bitter cup, and shrink—Nevertheless, glory be to the Father, and I partook and finished my preparations unto the children of men.
restoration.comment: Christ's own first-person account of His suffering — the Manuscript Chapter 9 anchor for the interior weight of what happened in Gethsemane and on the cross.

restoration.text: And lo, he shall suffer temptations, and pain of body, hunger, thirst, and fatigue, even more than man can suffer, except it be unto death; for behold, blood cometh from every pore, so great shall be his anguish for the wickedness and the abominations of his people.
restoration.comment: King Benjamin's prophetic preview of Gethsemane — the bloody sweat as the marker of suffering 'beyond our understanding.'

restoration.text: And he shall go forth, suffering pains and afflictions and temptations of every kind; and this that the word might be fulfilled which saith he will take upon him the pains and the sicknesses of his people. And he will take upon him death, that he may loose the bands of death which bind his people; and he will take upon him their infirmities, that his bowels may be filled with mercy.
restoration.comment: Alma's witness of the redemptive-suffering pattern — Christ taking upon Himself the full weight of human affliction. (Reasserted from Article 5 span 9 in different rhetorical direction: at s9 Christ-as-pastoral-companion; here Christ-as-suffering-redeemer.)

s13.panel_comment: The crucifixion claim. The biblical anchors carry both the obedience-unto-death and the redemptive significance: Philippians 2:8 names the Son's willing submission ('became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross'); John 19:30 ('It is finished') is Christ's own declaration of completion; Galatians 3:13 names the legal exchange ('being made a curse for us'); Colossians 1:20 names the reconciling work ('the blood of his cross'). The Restoration anchors confirm: 3 Nephi 27:14 records Christ's first-person framing ('my Father sent me that I might be lifted up upon the cross'), and 1 Nephi 11:33 records Nephi's vision of the Lamb 'lifted up upon the cross and slain for the sins of the world.'

biblical.text: And being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.
biblical.comment: Paul's claim that the cross was the climax of Christ's obedient self-emptying — the death framed as willing submission.

biblical.text: When Jesus therefore had received the vinegar, he said, It is finished: and he bowed his head, and gave up the ghost.
biblical.comment: Christ's own final declaration from the cross — the 'tetelestai' that names the completion of His mission in death.

biblical.text: Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us: for it is written, Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree.
biblical.comment: Paul's legal-exchange anchor — Christ becoming the curse so that the cursed might be redeemed.

biblical.text: And, having made peace through the blood of his cross, by him to reconcile all things unto himself; by him, I say, whether they be things in earth, or things in heaven.
biblical.comment: Paul's reconciling-work anchor — the cross as the means by which all things are reconciled to God.

restoration.text: And my Father sent me that I might be lifted up upon the cross; and after that I had been lifted up upon the cross, that I might draw all men unto me, that as I have been lifted up by men even so should men be lifted up by the Father, to stand before me, to be judged of their works.
restoration.comment: Christ's own first-person framing of the cross as the Father's mission — His being 'lifted up' as the means by which others are drawn to Him.

restoration.text: And I, Nephi, saw that he was lifted up upon the cross and slain for the sins of the world.
restoration.comment: Nephi's vision of the cross — the Lamb of God lifted up and slain for the sins of the world, the Restoration's most direct vision of Christ crucified.

s14.text: rose again from death in glory on the third day
s14.panel_comment: The resurrection claim — third-day, in glory. The biblical anchors carry the creedal pattern: 1 Corinthians 15:4 (the apostolic creedal formulation that the article paraphrases directly), Matthew 28:6 (the empty-tomb proclamation), Luke 24:6–7 (the angelic reminder of Christ's own prediction), and Romans 6:9 (the abiding-resurrection claim that Christ 'dieth no more'). The Restoration anchors record the resurrected Christ's manifestation in glory: 3 Nephi 11:8–15 records the New World theophany, and Mormon 7:5 names the resurrection's universal scope ('that he might bring all men unto him'). The phrase 'in glory' connects the resurrection event to its eschatological weight.

biblical.text: And that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures.
biblical.comment: The apostolic creedal formulation — 'rose again the third day' is the precise phrasing the article paraphrases. The article's most direct creedal anchor.

biblical.text: He is not here: for he is risen, as he said. Come, see the place where the Lord lay.
biblical.comment: The angelic empty-tomb proclamation — the Resurrection announced at the site of the burial.

biblical.text: He is not here, but is risen: remember how he spake unto you when he was yet in Galilee, Saying, The Son of man must be delivered into the hands of sinful men, and be crucified, and the third day rise again.
biblical.comment: The angelic reminder that Christ Himself had foretold the third-day resurrection — anchoring the timing in His own prophetic words.

biblical.text: Knowing that Christ being raised from the dead dieth no more; death hath no more dominion over him.
biblical.comment: Paul's claim of the abiding resurrection — Christ raised, and death's dominion broken.

restoration.text: And it came to pass, as they understood they cast their eyes up again towards heaven; and behold, they saw a Man descending out of heaven; and he was clothed in a white robe; and he came down and stood in the midst of them... Behold, I am Jesus Christ, whom the prophets testified shall come into the world... Arise and come forth unto me, that ye may thrust your hands into my side, and also that ye may feel the prints of the nails in my hands and in my feet.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's signature resurrection theophany — the Risen Christ descending in glory to the Nephites, His resurrected body bearing the wounds of the cross.

restoration.text: Know ye that ye must come to the knowledge of your fathers, and repent of all your sins and iniquities, and believe in Jesus Christ, that he is the Son of God, and that he was slain by the Jews, and by the power of the Father he hath risen again, whereby he hath gained the victory over the grave; and also in him is the sting of death swallowed up.
restoration.comment: Mormon's apostolic-style summary of the Resurrection's universal scope — Christ raised by the Father's power, the victory over the grave.

s15.text: the one perfect vessel in whom the will of God has been made flesh
s15.panel_comment: The Christological centerpiece. Aaron's distinctive phrasing — 'the one perfect vessel in whom the will of God has been made flesh' — closes the loop with the broken-vessels theme that runs through the prior articles, affirming Christ as the singular exception. The biblical anchors hold the will-of-God dimension: John 6:38 ('I came down from heaven, not to do mine own will, but the will of him that sent me') and Hebrews 10:5–7 ('Lo, I come... to do thy will, O God') name Christ's mission as obedient enactment of the Father's will. Philippians 2:5–8 carries the kenotic-hymn vocabulary (emptying, obedience, the form of a servant) that names the same claim across early Christian liturgy. John 1:14 is reasserted from Article 5 span 4 in a different rhetorical position — at s4 the claim is 'Divinity made flesh' (the nature claim); here the claim is 'the will of God made flesh' (the obedience-and-mission claim). Same anchor, different doctrinal direction. The Restoration anchors carry the will-of-Father claim with characteristic precision: 3 Nephi 11:11 records Christ's own claim ('I have suffered the will of the Father in all things from the beginning'), and Mosiah 15:7 names 'the will of the Son being swallowed up in the will of the Father.' The container-words 'perfect vessel' and 'will of God made flesh' are receivable by Chalcedonian readers (two natures, one person), Trinitarian readers, Restoration readers, and others — each tradition fills the biblical floor from its own theology.

biblical.text: For I came down from heaven, not to do mine own will, but the will of him that sent me.
biblical.comment: Christ's own claim that His descent and mission are framed as obedient submission to the Father's will — the most direct biblical anchor for 'the will of God made flesh.' (Reasserted from Article 5 span 8 in different rhetorical direction: at s8 the function is the Father's sending; here the function is the Son's willed obedience.)

biblical.text: Wherefore when he cometh into the world, he saith, Sacrifice and offering thou wouldest not, but a body hast thou prepared me: in burnt offerings and sacrifices for sin thou hast had no pleasure. Then said I, Lo, I come (in the volume of the book it is written of me,) to do thy will, O God.
biblical.comment: The author of Hebrews placing the kenotic claim in Christ's own mouth — the body prepared as the instrument of the Father's will, fulfilled in flesh.

biblical.text: Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus: who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God: but made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men: and being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.
biblical.comment: The kenotic hymn — early Christian liturgy naming the Incarnation as divine self-emptying into obedient human form. Carries 'perfect vessel' theology across every Christian tradition.

biblical.text: And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.
biblical.comment: The Word-made-flesh claim. (Reasserted from Article 5 span 4 in a different rhetorical position — at s4 the claim is 'Divinity made flesh' (the nature claim); here it grounds 'the will of God made flesh' (the obedience-and-mission claim). Deliberate cross-span resonance.)

restoration.text: And behold, I am the light and the life of the world; and I have drunk out of that bitter cup which the Father hath given me, and have glorified the Father in taking upon me the sins of the world, in the which I have suffered the will of the Father in all things from the beginning.
restoration.comment: Christ's own claim that He has 'suffered the will of the Father in all things from the beginning' — the Restoration's most direct anchor for 'the will of God made flesh.' (Reasserted from Article 5 span 8 in different rhetorical direction: at s8 the function is divine sonship and self-introduction; here the function is willed obedience to the Father.)

restoration.text: Yea, even so he shall be led, crucified, and slain, the flesh becoming subject even unto death, the will of the Son being swallowed up in the will of the Father.
restoration.comment: Abinadi's prophetic claim of 'the will of the Son being swallowed up in the will of the Father' — the Restoration's signature articulation of the obedience-and-mission claim that makes the Christological centerpiece coherent.

s16.text: the living reference by whom every other witness and follower is measured
s16.panel_comment: Christ as the measuring rod for both prophetic witness and Christian discipleship. The biblical anchors carry the dual claim: Ephesians 4:13 ('the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ') names Christ as the standard toward which the saints grow; John 14:6 ('I am the way, the truth, and the life') names Christ as the exclusive path; 1 Corinthians 11:1 ('Be ye followers of me, even as I also am of Christ') names Paul's discipleship as derivative — Christ is the original, the apostle is the imitator; Hebrews 12:2 ('looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith') names Christ as the framing point of every disciple's gaze. The Restoration anchors deepen: 3 Nephi 27:27 ('what manner of men ought ye to be? Verily I say unto you, even as I am') is Christ's own self-identification as the standard, and Moroni 7:48 names the becoming ('when he shall appear we shall be like him'). The 'living reference' phrase claims Christ as both static norm (the unchanging standard) and dynamic referent (the living person from whom the measure is taken).

biblical.text: Till we all come in the unity of the faith, and of the knowledge of the Son of God, unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ.
biblical.comment: Paul's claim that Christ is the measure toward which the saints grow — the most direct biblical anchor for 'the living reference by whom every other follower is measured.'

biblical.text: Jesus saith unto him, I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.
biblical.comment: Christ's own exclusive-claim — the way, the truth, the life. The 'living reference' for every soul's path to the Father.

biblical.text: Be ye followers of me, even as I also am of Christ.
biblical.comment: Paul's discipleship as derivative — Christ is the original, the apostle is the imitator. The article's 'every other witness and follower' framing in apostolic shape.

biblical.text: Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the Majesty on high.
biblical.comment: The author of Hebrews naming Christ as 'the author and finisher of our faith' — the framing point of every disciple's gaze. (Reasserted from Article 4 span 13 in Christological direction: at A4 s13 Hebrews 12:2 closes the Christological-hermeneutic exhortation; here it names Christ Himself as the standing reference point.)

restoration.text: Therefore, what manner of men ought ye to be? Verily I say unto you, even as I am.
restoration.comment: Christ's own self-identification as the standard — the Restoration's most direct anchor for Christ as 'the living reference.'

restoration.text: Wherefore, my beloved brethren, pray unto the Father with all the energy of heart, that ye may be filled with this love, which he hath bestowed upon all who are true followers of his Son, Jesus Christ; that ye may become the sons of God; that when he shall appear we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is; that we may have this hope; that we may be purified even as he is pure.
restoration.comment: Mormon's witness of the becoming — being made like Christ at His appearing, the eschatological scope of the measuring rod.

s1.text: Jesus Christ offers entrance to the Kingdom of God through His Gospel of Salvation
s1.panel_comment: The article's opening move — salvation framed first as entrance into the Kingdom, not as a private transaction. The biblical anchors carry Christ's own inaugural proclamation: Mark 1:15 names the gospel as the announcement of the kingdom drawn near and repentance as its threshold; Matthew 4:23 names "the gospel of the kingdom" as the content of Christ's preaching ministry; John 10:9 names Christ Himself as the door of entrance ("by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved"). The span also carries the retired old-A6 proclamation cluster — the exclusivity of the person by whom salvation comes: John 14:6 names Christ as the only way to the Father; Helaman 5:9 and 2 Nephi 25:26 name the same exclusivity in the Restoration's voice, the source to whom we look for a remission of sins. The Restoration confirms the deliverance the kingdom's entrance secures: 2 Nephi 9:19 names the Holy One of Israel delivering His saints from death and hell. The crossref to Article 7 is deliberate — A7 carries the already/not-yet kingdom in full; A6 s1 hands off to it, naming salvation as the doorway A7 describes the dwelling behind. (John 14:6 re-homed from the retired old A6 s8 in different rhetorical direction: at old s8 it grounded the proclamation of the person; here it grounds Christ as the door of entrance. Helaman 5:9 and 2 Nephi 25:26 re-homed from old A6 s8, preserving the proclamation cluster's exclusivity claim in the new entrance register.)

biblical.text: And saying, The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe the gospel.
biblical.comment: Christ''s inaugural proclamation — the gospel announced as the kingdom drawn near, with repentance as its threshold. The entrance the article names begins where Christ''s own preaching begins.

biblical.text: And Jesus went about all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues, and preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing all manner of sickness and all manner of disease among the people.
biblical.comment: Names "the gospel of the kingdom" as the content of Christ''s preaching ministry — salvation''s gospel is, from the first, the gospel of the Kingdom into which it grants entrance.

biblical.text: I am the door: by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved, and shall go in and out, and find pasture.
biblical.comment: Christ names Himself the door of entrance — "by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved." The most direct biblical anchor for salvation framed as entrance through Christ.

biblical.text: Jesus saith unto him, I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.
biblical.comment: Christ's own way-claim, grounding the exclusivity of the entrance. (Re-homed from the retired old A6 s8 in different rhetorical direction: at old s8 it grounded the proclamation of the person by whom salvation is offered; here it grounds Christ as the only way and door of entrance to the Kingdom.)

restoration.text: O the greatness of the mercy of our God, the Holy One of Israel! For he delivereth his saints from that awful monster the devil, and death, and hell, and that lake of fire and brimstone, which is endless torment.
restoration.comment: Jacob names the deliverance the kingdom''s entrance secures — the Holy One of Israel delivering His saints from the devil, death, and hell. The Restoration''s confirmation of what salvation saves from at the threshold.

restoration.text: O remember, remember, my sons, the words which king Benjamin spake unto his people; yea, remember that there is no other way nor means whereby man can be saved, only through the atoning blood of Jesus Christ, who shall come; yea, remember that he cometh to redeem the world.
restoration.comment: Helaman naming Christ as the only way and means of salvation. (Re-homed from the retired old A6 s8; carries the proclamation cluster's exclusivity into the entrance register, preserving the inbound chains that lean on it.)

restoration.text: And we talk of Christ, we rejoice in Christ, we preach of Christ, we prophesy of Christ, and we write according to our prophecies, that our children may know to what source they may look for a remission of their sins.
restoration.comment: Nephi's signature Christocentric passage — the source to whom we look for a remission of sins. (Re-homed from the retired old A6 s8, where it grounded the Christological hermeneutic for salvation-proclamation; here it names Christ as the source of the entrance salvation grants.)

crossref.label: See Article 7
crossref.title: The Kingdom at Hand

s2.text: what we are being saved from, and what we are being saved for—though we may never fully comprehend these things in mortality
s2.panel_comment: Merognosis turned upon salvation's scope before P3 turns it upon salvation's mechanism. The article confesses both ends — what we are saved from and what we are saved for — and then declares the full vision of both beyond mortal sight. 1 Corinthians 13:9–12 is reasserted from Article 1 span 1, where it grounds the universal merognostic posture; here it applies that posture to the horizon of salvation itself — we know the direction in part, and prophesy the destination in part. The Restoration confirms the framing: Mosiah 4:9 names that man does not comprehend all the things which the Lord can comprehend — the mechanism and scope of salvation exceed mortal comprehension, yet belief is asked on exactly that ground. The crossref to Article 1 names plainness as the discipline that lets the article confess a partial knowing without anxiety.

biblical.text: For we know in part, and we prophesy in part. But when that which is perfect is come, then that which is in part shall be done away… For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known.
biblical.comment: Paul's foundational statement on mortal epistemic limits. (Reasserted from Article 1 span 1, where it grounds the universal merognostic posture; here it applies that posture to the horizon of salvation — its scope known and prophesied in part.)

restoration.text: Believe in God; believe that he is, and that he created all things, both in heaven and in earth; believe that he has all wisdom, and all power, both in heaven and in earth; believe that man doth not comprehend all the things which the Lord can comprehend.
restoration.comment: King Benjamin pairs belief with frank acknowledgment of incomprehension. (Reasserted from Article 9 span 6 in different rhetorical direction: at A9 s6 it grounds the general cognitive-humility posture of navigation; here it confirms the merognosis of salvation's scope — what we are saved from and for exceeds mortal comprehension, yet belief is asked on that ground.)

crossref.label: See Article 1
crossref.title: Plainness

s3.text: "Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which God hath prepared for them that love him."
s3.panel_comment: A type: direct span — the article quotes 1 Corinthians 2:9 verbatim to close P1. Paul's promise does the merognostic and the encounter work at once: it does not merely admit that the destination exceeds comprehension, it names the destination as prepared — by God, for those who love Him. The restraint is hopeful, not agnostic. The verse is the hinge between P1's confession of partial knowing and P2's confident naming of the arc God has prepared. The Restoration confirms with its own direct parallel: D&C 76:10 promises that by His Spirit the Lord will make known "those things which eye has not seen, nor ear heard" — the salvation-things God hath prepared are reserved for disclosure by the Spirit, not by speculation.

biblical.text: But as it is written, Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which God hath prepared for them that love him.
biblical.comment: The verse the article quotes verbatim. Names the destination as prepared by God for those who love Him — the merognostic restraint made hopeful rather than agnostic.

restoration.text: For by my Spirit will I enlighten them, and by my power will I make known unto them the secrets of my will—yea, even those things which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor yet entered into the heart of man.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's own direct parallel to 1 Corinthians 2:9. (Reasserted from Article 12 span 7 in different rhetorical direction: at A12 s7 it grounds eschatological-glories restraint; here it confirms the salvation-things-God-hath-prepared register — reserved for disclosure by the Spirit.)

s4.text: Salvation from our sins and mortality through the grace and atonement of the Son of God
s4.panel_comment: The ground of the entire article: salvation is through the grace and atonement of the Son of God. Ephesians 2:8 carries the universal Christian floor (saved by grace through faith, the gift of God); Acts 4:12 carries the exclusivity (salvation in no other). The deliberately-paired Philippians 2:12–13 and 1 Corinthians 15:10 surround the Restoration's signature grace claim so that "after all we can do" reads as canonical chorus, not synergistic add-on: Paul's "work out your salvation… for it is God which worketh in you" and "I laboured… yet not I, but the grace of God" say in apostolic voice exactly what 2 Nephi 25:23 says — that the disciple labors and yet the grace is the saving power. Moroni 10:32 names grace as both source and sufficiency. This is where the ground/outworking distinction is anchored for the engaged reader; the bare clause confesses grace as ground without litigating the forensic order. (Acts 4:12 reused: at the old A6 s2 it grounded faith-in-the-name and at old s8 the proclamation of the person — both retired here; in the rebuild it grounds salvation-in-no-other as the ground itself.)

biblical.text: For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
biblical.comment: The universal Christian floor for grace-as-ground — saved by grace through faith, the gift of God. The verse every tradition affirms.

biblical.text: Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved.
biblical.comment: Peter's exclusivity claim — salvation in no other. (Reused from the retired old A6 s2/s8 in different rhetorical direction: there it grounded faith-in-the-name and the proclamation of the person; here it grounds salvation-in-no-other as the ground of the article itself.)

biblical.text: Wherefore, my beloved, as ye have always obeyed, not as in my presence only, but now much more in my absence, work out your own salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure.
biblical.comment: Paul''s labor-yet-grace pairing — "work out your own salvation… for it is God which worketh in you." Set beside 2 Nephi 25:23 so the Restoration''s grace claim reads as apostolic chorus, not synergistic add-on.

biblical.text: But by the grace of God I am what I am: and his grace which was bestowed upon me was not in vain; but I laboured more abundantly than they all: yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.
biblical.comment: Paul''s "yet not I, but the grace of God" — the disciple labors, and the grace is the saving power. The apostolic voice of "after all we can do."

restoration.text: Yea, come unto Christ, and be perfected in him, and deny yourselves of all ungodliness; and if ye shall deny yourselves of all ungodliness, and love God with all your might, mind and strength, then is his grace sufficient for you, that by his grace ye may be perfect in Christ; and if by the grace of God ye are perfect in Christ, ye can in nowise deny the power of God.
restoration.comment: Moroni names grace as both source and sufficiency — "his grace is sufficient for you." (Verse-scope use of the come-unto-Christ passage; the wholeness register of verses 32–33 is carried at s9.)

restoration.text: For we labor diligently to write, to persuade our children, and also our brethren, to believe in Christ, and to be reconciled to God; for we know that it is by grace that we are saved, after all we can do.
restoration.comment: The Restoration''s signature grace claim, seated between Philippians 2:12–13 and 1 Corinthians 15:10 so that "after all we can do" reads as the canonical labor-yet-grace chorus — the disciple labors and the grace saves.

s5.text: central to the grand arc of God's Plan
s5.panel_comment: Salvation set inside the whole counsel of God — the "grand arc" from creation to consummation. Ephesians 1:9–10 names the mystery of His will to gather together in one all things in Christ; Ephesians 3:11 names the eternal purpose accomplished in Christ Jesus. Alma 42:8 names the plan within which mortality, death, and restoration cohere, and Alma 12:25 names the plan of redemption "prepared from the foundation of the world" — confirming the grand arc as laid before the Fall, not improvised against it. The anchors keep the arc Christocentric and purposive: salvation is the center of a plan, not a rescue improvised against the Fall.

biblical.text: Having made known unto us the mystery of his will, according to his good pleasure which he hath purposed in himself: That in the dispensation of the fulness of times he might gather together in one all things in Christ, both which are in heaven, and which are on earth; even in him:
biblical.comment: Names the mystery of His will — to gather together in one all things in Christ. The arc''s Christocentric scope, purposed in God before the times.

biblical.text: According to the eternal purpose which he purposed in Christ Jesus our Lord:
biblical.comment: Names the eternal purpose accomplished in Christ Jesus — the architecture within which salvation is central, not incidental.

restoration.text: Now behold, it was not expedient that man should be reclaimed from this temporal death, for that would destroy the great plan of happiness.
restoration.comment: Names the great plan of happiness as the architecture within which mortality and death cohere — the arc''s Restoration register.

restoration.text: Now, if it had not been for the plan of redemption, which was laid from the foundation of the world, there could have been no resurrection of the dead; but there was a plan of redemption laid, which shall bring to pass the resurrection of the dead, of which has been spoken.
restoration.comment: Names the plan of redemption "laid from the foundation of the world" — confirming the grand arc as laid before the Fall. Distinct from Alma 42:8's plan-of-happiness register at the same span.

s6.text: from our creation in His image, passing through redemptive transformation, to receiving God's image in our countenance
s6.panel_comment: The transformation arc named in the language of image and countenance. Genesis 1:26–27 grounds where the arc begins — man created in the image and likeness of God. 2 Corinthians 3:18 is the keystone — beholding the glory of the Lord, we are "changed into the same image from glory to glory, even as by the Spirit," fusing face, image, glory, and Spirit in a single verse. Colossians 3:10 (renewed after the image of the Creator) and Romans 8:29 carry the conforming work — Romans 8:29 is anchored strictly on "conformed to the image of his Son," never on "predestinate"; the article does not teach predestination. Numbers 6:26 and Psalm 34:5 carry the countenance language (the Lord lifting up His countenance; faces lightened, not ashamed). Alma 5:14 carries the Restoration's question — whether the image of God is engraven upon our countenances. Firewall: this is the theosis-adjacent beat; every anchor is kept on the shared sanctification/transformation register (conformed, changed from glory to glory, His image in the countenance) — no becoming-gods texts, no exaltation gloss. The Restoration distinctive lives in Volume 2.

biblical.text: And God said, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over the cattle, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth. So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.
biblical.comment: The creation ground of the arc — man made in the image and likeness of God. Names where the transformation begins: the image given at creation is the image being restored and brought to its fullness in the countenance. Kept on the shared register — the image as creational gift, not a deification claim.

biblical.text: But we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory, even as by the Spirit of the Lord.
biblical.comment: The keystone — face, image, glory, and Spirit fused in one verse. Beholding the glory of the Lord, we are changed into the same image from glory to glory. Kept strictly on the shared sanctification register.

biblical.text: The LORD lift up his countenance upon thee, and give thee peace.
biblical.comment: The priestly blessing''s countenance language — the Lord lifting up His countenance. Grounds the "His image in our countenance" hook in the shared register.

biblical.text: They looked unto him, and were lightened: and their faces were not ashamed.
biblical.comment: The countenance lightened by looking unto Him — faces not ashamed. The transformation read on the face, kept on the shared sanctification register.

biblical.text: For whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brethren.
biblical.comment: Anchored strictly on "conformed to the image of his Son," not on "predestinate." The article does not teach predestination; the conforming-to-the-image work is the shared sanctification claim every tradition affirms.

biblical.text: And have put on the new man, which is renewed in knowledge after the image of him that created him:
biblical.comment: The new man renewed after the image of the Creator — the conforming work named as renewal into His image, on the shared register.

restoration.text: And now behold, I ask of you, my brethren of the church, have ye spiritually been born of God? Have ye received his image in your countenances? Have ye experienced this mighty change in your hearts?
restoration.comment: Alma's diagnostic question — whether the image of God is received in our countenances. (Reused from Article 13 span 5 in different rhetorical direction: at A13 s5 it grounds the indwelling/testimony register; here it grounds the image-in-countenance/transformation register of the arc. Kept on the shared sanctification register, no exaltation gloss.)

s7.text: we shall be like Him—flourishing and glorified together as co-heirs with Christ of the Kingdom of God
s7.panel_comment: The destination clause, anchored verbatim. 1 John 3:2 — "we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is" — is the article's own words and carries the merognosis forward (it does not yet appear what we shall be) while naming the likeness with confidence. Firewall: glorification is anchored on Romans 8:17 — "joint-heirs with Christ… that we may be also glorified together" — the shared glorification every tradition affirms, never on exaltation-specific texts. Romans 8:30 closes the golden chain at "them he also glorified." "Flourishing" carries the wholeness register (salus / sōzō — to save is to heal, to make whole); "co-heirs" is Romans 8:17's "joint-heirs" in plain English. The Restoration confirms with its own quotation of the verse: Moroni 7:48 — "when he shall appear we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is" — confirming glorification-as-christoformity without importing exaltation. Shared glorification, not exaltation; the distinctive is Volume 2.

biblical.text: Beloved, now are we the sons of God, and it doth not yet appear what we shall be: but we know that, when he shall appear, we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is.
biblical.comment: The article''s own words, anchored verbatim. Carries the merognosis forward ("it doth not yet appear what we shall be") while naming the likeness with confidence ("we shall be like him").

biblical.text: And if children, then heirs; heirs of God, and joint-heirs with Christ; if so be that we suffer with him, that we may be also glorified together.
biblical.comment: The firewall anchor for glorification — "joint-heirs with Christ… that we may be also glorified together," the shared glorification every tradition affirms. "Co-heirs" is this verse''s "joint-heirs" in plain English.

biblical.text: Moreover whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified.
biblical.comment: Closes the golden chain at "them he also glorified." Anchored on the glorification terminus, kept on the shared register.

restoration.text: Wherefore, my beloved brethren, pray unto the Father with all the energy of heart, that ye may be filled with this love, which he hath bestowed upon all who are true followers of his Son, Jesus Christ; that ye may become the sons of God; that when he shall appear we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is; that we may have this hope; that we may be purified even as he is pure. Amen.
restoration.comment: The Book of Mormon quoting 1 John 3:2 itself — "when he shall appear we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is." Confirms glorification-as-christoformity without importing exaltation. (Overlaps the Moroni 7:45–48 range deployed at A1 s19, where its function is the charity meditation; here verse 48 grounds the likeness/glorification claim.)

s8.text: We do not claim to know the full mechanisms by which salvation operates
s8.panel_comment: The signature interfaith pivot — merognosis applied to the mechanism of salvation, where the traditions divide most sharply (monergism/synergism, imputed/infused righteousness, eternal security/conditional perseverance, sacramental/non-sacramental causality). The article affirms the floor — salvation works, through grace and the whole that follows — and declares the deep machinery opaque to creaturely knowing. Deuteronomy 29:29 governs the revealed/unrevealed line; Isaiah 55:8–9 names the height of God's ways above ours; Romans 11:33–34 is Paul's doxological merognosis specifically about God's saving judgments ("how unsearchable… past finding out"). The Restoration confirms: Jacob 4:8 names that it is impossible that man should find out all His ways — here scoped to the salvation mechanism, how grace works in us is unsearchable. (Deuteronomy 29:29 and Isaiah 55:8–9 reasserted from Article 1 span 1, where they ground the universal merognostic posture; here they apply it to soteriological mechanism. Romans 11:33–34 reasserted from Article 2 span 8, where it grounds doxological restraint before God's nature; here before His saving wisdom. Jacob 4:8 reasserted from Article 1 span 1; here scoped to the salvation mechanism.) Crossref to Article 1.

biblical.text: The secret things belong unto the Lord our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever, that we may do all the words of this law.
biblical.comment: The revealed/unrevealed distinction that governs all merognostic claims. (Reasserted from Article 1 span 1; here it applies the secret/revealed line to the mechanism of salvation — what is revealed we receive, what is secret about its machinery we do not pretend to possess.)

biblical.text: For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, saith the Lord. For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways, and my thoughts than your thoughts.
biblical.comment: Names the height of God's ways above ours. (Reasserted from Article 1 span 1, where it grounds the universal merognostic posture; here it applies that posture to the mechanism of salvation.)

biblical.text: O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out! For who hath known the mind of the Lord? or who hath been his counsellor?
