biblical.comment: Paul's doxological merognosis about God's saving judgments — "how unsearchable… past finding out." (Reasserted from Article 2 span 8, where it grounds doxological restraint before God's nature; here before His saving wisdom specifically.)

restoration.text: Behold, great and marvelous are the works of the Lord. How unsearchable are the depths of the mysteries of him; and it is impossible that man should find out all his ways.
restoration.comment: Confirms the mechanism-merognosis: it is impossible that man should find out all His ways. (Reasserted from Article 1 span 1, where it grounds the general epistemic limit; here scoped to the salvation mechanism — how grace works in us is unsearchable.)

crossref.label: See Article 1
crossref.title: Plainness

s9.text: nor ought we to reduce it to any single aspect of the whole that Christ taught plainly
s9.panel_comment: The load-bearing thesis of the rebuilt article: salvation is not to be reduced to any single facet of the whole Christ taught. This is integral wholeness, not works-righteousness and not a single sola — the question "which facet saves?" is malformed because holiness is wholeness (teleios — complete, whole, mature — not flawless). Matthew 23:23 carries the exact grammar: "these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone" — do not pit weightier against lighter; keep the whole. James 2:10 names the whole-law principle (offend in one point, guilty of all) as the structural refusal of reduction. Moroni 10:32–33 names perfection-in-Christ as wholeness by His grace (perfect = teleios = whole), and Alma 7:23–24 names the integral catalog — humble, submissive, gentle, full of patience, faith, hope, and charity, abounding in good works — the strongest Restoration anchor for salvation as wholeness across every facet, never a single axis. (Moroni 10:32–33 reasserted from the retired old A6 grace-and-completion uses; here it grounds the wholeness thesis directly.)

biblical.text: Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye pay tithe of mint and anise and cummin, and have omitted the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy, and faith: these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone.
biblical.comment: Carries the exact grammar of the thesis — "these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone." Do not pit weightier against lighter; keep the whole.

biblical.text: For whosoever shall keep the whole law, and yet offend in one point, he is guilty of all.
biblical.comment: The whole-law principle — offend in one point, guilty of all — named as the structural refusal of reduction to a single facet.

restoration.text: Yea, come unto Christ, and be perfected in him, and deny yourselves of all ungodliness; and if ye shall deny yourselves of all ungodliness, and love God with all your might, mind and strength, then is his grace sufficient for you, that by his grace ye may be perfect in Christ; and if by the grace of God ye are perfect in Christ, ye can in nowise deny the power of God.
restoration.comment: Perfection-in-Christ as wholeness by His grace (perfect = teleios = whole). (Reasserted from the retired old A6 s1/s12 grace-and-completion uses; here it grounds the wholeness thesis directly.)

restoration.text: And now I would that ye should be humble, and be submissive and gentle; easy to be entreated; full of patience and long-suffering; being temperate in all things; being diligent in keeping the commandments of God at all times; asking for whatsoever things ye stand in need, both spiritual and temporal; always returning thanks unto God for whatsoever things ye do receive. And see that ye have faith, hope, and charity, and then ye will always abound in good works.
restoration.comment: The integral catalog — humility, gentleness, patience, faith, hope, and charity abounding in good works. The strongest Restoration anchor for salvation as wholeness across every facet, never a single axis.

s10.text: the justice, mercy, grace, and atonement freely offered in Him; the faith in God and belief in His Son, the prayer and repentance by which we turn to Him
s10.panel_comment: The first movement of the whole — the gift freely offered and the disciple's turning to receive it. Justice, mercy, and grace meet in the atonement "freely offered": Romans 3:23–24 names the universal need and the free justification by grace; Alma 42:15 names the atonement appeasing justice and extending mercy (the verse-scope split from Alma 42:8 at s5 is deliberate — s5 the arc, s10 the justice-mercy meeting). The turning: John 1:12 and Romans 10:9–10 name faith and confession as the receiving disposition; Acts 3:19 and 2 Corinthians 7:10 name repentance — Peter's "repent and be converted" and Paul's godly-sorrow-unto-salvation; Alma 34:31–32 names this life as the day to turn. These are inputs, not levers — the disciple turns toward a salvation already offered in grace. (Romans 3:23–24, Acts 3:19, 2 Corinthians 7:10, and Alma 34:31–32 re-homed from the retired old A6 spans s1/s3; John 1:12 reused from old A6 s2/s10; Romans 10:9–10 re-homed from old A6 s2 and reasserted intra-article at s15 in the confession-of-faith direction.)

biblical.text: For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God; Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.
biblical.comment: The universal need ("all have sinned") paired with the free justification by grace. (Re-homed from the retired old A6 s1; here it grounds the justice-mercy-grace meeting in the atonement freely offered.)

biblical.text: But as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name.
biblical.comment: The receiving-by-name pattern — faith and reception named together. (Reused from the retired old A6 s2/s10; here it names faith as the receiving disposition by which the disciple turns to the gift.)

biblical.text: That if thou shalt confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus, and shalt believe in thine heart that God hath raised him from the dead, thou shalt be saved. For with the heart man believeth unto righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.
biblical.comment: Paul's confession-and-belief formula. (Re-homed from the retired old A6 s2; reasserted intra-article at s15 in the confession-before-men direction — here it names belief and confession as the receiving disposition.)

biblical.text: Repent ye therefore, and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out, when the times of refreshing shall come from the presence of the Lord.
biblical.comment: Peter's "repent and be converted." (Re-homed from the retired old A6 s3; here it names repentance as the turning by which the disciple receives the salvation freely offered.)

biblical.text: For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death.
biblical.comment: Paul's godly-sorrow-unto-salvation. (Re-homed from the retired old A6 s3; here it names the interior quality of the turning toward grace.)

restoration.text: And now, the plan of mercy could not be brought about except an atonement should be made; therefore God himself atoneth for the sins of the world, to bring about the plan of mercy, to appease the demands of justice, that God might be a perfect, just God, and a merciful God also.
restoration.comment: Names the atonement appeasing justice and extending mercy — the justice-mercy meeting. (Verse-scope split from Alma 42:8 at s5: s5 carries the grand arc, s10 the justice-mercy meeting in the atonement.)

restoration.text: Yea, I would that ye would come forth and harden not your hearts any longer; for behold, now is the time and the day of your salvation; and therefore, if ye will repent and harden not your hearts, immediately shall the great plan of redemption be brought about unto you. For behold, this life is the time for men to prepare to meet God; yea, behold the day of this life is the day for men to perform their labors.
restoration.comment: Names this life as the day to turn — the time of repentance by which the plan of redemption is brought about. (Re-homed from the retired old A6 s3.)

s11.text: the rebirth, and the love, forgiveness, peace, humility, patience, gentleness, and kindness by which His life grows whole in us
s11.panel_comment: The organic center of the holism — His life growing whole in us. The named virtues are not a checklist of human achievement but the fruit of the Spirit and the shape of Christ's own life taking root: Galatians 5:22–23 names love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness as the Spirit's fruit. John 15:4–5 carries the vine-and-branches — "without me ye can do nothing" — the exact image of a life that grows whole only by abiding, not by self-construction. John 3:3–5 anchors the rebirth itself in Christ's own teaching — except a man be born of water and of the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God. Mosiah 5:2 names the mighty change of heart (rebirth) — "no more disposition to do evil, but to do good continually." The whole beat enacts the thesis of s9: these are facets of one organic wholeness, never a ranked mechanism. (Galatians 5:22–23 re-homed from the retired old A6 s12 and reasserted from A7 s11 in the kingdom-fruit direction, here in the wholeness direction; John 15:4–5 re-homed from old A6 s4's vine anchor; Mosiah 5:2 re-homed from old A6 s12.)

biblical.text: Jesus answered and said unto him, Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God. Nicodemus saith unto him, How can a man be born when he is old? can he enter the second time into his mother's womb, and be born? Jesus answered, Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born of water and of the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God.
biblical.comment: Christ's own born-again teaching — except a man be born of water and of the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God. The most direct biblical anchor for 'the rebirth,' naming it as Christ named it: a birth from above by water and Spirit, not a human self-renewal.

biblical.text: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, Meekness, temperance: against such there is no law.
biblical.comment: The fruit of the Spirit as the named virtues' true source — not human achievement but the Spirit's fruit. (Re-homed from the retired old A6 s12; reasserted from A7 s11 in the kingdom-fruit direction, here in the wholeness direction.)

biblical.text: Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, except it abide in the vine; no more can ye, except ye abide in me. I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing.
biblical.comment: The vine-and-branches — "without me ye can do nothing." The image of a life that grows whole only by abiding, not by self-construction. (Re-homed and verse-scope-extended from old A6 s4's John 15:5 vine anchor.)

restoration.text: And they all cried with one voice, saying: Yea, we believe all the words which thou hast spoken unto us; and also, we know of their surety and truth, because of the Spirit of the Lord Omnipotent, which has wrought a mighty change in us, or in our hearts, that we have no more disposition to do evil, but to do good continually.
restoration.comment: The mighty change of heart (rebirth) — "no more disposition to do evil, but to do good continually." (Re-homed from the retired old A6 s12; here it names the rebirth by which His life begins to grow whole in us.)

s12.text: the obedience, discipleship, perseverance, and good works that bear fruit to His glory
s12.panel_comment: The fruit — output, not input. The grammar is the article's whole argument in miniature: works "bear fruit to His glory," they do not earn the salvation that grace grounds. John 15:8 names the telos — "herein is my Father glorified, that ye bear much fruit." Ephesians 2:8–10 is the hinge verse, holding grace-not-works (v.8–9) and created-unto-good-works (v.10) in one breath; Galatians 2:16 keeps the firewall against works of the law. James 2:22, 24 and Matthew 7:21 ground the refusal to reduce salvation to faith-only by canonical witness — the verses that name works as the evidence and companion of living faith. 2 Nephi 31:20 names the active life (press forward, endure); D&C 130:20–21 names the law-blessing-obedience structure without making obedience the meritorious cause. This is the span where the honest difference lives — the panel names the ground/outworking distinction (grace = ground at s4; works = fruit here); it does not adopt sola fide's forensic vocabulary. Difference in form, not in whether works ground salvation. (2 Nephi 31:20 reused from A9 s20 in the press-forward direction; D&C 130:20–21 re-homed from the retired old A6 s4.)

biblical.text: Herein is my Father glorified, that ye bear much fruit; so shall ye be my disciples.
biblical.comment: Names the telos — "herein is my Father glorified, that ye bear much fruit." Works are fruit borne to His glory, not the cause of salvation.

biblical.text: For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them.
biblical.comment: The hinge verse — grace-not-works (v.8–9) and created-unto-good-works (v.10) held in one breath. The article''s whole argument in a single passage.

biblical.text: Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ, even we have believed in Jesus Christ, that we might be justified by the faith of Christ, and not by the works of the law: for by the works of the law shall no flesh be justified.
biblical.comment: Keeps the firewall against works of the law — justification by the faith of Christ, not by works of the law. The grace-ground guarded as the fruit is named.

biblical.text: Seest thou how faith wrought with his works, and by works was faith made perfect?… Ye see then how that by works a man is justified, and not by faith only.
biblical.comment: Names works as the evidence and companion of living faith — "by works was faith made perfect," "not by faith only." Grounds the refusal to reduce salvation to faith alone by canonical witness.

biblical.text: Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of my Father which is in heaven.
biblical.comment: Christ''s own naming of doing the Father''s will as the mark of entrance — the dominical refusal of confession-only as the whole of salvation.

restoration.text: Wherefore, ye must press forward with a steadfastness in Christ, having a perfect brightness of hope, and a love of God and of all men. Wherefore, if ye shall press forward, feasting upon the word of Christ, and endure to the end, behold, thus saith the Father: Ye shall have eternal life.
restoration.comment: Names the active life — press forward, feast, endure. (Reused from Article 9 span 20 in different rhetorical direction: at A9 s20 it grounds navigational perseverance; here it names the obedience-and-perseverance that bears fruit to His glory.)

restoration.text: There is a law, irrevocably decreed in heaven before the foundations of this world, upon which all blessings are predicated—And when we obtain any blessing from God, it is by obedience to that law upon which it is predicated.
restoration.comment: Names the law-blessing-obedience structure without making obedience the meritorious cause of salvation. (Re-homed from the retired old A6 s4.)

s13.text: the joy, sanctification, and sealing by the Holy Spirit that open unto resurrection, immortality, eternal life, and glorification
s13.panel_comment: The consummation — the Spirit's sealing opening unto resurrection and glorified life. Ephesians 1:13–14 carries the sealing in the deliberately interfaith-broad register ("sealed with that holy Spirit of promise… the earnest of our inheritance"), receivable by Reformed, Wesleyan, Pentecostal, Catholic, and Restoration readers alike. Romans 8:16 names the experiential signature — the Spirit's witness that we are children of God — and is retained here specifically because Article 7 s10 reasserts it from A6's sealing span; keeping it preserves that inbound pointer. 1 Corinthians 15:21–22 and John 11:25–26 carry the resurrection-and-immortality promise; Moroni 6:4 names the Spirit numbering the disciple into the body of Christ; Mosiah 16:7–8 names the resurrection victory ("the sting of death is swallowed up in Christ"). The article opens with grace (s4) and closes with the Spirit's sealing — an inclusio: grace begins the salvation, the Spirit consummates it. (All anchors re-homed from the retired old A6 sealing and resurrection spans s5/s10.)

biblical.text: In whom ye also trusted, after that ye heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation: in whom also after that ye believed, ye were sealed with that holy Spirit of promise, Which is the earnest of our inheritance, until the redemption of the purchased possession, unto the praise of his glory.
biblical.comment: The sealing in the interfaith-broad register — "sealed with that holy Spirit of promise… the earnest of our inheritance." (Re-homed from the retired old A6 s5.)

biblical.text: The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God.
biblical.comment: The experiential signature of the sealing — the Spirit's witness that we are children of God. (Re-homed from the retired old A6 s5; retained here because Article 7 s10 reasserts it from A6's sealing span — keeping it preserves that inbound pointer.)

biblical.text: For since by man came death, by man came also the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive.
biblical.comment: The universal-resurrection promise — "in Christ shall all be made alive." (Re-homed from the retired old A6 s10.)

biblical.text: Jesus said unto her, I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live: And whosoever liveth and believeth in me shall never die. Believest thou this?
biblical.comment: Christ's own immortality claim — "I am the resurrection, and the life." (Re-homed from the retired old A6 s10.)

restoration.text: And after they had been received unto baptism, and were wrought upon and cleansed by the power of the Holy Ghost, they were numbered among the people of the church of Christ; and their names were taken, that they might be remembered and nourished by the good word of God.
restoration.comment: The Spirit numbering the disciple into the body of Christ. (Re-homed from the retired old A6 s5; carries the sealing in the Restoration's church-handbook register.)

restoration.text: And if Christ had not risen from the dead, or have broken the bands of death that the grave should have no victory, and that death should have no sting, there could have been no resurrection. But there is a resurrection, therefore the grave hath no victory, and the sting of death is swallowed up in Christ.
restoration.comment: The resurrection victory — "the sting of death is swallowed up in Christ." (Re-homed from the retired old A6 s10.)

s14.text: We claim no right to sit upon the throne of Christ, judging no soul to be saved or condemned in His place
s14.panel_comment: The article's closing refusal — and its sharpest interfaith move. Scripture commits judgment to the Son (John 5:22), so that every soul stands before the judgment seat of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:10); to declare another soul saved or condemned is to take a seat that is His alone — "in His place." The gospel repeatedly checks the disciple's impulse to police the boundary: when the disciples tried to stop a man casting out demons in Christ's name "because he followeth not us," Christ corrected them — "he that is not against us is on our part" (Mark 9:38–40); when they would call down fire on the unreceptive Samaritans, He answered that they knew not what manner of spirit they were of (Luke 9:51–56). Paul presses the same restraint — "who art thou that judgest another man's servant?" (Romans 14:4) — and James names its ground: there is one Lawgiver and Judge (James 4:12; cf. Matthew 7:1–2). Because we do not see as God sees (1 Samuel 16:7), the verdict on a soul's standing is simply not ours to render. The Restoration confirms the line exactly: we may discern good from evil by the light of Christ, yet judge no soul wrongfully (Moroni 7:18), for to Christ the Father has given the drawing and the judging of all (3 Nephi 27:14), and the Lord reserves the verdict to Himself — "I, the Lord, will forgive whom I will forgive" (D&C 64:10). This is not indifference to truth — discernment of teaching remains the disciple's task (see Article 9) — but it refuses the zealous gatekeeping that mistakes the disciples' first impulse in Mark 9 for Christ's corrective answer. The span ties the cluster's judgment-refusals into one chord: A1 s16 ("Mysteries and judgment we leave to God"), A8 (fellowship without gatekeeping), and A10's call to repentance against those who would manage or restrict the grace of God. (Matthew 7:1–2 reasserted from Article 1 span 16; Romans 14:4 and James 4:12 reasserted from Article 9 span 19; 1 Samuel 16:7 reasserted from Article 9 span 21 — there they govern the soul's own navigation and the testing of teachers; here they ground the soul-status refusal specifically: not whom we fellowship or how we discern, but whose verdict a soul's salvation is. Moroni 7:18 re-homed from the retired old A6 s7. D&C 64:10 reasserted from Article 13 span 10, where it grounds the forgiveness imperative; here the reservation of judgment to the Lord.)

biblical.text: For the Father judgeth no man, but hath committed all judgment unto the Son:
biblical.comment: Scripture commits all judgment to the Son. To declare a soul saved or condemned is to take a seat committed to Christ alone.

biblical.text: For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ; that every one may receive the things done in his body, according to that he hath done, whether it be good or bad.
biblical.comment: Every soul stands before the judgment seat of Christ — the seat the disciple refuses to usurp "in His place."

biblical.text: And John answered him, saying, Master, we saw one casting out devils in thy name, and he followeth not us: and we forbad him, because he followeth not us. But Jesus said, Forbid him not: for there is no man which shall do a miracle in my name, that can lightly speak evil of me. For he that is not against us is on our part.
biblical.comment: Christ correcting the disciples'' impulse to police the boundary — "he that is not against us is on our part." The gospel''s own check on gatekeeping.

biblical.text: And it came to pass, when the time was come that he should be received up, he stedfastly set his face to go to Jerusalem, And sent messengers before his face: and they went, and entered into a village of the Samaritans, to make ready for him. And they did not receive him, because his face was as though he would go to Jerusalem. And when his disciples James and John saw this, they said, Lord, wilt thou that we command fire to come down from heaven, and consume them, even as Elias did? But he turned, and rebuked them, and said, Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of. For the Son of man is not come to destroy men's lives, but to save them. And they went to another village.
biblical.comment: Christ rebuking the would-be fire-callers — "ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of." The disciple''s zeal against the unreceptive is not Christ''s spirit.

biblical.text: Judge not, that ye be not judged. For with what judgment ye judge, ye shall be judged: and with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again.
biblical.comment: Christ's most direct command against judgment. (Reasserted from Article 1 span 16, where it grounds the article's closing posture; here it grounds the refusal to render a verdict on a soul's salvation.)

biblical.text: Who art thou that judgest another man's servant? to his own master he standeth or falleth. Yea, he shall be holden up: for God is able to make him stand.
biblical.comment: Paul's refusal of any human positioning as the disciple's judge — to his own master he stands or falls. (Reasserted from Article 9 span 19, where it grounds the no-human-approval claim; here the soul-status refusal.)

biblical.text: There is one lawgiver, who is able to save and to destroy: who art thou that judgest another?
biblical.comment: Names the ground — there is one Lawgiver and Judge. (Reasserted from Article 9 span 19; here it grounds the refusal to occupy the seat that saves and destroys.)

biblical.text: But the LORD said unto Samuel, Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.
biblical.comment: Because we do not see as God sees, the verdict on a soul's standing is not ours. (Reasserted from Article 9 span 21, where it grounds the Lord's reading of the heart in navigation; here the soul-status refusal — the heart we cannot read is the heart He judges.)

restoration.text: And now, my brethren, seeing that ye know the light by which ye may judge, which light is the light of Christ, see that ye do not judge wrongfully; for with that same judgment which ye judge ye shall also be judged. Wherefore, I beseech of you, brethren, that ye should search diligently in the light of Christ that ye may know good from evil.
restoration.comment: We may discern good from evil by the light of Christ, yet judge no soul wrongfully. (Re-homed from the retired old A6 s7; preserves the refuse-to-judge register in the new judgment-seat refusal.)

restoration.text: And my Father sent me that I might be lifted up upon the cross; and after that I had been lifted up upon the cross, that I might draw all men unto me, that as I have been lifted up by men even so should men be lifted up by the Father, to stand before me, to be judged of their works, whether they be good or whether they be evil—
restoration.comment: To Christ the Father has given the drawing and the judging of all — every soul stands before Him to be judged. The Restoration''s confirmation that the verdict is His.

restoration.text: I, the Lord, will forgive whom I will forgive, but of you it is required to forgive all men.
restoration.comment: The Lord reserves the verdict to Himself — "I, the Lord, will forgive whom I will forgive." (Reasserted from Article 13 span 10, where it grounds the forgiveness imperative; here the reservation of judgment to the Lord.)

s15.text: Rather, we remember that our charge before Christ is to love God and neighbor without ceasing, to profess our faith in Him, and to keep His commandments
s15.panel_comment: The positive charge that answers the refusal — judgment withheld is not obligation abandoned. Where we will not sit in Christ's seat, we are still given His commandments to keep. The clause gathers the whole article's holism into the two great commandments on which "hang all the law and the prophets" (Matthew 22:37–40): love of God and of neighbor, which Christ named as the sum. To that it adds the confession of faith — "with the mouth confession is made unto salvation" (Romans 10:9–10), the disciple who confesses Christ before men (Matthew 10:32) — and the keeping of His commandments as love's own expression: "this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments" (1 John 5:3). The mark Christ gave His disciples was never a verdict rendered on others but a love shown among them — "by this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another" (John 13:34–35), which is the gospel's own answer to the gatekeeping impulse s14 refuses. The Restoration confirms the same two-fold charge, love of God and neighbor (D&C 59:5–6), and names the disciple's posture as witness rather than judge — to stand as witnesses of God and bear one another's burdens (Mosiah 18:8–9). The clause deliberately recapitulates the third paragraph's holism — faith, love, obedience — gathering it into the commandments Christ Himself called greatest, so the article closes on what is ours to do rather than on what is His alone to decide. (Romans 10:9–10 reasserted intra-article from s10, there the receiving disposition, here the confession of faith.)

biblical.text: Jesus said unto him, Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind. This is the first and great commandment. And the second is like unto it, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets.
biblical.comment: The two great commandments on which "hang all the law and the prophets" — love of God and neighbor, which Christ named as the sum. The two great commandments enter the cluster here.

biblical.text: A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another; as I have loved you, that ye also love one another. By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another.
biblical.comment: The mark Christ gave His disciples — a love shown among them, not a verdict rendered on others. The gospel''s own answer to the gatekeeping impulse s14 refuses.

biblical.text: That if thou shalt confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus, and shalt believe in thine heart that God hath raised him from the dead, thou shalt be saved. For with the heart man believeth unto righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.
biblical.comment: "With the mouth confession is made unto salvation" — the confession of faith that is ours to make. (Reasserted intra-article from s10, where it names the receiving disposition; here the profession of faith in Him.)

biblical.text: Whosoever therefore shall confess me before men, him will I confess also before my Father which is in heaven.
biblical.comment: The disciple who confesses Christ before men — the profession of faith named as Christ''s own charge.

biblical.text: For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments: and his commandments are not grievous.
biblical.comment: Keeping His commandments as love''s own expression — "this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments." Love and obedience named as one.

restoration.text: Wherefore, I give unto them a commandment, saying thus: Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, with all thy might, mind, and strength; and in the name of Jesus Christ thou shalt serve him. Thou shalt love thy neighbor as thyself. Thou shalt not steal; neither commit adultery, nor kill, nor do anything like unto it.
restoration.comment: The Restoration''s confirmation of the same two-fold charge — love of God and neighbor named in Christ''s own modern word.

restoration.text: And it came to pass that he said unto them: Behold, here are the waters of Mormon (for thus were they called) and now, as ye are desirous to come into the fold of God, and to be called his people, and are willing to bear one another's burdens, that they may be light; Yea, and are willing to mourn with those that mourn; yea, and comfort those that stand in need of comfort, and to stand as witnesses of God at all times and in all things, and in all places that ye may be in, even until death, that ye may be redeemed of God, and be numbered with those of the first resurrection, that ye may have eternal life—
restoration.comment: Names the disciple''s posture as witness rather than judge — to bear one another''s burdens and stand as witnesses of God. The positive charge in the Restoration''s baptismal-covenant register.

s1.text: the kingdom of heaven is not only promised for a distant day
s1.panel_comment: The article's restraint hinge — the gating phrase that makes every present-tense claim that follows safe to make. The 'not only' carries critical theological weight: it concedes the future consummation of the kingdom without developing it, preserving the already/not-yet tension that serious eschatology requires. Without this gating phrase, the article would risk over-realized eschatology — collapsing the future into the present and compromising Article 12 (Immortality and Eternal Life) before that article arrives. The biblical anchors hold the future-promise pole: Matthew 25:31–34 carries the dominical 'inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world' as the future-consummation anchor; Revelation 11:15 carries the eschatological proclamation ('the kingdoms of this world are become the kingdoms of our Lord'); 2 Peter 3:13 carries the 'new heavens and a new earth' promise. The Restoration anchors confirm the future-pole reading: D&C 65:5–6 carries Joseph's prayer for the kingdom's coming ('that the kingdom of heaven may come') as a future-tense petition, and Articles of Faith 1:10 names the gathering of Israel and the millennial reign as future events the article concedes without developing. Container-word discipline: 'distant day' is left undefined — Catholic readers hear the parousia, Reformed readers hear consummation, Premillennial readers hear the millennium, Restoration readers hear the Second Coming and millennial reign. The article does not adjudicate; it simply concedes the future-pole and pivots to the present-tense focus that is the article's actual subject.

biblical.text: When the Son of man shall come in his glory, and all the holy angels with him, then shall he sit upon the throne of his glory: And before him shall be gathered all nations… Then shall the King say unto them on his right hand, Come, ye blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.
biblical.comment: The dominical anchor for the future-consummation pole the article concedes. 'Inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world' names the future kingdom as a real and coming reality, not merely a present-interior one — the very claim the article preserves with 'not only promised for a distant day.'

biblical.text: And the seventh angel sounded; and there were great voices in heaven, saying, The kingdoms of this world are become the kingdoms of our Lord, and of his Christ; and he shall reign for ever and ever.
biblical.comment: The eschatological proclamation of kingdom-consummation. The 'are become' names a future event from the perspective of John's vision — the cosmic completion of what the article will soon name as 'already come to those who receive it' (s11). The future-pole anchor.

biblical.text: Nevertheless we, according to his promise, look for new heavens and a new earth, wherein dwelleth righteousness.
biblical.comment: Peter's apostolic anchor for the future promise. The phrase 'we look for' names the disciple's posture toward the future-pole — expectation without collapse into present-tense claim. Pairs with the article's 'not only promised for a distant day' as the same balance.

restoration.text: Call upon the Lord, that his kingdom may go forth upon the earth, that the inhabitants thereof may receive it… Yea, a voice crying — Prepare ye the way of the Lord, prepare ye the supper of the Lamb, make ready for the Bridegroom. Pray unto the Lord, call upon his holy name, make known his wonderful works among the people. Call upon the Lord, that his kingdom may go forth, that the inhabitants of the earth may receive it, and be prepared for the days to come, in the which the Son of Man shall come down in heaven, clothed in the brightness of his glory, to meet the kingdom of God which is set up on the earth.
restoration.comment: Joseph's prayer for the kingdom's coming — pairs the present-tense kingdom-on-earth with the future-tense Son of Man's coming. The Restoration's most direct anchor for the very already/not-yet balance the article preserves at s1.

restoration.text: We believe in the literal gathering of Israel and in the restoration of the Ten Tribes; that Zion (the New Jerusalem) will be built upon the American continent; that Christ will reign personally upon the earth; and that the earth will be renewed and receive its paradisiacal glory.
restoration.comment: Joseph Smith's signature future-eschatology summary. The article concedes these future events ('promised for a distant day') without developing them — they belong to Article 12 (Immortality and Eternal Life), not here. The Restoration's most distinctive future-eschatology anchor.

s2.panel_comment: The article's load-bearing dominical claim and the type-direct anchor that grounds the entire kingdom-now teaching. The span is not the article asserting the kingdom is at hand on its own authority — it is the article echoing what Christ Himself proclaimed in His earliest preaching. The phrase 'at hand' translates the Greek ἤγγικεν (perfect tense of ἐγγίζω, 'has drawn near' or 'has come close'), naming a kingdom that has arrived in proximity even as its full consummation remains future. The biblical anchors carry the verba Christi: Mark 1:14–15 records the Markan summary of Christ's earliest Galilean preaching ('the time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand'); Matthew 4:17 records the parallel Matthean summary ('From that time Jesus began to preach, and to say, Repent: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand'); Matthew 10:7 records Christ commissioning the Twelve to carry the same proclamation forward ('And as ye go, preach, saying, The kingdom of heaven is at hand'); Luke 17:20–21 records Christ's distinctive answer to the Pharisees ('the kingdom of God is within you' or 'in the midst of you'), naming the kingdom's present-tense interiority. The Restoration anchors confirm and extend the dominical claim: 3 Nephi 9:15–17 records the resurrected Christ's New World proclamation ('I am the light and the life of the world… I have come unto my own, and my own received me not'), naming the same kingdom-arrival in a different hemisphere; D&C 65:2 carries Joseph's revelation naming the Restoration as the kingdom's continued going-forth ('The keys of the kingdom of God are committed unto man on the earth, and from thence shall the gospel roll forth unto the ends of the earth'). The article's choice of 'proclaimed' as the verb is itself dominical-echoing: Christ proclaimed; the article proclaims after Him. The verb at the article-level opening ('We proclaim') is an echo of the dominical proclamation this span anchors.

biblical.text: Now after that John was put in prison, Jesus came into Galilee, preaching the gospel of the kingdom of God, And saying, The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe the gospel.
biblical.comment: The Markan summary of Christ's earliest Galilean preaching — the most direct biblical anchor for the article's claim. The Greek ἤγγικεν ('has drawn near') names a kingdom whose arrival is already accomplished even while its consummation remains future. Mark places this proclamation as the inaugural moment of Jesus' public ministry. (Reasserted from Article 5 span 1 in different rhetorical direction: at A5 s1 the verse anchors the divine sovereignty over Messianic timing — 'the time is fulfilled'; here at A7 s2 the verse anchors the verba Christi proclamation of kingdom-arrival.)

biblical.text: From that time Jesus began to preach, and to say, Repent: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.
biblical.comment: The Matthean parallel to Mark 1:15 — same dominical proclamation, same inaugural placement. Matthew's preference for 'kingdom of heaven' (over Mark's 'kingdom of God') reflects Jewish circumlocution for the divine name; the kingdom proclaimed is the same.

biblical.text: And as ye go, preach, saying, The kingdom of heaven is at hand.
biblical.comment: Christ's commissioning of the Twelve to carry the same proclamation forward. Names the kingdom-at-hand claim not only as Christ's own preaching but as the apostolic mission entrusted to His followers. The article's 'We proclaim' stands within this commissioned line.

biblical.text: And when he was demanded of the Pharisees, when the kingdom of God should come, he answered them and said, The kingdom of God cometh not with observation: Neither shall they say, Lo here! or, lo there! for, behold, the kingdom of God is within you.
biblical.comment: Christ's distinctive answer to the Pharisees naming the kingdom's present-tense interiority. The Greek ἐντὸς ὑμῶν may be translated 'within you' or 'in the midst of you' — both readings name a kingdom already present, refusing to defer it to a future external event. The most direct biblical anchor for the article's central claim that the kingdom is accessible now.

restoration.text: Behold, I am Jesus Christ the Son of God. I created the heavens and the earth, and all things that in them are. I was with the Father from the beginning. I am in the Father, and the Father in me; and in me hath the Father glorified his name. I came unto my own, and my own received me not. And the scriptures concerning my coming are fulfilled. And as many as have received me, to them have I given to become the sons of God; and even so will I to as many as shall believe on my name, for behold, by me redemption cometh, and in me is the law of Moses fulfilled.
restoration.comment: The resurrected Christ's New World proclamation — names the same kingdom-arrival the article echoes, in a different hemisphere and at a later moment in the dominical timeline. The 'I came unto my own' phrasing names the kingdom's already-arrived character; the 'as many as have received me' names the present-tense reception that A7 will develop at s11. (Reasserted from Article 3 span 1 in different rhetorical direction: at A3 s1 verse 15 alone anchors Christ's identity as Creator; here verses 15–17 anchor His proclamation of kingdom-arrival in the New World.)

restoration.text: The keys of the kingdom of God are committed unto man on the earth, and from thence shall the gospel roll forth unto the ends of the earth, as the stone which is cut out of the mountain without hands shall roll forth, until it has filled the whole earth.
restoration.comment: Joseph's revelation naming the Restoration as the kingdom's continued going-forth. Echoes Daniel 2:34–35 (the stone cut out without hands) as the OT-prophetic anchor for the kingdom that grows from a present-tense beginning to fill the whole earth. Names the kingdom-at-hand claim as a continuing reality from Christ's day to the present.

s3.text: within reach of every soul who would open ears to hear, heart to feel, and eyes of the spirit to see
s3.panel_comment: The threefold receptive faculty — the article's distinctive expansion of the standard dominical idiom 'ears to hear / eyes to see' into a three-part structure that includes the heart's feeling. This is the ministry's own pastoral amplification: Christ's repeated invitation 'he that hath ears to hear, let him hear' (Matthew 11:15, 13:9, Mark 4:9, etc.) is the canonical pair the article echoes; the addition of 'heart to feel' names the affective dimension of spiritual perception that the bare hearing/seeing pair leaves implicit. The biblical anchors hold the architecture: Matthew 13:16 carries Christ's blessing on those whose faculties are open ('blessed are your eyes, for they see: and your ears, for they hear'); Isaiah 6:9–10 carries the OT prophetic anchor for the closed/open faculty dynamic ('hear ye indeed, but understand not… make the heart of this people fat… lest they… understand with their heart'); Mark 4:9 carries Christ's signature invitation in its Markan form ('he that hath ears to hear, let him hear'); Romans 10:17 carries the Pauline anchor for hearing as the means of faith ('faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God'). The Restoration anchors confirm the threefold receptivity: D&C 84:46–47 names the Spirit of Christ given to every soul as the ground of perception ('the Spirit enlighteneth every man through the world, that hearkeneth to the voice of the Spirit'), and Alma 32:27–28 names the heart's experiment-with-the-word as the entry into spiritual perception ('exercise a particle of faith… let this desire work in you, even until ye believe in a manner that ye can give place for a portion of my words'). Container-word discipline operates at the height of its precision here: 'within reach of every soul' refuses to specify what reaching means institutionally — Catholic readers bring baptism into the Church, Protestant readers bring conversion, Restoration readers bring baptism by authority, Orthodox readers bring entrance into the liturgical life of the Church, Pentecostal readers bring Spirit baptism. The article does not adjudicate; the means belong to Article 11 (Covenants and Commitments). This span carries the universal-access claim without trespassing the lane of mechanism.

biblical.text: But blessed are your eyes, for they see: and your ears, for they hear.
biblical.comment: Christ's blessing on those whose faculties are open — the most direct biblical anchor for the article's threefold receptivity claim. The verse follows Christ's quotation of Isaiah 6:9–10 in Matthew 13:14–15, naming the disciples' open faculties as the inverse of the closed faculties Isaiah lamented. The dominical pairing the article expands.

biblical.text: And he said, Go, and tell this people, Hear ye indeed, but understand not; and see ye indeed, but perceive not. Make the heart of this people fat, and make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and convert, and be healed.
biblical.comment: The OT prophetic anchor for the closed/open faculty dynamic — the passage Christ Himself quotes (Matthew 13:14–15) when explaining why He teaches in parables. Notable: Isaiah's full architecture names all three faculties (eyes, ears, heart), the very triad the article carries forward. The article's 'heart to feel' is not an addition to scripture but a recovery of the full Isaianic and dominical pattern.

biblical.text: And he said unto them, He that hath ears to hear, let him hear.
biblical.comment: Christ's signature invitation in its Markan form, repeated across the Synoptics and Revelation. Names hearing not as a passive reception but as an act of will — the soul that 'would open ears to hear' is the disciple posture the article requires. The most repeated dominical formula for spiritual receptivity in the New Testament.

biblical.text: So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.
biblical.comment: Paul's apostolic anchor for hearing as the means of faith. Names the hearing faculty as the channel through which faith enters the soul — grounds the article's claim that receptivity is the precondition of kingdom-access. The Pauline anchor for the article's reception-verb posture.

restoration.text: And the Spirit giveth light to every man that cometh into the world; and the Spirit enlighteneth every man through the world, that hearkeneth to the voice of the Spirit. And every one that hearkeneth to the voice of the Spirit cometh unto God, even the Father.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's most expansive anchor for universal spiritual receptivity. Names the Spirit as already given to every soul — the very faculty the article calls each soul to 'open.' Joseph's revelation grounds the article's universal-access claim ('every soul') in the prior universal gift of the Spirit.

restoration.text: But behold, if ye will awake and arouse your faculties, even to an experiment upon my words, and exercise a particle of faith, yea, even if ye can no more than desire to believe, let this desire work in you, even until ye believe in a manner that ye can give place for a portion of my words. Now, we will compare the word unto a seed. Now, if ye give place, that a seed may be planted in your heart, behold, if it be a true seed, or a good seed, if ye do not cast it out by your unbelief, that ye will resist the Spirit of the Lord, behold, it will begin to swell within your breasts.
restoration.comment: Alma's signature passage on the heart's experiment-with-the-word as the entry into spiritual perception. Names the threefold movement the article echoes: awakening of faculties (the article's 'open ears'), the heart's giving place (the article's 'heart to feel'), and the swelling within (the article's 'eyes of the spirit to see' as the soul's growing perception). The Restoration's most direct anchor for receptive-posture-as-entry. (Reasserted from Article 3 span 11 in different rhetorical direction: at A3 s11 verse 27 alone anchors interpretive choice — the soul's giving place for faith; here verses 27–28 anchor the threefold receptive faculty as the entry into kingdom-perception.)

s4.text: He calls us to enter it now, in this mortal life
s4.panel_comment: The article's central pastoral thesis — kingdom-entry as present-tense possibility within mortal life. The phrase 'in this mortal life' is the article's most direct refusal of any reading that defers kingdom-access to the afterlife. Where s2 carried the dominical claim that the kingdom is at hand, s4 carries the dominical invitation to enter it within mortality. The biblical anchors hold the architecture: John 3:3, 5 carries the load-bearing dominical anchor — Christ's instruction to Nicodemus that the new-birth is the gate of kingdom-seeing and kingdom-entering, and the new-birth happens now ('except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God… except a man be born of water and of the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God'); Matthew 11:12 carries the dominical claim that the kingdom is being seized now ('from the days of John the Baptist until now the kingdom of heaven suffereth violence, and the violent take it by force'); Colossians 1:13 carries the apostolic anchor for present-tense kingdom-translation ('who hath delivered us from the power of darkness, and hath translated us into the kingdom of his dear Son'). The Restoration anchors confirm and extend: Mosiah 27:25–26 carries Alma the Younger's signature passage on the new-birth as present-tense kingdom-entry ('all mankind, yea, men and women… must be born again; yea, born of God, changed from their carnal and fallen state to a state of righteousness, being redeemed of God, becoming his sons and daughters'); D&C 6:13 carries Christ's direct invitation to Oliver Cowdery and Joseph in the Restoration ('if thou wilt do good, yea, and hold out faithful to the end, thou shalt be saved in the kingdom of God, which is the greatest of all the gifts of God; for there is no gift greater than the gift of salvation'). Container-word discipline holds: 'enter it' refuses to specify the means of entry — Catholic readers bring sacramental initiation, Reformed readers bring effectual call, Restoration readers bring covenant baptism by authority, Pentecostal readers bring Spirit-baptism. The article carries the universal-invitation claim and leaves the means to Article 11 (Covenants and Commitments). Pairs with s5 ('begin to live eternal life now, while we yet walk in flesh') as a two-part articulation — s4 names the entry, s5 names the life that follows it.

biblical.text: Jesus answered and said unto him, Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God… Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born of water and of the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God.
biblical.comment: Christ's instruction to Nicodemus — the load-bearing dominical anchor for present-tense kingdom-entry. The two verses together carry both the seeing and the entering: the new-birth is the condition of both, and the new-birth happens now. The most direct biblical anchor for the article's claim that the kingdom is entered within mortal life.

biblical.text: And from the days of John the Baptist until now the kingdom of heaven suffereth violence, and the violent take it by force.
biblical.comment: Christ's claim that the kingdom is being seized now. The verse names the kingdom as a present-tense reality being entered actively in the days of John and Christ — not deferred to a future age. Grounds the article's 'enter it now' in the kingdom's already-present accessibility within Christ's own ministry.

biblical.text: Who hath delivered us from the power of darkness, and hath translated us into the kingdom of his dear Son.
biblical.comment: Paul's apostolic anchor for present-tense kingdom-translation. The verbs 'hath delivered' and 'hath translated' are perfect-tense — naming a transfer that has already happened in the disciple's life. The most direct Pauline anchor for the article's 'enter it now' claim.

restoration.text: And the Lord said unto me: Marvel not that all mankind, yea, men and women, all nations, kindreds, tongues and people, must be born again; yea, born of God, changed from their carnal and fallen state to a state of righteousness, being redeemed of God, becoming his sons and daughters; And thus they become new creatures; and unless they do this, they can in nowise inherit the kingdom of God.
restoration.comment: Alma the Younger's signature passage on the new-birth as present-tense kingdom-entry. The phrase 'must be born again… becoming his sons and daughters' names the same architecture as John 3:3, 5: the new-birth is the gate, kingdom-inheritance is its outcome, and both happen now. The Restoration's most direct echo of Christ's instruction to Nicodemus. (Reasserted from Article 3 span 9 in different rhetorical direction: at A3 s9 the passage anchors the fourfold mortal arc — choose, fall, rise, be made new — naming being-made-new as the closing motion of agency; here at A7 s4 the passage anchors the new-birth specifically as kingdom-entry within mortality. Same passage, two distinct soteriological directions: at A3 the becoming a new creature; at A7 the entering the kingdom.)

restoration.text: If thou wilt do good, yea, and hold out faithful to the end, thou shalt be saved in the kingdom of God, which is the greatest of all the gifts of God; for there is no gift greater than the gift of salvation.
restoration.comment: Christ's direct invitation to Oliver Cowdery and Joseph in the Restoration. Names kingdom-salvation as 'the gift of God' offered now — the present-tense invitation echoing Matthew 11:28 in its restoration moment. Grounds the article's 'He calls us' in Christ's own continuing voice through the Restoration.
