s5.text: begin to live eternal life now, while we yet walk in flesh
s5.panel_comment: The realized-eschatology claim — eternal life is entered, not only awaited. Where s4 named kingdom-entry as present-tense possibility, s5 names the life that follows entry as present-tense reality. The phrase 'while we yet walk in flesh' is the article's most direct refusal of any reading that makes mortality a barrier to eternal-life-participation. The biblical anchors hold the architecture: John 10:10 carries Christ's signature abundant-life claim ('I am come that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly'), naming the present-tense purpose of His coming; John 5:24 carries the most direct dominical anchor for the perfect-tense already-have-eternal-life claim ('he that heareth my word, and believeth on him that sent me, hath everlasting life… is passed from death unto life'); 1 John 5:11–13 carries John's apostolic confirmation ('these things have I written unto you that believe on the name of the Son of God; that ye may know that ye have eternal life'). The Restoration anchors confirm and extend: Mosiah 2:41 carries King Benjamin's signature 'blessed and happy state' passage, naming the joy of those who keep the commandments now ('they are blessed in all things, both temporal and spiritual; and if they hold out faithful to the end they are received into heaven') — the present-blessing pole paired with the future-reception pole; D&C 50:24 carries the light-groweth-brighter-and-brighter passage ('that which is of God is light; and he that receiveth light, and continueth in God, receiveth more light; and that light groweth brighter and brighter until the perfect day'), naming the progressive character of eternal-life-already-begun. The article's verb 'begin to live' is theologically precise: not 'enter into' (which s4 carries), and not the full 'know God' definition (which s6 carries), but the moment-of-beginning that signals entry has been made and life has commenced. Pairs with s4 as the consequence-claim: s4 names the entry, s5 names the life that follows it, s6 names what that life consists of. The article's three-step articulation across s4–s6 mirrors the biblical movement from new-birth (John 3:3, 5) to abundant-life (John 10:10) to knowing-God (John 17:3).

biblical.text: The thief cometh not, but for to steal, and to kill, and to destroy: I am come that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly.
biblical.comment: Christ's signature abundant-life claim — names the present-tense purpose of His coming. The Greek περισσὸν ('more abundantly') names life beyond mere subsistence — life that overflows. The most direct biblical anchor for the article's 'begin to live eternal life now' claim. Christ did not come merely that we might have life after death; He came that we might have abundant life now.

biblical.text: Verily, verily, I say unto you, He that heareth my word, and believeth on him that sent me, hath everlasting life, and shall not come into condemnation; but is passed from death unto life.
biblical.comment: Christ's most direct anchor for the perfect-tense already-have-eternal-life claim. The verbs 'hath' and 'is passed' are present and perfect — the disciple already has everlasting life and has already passed from death to life. The most theologically precise biblical anchor for the article's claim that eternal life is entered within mortality, not merely awaited beyond it.

biblical.text: And this is the record, that God hath given to us eternal life, and this life is in his Son. He that hath the Son hath life; and he that hath not the Son hath not life. These things have I written unto you that believe on the name of the Son of God; that ye may know that ye have eternal life, and that ye may believe on the name of the Son of God.
biblical.comment: John's apostolic confirmation of the present-tense possession of eternal life. The verb 'have' (Greek ἔχει) is present-tense — names eternal life as a present possession of those who have the Son, not a future inheritance only. The phrase 'that ye may know that ye have eternal life' grounds the disciple's present-tense assurance in the article's claim.

restoration.text: And moreover, I would desire that ye should consider on the blessed and happy state of those that keep the commandments of God. For behold, they are blessed in all things, both temporal and spiritual; and if they hold out faithful to the end they are received into heaven, that they may thereby dwell with God in a state of never-ending happiness. O remember, remember that these things are true; for the Lord God hath spoken it.
restoration.comment: King Benjamin's signature 'blessed and happy state' passage — names the present-tense blessing of those who keep the commandments now ('they are blessed in all things, both temporal and spiritual') alongside the future-reception pole ('if they hold out faithful to the end they are received into heaven'). The Restoration's most direct anchor for the present-blessing-paired-with-future-completion architecture the article carries at s5.

restoration.text: That which is of God is light; and he that receiveth light, and continueth in God, receiveth more light; and that light groweth brighter and brighter until the perfect day.
restoration.comment: The light-groweth-brighter-and-brighter passage — names the progressive character of eternal-life-already-begun. The disciple does not receive the full measure at the start, but begins with light and continues to receive more. Grounds the article's 'begin to live' verb in the Restoration's progressive-light architecture: eternal life is not all-at-once but begins-now-and-grows.

s6.text: Eternal life is not merely an unending existence beyond the grave — it is the life of knowing God and fellowship with His Son, which begins the moment we come to Him and can continue without end
s6.panel_comment: The article's most theologically dense span — the definitional redefinition of eternal life that grounds the entire kingdom-now teaching. Where s5 named the fact that eternal life is begun now, s6 names what that life consists of: knowing God and fellowship with His Son. This is the John 17:3 move, and it is the theological heart of the article. Christ's own definition of eternal life in His high-priestly prayer ('this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent') is the warrant for the entire kingdom-now claim. Eternal life is not primarily duration; it is a kind of life, characterized by knowing God and participation in Christ. The biblical anchors hold the architecture: John 17:3 carries the load-bearing definitional anchor — Christ's own definition of eternal life in His high-priestly prayer; 1 Corinthians 1:9 carries the most direct apostolic anchor for the fellowship-with-the-Son half ('God is faithful, by whom ye were called unto the fellowship of his Son Jesus Christ our Lord'); 1 John 1:3 carries the koinonia language explicitly ('that which we have seen and heard declare we unto you, that ye also may have fellowship with us: and truly our fellowship is with the Father, and with his Son Jesus Christ'); Jeremiah 9:23–24 carries the OT prophetic anchor for knowing-God as the supreme good ('let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me, that I am the Lord which exercise lovingkindness, judgment, and righteousness, in the earth'). The Restoration anchors confirm and extend: D&C 132:24 carries the Restoration's most direct echo of John 17:3 ('And this is life eternal, to know the only wise and true God, and Jesus Christ, whom he hath sent'), Joseph's repetition of Christ's high-priestly definition; D&C 88:49–50 carries the abiding-presence promise that grounds the 'continue without end' claim ('Then shall the angels be crowned with the glory of his might, and the saints shall be filled with his glory, and receive their inheritance and be made equal with him'). Container-word discipline operates with care here: 'fellowship' (Greek κοινωνία, koinōnia) names relationship rather than location, communion rather than geography. Catholic readers hear the beatific vision and sacramental communion. Reformed readers hear union with Christ. Restoration readers hear exaltation and continuing participation in divine glory. Orthodox readers hear theosis. Pentecostal readers hear Spirit-fellowship. The word accommodates all these pictures without specifying any. The phrase 'can continue without end' is theologically careful: it preserves the 'not yet' pole (the article does not collapse the future into the present at s6 any more than at s1), while affirming that what begins now is what continues then. Pairs with s5 as the consequence-claim: s5 names eternal-life-as-fact-of-life, s6 names eternal-life-as-content-of-life. The article's three-step articulation across s4–s6 mirrors the biblical movement from new-birth (John 3:3, 5) to abundant-life (John 10:10) to knowing-God (John 17:3).

biblical.text: And this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent.
biblical.comment: Christ's own definition of eternal life in His high-priestly prayer — the load-bearing biblical anchor for the entire kingdom-now teaching of the article. The verb 'know' (Greek γινώσκω, ginōskō) names relational knowing — not propositional information but the kind of knowing that exists between persons in relationship. Eternal life is not primarily duration; it is a kind of life, characterized by knowing God and participation in Christ. The most theologically precise anchor in the cluster for the article's redefinition of eternal life.

biblical.text: God is faithful, by whom ye were called unto the fellowship of his Son Jesus Christ our Lord.
biblical.comment: Paul's apostolic anchor for the fellowship-with-the-Son half of the article's definition. The Greek κοινωνία (koinōnia) names relational communion — not mere association, but participation in the Son's own life. The 'were called' (perfect tense) names the calling as an event already accomplished in the disciple's life, the present-tense ground for the present-tense fellowship the article describes.

biblical.text: That which we have seen and heard declare we unto you, that ye also may have fellowship with us: and truly our fellowship is with the Father, and with his Son Jesus Christ.
biblical.comment: John's apostolic anchor for the threefold koinōnia: among the disciples, with the Father, and with the Son. The article's 'fellowship with His Son' is the second of these — names participation in Christ's own life as the present-tense reality the disciple already enters. Pairs with 1 Corinthians 1:9 as the apostolic ground for the fellowship-with-Son claim.

biblical.text: Thus saith the Lord, Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, let not the rich man glory in his riches: But let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me, that I am the Lord which exercise lovingkindness, judgment, and righteousness, in the earth: for in these things I delight, saith the Lord.
biblical.comment: The OT prophetic anchor for knowing-God as the supreme good. Names the knowing of God not as one good among many but as the only legitimate ground of the disciple's glorying. Grounds Christ's John 17:3 definition in Jeremiah's prior prophetic declaration that knowing-God is the highest end of human life.

restoration.text: This is eternal lives — to know the only wise and true God, and Jesus Christ, whom he hath sent. I am he. Receive ye, therefore, my law.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's most direct echo of John 17:3 — Joseph's revelation reproducing Christ's high-priestly definition of eternal life. The variation 'eternal lives' (plural) is distinctively Restoration in formulation but holds the same definitional architecture as the original. Names the knowing-God-and-Christ as the content of eternal life. The most direct Restoration anchor for the article's redefinition.

restoration.text: The light shineth in darkness, and the darkness comprehendeth it not; nevertheless, the day shall come when you shall comprehend even God, being quickened in him and by him. Then shall ye know that ye have seen me, that I am, and that I am the true light that is in you, and that you are in me; otherwise ye could not abound.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's signature passage on the progressive comprehending-of-God that grounds the 'continue without end' claim. Names knowing-God as a movement that begins in mortal partial-comprehension and continues into the disciple's full participation in divine life. The 'I am the true light that is in you, and that you are in me' is the Restoration's most direct echo of John 14:20 and 17:21 — mutual indwelling as the architecture of fellowship that begins now and continues without end.

s7.text: We do not have to wait for death to find His rest
s7.panel_comment: The first of three triadic refusals — rest released from death-deferral. The article's signature triple-register pattern opens here at s7 and closes at s9, mirroring the merognosis dagger's triple-register architecture in Article 1. Each refusal closes a specific deferral-trap by which readers commonly defer the kingdom into an indefinite future: this span closes the death-deferral trap. The biblical anchors hold the architecture: Matthew 11:28–30 carries the load-bearing dominical anchor — Christ's signature invitation, where the verb 'I will give' is future-immediate (not eschatological) and the rest is offered to those who come now ('Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls'); Hebrews 4:9–11 carries the apostolic anchor for present-tense rest as already-entered ('there remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God. For he that is entered into his rest, he also hath ceased from his own works… Let us labour therefore to enter into that rest'); Psalm 62:1, 5 carries the OT lyrical anchor for the soul's present-tense waiting on God ('Truly my soul waiteth upon God: from him cometh my salvation… My soul, wait thou only upon God; for my expectation is from him'). The Restoration anchors confirm: D&C 84:23–24 carries Joseph's revelation naming the rest of the Lord as accessible in mortality ('Now this Moses plainly taught to the children of Israel in the wilderness, and sought diligently to sanctify his people that they might behold the face of God; But they hardened their hearts and could not endure his presence; therefore, the Lord in his wrath… sware that they should not enter into his rest'); Alma 13:12 carries the most direct anchor for entered-into-the-rest-of-the-Lord as a present-tense reality among Alma's people ('they could not look upon sin save it were with abhorrence; and there were many, exceedingly great many, who were made pure and entered into the rest of the Lord their God'). Pairs with s8 (joy released from perfection-deferral) and s9 (peace released from glory-deferral) as a unified triadic refusal — the article's signature mode echoing the merognosis dagger's triple-register pattern. The triad's rhetorical function: each clause opens a deferral-trap and closes it with a Christ-promise, freeing the disciple's experience of the kingdom from any precondition that would defer it beyond mortal reach.

biblical.text: Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.
biblical.comment: Christ's signature invitation — the load-bearing dominical anchor for the article's first refusal. The verb 'I will give' is future-immediate, not eschatological; the rest is offered to those who come now. Christ does not promise rest after death but rest unto the soul that comes to Him in mortal labor and burden. The most direct biblical refusal of the death-deferral trap.

biblical.text: There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God. For he that is entered into his rest, he also hath ceased from his own works, as God did from his. Let us labour therefore to enter into that rest, lest any man fall after the same example of unbelief.
biblical.comment: The author of Hebrews' apostolic anchor for present-tense rest as already-entered. The verb 'is entered' (perfect tense) names the rest as a reality the disciple has already entered, not a future-only promise. Pairs the entered-rest claim with the labour-to-enter exhortation — naming the present-tense rest as something to be sought now.

biblical.text: Truly my soul waiteth upon God: from him cometh my salvation… My soul, wait thou only upon God; for my expectation is from him.
biblical.comment: David's OT lyrical anchor for the soul's present-tense waiting on God. Names the rest of the soul not as the cessation of mortal labor but as the soul's quiet attentiveness to God in the midst of mortal labor. The OT anchor for the kind of rest the disciple finds within mortality, not after it.

restoration.text: Now this Moses plainly taught to the children of Israel in the wilderness, and sought diligently to sanctify his people that they might behold the face of God; But they hardened their hearts and could not endure his presence; therefore, the Lord in his wrath, for his anger was kindled against them, sware that they should not enter into his rest while in the wilderness, which rest is the fulness of his glory.
restoration.comment: Joseph's revelation naming the rest of the Lord as a reality Moses sought to bring his people into during their mortal journey. The phrase 'enter into his rest while in the wilderness' is the Restoration's most direct anchor for present-tense rest within mortal life. The rest was withheld not because rest is post-mortem-only but because of hardened hearts; the present-tense rest was the original intent.

restoration.text: Now they, after being sanctified by the Holy Ghost, having their garments made white, being pure and spotless before God, could not look upon sin save it were with abhorrence; and there were many, exceedingly great many, who were made pure and entered into the rest of the Lord their God.
restoration.comment: Alma's signature passage on entered-into-the-rest-of-the-Lord as a present-tense reality among his people. The phrase 'entered into the rest' is past tense, naming a completed action in the lives of mortal disciples — the most direct Restoration anchor for the article's claim that the rest of the Lord is found within mortality, not after it.

s8.text: We do not have to wait for perfection to taste His joy
s8.panel_comment: The middle position in the triadic refusal — joy released from perfection-deferral. Where s7 closed the death-deferral trap, s8 closes the perfection-deferral trap, the most pernicious of the three because it defers the kingdom not by an external event but by an internal moral standard the disciple feels obligated to meet first. The article refuses this deferral directly: joy is not the reward for completed sanctification but the present gift of the Spirit to those who are still becoming. The verb 'taste' is theologically careful — it names a real but partial experience of joy that grows toward fullness without requiring fullness as a precondition. The biblical anchors hold the architecture: John 15:11 carries the load-bearing dominical anchor — Christ's stated purpose for His teaching was that His disciples' joy might be full now ('these things have I spoken unto you, that my joy might remain in you, and that your joy might be full'); John 17:13 carries the parallel claim from the high-priestly prayer naming the joy as already-given to the disciples in the world ('that they might have my joy fulfilled in themselves'); Philippians 4:4 carries the apostolic command of joy as a present-tense disposition ('Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice') — Paul wrote from imprisonment and named joy without perfection-preconditions; Galatians 5:22 carries the Pauline anchor for joy as a fruit of the Spirit, naming joy as something that grows now in mortal life. The Restoration anchors confirm: 2 Nephi 2:25 carries Lehi's signature claim that joy is the very purpose of mortal existence ('Adam fell that men might be; and men are, that they might have joy') — the Restoration's most direct anchor for the article's refusal of the perfection-deferral trap, naming joy as the telos of mortal life itself, not its reward; D&C 11:13 carries Joseph's revelation naming the Spirit's filling-with-joy as a present-tense gift ('Verily, verily, I say unto thee, I will impart unto you of my Spirit, which shall enlighten your mind, which shall fill your soul with joy'). Pairs with s7 (rest released from death-deferral) and s9 (peace released from glory-deferral) as the unified triadic refusal — s8 holds the middle position, the deferral most disciples actually struggle with. The verb 'taste' (echoing Psalm 34:8 'O taste and see that the Lord is good') signals partial-but-real experience: the disciple does not yet have the fullness of joy in glory, but tastes its substance now.

biblical.text: These things have I spoken unto you, that my joy might remain in you, and that your joy might be full.
biblical.comment: Christ's stated purpose for His teaching — the load-bearing dominical anchor for the article's middle refusal. The verbs 'might remain' and 'might be full' are present-tense; Christ's joy is offered to the disciples as something to remain in them now and to be full now. The most direct biblical anchor for the article's claim that joy is not deferred to a future perfection.

biblical.text: And now come I to thee; and these things I speak in the world, that they might have my joy fulfilled in themselves.
biblical.comment: Christ's parallel claim from the high-priestly prayer. The phrase 'in the world' is decisive: the joy is fulfilled in the disciples while they yet walk in mortality, not after they leave it. Pairs with John 15:11 as the dominical pair for the article's claim that joy belongs to the present life.

biblical.text: Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice.
biblical.comment: Paul's apostolic command of joy as a present-tense disposition. Paul wrote from imprisonment in Rome and named joy without perfection-preconditions, without circumstance-preconditions, without any precondition at all except the Lord Himself. The most direct apostolic refusal of the perfection-deferral trap — joy 'alway' means joy now, in whatever imperfect circumstance the disciple finds herself.

biblical.text: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith.
biblical.comment: The Pauline anchor for joy as a fruit of the Spirit. Names joy as something that grows in the disciple's life through the Spirit's present operation — not as a reward earned by perfected discipleship but as a gift produced by the Spirit's own work. Grounds the article's claim that joy is given to imperfect disciples through the Spirit who is given to them now.

restoration.text: Adam fell that men might be; and men are, that they might have joy.
restoration.comment: Lehi's signature claim that joy is the very purpose of mortal existence — the Restoration's most direct anchor for the article's refusal of the perfection-deferral trap. The verse names joy not as the reward for completed mortality but as the telos of mortal life itself. Men are, that they might have joy now — not after they have perfected themselves. The most concise theological refusal of perfection-deferred-joy in the Restoration canon.

restoration.text: Verily, verily, I say unto thee, I will impart unto you of my Spirit, which shall enlighten your mind, which shall fill your soul with joy.
restoration.comment: Joseph's revelation naming the Spirit's filling-with-joy as a present-tense gift. The promise is given to a disciple who is yet imperfect — naming the joy as a gift of the Spirit, not a reward of the soul's perfection. Pairs with Galatians 5:22 as the Restoration's confirmation of joy-as-Spirit-fruit, given to those still becoming.

s9.text: We do not have to wait for glory to know His peace
s9.panel_comment: The third and closing position in the triadic refusal — peace released from glory-deferral. Where s7 closed the death-deferral trap and s8 closed the perfection-deferral trap, s9 closes the glory-deferral trap: the eschatological reading that defers the kingdom's gifts to the disciple's future glorification. The article refuses this deferral directly: peace is not the reward of attained glory but the present gift of Christ to those still walking the path. The verb 'know' is theologically careful — it names experiential knowing, not merely cognitive awareness. The disciple knows His peace by tasting it, by being kept by it, by walking in it. The biblical anchors hold the architecture: John 14:27 carries the load-bearing dominical anchor — Christ's signature peace-bequest to His disciples on the night of His betrayal, given precisely as they faced the worst of mortal trials, not after their glorification ('Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid'); John 16:33 carries the parallel dominical claim naming peace as already-given in tribulation ('These things I have spoken unto you, that in me ye might have peace. In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world'); Philippians 4:7 carries the apostolic anchor for peace as a present-tense guard for hearts in mortal life ('the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus'); Romans 5:1 carries the Pauline anchor for peace-with-God as the present-tense fruit of justification ('being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ'). The Restoration anchors confirm and extend with theological precision: D&C 19:23 carries Christ's direct invitation in the Restoration ('Learn of me, and listen to my words; walk in the meekness of my Spirit, and you shall have peace in me') — the most direct echo of John 14:27 in Restoration formulation; D&C 59:23 carries the doctrinally precise distinction between present-tense peace and future-tense eternal-life ('he who doeth the works of righteousness shall receive his reward, even peace in this world, and eternal life in the world to come') — the Restoration's most direct refusal of the glory-deferral trap, naming peace explicitly as a 'this world' reward, not a 'world to come' reward. Pairs with s7 (rest released from death-deferral) and s8 (joy released from perfection-deferral) as the unified triadic refusal — s9 holds the closing position and seals the inclusio. The triad as a whole functions architecturally like the merognosis dagger in Article 1: three specifications, three deferral-traps closed, the disciple's experience of the kingdom freed from any precondition that would defer it beyond mortal reach. The triadic structure is itself the article's signature voice — the Sermon-on-the-Mount cadence that the kingdom-now claim cannot be made through prose development alone.

biblical.text: Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid.
biblical.comment: Christ's signature peace-bequest to His disciples on the night of His betrayal — the load-bearing dominical anchor for the article's third refusal. The peace is given precisely as the disciples face the worst of mortal trials (Christ's arrest, trial, and crucifixion are about to begin), not after their glorification. The phrase 'not as the world giveth' is theologically decisive: this is not conventional peace as a future-tense good wish but a present-tense substantive gift. The most direct biblical anchor for the article's refusal of the glory-deferral trap.

biblical.text: These things I have spoken unto you, that in me ye might have peace. In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.
biblical.comment: Christ's parallel claim from the same Last Discourse, naming peace as already-given in the very world where tribulation reigns. The contrast is decisive: peace is not the absence of tribulation but its companion in the disciple's mortal experience. The verb 'might have' is present-tense; peace is for now, in the world, while tribulation is also present. Pairs with John 14:27 as the dominical pair for the article's claim that peace belongs to the present life.

biblical.text: And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus.
biblical.comment: Paul's apostolic anchor for peace as a present-tense guard for hearts in mortal life. The verb 'shall keep' (Greek φρουρήσει, phrourēsei, from a military root meaning 'garrison') names peace as an active protection given to the disciple now — not a future condition but a present operation. Grounds the article's claim that the disciple knows His peace within mortality, not after it.

biblical.text: Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.
biblical.comment: Paul's apostolic anchor for peace-with-God as the present-tense fruit of justification. The verb 'we have' is present-tense; the peace with God is already accomplished in the justified disciple, not a future reward. The most theologically precise apostolic anchor for the article's refusal of the glory-deferral trap: peace with God belongs to the justified, who are justified now.

restoration.text: Learn of me, and listen to my words; walk in the meekness of my Spirit, and you shall have peace in me.
restoration.comment: Christ's direct invitation in the Restoration — the most direct echo of John 14:27 in Restoration formulation. The phrase 'peace in me' is decisive: the peace is found in Christ's own person, accessible now to those who learn of Him and walk in His Spirit. The verb 'shall have' (immediate-future) names the peace as present-tense reality for those who walk the path.

restoration.text: But learn that he who doeth the works of righteousness shall receive his reward, even peace in this world, and eternal life in the world to come.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's most theologically precise refusal of the glory-deferral trap. The verse explicitly distinguishes the disciple's two rewards: peace in this world, and eternal life in the world to come. The article's refusal at s9 is anchored here in its sharpest form — peace is named explicitly as a 'this world' reward, not deferred to glory. The Restoration's signature anchor for the doctrinal architecture of present-peace-paired-with-future-completion.

s10.text: We can feel His peace now. We can perceive His power and Spirit operating in our lives to the healing and renewal of our souls
s10.panel_comment: The pneumatological ground of the article — the experiential signature of the kingdom-already-come. Where the triadic refusal at s7–s9 named what the kingdom-now releases the disciple from (death-deferral, perfection-deferral, glory-deferral), s10 names what the kingdom-now gives the disciple to feel and perceive. The compound 'power and Spirit' (Greek δύναμις and πνεῦμα) names both the operative force and the personal agent — the same compound the New Testament uses to describe Christ's own ministry (Acts 10:38) and the Spirit's continuing work in the disciple. The pair 'healing and renewal' is theologically deliberate: healing addresses past wounds (Malachi 4:2, Acts 10:38), renewal addresses ongoing formation (2 Corinthians 4:16, Romans 12:2, Titus 3:5). Together the pair carries both dimensions of the Spirit's work in the soul — what is damaged is healed, what is alive is renewed. The word 'souls' (Hebrew nephesh, Greek psychē) names the whole person, not merely an immaterial element — the Spirit's transforming work reaches the whole of the disciple, not only their spiritual interior. This whole-person anthropology is also more ecumenically receivable than 'spirits' would have been (which can carry trichotomist freight not every reader accepts). The dual verbs 'feel' and 'perceive' name two distinct dimensions of present spiritual experience: feeling is affective and immediate (the disciple knows peace as something experienced); perceiving is cognitive and discerning (the disciple recognizes the Spirit's operations through reflection on her own life). The biblical anchors hold the architecture: Acts 10:38 carries the most direct biblical anchor for the article's word choice ('how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Ghost and with power: who went about doing good, and healing all that were oppressed of the devil') — names the Spirit-and-power compound and the healing operation; 2 Corinthians 4:16 carries the apostolic anchor for ongoing renewal in mortal life ('though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day'); Romans 8:16 carries the Pauline anchor for the Spirit's present bearing-witness ('the Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God') — grounds the article's 'feel' verb in the Spirit's interior operation; Romans 8:26 carries the Pauline anchor for the Spirit's present-tense helping operation ('Likewise the Spirit also helpeth our infirmities… maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered') — grounds the article's 'perceive' verb in the disciple's discernment of the Spirit's continuing work. The Restoration anchors confirm: Mosiah 4:3 carries the most direct anchor for the article's healing/renewal pair almost verbatim ('they were filled with joy, having received a remission of their sins, and having peace of conscience, because of the exceeding faith which they had in Jesus Christ') — peace of conscience (healing of past wounds) and being filled with joy (renewal); 2 Nephi 32:5 carries the Restoration's most direct anchor for the Spirit's present-tense operative guidance ('if ye will enter in by the way, and receive the Holy Ghost, it will show unto you all things what ye should do') — grounds the article's 'perceive' verb in Nephi's signature pneumatology. Pairs with s11 as the experiential ground for the inaugurated-eschatology claim — s10 names what the disciple feels and perceives; s11 names that those experiences are themselves the witness of the kingdom's already-arrival.

biblical.text: How God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Ghost and with power: who went about doing good, and healing all that were oppressed of the devil; for God was with him.
biblical.comment: Peter's apostolic summary of Christ's ministry — names the Holy Ghost-and-power compound and the healing operation that the article echoes. The verbs 'anointed' and 'went about… healing' name the Spirit's operative work as continuing through Christ's ministry and, by extension, through the lives of those filled with the same Spirit. The most direct biblical anchor for the article's word choice. (Reasserted from Article 5 span 11 in different rhetorical direction: at A5 s11 the verse anchors Christ's own ministry as the verbatim source of 'He went about doing good' — type direct, the apostolic description of Christ's mortal labors; here at A7 s10 the same verse anchors the disciple's continuing experience of the same Holy-Ghost-and-power compound operating in their lives. The verse moves from describing what Christ did to naming what the disciple now perceives the Spirit doing.)

biblical.text: For which cause we faint not; but though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day.
biblical.comment: Paul's apostolic anchor for ongoing renewal in mortal life. The verb 'is renewed' (present passive) names renewal not as a one-time event but as the Spirit's continuing daily work in the disciple's interior. The most direct biblical anchor for the article's 'renewal of our souls' phrase — names the renewal as happening day by day, while the outward man yet walks in flesh.

biblical.text: The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God.
biblical.comment: Paul's anchor for the Spirit's present bearing-witness — grounds the article's 'feel' verb in the Spirit's interior operation upon the disciple's own spirit. Names the witness as a co-witness, not a replacement-witness: the Spirit's operation is felt as the disciple's own felt-knowing of being God's child. The most direct biblical anchor for the felt-knowing the article describes. (Reasserted from Article 6 span 5 in different rhetorical direction: at A6 s5 the verse anchors the experiential signature of the Spirit-sealing — what the seal feels like in the disciple's life; here at A7 s10 the verse anchors the Spirit's bearing-witness operation as what the disciple feels of the kingdom's already-arrival. Sister claims with shared experiential register.)

biblical.text: Likewise the Spirit also helpeth our infirmities: for we know not what we should pray for as we ought: but the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered.
biblical.comment: Paul's anchor for the Spirit's present-tense helping operation. Names the Spirit's continuing intercession in the disciple's life — operations that the disciple comes to perceive through reflection on her own infirmities and the Spirit's secret work within them. Grounds the article's 'perceive' verb in the disciple's discernment of the Spirit's continuing presence.

restoration.text: And it came to pass that after they had spoken these words the Spirit of the Lord came upon them, and they were filled with joy, having received a remission of their sins, and having peace of conscience, because of the exceeding faith which they had in Jesus Christ who should come.
restoration.comment: King Benjamin's people receiving the Spirit's transforming work — the most direct Restoration anchor for the article's healing-and-renewal pair almost verbatim. 'Peace of conscience' names the healing of past wounds (the consequence of received remission of sins); 'filled with joy' names the renewal that follows (the present operation of the Spirit upon souls who have come to Christ). The doctrinal architecture the article describes, witnessed in narrative form among Restoration disciples.

restoration.text: For behold, again I say unto you that if ye will enter in by the way, and receive the Holy Ghost, it will show unto you all things what ye should do.
restoration.comment: Nephi's signature anchor for the Spirit's present-tense operative guidance. Names the Holy Ghost not as a future-promised gift but as a present-operating presence given to those who enter in by the way. The most direct Restoration anchor for the article's 'perceive His power and Spirit operating in our lives' claim — the Spirit's continuing operation is what the disciple comes to perceive in her ordinary moments of decision. (Reasserted from Article 4 span 14 in different rhetorical direction: at A4 s14 verses 3–5 together anchor the integration of receiving-truth and right-living through the Spirit's comprehensive guidance; here at A7 s10 verse 5 alone anchors the disciple's perceiving the Spirit's operations in her daily life. The earlier passage names the Spirit's office of guidance; this passage extracts the disciple's perception of that office at work.)

s11.text: These fruits are the witness that the kingdom has already come to those who receive it
s11.panel_comment: The article's most theologically precise eschatological claim — the inaugurated-eschatology position stated explicitly. The phrasing is theologically calibrated with care: the article does not say 'the kingdom is already fully come' (which would be over-realized eschatology, collapsing the future into the present and compromising Article 12 before it arrives); it says 'the kingdom has already come to those who receive it' — kingdom already-arrived in the lives of disciples who have received it, without claiming it has fully arrived in the world. This is the position consistent with serious Christian eschatology across traditions. Two precise theological moves operate here. First, 'these fruits are the witness' grounds the kingdom-now claim in observable evidence rather than institutional authority. The article does not point to the disciple's church membership or sacramental status as proof that the kingdom is at hand; it points to the disciple's experienced rest, joy, peace, healing, and renewal as the lived evidence. This is Christ's own 'by their fruits ye shall know them' principle (Matthew 7:16, 20) applied to the kingdom's present arrival. Second, 'those who receive it' carries the article's container-word reception-discipline forward — the kingdom comes to those who receive it, with reception again left without mechanism. Catholic readers bring sacramental reception, Reformed readers bring effectual call, Restoration readers bring covenant baptism by authority, Pentecostal readers bring Spirit-baptism, Orthodox readers bring entrance into the liturgical life. The verb 'receive' echoes Mark 10:15, where Christ names childlike receiving as the kingdom-entry posture — reception as the opposite of gatekeeping. The biblical anchors hold the architecture: Matthew 7:16, 20 carries the load-bearing dominical anchor for fruits-as-witness ('Ye shall know them by their fruits… Wherefore by their fruits ye shall know them'); Mark 10:15 carries the dominical anchor for kingdom-receiving as the entry-posture ('Verily I say unto you, Whosoever shall not receive the kingdom of God as a little child, he shall not enter therein'); Galatians 5:22–23 carries the apostolic anchor for the full list of fruits the article aggregates as witness ('the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance'); John 13:35 carries the parallel dominical claim that disciples are recognized by their fruit ('By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another'). The Restoration anchors confirm: 3 Nephi 14:16, 20 carries the resurrected Christ's New World repetition of the fruits-witness claim ('Ye shall know them by their fruits… Wherefore, by their fruits ye shall know them'); Moroni 7:5–8 carries Mormon's signature passage on fruit-witness as the test of discipleship ('by their works ye shall know them; for if their works be good, then they are good also'). Note on Galatians 5:22–23 reuse: the verse appeared at s8 in a different rhetorical function (joy as a single fruit of the Spirit, given to imperfect disciples). At s11 the verse functions as the full fruit-list aggregated as the disciple's lived witness of the kingdom's arrival. Cross-reference annotation: see s8 / Galatians 5:22 for the perfection-deferral refusal use. The two uses are genuinely divergent rhetorical functions: s8 extracts a single fruit; s11 names the full list as eschatological evidence. (Reasserted from Article 6 span 12 in different rhetorical direction: at A6 s12 the passage anchors the Spirit's transformative-labors operational signature — what the Spirit's sanctifying work produces empirically in the disciple's life; here at A7 s11 the same passage anchors the eschatological inference from observed fruit to kingdom-arrival. A6 s12 names the fruit as evidence the Spirit is at work; A7 s11 names the fruit as evidence the kingdom has come. Sister claims with distinct doctrinal directions.) Pairs with s10 as the inferential bridge — s10 names what the disciple feels and perceives; s11 names that those experiences are themselves the evidence that the kingdom has come.

biblical.text: Ye shall know them by their fruits. Do men gather grapes of thorns, or figs of thistles?… Wherefore by their fruits ye shall know them.
biblical.comment: Christ's signature dominical principle — the load-bearing biblical anchor for the article's fruits-as-witness claim. The principle is Christ's own answer to the question of how to recognize true discipleship: not by claims, not by credentials, not by institutional placement, but by the fruit observable in lives. The article's move at s11 applies this principle to the kingdom's arrival itself: the kingdom has come where its fruits are observable in the lives of those who have received it.

biblical.text: Verily I say unto you, Whosoever shall not receive the kingdom of God as a little child, he shall not enter therein.
biblical.comment: Christ's anchor for the kingdom-receiving verb the article carries at s11. The image is decisive: the child's reception is the opposite of gatekeeping or institutional control. The kingdom comes to those who receive it as a gift, not those who earn it or qualify for it through credentials. Grounds the article's 'those who receive it' as a posture-claim, not a status-claim.

biblical.text: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance: against such there is no law.
biblical.comment: Paul's apostolic anchor for the full list of fruits the article aggregates as witness. Where s8 extracted joy from this list as a single fruit refusing perfection-deferral, s11 names the full fruit-list as the lived evidence that the Spirit is operating and the kingdom has therefore arrived. The two uses of the verse hold genuinely divergent rhetorical functions: s8 is extractive (one fruit, one refusal), s11 is aggregative (the fruit-list as eschatological evidence).

biblical.text: By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another.
biblical.comment: Christ's parallel claim that disciples are recognized by their fruit — specifically by their love. Names love as the public, observable fruit by which the disciple's identity is testified to the world. Pairs with Matthew 7:16, 20 as the dominical pair on fruit-recognition, with this verse focusing the witness on the disciple's love specifically.

restoration.text: Ye shall know them by their fruits. Do men gather grapes of thorns, or figs of thistles?… Wherefore, by their fruits ye shall know them.
restoration.comment: The resurrected Christ's New World repetition of Matthew 7:16, 20 — verbatim echo of the dominical principle in the Restoration's own scriptural witness. Confirms the article's fruits-witness claim with the additional weight of the Restoration's confirming witness to the same dominical teaching. The Book of Mormon's most direct anchor for the article's central inferential move at s11.

restoration.text: For I remember the word of God which saith by their works ye shall know them; for if their works be good, then they are good also. For behold, God hath said a man being evil cannot do that which is good… For behold, a bitter fountain cannot bring forth good water; neither can a good fountain bring forth bitter water; wherefore, a man being a servant of the devil cannot follow Christ; and if he follow Christ he cannot be a servant of the devil.
restoration.comment: Mormon's signature passage on fruit-witness as the test of discipleship. The fountain-and-water imagery names the deep ontological connection between the disciple's interior reality and her observable fruit — the kingdom's arrival in the soul produces fruit consistent with that arrival, and the absence of fruit testifies to the kingdom's absence. The Restoration's most precise anchor for the article's inferential move from observed-fruit to kingdom-arrival.

s12.text: and who seek to build it
s12.panel_comment: The article's dual-disposition refinement — kingdom-reception paired with kingdom-building. Where s11 named those who receive the kingdom as the disciples in whose lives the kingdom has already come, s12 corrects any reading of s11 that would make kingdom-reception purely interior or passive. The disciple receives the kingdom; the disciple also seeks to build it. The two dispositions are inseparable in Christ's own teaching: those who receive the kingdom are called to pray for its coming, to labor in its harvest, and to participate in its growth. The verb 'seek to build' is theologically precise — it names the disciple's active disposition without claiming that the disciple constructs the kingdom by her own works. The kingdom is built by God, but disciples are summoned to participate in the building as labourers together with Him. The biblical anchors hold the architecture: Matthew 6:10 carries the load-bearing dominical anchor for present-tense kingdom-building participation — the Lord's Prayer petition Christ taught His disciples to pray ('Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven'); Matthew 13:31–33 carries the dominical kingdom-growth parables of mustard seed and leaven, naming the kingdom as a present-tense growing reality through which the disciple participates by being the soil in which the seed grows and the meal in which the leaven works; 1 Corinthians 3:9 carries Paul's apostolic anchor for the disciple's active kingdom-labor participation ('we are labourers together with God: ye are God's husbandry, ye are God's building'). The Restoration anchors confirm: D&C 4:2–4 carries the canonical Restoration kingdom-labor passage, echoing Matthew 9:37–38's harvest imagery and naming the disciple's active embarkation in the work ('therefore, O ye that embark in the service of God, see that ye serve him with all your heart, might, mind and strength… For behold the field is white already to harvest'); Alma 26:5 carries Ammon's witness of the kingdom-harvest already underway ('ye behold that the field was ripe, and blessed are ye, for ye did thrust in the sickle, and did reap with your might'). Container-word discipline holds: 'seek to build it' refuses to specify what kingdom-building looks like institutionally — Catholic readers bring sacramental and ecclesial building, Reformed readers bring Word-and-deed witness, Restoration readers bring covenant-keeping and ordinance-administration, Pentecostal readers bring evangelism and Spirit-empowered ministry. The article does not adjudicate the form; it names the disposition. The s11–s12 pairing balances the article's previous container-word emphasis on reception with the active-participation disposition that completes the disciple's relationship to the kingdom. Pairs with s4 and s5 as the kingdom-now triad of dispositions: enter (s4), live in (s5), build (s12).

biblical.text: Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven.
biblical.comment: The Lord's Prayer petition Christ taught His disciples to pray — the load-bearing dominical anchor for present-tense kingdom-building participation. The petition is not 'we will build the kingdom' but 'Thy kingdom come' — the disciple's active participation is invocational, not constructional. The kingdom comes by God's hand; the disciple is summoned to ask for its coming and to labor in alignment with that prayer. The most concise biblical anchor for the article's 'seek to build it' verb.

biblical.text: The kingdom of heaven is like to a grain of mustard seed, which a man took, and sowed in his field: which indeed is the least of all seeds: but when it is grown, it is the greatest among herbs, and becometh a tree, so that the birds of the air come and lodge in the branches thereof. Another parable spake he unto them; The kingdom of heaven is like unto leaven, which a woman took, and hid in three measures of meal, till the whole was leavened.
biblical.comment: Christ's classic dominical kingdom-growth parables — mustard seed and leaven. Both parables name the kingdom as a present-tense growing reality from a small beginning to a great consummation. The disciple's role is to be the soil in which the seed grows and the meal in which the leaven works — active participation in kingdom-growth without constructional claim. Grounds the article's 'seek to build' as a participatory disposition aligned with the kingdom's own organic growth.

biblical.text: For we are labourers together with God: ye are God's husbandry, ye are God's building.
biblical.comment: Paul's apostolic anchor for the disciple's active kingdom-labor participation. The phrase 'labourers together with God' (Greek συνεργοί, synergoi, 'co-workers') names the disciple's role as active collaborator in the kingdom-work, not as passive recipient only. Paul's threefold 'God's husbandry, God's building' names the kingdom as both organic (husbandry/farming) and constructed (building) — the article's 'seek to build it' echoes the second pole of Paul's compound.

restoration.text: Therefore, O ye that embark in the service of God, see that ye serve him with all your heart, might, mind and strength, that ye may stand blameless before God at the last day. Therefore, if ye have desires to serve God ye are called to the work; For behold the field is white already to harvest; and lo, he that thrusteth in his sickle with his might, the same layeth up in store that he perisheth not, but bringeth salvation to his soul.
restoration.comment: The canonical Restoration kingdom-labor passage — Joseph Sr.'s revelation echoing Matthew 9:37–38's harvest imagery directly. The phrase 'embark in the service of God' names the disciple's active disposition of kingdom-building participation; 'the field is white already to harvest' names the kingdom-work as present-tense and ongoing. The most direct Restoration anchor for the article's 'seek to build it' verb.

restoration.text: And now behold, my brethren, what natural brother can boast of more than we can boast? Have we not reason to rejoice? Yea, I say unto you, there never were men that had so great reason to rejoice as we, since the world began; yea, and my joy is carried away, even unto boasting in my God; for he has all power, all wisdom, and all understanding; he comprehendeth all things, and he is a merciful Being, even unto salvation, to those who will repent and believe on his name. For behold, ye behold that the field was ripe, and blessed are ye, for ye did thrust in the sickle, and did reap with your might, yea, all the day long did ye toil.
restoration.comment: Ammon's witness of the kingdom-harvest already underway. Names the disciple's active kingdom-labor in the missionary work among the Lamanites — concrete present-tense participation in kingdom-building. The phrases 'thrust in the sickle' and 'reap with your might' name the disciple's active disposition; 'all the day long did ye toil' names the sustained character of kingdom-labor. The Restoration's most direct narrative witness of disciples engaged in kingdom-building.

s13.text: His will is that we should live — really live — beginning now
s13.panel_comment: The article's closing affirmation — pastoral, providential, and life-affirming. The full sentence preceding s13 ('The Father's will was never that we should merely endure mortality while awaiting Him') names the providence claim that grounds s13: the Father's purpose for mortal life is not mere endurance but real living. The article's closing move shifts register decisively. Through the previous twelve spans the article has held a creedal-declarative voice; at s13 it breaks through that formality with the colloquial phrase 'really live' — letting the reader hear their own voice in the text. The conversational register is theologically deliberate, not stylistically careless: the article's pastoral purpose is to free the disciple's experience of the kingdom from any precondition that would defer it, and the colloquial register completes that freeing by making the closing affirmation directly receivable rather than mediated through high creedal language. The phrase 'really live' is an explicit echo of Christ's John 10:10 abundant-life promise — the verse already anchored at s5 (where it grounded the fact of present-tense eternal life). At s13 the verse functions in a divergent rhetorical role: not as the fact-anchor for life-begun-now, but as the will-anchor for the Father's purpose-of-our-living. The disciple already has abundant life as fact (s5); the Father wills for the disciple to live that abundant life as His paternal purpose for them (s13). The biblical anchors hold the architecture: John 6:39–40 carries the load-bearing anchor naming the Father's will explicitly ('this is the Father's will which hath sent me, that of all which he hath given me I should lose nothing… that every one which seeth the Son, and believeth on him, may have everlasting life: and I will raise him up at the last day') — the verse pairs the Father's will with both present-tense everlasting life (the article's closing affirmation) and future-tense resurrection (the future-pole the article preserves throughout); Deuteronomy 30:19–20 carries the OT prophetic anchor for Moses's signature 'choose life' call ('I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life, that both thou and thy seed may live: that thou mayest love the Lord thy God, and that thou mayest obey his voice, and that thou mayest cleave unto him: for he is thy life'); John 10:10 carries the dominical anchor for the abundant-life promise the article's 'really live' explicitly echoes — reused from s5 with divergent rhetorical function (s5: present-tense fact of abundant life; s13: Father's will that we should live that abundant life); Romans 14:17 carries the Pauline anchor for the kingdom's character ('the kingdom of God is not meat and drink; but righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost') — names the kingdom-life as the Spirit's joy, peace, and righteousness, completing the inclusio with the rest/joy/peace triad of s7–s9. The Restoration anchors confirm: Moses 1:39 carries the most concise Restoration statement of the Father's will ('For behold, this is my work and my glory — to bring to pass the immortality and eternal life of man') — pairs the Father's will with both immortality (future-pole, the consummation) and eternal life (already-begun-now, the article's whole movement); 1 Nephi 17:36 carries Nephi's signature anchor for the Father's purpose for mortal life ('Behold, the Lord hath created the earth that it should be inhabited; and he hath created his children that they should possess it') — the Restoration's most direct refusal of mortality-as-mere-endurance, naming inhabitation and possession as the disciple's birthright purpose. Note on John 10:10 reuse: the verse appeared at s5 in a different rhetorical function (Christ's signature abundant-life claim grounding the fact of present-tense eternal life). At s13 the verse functions as the will-anchor for the Father's purpose-of-our-living. The two uses are genuinely divergent rhetorical functions: s5 is fact-grounding (life is begun now), s13 is will-grounding (the Father wills for that begun-life to be lived). Cross-reference annotation: see s5 / John 10:10 for the fact-of-abundant-life use. The s13 closing completes the article's threefold relational architecture: Christ proclaims (s2), the Father wills (s13), the Spirit operates (s10) — naming each Person's distinct work in the kingdom-now economy without theological speculation about their inter-relations.

biblical.text: And this is the Father's will which hath sent me, that of all which he hath given me I should lose nothing, but should raise it up again at the last day. And this is the will of him that sent me, that every one which seeth the Son, and believeth on him, may have everlasting life: and I will raise him up at the last day.
biblical.comment: Christ's two-fold naming of the Father's will — the load-bearing biblical anchor for the article's closing affirmation. The verses pair the Father's will with both present-tense everlasting life ('may have everlasting life') and future-tense resurrection ('I will raise him up at the last day'), preserving the already/not-yet architecture the article has held throughout. The most direct biblical anchor for the article's claim that the Father wills for the disciple to live, beginning now.

biblical.text: I call heaven and earth to record this day against you, that I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life, that both thou and thy seed may live: That thou mayest love the Lord thy God, and that thou mayest obey his voice, and that thou mayest cleave unto him: for he is thy life, and the length of thy days.
biblical.comment: Moses's signature 'choose life' call — the OT prophetic anchor for the article's life-affirming closing posture. The verbs 'choose life' and 'cleave unto him' name the disciple's active disposition aligned with God-as-life-source. The phrase 'for he is thy life' grounds the article's closing affirmation in the OT prophetic claim that real life is not life-apart-from-God but life-cleaving-to-God. (Reasserted from Article 3 span 3 in different rhetorical direction: at A3 s3 verse 19 alone anchors divinely-endowed agency — Moses placing life and death before Israel and commanding the choice; here at A7 s13 verses 19–20 together anchor the Father's will-claim that the disciple should live abundantly, with verse 20's 'for he is thy life' carrying the relational weight Moses's verse 19 makes the precondition for. The passage moves from the choice itself at A3 to the life that the choice opens at A7.)

biblical.text: I am come that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly.
biblical.comment: Christ's dominical anchor for the abundant-life promise — the verse the article's 'really live' explicitly echoes. Reused from s5 (where it anchored the fact of present-tense eternal life) with divergent rhetorical function: at s13 the verse anchors the Father's will-purpose for the disciple's abundant-living, not the fact-claim about that living's accessibility. See cross-reference to s5 for the fact-anchor use.

biblical.text: For the kingdom of God is not meat and drink; but righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost.
biblical.comment: Paul's apostolic anchor for the kingdom's character. The verse names the kingdom-life specifically as the Spirit's righteousness, peace, and joy — completing the article's inclusio with explicit echo of the rest/joy/peace triad at s7–s9. Grounds the article's closing affirmation in Paul's most direct apostolic statement that the kingdom is qualitatively a Spirit-life, not a future-circumstance.

restoration.text: For behold, this is my work and my glory — to bring to pass the immortality and eternal life of man.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's most concise statement of the Father's will. Names the divine purpose with theological precision: the Father's work and glory is to bring to pass both immortality (the future-pole consummation) and eternal life (the already-begun-now, the article's whole movement). Pairs both poles in one verse, the architecture the article has carried throughout from s1's 'not only promised for a distant day' to s13's 'beginning now.' The most direct Restoration anchor for the article's closing affirmation. (Reasserted from Article 3 span 1 in different rhetorical direction: at A3 s1 verses 33 and 39 together anchor creation's teleology — God naming the cosmic scope of creation and its purpose; here at A7 s13 verse 39 alone anchors the Father's will-claim for the disciple's living. Same verse, two distinct doctrinal moments: at A3 the cosmic purpose of creation; at A7 the personal purpose for the soul who lives within that creation.)

restoration.text: Behold, the Lord hath created the earth that it should be inhabited; and he hath created his children that they should possess it.
restoration.comment: Nephi's signature anchor for the Father's purpose for mortal life. The verbs 'inhabited' and 'should possess it' name the disciple's birthright purpose as active mortal possession of the earth, not passive endurance of mortality. The Restoration's most direct refusal of the mortality-as-mere-endurance reading the article rejects in the sentence preceding s13. Grounds the article's closing affirmation in the doctrinal claim that the Father created His children for real living within mortal life, not for waiting through it.

crossref.title: Creation and Life

s14.text: merely endure mortality while awaiting Him
s14.panel_comment: The article's penultimate move — the negation that grounds s13's positive affirmation. The phrase makes a paired denial: that the Father's will for mortality is mere endurance, and that the disciple's posture toward Him is mere awaiting. Both denials carry explicit scriptural witness. Christ Himself names mortality as the working-day, not the awaiting-night (John 9:4); the disciple's posture is to actively run the race set before us (Hebrews 12:1); even Isaiah's 'waiting upon the Lord' is strength-renewal, not passivity (Isaiah 40:31); the parable of the Talents judges merely-awaiting servants while commending those who acted in the Master's absence (Matthew 25:14–30). The Restoration confirms: Amulek refuses procrastination as the Father's purpose for mortal life (Alma 34:33–34); modern revelation names His will as anxious engagement of free agency (D&C 58:27–28). s13 names this span as its grounding providence claim; together they form the article's closing pair.

biblical.text: I must work the works of him that sent me, while it is day: the night cometh, when no man can work.
biblical.comment: Christ Himself naming mortality as the working-day. The verbs 'must work' and 'while it is day' frame the present life as the active vocation, not as a holding pattern. The contrast with 'the night cometh, when no man can work' makes mortality's working window a positive theological fact rather than a survival horizon. The dominical anchor for the negation that the Father's will is mere endurance.

biblical.text: Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us.
biblical.comment: The disciple's posture under the Father's purpose — actively running the race set before us, not awaiting its end. The hortatory subjunctive 'let us run' (Greek τρέχωμεν) names the present participation in the disciple's vocation. Cross-reference annotation: the cluster carries Hebrews 12:2 at A4 s13 and A5 s16, where the verse anchors Christ as the author and finisher of faith. Here verse 1 functions distinctly — the disciple's posture toward the Father's set-before-us race, distinct from the Christological capstone of verse 2.

biblical.text: But they that wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.
biblical.comment: The OT prophetic anchor reframing 'waiting' itself. The Hebrew קָוָה (qavah) names not passive expectation but active hopeful expectancy — the verb in cognate forms produces the verbs 'mount up,' 'run,' and 'walk' that follow. The 'awaiting Him' the article negates is therefore not biblical waiting but its counterfeit. Cross-reference annotation: A4 s10 carries Isaiah 40:8 (the word that standeth forever) — different chapter-section, different rhetorical work.

biblical.text: For the kingdom of heaven is as a man travelling into a far country, who called his own servants, and delivered unto them his goods… After a long time the lord of those servants cometh, and reckoneth with them.
biblical.comment: The parable of the Talents — Christ's most direct judgment on the merely-awaiting posture. The unprofitable servant who 'hid' the talent and awaited the Master's return is condemned not for losing the gift but for failing to engage it; the servants commended are those who 'traded' (Greek εἰργάσατο, 'worked with') what they were given. Cross-reference annotation: A7 s1 carries Matthew 25:31–34 (the Sheep and Goats pericope), which anchors the future-consummation pole the article concedes. Here Matthew 25:14–30 anchors the active stewardship Christ commends in the Master's absence — different parable in the same chapter, distinct rhetorical function.

restoration.text: And now, my brethren, I would that, after ye have received so many witnesses, seeing that the holy scriptures testify of these things, ye come forth and bring fruit unto repentance. Yea, I would that ye would come forth and harden not your hearts any longer; for behold, now is the time and the day of your salvation; and therefore, if ye will repent and harden not your hearts, immediately shall the great plan of redemption be brought about unto you. For behold, this life is the time for men to prepare to meet God; yea, behold the day of this life is the day for men to perform their labors. And now, as I said unto you before, as ye have had so many witnesses, therefore, I beseech of you that ye do not procrastinate the day of your repentance until the end.
restoration.comment: Amulek's signature anti-procrastination passage. The verses name mortality explicitly as the working-day: 'this life is the time for men to prepare to meet God; yea, behold the day of this life is the day for men to perform their labors.' The injunction against procrastination directly negates the merely-awaiting posture the article rejects. Cross-reference annotation: A6 s3 carries Alma 34:31–32, which grounds the immediate appeal of faith for salvation. Here verses 33–34 anchor mortality's positive vocation under the Father's purpose — a distinct rhetorical function on the same Amulek discourse.

restoration.text: Verily I say, men should be anxiously engaged in a good cause, and do many things of their own free will, and bring to pass much righteousness; for the power is in them, wherein they are agents unto themselves. And inasmuch as men do good they shall in nowise lose their reward.
restoration.comment: Modern revelation framing the Father's will explicitly as anxious engagement of free agency rather than awaiting commands. The phrase 'agents unto themselves' names the disciple as commissioned actor in the Father's purpose, not as recipient awaiting deployment. Cross-reference annotation: A3 s9 carries D&C 58:42–43 (the Lord's forgiveness of confessed sin) — same section, completely distinct pericope and rhetorical function.

s1.text: We receive every soul who comes to Jesus Christ as brother, as sister, as fellow child of the same Father
s1.panel_comment: The article's opening reception thesis. The sentence carries three distinct theological claims welded into one declaration: a Christological criterion (comes to Jesus Christ), a relational triad (brother, sister, fellow child), and a paternal common ground (the same Father). The grammatical hinge is the comma series after Christ — every soul who comes to Him is received as the threefold relational kin. The Christological criterion governs the universality; the paternal claim grounds the relational triad in shared divine sonship. The biblical anchors hold the foundation: Galatians 3:26–28 names how all who are in Christ Jesus are children of God and the dividing markers of ethnicity, status, and gender are subordinated to that shared identity; Romans 8:14–17 names the Spirit of adoption by which we cry Abba, Father, making the divine sonship operational rather than honorary; Matthew 12:48–50 records Christ's own redefinition of family — whoever does the will of His Father is His brother, sister, and mother — the dominical anchor for the relational triad the article uses; Ephesians 4:4–6 grounds the article's catholicity in apostolic confession (one body, one Spirit, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all). The Restoration anchors confirm and deepen: Mosiah 5:7 carries King Benjamin's covenant rebirth language — those who covenant with Christ become His sons and daughters, with the family-claim grounded in Christ's own paternity in the new covenant; 2 Nephi 26:33 carries the Restoration's most sweeping universality claim — Christ denies none who come to Him, and all are alike unto God. (Reasserted from Article 1 Span 12 in different rhetorical direction: at A1 s12 the verse anchors that no soul is barred from Christ for lacking perfect understanding — the soteriological negation; here at A8 s1 the verse anchors that those received in Christ are received as family — the relational positive ground. A1 names what Christ never excludes; A8 names what Christ thereby includes.) Moses 6:8–9 supplies the foundational creation-paternity claim — every soul is a child of Adam, who is a child of God — naming the universal paternity by creation that holds for every soul regardless of covenant status. Together with Mosiah 5:7 the two poles carry the article's reception thesis: every soul is already a child of God by creation (the floor); those who come to Christ are received as kin in covenant (the article's positive claim). The article does not adjudicate the deeper theological questions about how the divine paternity operates (literal pre-mortal Fatherhood as Latter-day Saint readers carry it; creational and adoptive Fatherhood as Trinitarian traditions carry it) — that work belongs to Article 2 and to the cluster's container-word discipline. This span only names the door: those who come to Christ are received as kin, on the ground of a Father common to all.

biblical.text: For ye are all the children of God by faith in Christ Jesus. For as many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ. There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus.
biblical.comment: Paul's foundational statement — the dividing markers of ethnicity, social status, and gender are subordinated to shared identity in Christ. The phrase 'all one in Christ Jesus' names the catholicity the article opens with; 'children of God by faith in Christ Jesus' names the paternal ground the article rests on. The single most concentrated biblical anchor for the article's reception thesis.

biblical.text: For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, they are the sons of God. For ye have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear; but ye have received the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father. The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God: And if children, then heirs; heirs of God, and joint-heirs with Christ.
biblical.comment: Paul names the operational mechanism by which the divine sonship is real to the disciple — the Spirit of adoption witnessing with the disciple's own spirit. The Aramaic 'Abba' makes the paternal claim intimate, not formal. The pairing with 'joint-heirs with Christ' grounds the brother/sister relation the article carries: those received as kin are joint-heirs with Christ Himself.

biblical.text: But he answered and said unto him that told him, Who is my mother? and who are my brethren? And he stretched forth his hand toward his disciples, and said, Behold my mother and my brethren! For whosoever shall do the will of my Father which is in heaven, the same is my brother, and sister, and mother.
biblical.comment: The dominical anchor for the relational triad. Christ Himself redefines family from biological to covenantal — whoever does the will of His Father is His brother, sister, and mother. The article's 'brother, sister, fellow child' echoes Christ's own grouping in Matthew 12:50 with high fidelity. Notable: Christ's redefinition is grounded in doing the Father's will, not in doctrinal completeness — consistent with A1 s18's negation that Christ never required theological sorting before fellowship.

biblical.text: There is one body, and one Spirit, even as ye are called in one hope of your calling; One Lord, one faith, one baptism, One God and Father of all, who is above all, and through all, and in you all.
biblical.comment: The apostolic catholicity confession — sevenfold 'one' binding the body of Christ to the Father common to all. The closing phrase 'Father of all, who is above all, and through all, and in you all' is the most concentrated NT statement of the paternal common ground the article rests on. Anticipates s7 (the body of Christ larger than any single denomination) by establishing the apostolic frame.

restoration.text: And now, because of the covenant which ye have made ye shall be called the children of Christ, his sons, and his daughters; for behold, this day he hath spiritually begotten you; for ye say that your hearts are changed through faith on his name; therefore, ye are born of him and have become his sons and his daughters.
restoration.comment: King Benjamin's covenant-rebirth language. Names the operational mechanism by which those who come to Christ become His sons and daughters — spiritual begetting through faith on His name and heart-change. The Restoration's most direct articulation of the family-claim grounded in covenant rather than biology. Pairs with Galatians 3:26 (children of God by faith) as the cross-canonical witness that covenant relation, not lineage, is the Christian family-ground.

restoration.text: He inviteth them all to come unto him and partake of his goodness; and he denieth none that come unto him, black and white, bond and free, male and female; and he remembereth the heathen; and all are alike unto God, both Jew and Gentile.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's most sweeping universality statement, with explicit verbal echo of Galatians 3:26–28's dividing-marker subordination ('black and white, bond and free, male and female' / 'neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female'). Reasserted from Article 1 Span 12 in different rhetorical direction: at A1 s12 the verse anchors that no soul is barred from Christ for lacking perfect understanding — the soteriological negation against gatekeeping. Here at A8 s1 the verse anchors that those received in Christ are received as kin — the relational positive ground. A1 names what Christ never excludes; A8 names what Christ thereby includes. Same verse, distinct doctrinal moments in the cluster's architecture.

restoration.text: Now this same Priesthood, which was in the beginning, shall be in the end of the world also. Now this prophecy Adam spake, as he was moved upon by the Holy Ghost, and a genealogy was kept of the children of God. And this was the book of the generations of Adam, saying: In the day that God created man, in the likeness of God made he him; In the image of his own body, male and female, created he them, and blessed them, and called their name Adam, in the day when they were created and became living souls in the land upon the footstool of God.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's foundational creation-paternity anchor. The phrase 'the genealogy of the children of God' (and verse 22's 'genealogy of the sons of Adam, who was the son of God') names the divine paternity at the level of creation itself — every soul is a child of Adam, who is a child of God. The article's 'fellow child of the same Father' rests on this paternal common ground that holds across humanity by creation regardless of covenant status. Pairs with Mosiah 5:7 as the cluster's two-pole Restoration paternity witness: Moses 6:8–9 names the universal paternity by creation that holds for every soul; Mosiah 5:7 names the covenantal sonship and daughtership added when souls come to Christ. The article's reception thesis stands on both poles together.
