s2.panel_comment: The universality clause held as standalone span. The phrase carries the weight of every gatekeeping refusal the article will make: 'every' admits no qualifier — not doctrinal completeness, not denominational alignment, not liturgical conformity, not credential, not credal precision. Where s1 names the reception relation, s2 names the scope of that reception with byte-level precision. The biblical anchors carry the universal scope explicit: John 3:16 names 'whosoever believeth' as the Greek 'pas ho pisteuon' — every-one-who-believes, with no qualifier admitted; Romans 10:13 carries Joel's prophetic universal 'whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved,' the Pauline foundation for universal-call evangelism; 1 Timothy 2:3–4 names God's salvific will as 'all men' with explicit 'who will have all men to be saved' extension; Revelation 22:17 closes the canon with 'whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely' — the final invitational universal in scripture. The Restoration anchors confirm at maximum scope: 2 Nephi 26:33 (already cited at s1 in the relational direction; reasserted here for the universality direction with rhetorical-divergence note); Alma 5:33 carries Christ's pastoral universal 'Behold, he sendeth an invitation unto all men, for the arms of mercy are extended towards them'; Moroni 8:17 carries the most sweeping Restoration affirmation that 'all are alike and partakers of salvation.' Pairs with A1 s12 (no soul barred from Christ for lacking perfect understanding) as the affirmative universal counterpart to A1's negative universal: A1 s12 names what is not required for reception; A8 s2 names that every soul is received without qualification. The two universals together close the gatekeeping question completely.

biblical.text: For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.
biblical.comment: The most universally received biblical statement of universal scope — 'whosoever' (Greek pas ho pisteuon, every-one-who-believes) with no qualifier admitted. The verse Christian tradition has memorized across every denomination as the foundational universal-offer text. Reasserted from Article 1 Span 12 in different rhetorical direction: at A1 s12 the verse anchors that no soul is barred from salvation for lacking perfect understanding (the soteriological direction); here at A8 s2 the verse anchors the universal scope of the article's reception (the ecclesial direction). Same verse, two distinct moments in the cluster's architecture.

biblical.text: For whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.
biblical.comment: Paul quoting Joel 2:32 and applying it explicitly to the universal call of the gospel. The verse's surrounding context (Romans 10:9–13) is the Pauline foundation for universal-call evangelism — 'there is no difference between the Jew and the Greek: for the same Lord over all is rich unto all that call upon him.' Reasserted from Article 1 Span 12 in different rhetorical direction: at A1 s12 the verse grounds the universal salvific offer; here at A8 s2 it grounds the universal ecclesial reception. The same Christological universal under two doctrinal aspects.

biblical.text: For this is good and acceptable in the sight of God our Saviour; Who will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth.
biblical.comment: Paul's most concentrated statement of God's salvific will toward 'all men.' The phrase 'will have all men to be saved' names divine intent at the broadest possible scope. The pairing with 'come unto the knowledge of the truth' anticipates the article's distinction between Christ-reception (the universal scope) and theological completeness (which the article elsewhere refuses to make a precondition).

biblical.text: And the Spirit and the bride say, Come. And let him that heareth say, Come. And let him that is athirst come. And whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely.
biblical.comment: The closing verse-cluster of the canon — the final invitational universal in scripture. The Spirit, the bride (the Church), and the disciple all speak the same word: 'Come.' The phrase 'whosoever will, let him take' is the most concentrated NT statement of universal availability without precondition. Anticipates s17 (free, plain, and without price) by establishing the closing-canon resonance.

restoration.text: He inviteth them all to come unto him and partake of his goodness; and he denieth none that come unto him, black and white, bond and free, male and female; and he remembereth the heathen; and all are alike unto God, both Jew and Gentile.
restoration.comment: Reasserted from s1 above in different rhetorical direction. At s1 the verse anchors the relational kin-claim — those received are received as family. Here at s2 the verse anchors the universal scope — 'every soul' is the article's verbal echo of 'all are alike unto God.' The cluster's most-reused universality verse, doing distinct work at each surfacing.

restoration.text: Behold, he sendeth an invitation unto all men, for the arms of mercy are extended towards them, and he saith: Repent, and I will receive you.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's most pastorally direct universal-invitation statement. The phrase 'arms of mercy are extended towards them' names the divine posture toward 'all men' before any human response. The verb 'receive' in Christ's first-person voice ('I will receive you') is the article's own opening verb — Christ's self-naming of the act the article carries forward.

restoration.text: And I am filled with charity, which is everlasting love; wherefore, all children are alike unto me; wherefore, I love little children with a perfect love; and they are all alike and partakers of salvation.
restoration.comment: Mormon's most sweeping affirmation of universal participation in salvation. Reasserted from Article 1 Span 12 in different rhetorical direction: at A1 s12 the verse anchors the universality of salvation against gatekeeping; here at A8 s2 it anchors the universality of reception in the body of Christ. Same passage, distinct ecclesial vs. soteriological functions.

s3.panel_comment: The Christological criterion that qualifies s2's universality without compromising it. The article's reception is Christological, not credal — every soul who comes to Jesus Christ, not every soul who has subscribed to a creed nor every soul who has been institutionally received. The verb 'comes to' is theologically deliberate and editorially load-bearing: it carries Christ's own invitation language and was specifically chosen during the April 22, 2026 revision pass over the alternative 'confesses' precisely to encompass both articulated confessors and souls in motion toward Christ before articulation. 'Confesses' (Romans 10:9) names a speech-act — articulated, declarative, the moment the disciple verbally affirms Christ. 'Comes to' names the movement that includes the speech-act and reaches earlier — the drawing before the declaring, the seeking before the finding, the approach before the confession. Christ's own invitation language is built on 'come': Matthew 11:28's 'Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest'; John 6:37's 'him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out'; John 7:37's 'If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink.' Each names the relationship Christ Himself welcomes, with the verb at the center of the welcome. The article's reception thus tracks Christ's own reception — receiving the souls Christ Himself names His own as those who come to Him. The biblical anchors hold this Christological criterion at apostolic depth: the three 'come' invitations from Christ's mortal ministry, and Hebrews 11:6 carrying the Christological grammar at its most foundational ('he that cometh to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him') — naming the verb as the disciple's standing posture toward God Himself. The Restoration anchors confirm and extend: 3 Nephi 9:14 records the resurrected Christ in Bountiful issuing the post-Resurrection universal invitation in Christ's own first-person voice ('Yea, verily I say unto you, if ye will come unto me ye shall have eternal life'); 3 Nephi 12:19–20 carries the Sermon at the Temple's beatitude-opener with explicit 'come unto me' phrasing for the contrite of heart; D&C 88:63 carries Christ's modern-revelation reaffirmation in Doctrine and Covenants form ('draw near unto me and I will draw near unto you; seek me diligently and ye shall find me; ask, and ye shall receive; knock, and it shall be opened unto you'). The verb 'comes to' is the article's hermeneutical key — it is the thing the article's reception thesis is calibrated to, and it is Christ Himself who set the calibration.

biblical.text: Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
biblical.comment: Christ's signature invitation. The most concentrated dominical anchor for the verb 'come' as the standing posture toward Him. The universal scope ('all ye that labour and are heavy laden') and the relational promise ('I will give you rest') make this the foundational text for the article's Christological criterion. The verb is at the center of Christ's own reception of the weary.

biblical.text: All that the Father giveth me shall come to me; and him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.
biblical.comment: Christ's most direct articulation of the reception promise the article echoes. The double 'come' — those given by the Father come, and those who come are not cast out — frames the entire Christological reception structure. The phrase 'in no wise cast out' (Greek ou me ekbalo exo, double-negative emphatic) is the strongest grammatical denial of rejection in the New Testament. The article's 'we receive every soul who comes' tracks Christ's own 'I will in no wise cast out him that cometh.'

biblical.text: In the last day, that great day of the feast, Jesus stood and cried, saying, If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink.
biblical.comment: Christ's public proclamation at the Feast of Tabernacles — the third of the great 'come' invitations alongside Matthew 11:28 and John 6:37. The setting (the great day of the feast, water-pouring liturgy) gives the verb 'come' its richest sacramental resonance. 'Any man' matches the article's 'every soul' at the universality scope.

biblical.text: But without faith it is impossible to please him: for he that cometh to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him.
biblical.comment: The apostolic anchor for the verb 'come' as the standing posture toward God Himself. The faith required is minimal and foundational — 'that he is, and that he is a rewarder' — not doctrinally elaborate. The article's Christological criterion echoes this foundation: the disciple comes; what is required is the coming and the believing-He-is, not theological completeness. Pairs with John 6:37 as the cross-Testamental witness that the verb 'come' names the Christian's defining posture.

restoration.text: Yea, verily I say unto you, if ye will come unto me ye shall have eternal life. Behold, mine arm of mercy is extended towards you, and whosoever will come, him will I receive; and blessed are those who come unto me.
restoration.comment: The resurrected Christ's universal invitation in His own first-person voice — issued in the Bountiful theophany. The triple 'come' ('if ye will come... whosoever will come... blessed are those who come') is the most concentrated Christological invitation in Restoration scripture. The phrase 'him will I receive' uses the article's own opening verb in Christ's first-person — Christ's own naming of the reception the article performs. The strongest single Restoration anchor for the article's Christological criterion.

restoration.text: And behold, I have given you the law and the commandments of my Father, that ye shall believe in me, and that ye shall repent of your sins, and come unto me with a broken heart and a contrite spirit. Behold, ye have the commandments before you, and the law is fulfilled.
restoration.comment: The resurrected Christ's Sermon at the Temple, opening the beatitudes with the explicit 'come unto me' phrasing for the contrite of heart. The pairing with the broken heart and contrite spirit (the post-Pentecost beatitude register) names what 'coming to Christ' requires of the disciple's interior — not doctrinal alignment, but humility and contrition. The Restoration's most direct dominical anchor for the qualitative content of the verb 'come.'

restoration.text: Draw near unto me and I will draw near unto you; seek me diligently and ye shall find me; ask, and ye shall receive; knock, and it shall be opened unto you.
restoration.comment: Christ's modern-revelation reaffirmation of the 'come' invitation in Doctrine and Covenants form. The verbal cluster ('draw near,' 'seek,' 'ask,' 'knock') is a fourfold expansion of the single dominical verb 'come,' with each naming a posture Christ welcomes. The chiasmic 'draw near unto me / I will draw near unto you' mirrors John 6:37's 'him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out' — the same Christological reception in modern-revelation form.

s4.text: We love them whether they return our love or not
s4.panel_comment: The first of the article's three unconditional clauses, naming Christ's love-without-reciprocation as the disciple's standing posture. The clause radicalizes the second great commandment by removing the implicit reciprocity that fallen love depends on — we love whether or not love returns to us. The biblical anchors carry the dominical and apostolic foundation: Matthew 5:43–48 records Christ's most direct anti-reciprocity instruction, with the closing line ('what reward have ye? do not even the publicans the same?') making transactional love the very thing Christ's love transcends; Luke 6:32–35 carries the parallel with the most concentrated NT phrase against love-as-transaction, 'lend, hoping for nothing again'; Romans 5:8 supplies the theological ground — God commendeth His love toward us 'while we were yet sinners,' before any return was possible, naming the pattern the article asks the disciple to imitate; 1 John 4:19–21 closes the door to pretending love-of-God while withholding love-of-neighbor, the Johannine grammatical anchor for the impossibility of selective love. The Restoration anchors confirm and extend: Moroni 7:45–48 (reasserted from Article 1 Span 19 with rhetorical-divergence note) names the texture of love that endures non-reciprocation — 'suffereth long, beareth all things, endureth all things' — distinct from A1 s19's commandment-content function; 3 Nephi 12:43–48 carries the resurrected Christ's Bountiful sermon, His own first-person dominical reaffirmation of the Sermon on the Mount's love ethic in Western-hemisphere voice; D&C 121:41–46 supplies the Liberty Jail revelation's pastoral pattern — 'long-suffering, by gentleness and meekness, and by love unfeigned... charity, charity towards all men' — the Restoration's most concentrated statement of the unfeigned love that survives mistreatment. Pairs with s5 (honor) and s6 (family) as the article's triple-unconditional clause, with s4 establishing the Christological grammar the other two extend.

biblical.text: Ye have heard that it hath been said, Thou shalt love thy neighbour, and hate thine enemy. But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you and persecute you... For if ye love them which love you, what reward have ye? do not even the publicans the same?... Be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect.
biblical.comment: Christ's most direct anti-reciprocity instruction. The dominical anchor for love that transcends transactional return. The phrase 'what reward have ye? do not even the publicans the same?' makes reciprocity the very thing Christ's love is meant to surpass. The closing 'be ye therefore perfect' frames unconditional love as the perfecting movement — the article's whole claim in dominical voice. The strongest single biblical anchor for s4.

biblical.text: For if ye love them which love you, what thank have ye? for sinners also love those that love them. And if ye do good to them which do good to you, what thank have ye? for sinners also do even the same... But love ye your enemies, and do good, and lend, hoping for nothing again; and your reward shall be great, and ye shall be the children of the Highest: for he is kind unto the unthankful and to the evil.
biblical.comment: Luke's parallel to the Matthew 5 pericope. The most concentrated NT phrase against love-as-transaction is here — 'lend, hoping for nothing again' (Greek apelpizontes, expecting nothing in return). The closing 'for he is kind unto the unthankful and to the evil' grounds the disciple's unconditional love in the Father's own posture. Two-witness biblical confirmation of Christ's anti-reciprocity ethic.

biblical.text: But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.
biblical.comment: Paul's theological ground for unconditional love. God loved us before any return was possible — indeed, while we were enemies of God (Romans 5:10 extends the same logic). The Pauline anchor for the *pattern* the article asks the disciple to imitate: Christ's love precedes our response and does not depend on it. Names the Christological precedent the disciple's love is conformed to.

biblical.text: We love him, because he first loved us. If a man say, I love God, and hateth his brother, he is a liar: for he that loveth not his brother whom he hath seen, how can he love God whom he hath not seen? And this commandment have we from him, That he who loveth God love his brother also.
biblical.comment: John's grammatical anchor for the impossibility of selective love. The argument moves in two directions: God's prior love grounds ours ('we love him, because he first loved us'), and love-of-God cannot exist while love-of-neighbor is withheld ('he is a liar'). Closes the door to 'I love God but not these particular Christians' — the very evasion the article's unconditional clause refuses.

restoration.text: And charity suffereth long, and is kind, and envieth not, and is not puffed up, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil, and rejoiceth not in iniquity but rejoiceth in the truth, beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things... Wherefore, my beloved brethren, pray unto the Father with all the energy of heart, that ye may be filled with this love.
restoration.comment: Reasserted from Article 1 Span 19 in different rhetorical direction. At A1 s19 the passage anchored charity-as-the-commandment-content of the Great Commandments framework — the *what* of the second commandment. Here at A8 s4 the passage anchors charity's specific texture of endurance — 'suffereth long, beareth all things, endureth all things' — the *how* of love that survives non-reciprocation. Same passage, distinct rhetorical functions: A1 s19 names what is commanded; A8 s4 names what that obedience looks like when love is not returned. The cluster's most-reused charity passage.

restoration.text: And behold it is written, thou shalt love thy neighbor and hate thine enemy; but behold I say unto you, love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them who despitefully use you and persecute you... Therefore those things which were of old time, which were under the law, in me are all fulfilled. Old things are done away, and all things have become new. Therefore I would that ye should be perfect even as I, or your Father who is in heaven is perfect.
restoration.comment: The resurrected Christ's Bountiful sermon — His own first-person dominical reaffirmation of the Sermon on the Mount's love ethic, given in the Western hemisphere after the Resurrection. Notable: where Matthew 5:48 says 'be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect,' the resurrected Christ here adds 'even as I, or your Father who is in heaven is perfect' — explicitly including Himself in the perfection-pattern. The Christological intensification of the love-your-enemies instruction in the Restoration's voice.

restoration.text: No power or influence can or ought to be maintained by virtue of the priesthood, only by persuasion, by long-suffering, by gentleness and meekness, and by love unfeigned; By kindness, and pure knowledge, which shall greatly enlarge the soul without hypocrisy, and without guile... Let thy bowels also be full of charity towards all men, and to the household of faith, and let virtue garnish thy thoughts unceasingly; then shall thy confidence wax strong in the presence of God.
restoration.comment: The Liberty Jail revelation's pastoral love-without-condition pattern — the Restoration's most concentrated statement of the unfeigned (Greek anypokritos, un-counterfeited) love that survives mistreatment. The phrase 'love unfeigned... charity towards all men, and to the household of faith' explicitly extends charity beyond the household of faith, the precise scope the article's unconditional clause assumes. Joseph Smith received this in the dungeon while being mistreated by professed Christians — the experiential ground for the doctrinal claim.

s5.text: We honor them whether they honor us or not
s5.panel_comment: The article's second unconditional clause, distinct from love (s4) at the level of theological vocabulary and pastoral function. Honor is the *recognition of intrinsic worth* in another person — image-bearer, soul redeemed by Christ — and does not depend on the other's behavior toward us. The biblical word group (Greek timē, timáō) carries the specific note of *ascribed worth*, a deliberate cognitive act of esteem, distinct from the affective movement of love (agape). The biblical anchors carry the apostolic instruction at four registers: Romans 12:10 names honor as initiative-taking ('in honour preferring one another' — Greek proēgeomai, going before in ascribing worth); 1 Peter 2:17 places 'honour all men' in the same compact instruction as 'fear God,' grounding honor in the same theological seriousness as worship; Philippians 2:3 names honor as deliberate cognition ('let each esteem other better than themselves' — Greek hēgeomai, to count or consider) rather than mere feeling; James 2:1–9 supplies the negative anchor by naming the very failure the article refuses — 'respect of persons' (Greek prosōpon lambanete, accepting faces) is the partiality that withholds honor based on social return. The Restoration anchors complete the architecture: D&C 121:36–37 names the spiritual cost of dishonoring fellow believers — 'when we undertake to cover our sins, or to gratify our pride, our vain ambition... behold, the heavens withdraw themselves'; Mosiah 23:7 supplies the Restoration's most direct egalitarian-honor statement, refusing the very hierarchies that make honor reciprocal-only ('one man shall not think himself above another'); D&C 38:24–27 grounds honor in covenant identity ('let every man esteem his brother as himself... be one; and if ye are not one ye are not mine'). Pairs with s4 (love) and s6 (family) as the article's triple-unconditional clause, distinct from each through its theological vocabulary while sharing the unconditional grammar.

biblical.text: Be kindly affectioned one to another with brotherly love; in honour preferring one another.
biblical.comment: Paul's anchor for honor as initiative-taking. The Greek verb proēgeomai — 'going before' in ascribing honor — frames honor as the disciple's first move, not a response to the other's worthiness. The construction names honor as competitive in the right direction: a contest of who can ascribe more worth to the other, not who can claim more for themselves. The single most concentrated NT statement of honor's active disposition.

biblical.text: Honour all men. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honour the king.
biblical.comment: Peter's fourfold mandate places honor of *all men* alongside fear of God in the same compact apostolic instruction. The unconditional scope of 'all men' is the load-bearing biblical anchor for the span. Notable structural detail: Peter uses the same verb (timao) for 'honour all men' and 'honour the king' — the honor due to every soul is the same kind of honor due to the highest visible authority. The article's claim that honor does not depend on reciprocation is grounded in this apostolic universal.

biblical.text: Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves.
biblical.comment: Paul's hymn-prelude anchor for honor as anti-vainglory disposition. The verb hēgeomai — to *consider* or *count* — names honor as a deliberate cognitive act, not merely a feeling that arises and recedes. The phrase 'let each esteem other better than themselves' radicalizes honor by inverting the natural calculus of self-elevation. Sets up the Carmen Christi (Philippians 2:5–11) where Christ Himself models the kenotic pattern — the Christological ground for the disciple's honor-disposition.

biblical.text: My brethren, have not the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, with respect of persons. For if there come unto your assembly a man with a gold ring, in goodly apparel, and there come in also a poor man in vile raiment; And ye have respect to him that weareth the gay clothing... are ye not then partial in yourselves, and are become judges of evil thoughts?... If ye fulfil the royal law according to the scripture, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself, ye do well: But if ye have respect to persons, ye commit sin, and are convicted of the law as transgressors.
biblical.comment: James's negative anchor — the failure the article's unconditional clause specifically refuses. 'Respect of persons' (Greek prosōpon lambanete, accepting faces) names exactly the failure of withholding honor based on social return or apparent worthiness. James calls partial honor a transgression of the royal law itself, making it not a minor pastoral oversight but a theological breach. Ancient practice surfaces precisely the dynamic the article addresses in modern denominational form.

restoration.text: That the rights of the priesthood are inseparably connected with the powers of heaven, and that the powers of heaven cannot be controlled nor handled only upon the principles of righteousness. That they may be conferred upon us, it is true; but when we undertake to cover our sins, or to gratify our pride, our vain ambition, or to exercise control or dominion or compulsion upon the souls of the children of men, in any degree of unrighteousness, behold, the heavens withdraw themselves; the Spirit of the Lord is grieved; and when it is withdrawn, Amen to the priesthood or the authority of that man.
restoration.comment: The Liberty Jail revelation's most direct anchor for the spiritual cost of dishonoring fellow believers. Pride and 'vain ambition' — the disposition of receiving honor while withholding it — grieves the Spirit and withdraws the heavens. The verse names honor-withheld as not just a relational failure but a spiritual one, with consequences for the disciple's own connection to God. The strongest Restoration anchor for the unconditional honor the article describes.

restoration.text: Ye shall not esteem one flesh above another, or one man shall not think himself above another; therefore I say unto you, it is not expedient that ye should have a king.
restoration.comment: King Mosiah's pastoral anchor refusing the hierarchies that make honor reciprocal-only. The Restoration's most direct egalitarian-honor statement. Notable that the king himself is refusing kingship as a way of preserving the people's mutual honor — the disposition the article asks the disciple to maintain across denominational lines is the same disposition Mosiah identifies as the political precondition for righteous community. Honor without rank-comparison.

restoration.text: And let every man esteem his brother as himself, and practise virtue and holiness before me. And again I say unto you, let every man esteem his brother as himself... I say unto you, be one; and if ye are not one ye are not mine.
restoration.comment: Christ's covenant-anchor for honor as the disciple's standing posture toward every brother. The doubled command 'esteem his brother as himself' uses the same hēgeomai-family verb Paul uses in Philippians 2:3 — deliberate cognition of equal worth. The closing line ('be one; and if ye are not one ye are not mine') makes the honor-as-equality move covenantal, not optional. Christ's recognition of His disciples is conditioned on their honoring of one another. Reasserted from Article 1 Span 18 — different in this surfacing: A1 s18 used the unity language to ground fellowship-without-doctrinal-credential; A8 s5 uses the same passage to ground unconditional honor as covenant grammar.

s6.text: We hold them as family whether or not their tradition recognizes ours, and whether or not ours has treated them rightly
s6.panel_comment: The article's third and most demanding unconditional clause, doing two distinct theological moves at once: (1) refusing to make family-recognition reciprocal between traditions — the disciple holds others as family even when others' ecclesiology denies the disciple's tradition is part of the body of Christ; and (2) confessing corporate fault — acknowledging that 'ours' (the disciple's own tradition) has not always treated other Christians rightly, and refusing to weaponize that history against present-day fellowship. This second move makes s6 the most theologically distinctive of the triple-unconditional clauses, and warrants the densest anchor work — eight anchors instead of seven, four biblical and four restoration. The biblical anchors carry both theological moves: Ephesians 2:14–16 supplies the strongest single biblical anchor for refusing dividing walls between Christ-confessing peoples — Christ Himself has 'broken down the middle wall of partition' between groups previously divided, by His own work, the body of Christ is one body; John 17:20–23 carries Christ's high-priestly prayer for unity that transcends visible institutional boundaries — the dominical anchor for family-claim that does not depend on tradition's reciprocal recognition; Daniel 9:4–11 supplies the OT model of confessing one's own people's sins without disowning the people — Daniel speaks 'we have sinned' while clean himself, the prophetic anchor for confessing corporate fault as part of corporate identity; 1 John 1:8–9 supplies the Johannine grammatical anchor for the confessing posture — honest confession of fault is a Christian virtue, not a betrayal. The Restoration anchors complete the architecture: 3 Nephi 11:28–30 (reasserted from Article 1 Span 18 with rhetorical-divergence note) is here applied to historical contention between traditions; D&C 38:27 (reasserted from s5 above with rhetorical-divergence note) here grounds the unity-claim as Christ-required rather than honor-as-equality; D&C 124:49–50 supplies the modern-revelation anchor for confession of historical fault — Christ Himself names that human enemies (including, by extension, fellow Christians who became enemies) can hinder the people of God, with the burden falling on the hindering rather than the prevented; Mosiah 18:8–10 supplies the Waters of Mormon covenant-formula for the family-claim — those entering Christ's fellowship are willing to bear and mourn *with*, not adjudicate or rank. Pairs with s4 (love) and s5 (honor) as the article's triple-unconditional clause; closes the triple with the most ecclesially demanding move.

biblical.text: For he is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us; Having abolished in his flesh the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances; for to make in himself of twain one new man, so making peace; And that he might reconcile both unto God in one body by the cross, having slain the enmity thereby.
biblical.comment: The single most direct biblical anchor for refusing dividing walls between Christ-confessing peoples. Paul applies it to Jew/Gentile but the Christological logic extends to denominational dividing walls — if Christ has by His own work made both one, the disciple cannot maintain the walls Christ has already torn down. The phrase 'one new man' (Greek hena kainon anthrōpon) names the new ecclesial reality the article's family-claim presumes. Notable that the wall-breaking is past tense and accomplished — the article's claim is not a goal but a recognition of an already-completed work of Christ.

biblical.text: Neither pray I for these alone, but for them also which shall believe on me through their word; That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee, that they also may be one in us: that the world may know that thou hast sent me. And the glory which thou gavest me I have given them; that they may be one, even as we are one: I in them, and thou in me, that they may be made perfect in one; and that the world may know that thou hast sent me, and hast loved them, even as thou hast loved me.
biblical.comment: Christ's high-priestly prayer. The dominical anchor for unity that transcends visible institutional boundaries. Christ Himself prays for the future church (those who shall believe through the apostles' word) — every present-day Christian is included in the prayer's scope. The unity Christ prays for is qualitative ('as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee'), not bureaucratic, and Christ names the missional consequence: 'that the world may know that thou hast sent me.' The article's family-claim is therefore not a sentiment but a participation in Christ's own prayer.

biblical.text: And I prayed unto the Lord my God, and made my confession, and said, O Lord, the great and dreadful God, keeping the covenant and mercy to them that love him, and to them that keep his commandments; We have sinned, and have committed iniquity, and have done wickedly, and have rebelled, even by departing from thy precepts and from thy judgments: Neither have we hearkened unto thy servants the prophets... O Lord, righteousness belongeth unto thee, but unto us confusion of faces, as at this day; to the men of Judah, and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and unto all Israel.
biblical.comment: The OT model of confessing one's *own people's* sins without disowning the people. Daniel speaks 'we have sinned' while himself clean — he stands as part of his people while confessing what his people have done. The prophetic anchor for the article's second theological move: confessing corporate fault as part of corporate identity. The disciple does not say 'they sinned, but I am clean'; the disciple says 'we have not always treated them rightly,' identifying with the corporate body even in confessing its fault. The grammatical pattern Christian intercession should preserve.

biblical.text: If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
biblical.comment: The Johannine grammatical anchor for the confessing posture. The article's clause 'whether or not ours has treated them rightly' implies rightly that ours has not always done so — the implication is structurally Christian, since the Johannine logic forecloses the option of claiming no sin. Honest confession of fault is presented in the apostolic witness as a Christian virtue and the precondition of God's faithful forgiveness, not as a betrayal of one's tradition. The article's confessing posture is therefore in line with apostolic confession-grammar.

restoration.text: And there shall be no disputations among you, as there have hitherto been; neither shall there be disputations among you concerning the points of my doctrine, as there have hitherto been. For verily, verily I say unto you, he that hath the spirit of contention is not of me, but is of the devil, who is the father of contention, and he stirreth up the hearts of men to contend with anger, one with another. Behold, this is not my doctrine, to stir up the hearts of men with anger, one against another; but this is my doctrine, that such things should be done away.
restoration.comment: Reasserted from Article 1 Span 18 in different rhetorical direction. At A1 s18 the passage anchored Christ's pattern of receiving the stranger casting out devils in His name — contention itself as not of Him in Christ's general teaching. Here at A8 s6 the article applies the same anchor to *historical* contention between Christian traditions, asking the disciple to refuse to perpetuate it. The phrase 'as there have hitherto been' makes contention's history Christ-named, not denied; what Christ refuses is its perpetuation. The same anchor doing the work of historical reckoning rather than abstract pattern-naming.

restoration.text: Behold, this I have given unto you as a parable, and it is even as I am. I say unto you, be one; and if ye are not one ye are not mine.
restoration.comment: Reasserted from s5 above in different rhetorical direction. At s5 the verse anchored honor-as-active-equality, the disposition the disciple maintains. Here at s6 the verse grounds the unity-claim as Christ-required rather than disciple-volunteered. The covenant grammar makes oneness Christ-required ('if ye are not one ye are not mine'), conditioning Christ's recognition of His disciples on their unity-claim toward one another. The article's family-claim is therefore not optional fellowship but covenant participation. Same passage, distinct rhetorical functions: s5 names the disposition; s6 names the covenant ground.

restoration.text: Verily, verily, I say unto you, that when I give a commandment to any of the sons of men to do a work unto my name, and those sons of men go with all their might and with all they have to perform that work, and cease not their diligence, and their enemies come upon them and hinder them from performing that work, behold, it behooveth me to require that work no more at the hands of those sons of men, but to accept of their offerings. And the iniquity and transgression of my holy laws and commandments I will visit upon the heads of those who hindered my work, unto the third and fourth generation, so long as they repent not, and hate me, saith the Lord God.
restoration.comment: Christ Himself in modern revelation naming that human enemies can hinder the people of God, and the burden falls on the hindering rather than the prevented. The Restoration's anchor for confession of historical fault that does not collapse into denominational self-abnegation — Christ acknowledges that some hindrance comes from human enemies, but the article's confession 'whether or not ours has treated them rightly' refuses to claim only the position of the prevented. The disciple holds both: that wrongs were done in both directions, and that the question of historical adjudication is Christ's, not the disciple's. The verse grounds the moral seriousness of historical wrong without licensing the disciple to make it the basis of present fellowship.

restoration.text: And it came to pass that he said unto them: Behold, here are the waters of Mormon (for thus were they called) and now, as ye are desirous to come into the fold of God, and to be called his people, and are willing to bear one another's burdens, that they may be light; Yea, and are willing to mourn with those that mourn; yea, and comfort those that stand in need of comfort, and to stand as witnesses of God at all times and in all things, and in all places that ye may be in, even until death, that ye may be redeemed of God, and be numbered with those of the first resurrection, that ye may have eternal life — Now I say unto you, if this is the desire of your hearts, what have you against being baptized in the name of the Lord, as a witness before him that ye have entered into a covenant with him, that ye shall serve him and keep his commandments, that he may pour out his Spirit more abundantly upon you?
restoration.comment: Alma's Waters of Mormon covenant-formula. The Restoration's anchor for the family-claim as covenant willingness rather than recognition-by-status. Those entering Christ's fellowship are willing to 'bear one another's burdens, that they may be light' and 'mourn with those that mourn, comfort those that stand in need of comfort' — the disposition of bearing-with-and-mourning-with rather than adjudicating or ranking. The article's family-claim presumes this Restoration pattern: family is constituted by mutual burden-bearing across difference, not by reciprocal institutional recognition. The covenant-formula naming the texture of the family-relation the article confesses.

s7.text: the body of Christ is larger than any single denomination and older than every division
s7.panel_comment: The catholicity claim. The article moves from the triple-unconditional clauses (s4–s5–s6) to a constructive thesis: the body of Christ exceeds every denominational boundary in two dimensions — spatial (larger than any single denomination) and temporal (older than every division). Both dimensions matter for the article’s pastoral function. The spatial claim refuses the implicit identification of the body of Christ with any one ecclesial container; the temporal claim refuses the implicit identification of the body with any one historical fracture’s defining moment. The body’s reality precedes its visible divisions and exceeds its visible boundaries. The biblical anchors hold both dimensions: 1 Corinthians 12:12–14, 27 supplies the foundational Pauline architecture — the body is one body with many members, baptized by one Spirit, all together constituting Christ’s body in particular; Ephesians 4:4–6 (reasserted from A8 s1 with rhetorical-divergence note) here grounds the catholic-ecclesiology claim distinct from the receptive-identity function it carried at s1; John 10:16 supplies Christ’s own dominical anchor for the body’s scope exceeding any single visible fold (“other sheep I have, which are not of this fold”); Hebrews 12:22–24 supplies the apostolic anchor for the temporal dimension — the disciple in Christ has come to a fellowship that includes “the spirits of just men made perfect,” the faithful from every age. The Restoration anchors complete the architecture: D&C 10:67–68 supplies Christ’s own modern-revelation definition of “my church” by repentance and coming, not by institutional roster — the strongest Restoration anchor for the article’s claim that the body exceeds any single denomination; Moses 7:18–21 supplies the Restoration’s most ancient-Zion anchor for “older than every division” — Enoch’s city, the original one-heart-and-one-mind community in the antediluvian generations, naming the body’s pattern as preceding by definition every later fracture. Pairs with s6 (where the article’s family-claim was grounded in the wall-breaking work of Christ) as the constructive consequence: if Christ has by His own work made one body, then that body is by definition larger than any human-bounded subset and older than any division-event.

biblical.text: For as the body is one, and hath many members, and all the members of that one body, being many, are one body: so also is Christ. For by one Spirit are we all baptized into one body, whether we be Jews or Gentiles, whether we be bond or free; and have been all made to drink into one Spirit. For the body is not one member, but many— Now ye are the body of Christ, and members in particular.
biblical.comment: The foundational Pauline architecture for the body of Christ as one body with many members. The phrase “so also is Christ” (verse 12) makes the body-and-Christ identification explicit: the body is not a metaphor for a community that follows Christ; the body is Christ as He continues to be present in the world through His members. The phrase “Now ye are the body of Christ, and members in particular” (verse 27) closes the claim with direct address. The single most concentrated NT statement of the body’s plurality-and-unity, and the strongest biblical anchor for the article’s catholicity claim. The dividing markers (“Jews or Gentiles— bond or free”) are subordinated to the one-body baptism — the very pattern A8 s1 grounds in Galatians 3:26–28, here applied at the ecclesial scale. First-time in the cluster.

biblical.text: There is one body, and one Spirit, even as ye are called in one hope of your calling; One Lord, one faith, one baptism, One God and Father of all, who is above all, and through all, and in you all.
biblical.comment: Reasserted from A8 s1 in different rhetorical direction. At s1 the sevenfold “one” anchored the receptive-identity claim — the disciple receives every soul as fellow child of the same Father, with the apostolic confession grounding the relational kin-claim. Here at s7 the same passage anchors the catholic-ecclesiology claim — the body of Christ is one body across denominations, with the apostolic confession grounding the institutional-transcendence claim. A8 s1 names what binds disciples to one another; A8 s7 names what binds the visible-and-invisible body across history. Same passage, distinct rhetorical functions in the cluster’s architecture.

biblical.text: And other sheep I have, which are not of this fold: them also I must bring, and they shall hear my voice; and there shall be one fold, and one shepherd.
biblical.comment: Christ’s own dominical anchor for the body’s scope exceeding any single visible fold. The verse names a fold-distinction Christ Himself acknowledges (“not of this fold”) while declaring the deeper unity that resolves it (“one fold, and one shepherd”). The article’s “larger than any single denomination” has its strongest dominical warrant here — Christ Himself is the one whose work establishes the body’s scope, and that scope exceeds the visible fold the disciple finds herself in. First-time in the cluster.

biblical.text: But ye are come unto mount Sion, and unto the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to an innumerable company of angels, To the general assembly and church of the firstborn, which are written in heaven, and to God the Judge of all, and to the spirits of just men made perfect, And to Jesus the mediator of the new covenant, and to the blood of sprinkling, that speaketh better things than that of Abel.
biblical.comment: The apostolic anchor for the temporal dimension of the body’s catholicity. The disciple has “come unto” — perfect tense, naming a present reality — the heavenly Jerusalem, the general assembly and church of the firstborn, and the spirits of just men made perfect. “General assembly” (Greek pan’gyris, festival-gathering) names the full convocation of the faithful from every age. The phrase “spirits of just men made perfect” explicitly names the temporal scope: faithful from every age are part of the body the disciple has now joined. The strongest single biblical anchor for “older than every division” — the body precedes by definition every visible fracture in mortal time. First-time in the cluster.

restoration.text: Behold, this is my doctrine—whosoever repenteth and cometh unto me, the same is my church. Whosoever declareth more or less than this, the same is not of me, but is against me; therefore he is not of my church.
restoration.comment: Christ’s modern-revelation definition of “my church” by repentance and coming, not by institutional roster. The Restoration’s strongest anchor for the article’s claim that the body exceeds any single denomination. The phrase “whosoever repenteth and cometh unto me” makes the boundary Christological, not credentialed; “the same is my church” makes the inclusion-claim Christ’s own first-person declaration. Notable: the verse refuses both expansion-beyond-the-plain-center (“declareth more”) and contraction-of-the-plain-center (“declareth less”) — the church is precisely those who repent and come, no more, no less. First-time in the cluster.

restoration.text: And the Lord called his people Zion, because they were of one heart and one mind, and dwelt in righteousness; and there was no poor among them. And Enoch continued his preaching in righteousness unto the people of God. And it came to pass in his days, that he built a city that was called the City of Holiness, even Zion— And the Lord came and dwelt with his people, and they dwelt in righteousness. And it came to pass that Zion was not, for God received it up into his own bosom; and from thence went forth the saying, Zion is fled.
restoration.comment: The Restoration’s most ancient-Zion anchor for “older than every division.” Enoch’s city, the original Zion-pattern, was a community of one heart and one mind in the antediluvian generations — the body’s pattern as preceding by definition every later division-event in human history. The phrase “the Lord came and dwelt with his people” names Christ’s presence as the constitutive ground of the community, not denominational structure; the unity of heart and mind names the body’s qualitative character. The Restoration’s strongest single anchor for the temporal dimension of the article’s catholicity claim. First-time in the cluster.

s8.text: We are not indifferent to Christian institutions or traditions
s8.panel_comment: The institutional-honoring claim — naming what the article is NOT before the wall-diagnostic at s9. The disciple’s posture is not anti-institutional dismissal but engaged honoring. The clause performs a critical pastoral function: the previous spans (s4–s6) establish the radical reception that does not depend on tradition’s reciprocal recognition; the next span (s9) will name the dividing walls as not built by Christ. Without s8, those moves could be read as anti-institutional sentiment — as if the article’s critique of walls is also a critique of the institutions in which they appear. s8 closes that misreading: institutions and traditions are not the problem; the walls humans have built within them are. The article honors Christian institutions and traditions for the genuine good they carry, while refusing to defend the walls that have arisen between them. The biblical anchors carry the apostolic instruction at four registers: Romans 12:18 grounds the disciple’s peaceable disposition toward all; 1 Thessalonians 5:21 names engaged discernment (“prove all things; hold fast that which is good”) as the alternative to blanket dismissal or blanket acceptance; Philippians 4:8 names the disciple’s habitual seeking of the good — truth, honesty, justice, purity, loveliness, good report — wherever it surfaces; Acts 17:22–23 supplies the apostolic model of engaged honoring at Mars Hill — Paul does not dismiss Athenian devotions; he locates them precisely and builds from them. The Restoration anchors complete the architecture: Moroni 7:12–18 supplies the Light of Christ as the discerning faculty by which the disciple recognizes good wherever it surfaces, with the explicit standard “every thing which inviteth and enticeth to do good, and to love God, and to serve him, is inspired of God”; Articles of Faith 1:13 supplies the Restoration’s most direct interfaith-honoring statement, naming the disposition of seeking after anything virtuous, lovely, of good report, or praiseworthy — the disposition the article confesses; 2 Nephi 32:7 (reasserted from A4 s8 with rhetorical-divergence note) here names what indifference to traditions costs — Nephi’s lament that those who “will not search knowledge” remain ignorant even when truth is given plainly. Cross-references A1 s2 (which already pointed forward to A8) — the article’s refusal to reject or disrespect institutions, traditions, or their formalized creeds and theologies finds its explicit landing here.

biblical.text: If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.
biblical.comment: Paul’s apostolic anchor for the disciple’s peaceable disposition toward all — including all Christian traditions. The conditional “if it be possible” honors the reality that peaceableness depends on more than one party, but the phrase “as much as lieth in you” locates the disciple’s responsibility in the burden being carried from her side. The disciple does not control whether peace is achieved; the disciple controls whether her own posture obstructs it. The most direct biblical anchor for the article’s refusal of indifference — indifference is itself a posture-failure on the disciple’s side. First-time in the cluster.

biblical.text: Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
biblical.comment: Paul’s most concentrated directive against indifference. The disciple does not dismiss traditions wholesale; the disciple proves (Greek dokimazete, tests by examination) and holds fast what is good. The verse names the alternative to blanket acceptance and blanket dismissal alike — engaged discernment. Where indifference treats all traditions as equally unworthy of attention, the article’s posture treats them as worthy of careful examination, with the good held fast and the rest left honestly named. First-time in the cluster.

biblical.text: Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things.
biblical.comment: Paul’s apostolic anchor for the disciple’s habitual seeking of the good across whatever tradition surfaces it. The sixfold list (truth, honesty, justice, purity, loveliness, good report) plus the closing virtue-and-praise pair names the comprehensive scope of what the disciple actively pursues. Pairs verbally with Articles of Faith 1:13 below — Joseph Smith echoes Philippians 4:8 directly in the Restoration’s most concentrated interfaith-honoring statement. The verbal echo is the Restoration’s explicit acknowledgment that this disposition is biblical, not innovative. First-time in the cluster.

biblical.text: Then Paul stood in the midst of Mars’ hill, and said, Ye men of Athens, I perceive that in all things ye are too superstitious. For as I passed by, and beheld your devotions, I found an altar with this inscription, TO THE UNKNOWN GOD. Whom therefore ye ignorantly worship, him declare I unto you.
biblical.comment: The apostolic model of engaged honoring rather than dismissive engagement. Paul does not dismiss Athenian religious practice as paganism unworthy of attention; he locates a specific altar precisely and builds from it. The verb “I perceive” (Greek theoro, observe carefully) names the engaged attention the article’s posture asks of the disciple. The strongest biblical narrative anchor for non-indifference toward another tradition’s reach toward God — Paul honored the seeking even where he understood it to be incomplete, and built apostolic witness from that honoring rather than from dismissal. First-time in the cluster.

restoration.text: Wherefore, all things which are good cometh of God; and that which is evil cometh of the devil; for the devil is an enemy unto God, and fighteth against him continually, and inviteth and enticeth to sin, and to do that which is evil continually. But behold, that which is of God inviteth and enticeth to do good continually; wherefore, every thing which inviteth and enticeth to do good, and to love God, and to serve him, is inspired of God— For behold, the Spirit of Christ is given to every man, that he may know good from evil; wherefore, I show unto you the way to judge; for every thing which inviteth to do good, and to persuade to believe in Christ, is sent forth by the power and gift of Christ; wherefore ye may know with a perfect knowledge it is of God.
restoration.comment: The Restoration’s Light of Christ teaching as the discerning faculty by which the disciple recognizes good wherever it surfaces. The standard is explicit: “every thing which inviteth and enticeth to do good, and to love God, and to serve him, is inspired of God.” The standard does not require institutional alignment; it does not require denominational agreement; it does not require credal completion. It requires only the fruit-test — does it invite and entice to do good, to love God, to serve Him? Where the answer is yes, the article confesses, indifference would be a refusal to recognize what God Himself has inspired. The Restoration’s most direct anchor for the article’s refusal of indifference toward Christian institutions and traditions — they carry, by Moroni’s own standard, what the Light of Christ Himself inspires when they invite the good. First-time in the cluster.

restoration.text: We believe in being honest, true, chaste, benevolent, virtuous, and in doing good to all men; indeed, we may say that we follow the admonition of Paul—We believe all things, we hope all things, we have endured many things, and hope to be able to endure all things. If there is anything virtuous, lovely, or of good report or praiseworthy, we seek after these things.
restoration.comment: The Restoration’s most direct interfaith-honoring statement and verbal echo of Philippians 4:8. Joseph Smith’s explicit acknowledgment (“we follow the admonition of Paul”) makes the apostolic source of the disposition explicit. The closing clause — “If there is anything virtuous, lovely, or of good report or praiseworthy, we seek after these things” — names the active disposition the article’s s8 confesses. The disciple does not wait passively for good to surface; the disciple seeks it. The strongest single Restoration anchor for the article’s s8 claim, with the additional weight of being part of the Restoration’s own confessional canon. First-time in the cluster.

restoration.text: And now I, Nephi, cannot say more; the Spirit stoppeth mine utterance, and I am left to mourn because of the unbelief, and the wickedness, and the ignorance, and the stiffneckedness of men; for they will not search knowledge, nor understand great knowledge, when it is given unto them in plainness, even as plain as word can be.
restoration.comment: Reasserted from A4 s8 in different rhetorical direction. At A4 s8 the verse anchored the imperative not-optionality of study — those who refuse to search remain ignorant even when truth is given plainly, the diagnostic for interpretive humility’s opposite. Here at A8 s8 the same verse anchors what indifference to traditions costs — the soul who treats Christian institutions and traditions as unworthy of careful searching repeats the very failure Nephi laments. A4 s8 names the disposition study requires; A8 s8 names what indifference loses. Same passage, distinct rhetorical functions: A4 names the disciple’s discipline; A8 names the cost of refusing it across traditions.

s9.text: the walls that often separate the Lord’s people were not built by Him
s9.panel_comment: The wall-diagnostic claim — the article’s most direct theological-historical declaration. The article does not say “there are no walls”; it says “walls that often separate” — acknowledging their reality and their separating power. What it refuses is the attribution of those walls to divine architecture. Christ has broken down dividing walls (Eph 2:14); humans have built up new ones in subsequent centuries. The article’s claim is therefore theological-historical: the divisions are not divine, therefore the disciple is not bound to perpetuate them. The biblical anchors carry the architecture: Ephesians 2:14–16 (reasserted from A8 s6 with rhetorical-divergence note) here grounds the Christological diagnosis distinct from its corporate-confession function at s6 — Christ has broken these walls down, therefore any walls that remain are human reconstruction, not divine architecture; John 17:11 supplies Christ’s first mention of unity in the high-priestly prayer (distinct from John 17:20–23 used at s6) — unity as Christ’s own petition for His people, with the walls that separate being precisely what Christ asks the Father to prevent; 1 Corinthians 1:10–13 supplies the single most direct biblical diagnosis of denominational division as not-of-Christ — Paul’s rhetorical question “Is Christ divided?” is the article’s wall-diagnostic in apostolic voice; Colossians 3:11 supplies the Pauline universal-erasure of dividing markers in Christ (“where there is neither Greek nor Jew, circumcision nor uncircumcision, Barbarian, Scythian, bond nor free: but Christ is all, and in all”). The Restoration anchors complete the architecture: Mosiah 18:21 supplies Alma’s commandment-against-contention at the Waters of Mormon, with explicit linguistic echo of Ephesians 4:5 (“one faith and one baptism”) within the Restoration’s voice; D&C 6:32 supplies the Restoration’s reaffirmation of Christ’s Matthean dominical promise of presence-in-gathering (“where two or three are gathered together in my name— behold, there am I in the midst of them”) — the walls humans build between two or three gathered in His name divide what He has joined; Moroni 8:18 supplies the impartiality-and-immutability anchor (“God is not a partial God, neither a changeable being; but he is unchangeable from all eternity to all eternity”) — divine immutability as the ground of unity-claim, with the partiality the disciple refuses being itself a denial of God’s own character. Pairs with s7 (the body’s catholic scope) and s8 (engagement with institutions) as the article’s ecclesial diagnostic triad: s7 names what the body is, s8 names what the disciple’s posture toward institutions is, s9 names what the walls between them are not.

biblical.text: For he is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us; Having abolished in his flesh the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances; for to make in himself of twain one new man, so making peace; And that he might reconcile both unto God in one body by the cross, having slain the enmity thereby.
biblical.comment: Reasserted from A8 s6 in different rhetorical direction. At s6 the passage anchored the corporate-confession dimension — Christ has by His own work torn down dividing walls, the ground for the article’s family-claim across traditions despite historical wrongs. Here at s9 the same passage anchors the Christological diagnosis itself — the walls Christ has broken down do not stay broken in human history; they get rebuilt, and any walls that remain between Christ-confessing peoples are by definition human reconstruction rather than divine architecture. A8 s6 names what Christ has done; A8 s9 names what humans have done in spite of it. Same passage, distinct rhetorical functions in the cluster’s architecture — the strongest single biblical anchor in both spans, deployed for the corporate-confession move at s6 and the wall-diagnostic move at s9.

biblical.text: And now I am no more in the world, but these are in the world, and I come to thee. Holy Father, keep through thine own name those whom thou hast given me, that they may be one, as we are.
biblical.comment: Christ’s high-priestly prayer in its first mention of unity — distinct from verses 20–23 (used at A8 s6) where the prayer extends to future believers. Here at s9 the focus is Christ’s petition itself: He asks the Father to keep His disciples that they may be one as the Father and Son are one. The walls that separate are precisely what Christ asks the Father to prevent. The dominical anchor for unity as Christ’s own first request, not the disciple’s aspiration. The verse names what Christ has prayed for — which makes the human walls that have arisen since the prayer not just regrettable, but contrary to Christ’s own petition. First-time in the cluster.

biblical.text: Now I beseech you, brethren, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you; but that ye be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment— Now this I say, that every one of you saith, I am of Paul; and I of Apollos; and I of Cephas; and I of Christ. Is Christ divided?
biblical.comment: The single most direct biblical diagnosis of denominational division as not-of-Christ. Paul names the Corinthian factions (“I of Paul— I of Apollos— I of Cephas— I of Christ”) and asks the question that diagnoses every later denominational identification: “Is Christ divided?” The grammar is rhetorical — Paul expects the answer no. The wall-diagnostic the article carries at s9 is Paul’s wall-diagnostic in apostolic voice. The strongest single biblical anchor for the article’s claim that the walls are not built by Christ — because Christ Himself is not divided, the divisions among His people cannot be of Him. First-time in the cluster.

biblical.text: Where there is neither Greek nor Jew, circumcision nor uncircumcision, Barbarian, Scythian, bond nor free: but Christ is all, and in all.
biblical.comment: Paul’s universal-erasure of dividing markers in Christ. Where Galatians 3:28 (used at A8 s1) names three pairs of dividing markers (Jew/Greek, bond/free, male/female), Colossians 3:11 expands the list with Barbarian and Scythian — naming the broadest scope of human division Paul could imagine in the first-century Mediterranean. The closing line (“but Christ is all, and in all”) names what fills the space the dividing markers vacated: not undifferentiated unity, but Christ’s own all-in-all presence. The article’s wall-diagnostic stands here — the markers on which dividing walls were built have been erased in Christ, and the walls that humans have built since then have no Christological warrant. First-time in the cluster.

restoration.text: And he commanded them that there should be no contention one with another, but that they should look forward with one eye, having one faith and one baptism, having their hearts knit together in unity and in love one towards another.
restoration.comment: Alma’s commandment at the Waters of Mormon — the Restoration’s most direct anchor for the wall-diagnostic. The phrase “one faith and one baptism” is a direct linguistic echo of Ephesians 4:5, embedded in the Restoration’s own foundational covenant moment. Notable that the contention-prohibition is paired with the unity-affirmation: Alma names the negative (no contention) and the positive (hearts knit together in unity and love) as a single covenant. The walls that separate are by Alma’s definition contention-walls — and contention is what the covenant explicitly forbids. The Restoration’s baptismal community was constituted on the very ground the article’s s9 claim defends. First-time in the cluster.

restoration.text: Verily, verily, I say unto you, as I said unto my disciples, where two or three are gathered together in my name, as touching one thing, behold, there will I be in the midst of them—even so am I in the midst of you.
restoration.comment: Christ’s reaffirmation in modern revelation of the Matthean dominical promise (Matthew 18:20). The phrase “as I said unto my disciples” explicitly identifies Christ’s continuing voice across the Restoration with His mortal voice — the same Christ who promised His presence to two or three gathered now reaffirms it. The wall-diagnostic implication is direct: where Christ Himself promises His presence in gathering-in-His-name, the walls humans have built between gatherings of Christ-confessing peoples are walls that divide what He has joined. The verse names presence as the gathering’s ground, not denominational alignment as its precondition. First-time in the cluster.

restoration.text: For I know that God is not a partial God, neither a changeable being; but he is unchangeable from all eternity to all eternity.
restoration.comment: Mormon’s impartiality-and-immutability anchor. The wall-diagnostic’s deepest theological ground: if God is not partial and not changeable, then the walls that have arisen since the apostolic generation cannot be His doing — they would require Him to be both partial (preferring some Christ-confessing peoples to others) and changeable (rebuilding what He had joined). Mormon’s claim makes wall-construction theologically impossible from the divine side. The Restoration’s most direct anchor for the “not built by Him” half of the article’s claim — the impossibility of attributing dividing walls to a God who is by character unchangeable and impartial. First-time in the cluster.

s10.definition: The disciple's deliberate refusal to take up arms — rhetorical, doctrinal, or institutional — in defense of the dividing walls humans have built between Christ-confessing peoples. Not a refusal to honor traditions (s8) or to acknowledge that walls separate (s9); a refusal to defend them as if they were Christ's architecture.
s10.panel_comment: The article's active-refusal claim, marked by the dagger (†) cross-reference to the companion study Contention and the Reach of Christ. The named concept is not the existence of the walls (s9 has already named them), nor disrespect toward the institutions in which they appear (s8 has already refused that disrespect). The named concept is the disciple's posture toward the walls themselves: we will not defend them. The verb 'defend' is editorially load-bearing — selected April 25, 2026 over 'uphold' for consistency with the live Contention companion study introduction, and theologically distinct from 'honor' (s8) and 'acknowledge' (s9). To defend a wall is to take up arms in its preservation; the disciple lays those arms down. The biblical anchors carry the dominical and apostolic foundation for the refusal. Matthew 26:51–52 supplies the strongest single dominical anchor — Christ's own 'put up again thy sword' to Peter in Gethsemane, refusing armed defense even of His own person at the moment of His arrest. The verse establishes that the disciple's posture toward Christ's body is not preserved by taking up weapons against fellow human beings, even when the cause appears most clearly to be Christ's own. Romans 14:19 supplies the affirmative Pauline directive — the disciple follows after the things which make for peace, the things wherewith one may edify another, with the implicit refusal of the disposition that fights for ground over edifying. 2 Timothy 2:23–25 supplies the most direct apostolic instruction against contentious posture: the servant of the Lord must not strive, but be gentle unto all, apt to teach, patient — Paul names the very disposition the article's s10 confesses. 1 Peter 3:9 supplies the closing biblical anchor for non-retaliation in kind, with the explicit 'contrariwise blessing' inversion that anticipates s13's non-retaliation triple. The Restoration anchors confirm and extend. 3 Nephi 11:29–30 (already deployed at A1 s18 and A8 s6) is reasserted here in a third distinct rhetorical direction: at A1 s18 the passage anchored Christ's general teaching that contention itself is not of Him — the dominical pattern; at A8 s6 the passage anchored the article's corporate confession of historical contention between traditions — the disciple's honest reckoning with what has been; here at A8 s10 the passage anchors the article's active refusal to perpetuate that contention going forward — the forward-looking declaration. The three surfacings together carry an architectural arc: A1 s18 names what Christ refuses; A8 s6 confesses what we have done in contradiction; A8 s10 declares what we will not do from this point on. Same passage, three load-bearing rhetorical functions across the cluster. D&C 19:23 supplies Christ's modern-revelation pairing of meekness with the disciple's peace — 'learn of me, and listen to my words; walk in the meekness of my Spirit, and you shall have peace in me' — naming meekness as the alternative posture to defending walls, with peace as the dominical reward of that posture. D&C 105:24 supplies Christ's direct counsel in modern revelation against boasting and contentious posture even when the disciple is being persecuted: 'talk not of judgments, neither boast of faith nor of mighty works, but carefully gather together, as much in one place as it is possible.' The verse names what the disciple does instead of defending — gathers together in one place as much as it is possible — the constructive movement that replaces the defensive one.

biblical.text: And, behold, one of them which were with Jesus stretched out his hand, and drew his sword, and struck a servant of the high priest's, and smote off his ear. Then said Jesus unto him, Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.
biblical.comment: The strongest single dominical anchor for the disciple's refusal of armed defense. Christ Himself, at the moment of His arrest, refuses armed defense even of His own person — and rebukes the disciple who attempts it. The phrase 'put up again thy sword into his place' names the active movement of laying down what was taken up in defense. The closing 'all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword' names the spiritual cost of weaponized defense in any cause, including a cause apparently in Christ's own service. The article's s10 stands on this Gethsemane refusal: if Christ would not have His own person defended by the sword, the disciple does not defend the dividing walls between His people by their rhetorical, doctrinal, or institutional analogues.

biblical.text: Let us therefore follow after the things which make for peace, and things wherewith one may edify another.
biblical.comment: Paul's affirmative directive in the very chapter that grounds A1 s2 ('him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations'). The verse names what the disciple does instead of defending walls — pursues peace, pursues edifying. The Greek dioko (follow after) carries an active, pursuing connotation; the disciple does not merely avoid contention but actively pursues its alternative. The verbal echo of A1 s2's receive-without-disputation pattern makes this the article cluster's natural Pauline anchor for the active-refusal claim.

biblical.text: But foolish and unlearned questions avoid, knowing that they do gender strifes. And the servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient, In meekness instructing those that oppose themselves; if God peradventure will give them repentance to the acknowledging of the truth.
biblical.comment: Paul's most direct apostolic instruction against contentious posture for the servant of Christ. The verb me machesthai (must not strive) is grammatically prohibitive — the servant's standing posture is non-striving, not occasionally non-striving. The companion virtues (gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient, in meekness instructing) name the texture of the alternative. The closing clause ('if God peradventure will give them repentance') names the disciple's humility — even those who oppose are addressed in the hope of God's work, not in the disposition of defeating them. The strongest single Pauline anchor for the article's s10 named-concept.

biblical.text: Not rendering evil for evil, or railing for railing; but contrariwise blessing; knowing that ye are thereunto called, that ye should inherit a blessing.
biblical.comment: Peter's anchor for the disciple's refusal of defensive counterattack. The phrase 'rendering railing for railing' names exactly the rhetorical-defense disposition the article's s10 refuses; the inversion 'contrariwise blessing' names what replaces it. The closing claim — 'ye are thereunto called, that ye should inherit a blessing' — locates the refusal within the disciple's vocation, not as an optional pacifist preference. Anticipates s13's non-retaliation triple (insult for insult, exclusion for exclusion, suspicion for suspicion) by establishing the apostolic register the triple will draw on.

restoration.text: For verily, verily I say unto you, he that hath the spirit of contention is not of me, but is of the devil, who is the father of contention, and he stirreth up the hearts of men to contend with anger, one with another. Behold, this is not my doctrine, to stir up the hearts of men with anger, one against another; but this is my doctrine, that such things should be done away.
restoration.comment: Reasserted from Article 1 Span 18 and Article 8 Span 6 in different rhetorical direction. At A1 s18 the passage anchored Christ's general teaching that contention itself is not of Him — the dominical pattern. At A8 s6 the passage anchored the article's corporate confession of historical contention between Christian traditions — the disciple's honest reckoning with what has been. Here at A8 s10 the same passage anchors the disciple's active refusal to perpetuate that contention going forward — the forward-looking declaration. Three rhetorical functions of the same passage across the cluster: A1 s18 names what Christ refuses (dominical pattern); A8 s6 confesses what we have done in contradiction (corporate reckoning); A8 s10 declares what we will not do from this point on (active refusal). The closing phrase 'such things should be done away' carries the imperative weight of s10's refusal: Christ Himself names the doing-away as His doctrine, and the disciple's refusal to defend the walls participates in that doing-away.

restoration.text: Learn of me, and listen to my words; walk in the meekness of my Spirit, and you shall have peace in me.
restoration.comment: Christ's modern-revelation pairing of meekness with the disciple's peace. The verse names meekness as the alternative posture to defending walls, with peace as the dominical reward. The walking-in-meekness disposition is not absence of conviction (the article's prior spans s4–s9 carry strong conviction); it is the refusal to translate conviction into the posture of armed defense. The verbal echo of Matthew 11:29 ('Learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart') makes the modern-revelation continuous with the dominical original — the same Christ teaching the same posture across canons.

restoration.text: Talk not of judgments, neither boast of faith nor of mighty works, but carefully gather together, as much in one place as it is possible.
restoration.comment: Christ's direct counsel in modern revelation against boasting and contentious posture, given to a Latter-day Saint people who were themselves being persecuted. The triple prohibition ('talk not of judgments, neither boast of faith nor of mighty works') addresses the very dispositions that arise when the disciple is hurt and tempted to defend. The affirmative — 'carefully gather together, as much in one place as it is possible' — names the constructive alternative to defending walls: the gathering of the saints across whatever divisions surround them. The verse grounds the article's s10 in the Restoration's own experience of being on the wrong end of contention, with Christ Himself directing His people toward gathering rather than defending.
