s11.text: Nor will we defend any doctrine or teaching made into a weapon against a brother or sister who names His name
s11.panel_comment: The weaponization-refusal claim. Where s10 named the refusal to defend the walls themselves, s11 names the refusal to defend the means by which the walls are often kept up: doctrines and teachings bent into weapons against fellow Christ-confessing peoples. The article does not refuse doctrine — A1, A4, and A8 s8 already establish the cluster's honoring of doctrine in its proper function. The article refuses the bending of doctrine into a weapon, with the implicit theological claim that weaponization-against-believers is not what doctrine is for. The biblical anchors carry the architecture at four registers. 2 Corinthians 10:3–5 supplies the foundational Pauline distinction between the disciple's spiritual weapons and carnal weaponization — 'the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds' — naming what the disciple's scriptural and doctrinal resources are for, with the implicit refusal of their carnal-against-believers use. The pulling-down is of strong holds, of imaginations exalted against God, of every high thing — not of fellow believers themselves. Matthew 23:13 supplies Christ's most direct dominical diagnosis of doctrine-as-gatekeeping-weapon: the woe against scribes and Pharisees who shut up the kingdom of heaven against men, neither entering in themselves nor suffering them that are entering to go in. The verse identifies the specific perversion s11 refuses — using one's own doctrinal position to bar others from the kingdom — and locates it under Christ's explicit woe. James 3:9–10 supplies the apostolic anchor for the impossibility of weaponized speech against image-bearers: 'therewith bless we God, even the Father; and therewith curse we men, which are made after the similitude of God. Out of the same mouth proceedeth blessing and cursing. My brethren, these things ought not so to be.' The verse names the contradiction that weaponization performs — blessing God in one breath while cursing those made in His image in the next — and James's 'these things ought not so to be' is the apostolic equivalent of s11's 'nor will we.' 2 Timothy 2:14 supplies the closing biblical anchor in the same epistolary context as 2:23–25 used at s10: 'charging them before the Lord that they strive not about words to no profit, but to the subverting of the hearers.' The verse names the specific damage of weaponized words: subverting the hearers — the very fellow believers the article's s11 refuses to use doctrine against. The Restoration anchors complete the architecture. 3 Nephi 11:32 (already deployed at A1 s13 and A4 s13) is reasserted here in a third distinct rhetorical direction: at A1 s13 the passage anchored the canonical brevity of Christ's doctrine — what Christ's doctrine is at its floor; at A4 s13 the passage anchored the Christological hermeneutic for scripture-reading — how to read scripture toward Christ; here at A8 s11 the same passage functions as the diagnostic against weaponization — what gets weaponized is always more than this canonical floor, with the floor itself standing as the measure against which weaponized doctrines are revealed as excess. Three rhetorical functions across the cluster: A1 s13 names the floor; A4 s13 reads toward the floor; A8 s11 measures against the floor. D&C 121:39 supplies the Restoration's most direct anchor for the human propensity behind weaponization: 'we have learned by sad experience that it is the nature and disposition of almost all men, as soon as they get a little authority, as they suppose, they will immediately begin to exercise unrighteous dominion.' The verse names weaponization not as an aberration but as a near-universal human disposition — making s11's refusal not a charge against any particular tradition but a confession of what every tradition (including the disciple's own) is constantly tempted toward. Pairs with D&C 121:36–37 already deployed at A8 s5 to complete the Liberty Jail revelation's diagnostic of unrighteous dominion across the article. Alma 31:5 supplies the Restoration's most direct anchor for word-against-sword in the right direction: 'the preaching of the word had a great tendency to lead the people to do that which was just — yea, it had had more powerful effect upon the minds of the people than the sword.' The verse names the proper instrument of doctrine — preaching that leads to justice — distinct from the weaponized form s11 refuses. Word as such overcomes; word weaponized perverts what word is for. D&C 64:9–10 supplies the closing Restoration anchor at the relational level: 'wherefore, I say unto you, that ye ought to forgive one another; for he that forgiveth not his brother his trespasses standeth condemned before the Lord; for there remaineth in him the greater sin. I, the Lord, will forgive whom I will forgive, but of you it is required to forgive all men.' The verse names what the disciple does in the place where weaponization would otherwise occur — forgives — and Christ's reservation of judgment to Himself ('I, the Lord, will forgive whom I will forgive') closes the door on the disciple weaponizing doctrine in His name.

biblical.text: For though we walk in the flesh, we do not war after the flesh: (For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds;) Casting down imaginations, and every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ.
biblical.comment: Paul's foundational distinction between the disciple's spiritual weapons and carnal weaponization. The phrase 'our warfare' acknowledges that the disciple is engaged in genuine spiritual contest; 'not carnal' refuses the weaponization of that contest against fellow human beings. The pulling-down is of strong holds, of imaginations exalted against God, of every high thing — not of fellow believers. The article's s11 stands precisely at this Pauline distinction: doctrine and teaching are the disciple's spiritual resources for their proper warfare, never to be carnally turned against a brother or sister who names His name.

biblical.text: But woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye shut up the kingdom of heaven against men: for ye neither go in yourselves, neither suffer ye them that are entering to go in.
biblical.comment: Christ's most direct dominical diagnosis of doctrine-as-gatekeeping-weapon. The woe against scribes and Pharisees identifies the specific perversion s11 refuses — using one's own position to shut up the kingdom against others. Notable: the woe is not against the scribes and Pharisees for being scribes and Pharisees; it is against them for the gatekeeping disposition. The article's s11 refuses the same disposition wherever it surfaces — including, by structural implication, in the disciple's own tradition. The dominical anchor for the article's most pointed refusal.

biblical.text: Therewith bless we God, even the Father; and therewith curse we men, which are made after the similitude of God. Out of the same mouth proceedeth blessing and cursing. My brethren, these things ought not so to be.
biblical.comment: James's apostolic anchor for the impossibility of weaponized speech against image-bearers. The argument moves on the ground of imago Dei: men are made after the similitude of God, and to weaponize speech against them while blessing God with the same mouth is a contradiction the disciple's tongue cannot sustain coherently. The phrase 'these things ought not so to be' is the apostolic equivalent of the article's 'nor will we' — a refusal grounded in apostolic instruction, not in the disciple's preference. The verse extends the refusal beyond doctrinal weaponization to the broader register of speech against fellow believers as image-bearers.

biblical.text: Of these things put them in remembrance, charging them before the Lord that they strive not about words to no profit, but to the subverting of the hearers.
biblical.comment: Paul in the same epistolary context as 2:23–25 used at s10. The verse names the specific damage weaponized words inflict: subverting the hearers — the very fellow believers the article's s11 refuses to use doctrine against. The phrase 'strive not about words to no profit' identifies the refusal's object precisely — not all doctrinal conversation (the article honors that), but striving about words in ways that produce no profit and subvert the hearers. The article's s11 honors the same Pauline distinction.

restoration.text: And this is my doctrine, and it is the doctrine which the Father hath given unto me; and I bear record of the Father, and the Father beareth record of me, and the Holy Ghost beareth record of the Father and me; and I bear record that the Father commandeth all men, everywhere, to repent and believe in me.
restoration.comment: Reasserted from Article 1 Span 13 and Article 4 Span 13 in different rhetorical direction. At A1 s13 the passage anchored the canonical brevity of Christ's doctrine — what His doctrine is at its floor: repent and believe in Him. At A4 s13 the passage anchored the Christological hermeneutic for scripture-reading — how to read scripture toward this floor. Here at A8 s11 the same passage functions as the diagnostic against weaponization: what gets weaponized is always more than this canonical floor, with the floor itself standing as the measure that reveals weaponized doctrines as excess. Three rhetorical functions across the cluster: A1 s13 names the floor; A4 s13 reads toward the floor; A8 s11 measures against the floor. The cluster's most-reused doctrine-floor anchor, doing distinct theological work at each surfacing.

restoration.text: We have learned by sad experience that it is the nature and disposition of almost all men, as soon as they get a little authority, as they suppose, they will immediately begin to exercise unrighteous dominion.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's most direct anchor for the human propensity behind weaponization. Joseph Smith's 'sad experience' was acquired while being mistreated by professed Christians, including those who claimed authority; the diagnostic he offers is not aimed at any particular tradition but at the near-universal human propensity ('almost all men'). The verse makes s11's refusal a confession of what every tradition is constantly tempted toward, including the disciple's own. Pairs with D&C 121:36–37 already deployed at A8 s5 to complete the Liberty Jail revelation's diagnostic of unrighteous dominion across the article — s5 names the spiritual cost of dishonoring fellow believers; s11 names the propensity behind that dishonoring.

restoration.text: And now, as the preaching of the word had a great tendency to lead the people to do that which was just — yea, it had had more powerful effect upon the minds of the people than the sword, or anything else, which had happened unto them — therefore Alma thought it was expedient that they should try the virtue of the word of God.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's most direct anchor for word-against-sword in the right direction. Alma's reflection names the proper instrument of doctrine — preaching that leads to justice — and contrasts it explicitly with the sword, the weaponized alternative. The phrase 'more powerful effect upon the minds of the people than the sword' carries the article's s11 claim in narrative form: word as such has greater power than weaponized force; the disciple who weaponizes doctrine forfeits the very power that doctrine carries when used in its proper register. The Restoration's narrative anchor for the theological refusal s11 makes.

restoration.text: Wherefore, I say unto you, that ye ought to forgive one another; for he that forgiveth not his brother his trespasses standeth condemned before the Lord; for there remaineth in him the greater sin. I, the Lord, will forgive whom I will forgive, but of you it is required to forgive all men.
restoration.comment: The closing Restoration anchor at the relational level. Where s11's prior anchors name what the disciple refuses (weaponization, gatekeeping, subverting), this anchor names what the disciple does in the place where weaponization would otherwise occur: forgives. Christ's reservation of judgment to Himself ('I, the Lord, will forgive whom I will forgive') closes the door on the disciple weaponizing doctrine in His name — the disciple is not Christ's vicar in matters of judgment, and the doctrine the disciple holds is not the disciple's instrument of judgment against fellow believers. 'Of you it is required to forgive all men' makes the affirmative requirement universal in scope, matching the article's 'every soul who comes to Jesus Christ' opening at s1.

s12.panel_comment: The article's most generous boundary marker, held as standalone span. Where s3 named the Christological criterion ('who comes to Jesus Christ') in Christ's own invitation language, s12 paraphrases that criterion at its most accessible threshold: naming the name. The phrase functions as the article's structural answer to the question 'whom does the article receive?' — every soul who names His name. Not those who name Him with creedal completeness; not those who name Him within institutional alignment with the disciple's tradition; not those who name Him with theological precision that matches the disciple's own. Those who name His name. The verb 'names' is editorially deliberate — it includes the speech-act of confession, the prayer addressed to Him, the witness offered in His name, the worship rendered to His name — without requiring any of these to take a particular doctrinal form. The biblical anchors hold this generosity at apostolic depth. Mark 9:38–40 supplies the strongest single dominical anchor: the disciples' attempt to forbid one casting out devils in Christ's name because 'he followeth not us,' and Christ's direct refusal — 'Forbid him not... For he that is not against us is on our part.' The pericope is the gospel's most direct illustration of the generosity s12 names: a soul outside the disciples' immediate circle is operating in Christ's name, the disciples raise the boundary-question, and Christ Himself widens the circle to include the name-bearing operator. The article's s12 stands precisely at this Markan refusal — the boundary-marker is not 'follows us' but 'names His name.' Romans 10:9–10 supplies the apostolic anchor for confession of the name as sufficient ground: 'if thou shalt confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus, and shalt believe in thine heart that God hath raised him from the dead, thou shalt be saved.' The verse names confession-of-the-name as the saving threshold — a threshold the article's s12 honors as also the receiving threshold. 1 Corinthians 12:3 supplies the pneumatological ground for treating naming-the-name as Spirit-given: 'no man can say that Jesus is the Lord, but by the Holy Ghost.' The implication for the article is direct: where a soul confesses Jesus as Lord, the Holy Ghost has been at work; the disciple who refuses to receive that soul refuses what the Holy Ghost has done. Acts 2:21 supplies the closing biblical anchor in the proclamation register: 'and it shall come to pass, that whosoever shall call on the name of the Lord shall be saved.' Peter's Pentecost quotation of Joel 2:32 pairs verbally with Romans 10:13 (deployed at A1 s12 and A8 s2) but in a distinct rhetorical position — there the universality scope; here the proclamation register naming who is calling. The Restoration anchors complete the architecture at four registers. D&C 18:21 supplies Christ's direct command to take upon the name: 'take upon you the name of Christ, and speak the truth in soberness.' The verse names the active disposition the disciple recognizes in others who do the same — the active taking-upon, not the passive registering. D&C 20:37 supplies the Restoration's most direct ecclesial-recognition formula: 'all those who humble themselves before God, and desire to be baptized... and witness before the church that they have truly repented of all their sins, and are willing to take upon them the name of Jesus Christ.' The verse identifies willing-to-take-upon-the-name as the gateway covenant of the disciple's own tradition — and by structural implication, recognizes the same willing-to-take-upon-the-name in souls outside that tradition as participation in the same Christological reality. 3 Nephi 27:5–7 supplies the resurrected Christ's own dominical anchor for the name as identity-marker: 'have they not read the scriptures, which say ye must take upon you the name of Christ, which is my name? For by this name shall ye be called at the last day.' The verse names the eschatological weight of the name-bearing — by this name the disciple shall be called at the last day — making the article's s12 not merely a generous receiving but a recognition of the eschatological identity the name confers. 4 Nephi 1:17 supplies the Restoration's strongest narrative anchor for the unifying name-bearing identity: 'there were no robbers, nor murderers, neither were there Lamanites, nor any manner of -ites; but they were in one, the children of Christ, and heirs to the kingdom of God.' The verse names what name-bearing accomplishes when it is permitted to do its work: the prior tribal categories collapse, replaced by the unifying 'children of Christ.' The article's s12 stands on this Restoration narrative — the name-bearing the disciple recognizes is the same name-bearing that, in 4 Nephi's narrative, dissolved every -ite-distinction in favor of the one Christ-identity. The cluster's most direct narrative anchor for the article's most generous boundary-marker.

biblical.text: And John answered him, saying, Master, we saw one casting out devils in thy name, and he followeth not us: and we forbad him, because he followeth not us. But Jesus said, Forbid him not: for there is no man which shall do a miracle in my name, that can lightly speak evil of me. For he that is not against us is on our part.
biblical.comment: The strongest single dominical anchor for the article's s12. The pericope is the gospel's most direct illustration of the generosity the article carries: a soul outside the disciples' immediate circle is operating in Christ's name, the disciples raise the boundary-question ('he followeth not us'), and Christ Himself widens the circle by His own first-person command ('Forbid him not'). The reasoning Christ supplies — 'he that is not against us is on our part' — sets the threshold of receiving at name-bearing rather than institutional alignment. The article's s12 stands precisely at this Markan refusal of the disciples' first-instinct boundary, with Christ's own widening-of-the-circle as its dominical warrant.

biblical.text: That if thou shalt confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus, and shalt believe in thine heart that God hath raised him from the dead, thou shalt be saved. For with the heart man believeth unto righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.
biblical.comment: Paul's apostolic anchor for confession of the name as the saving threshold. The verse names two coordinated movements — heart-belief and mouth-confession — that together constitute the disciple's reception of salvation. The article's s12 honors this Pauline grammar: where there is mouth-confession of the Lord Jesus and heart-belief in His resurrection, the article confesses there is no further threshold the disciple may impose for receiving the soul as a brother or sister. What is sufficient for salvation is sufficient for receiving.

biblical.text: Wherefore I give you to understand, that no man speaking by the Spirit of God calleth Jesus accursed: and that no man can say that Jesus is the Lord, but by the Holy Ghost.
biblical.comment: Paul's pneumatological ground for treating naming-the-name as Spirit-given. The verse closes the door on the disciple's temptation to suspect the name-bearing of others as merely verbal or insufficiently inhabited: where a soul says 'Jesus is the Lord,' the Holy Ghost has been at work, by Paul's own apostolic claim. The implication for the article's s12 is direct: refusing to receive the name-bearing soul is structurally a refusal of what the Holy Ghost has done in that soul. The verse makes the article's generosity not a pastoral choice but an apostolic recognition.

biblical.text: And it shall come to pass, that whosoever shall call on the name of the Lord shall be saved.
biblical.comment: Peter's Pentecost quotation of Joel 2:32, spoken at the foundational moment of the apostolic church. The verse pairs verbally with Romans 10:13 (deployed at A1 s12 and A8 s2) but in a distinct rhetorical position — there the universality scope of the gospel offer; here the proclamation register naming the one who is calling. The article's s12 honors the Petrine grammar: those who call on the name are those whom Peter's gospel recognizes as the called and the saved, and the article extends the same recognition to its receiving threshold.

restoration.text: Take upon you the name of Christ, and speak the truth in soberness.
restoration.comment: Christ's direct command in modern revelation to take upon the name. The verse names the active disposition the disciple recognizes in others who do the same — the active taking-upon, the soberly-spoken truth, the conscious identification with Christ that the name-bearing involves. The pairing of name-taking with truth-speaking-in-soberness matters for the article's s12: name-bearing is not merely vocative but constitutive of how the disciple speaks and lives. Where the disciple recognizes that constitutive name-bearing in another soul, the recognition is not optional generosity but acknowledgment of a participation in the same Christological reality the disciple herself participates in.

restoration.text: And again, by way of commandment to the church concerning the manner of baptism — All those who humble themselves before God, and desire to be baptized, and come forth with broken hearts and contrite spirits, and witness before the church that they have truly repented of all their sins, and are willing to take upon them the name of Jesus Christ, having a determination to serve him to the end, and truly manifest by their works that they have received of the Spirit of Christ unto the remission of their sins, shall be received by baptism into his church.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's most direct ecclesial-recognition formula. The verse identifies willing-to-take-upon-the-name as the gateway covenant of the disciple's own tradition. By structural implication, the article's s12 recognizes the same willing-to-take-upon-the-name in souls outside that gateway as participation in the same Christological reality the gateway formalizes. The article does not collapse the gateway — that work belongs to A11's covenant treatment — but it refuses to make the gateway's formal completion the precondition of receiving. The verse grounds the article's generosity in the Restoration's own ecclesial language: the threshold the article confesses for receiving is the same threshold the Restoration confesses for baptizing, with the formal sealing held in its proper place.

restoration.text: Have they not read the scriptures, which say ye must take upon you the name of Christ, which is my name? For by this name shall ye be called at the last day; And whoso taketh upon him my name, and endureth to the end, the same shall be saved at the last day. Therefore, whatsoever ye shall do, ye shall do it in my name; therefore ye shall call the church in my name; and ye shall pray unto the Father in my name that he will bless the church for my sake.
restoration.comment: The resurrected Christ's dominical anchor for the name as identity-marker of His people, given in the Bountiful theophany. The verse names the eschatological weight of name-bearing — by this name the disciple shall be called at the last day — making the article's s12 not merely a generous present-tense receiving but a recognition of the eschatological identity the name confers. The triple-clause closing ('whatsoever ye shall do, ye shall do it in my name; therefore ye shall call the church in my name; and ye shall pray unto the Father in my name') extends the name's reach across action, ecclesial identity, and prayer — the article's s12 recognizes the name-bearing soul wherever any of these registers is operative.

restoration.text: There were no robbers, nor murderers, neither were there Lamanites, nor any manner of -ites; but they were in one, the children of Christ, and heirs to the kingdom of God.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's strongest narrative anchor for the unifying name-bearing identity. The verse names what name-bearing accomplishes when it is permitted to do its work across a community: the prior tribal categories collapse ('no manner of -ites'), replaced by the unifying 'children of Christ.' The phrase 'nor any manner of -ites' is a structural anchor for the article's claim that the boundary-marker is not the disciple's -ite-of-origin but the name-bearing itself. The article's s12 stands on this 4 Nephi narrative: the name-bearing the disciple recognizes today is the same name-bearing that, in the Bountiful generation following Christ's post-resurrection ministry, dissolved every -ite-distinction in favor of the one Christ-identity. The cluster's most direct Restoration narrative anchor for the article's most generous boundary-marker.

s13.text: We will not return insult for insult, exclusion for exclusion, or suspicion for suspicion
s13.panel_comment: The non-retaliation triple. Where s10 named the refusal to defend the walls and s11 named the refusal to weaponize doctrine, s13 names the refusal at its most personal register: the three specific in-kind responses the disciple declines when treated as an outsider, a suspect, or an enemy by those who themselves name Christ. The triple is structurally Pauline (cf. Romans 12:17 'recompense to no man evil for evil'; 1 Peter 3:9 'not rendering evil for evil, or railing for railing'), but the article's formulation is more specific than its biblical sources — naming the exact three currencies in which inter-Christian retaliation typically trades: rhetorical (insult), social (exclusion), and dispositional (suspicion). The biblical anchors carry the apostolic foundation. Romans 12:17–21 supplies the strongest single Pauline anchor — the most extended NT non-retaliation pericope, with its closing 'be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good' naming the affirmative posture that replaces the in-kind response. Matthew 5:38–42 supplies the dominical anchor at its source: Christ's antithesis 'ye have heard that it hath been said, An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth: But I say unto you, That ye resist not evil.' The article's s13 stands in the lineage of this Sermon-on-the-Mount antithesis — the disciple's refusal of in-kind response is not a personal preference but a dominical instruction. 1 Peter 3:9 (already deployed at A8 s10) is reasserted here in different rhetorical direction. At s10 the verse anchored the general framing of non-retaliation as the disciple's standing posture toward defending the walls; here at s13 the verse anchors the specific in-kind currencies (railing for railing) that the article's triple makes explicit. The s10 deployment carried the disposition; the s13 deployment carries the operation. 1 Thessalonians 5:15 supplies the closing biblical anchor with universality scope: 'see that none render evil for evil unto any man.' The phrase 'unto any man' matches the article's 'we will not' in scope — the refusal is not selectively applied to certain offenders but is the disciple's standing posture toward all. The Restoration anchors deepen and extend. 3 Nephi 12:38–42 supplies the resurrected Christ's Bountiful reaffirmation of the Sermon-on-the-Mount antithesis: 'ye have heard that it hath been said, An eye for an eye... but I say unto you, that ye shall not resist evil, but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also.' The verbal continuity between Matthew 5 and 3 Nephi 12 ratifies the dominical instruction across two sermons in two hemispheres — the same Christ teaching the same posture to two assemblies. D&C 98:23–27 supplies the Restoration's most extended anti-retaliation pericope, with the multi-bearing structure ('first time bear it patiently and revile not against them; second time bear it patiently; third time bear it patiently'). The verse names what the disciple does *across time* when the in-kind temptation is repeated — bears patiently again and again, not because the disciple is exhausted of will but because the bearing is itself the disciple's witness. Mosiah 3:19 supplies the closing Restoration anchor at the dispositional level: King Benjamin's naming of 'the natural man' that 'putteth off' through becoming 'as a child, submissive, meek, humble, patient, full of love, willing to submit.' The verse names the very disposition that replaces the retaliatory instinct — submission, meekness, patience — and locates the disciple's s13 refusal not as suppression of native impulse but as the natural-man-put-off and the saint-put-on.

biblical.text: Recompense to no man evil for evil. Provide things honest in the sight of all men. If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men. Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord. Therefore if thine enemy hunger, feed him; if he thirst, give him drink: for in so doing thou shalt heap coals of fire on his head. Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good.
biblical.comment: The most extended NT non-retaliation pericope and the strongest single Pauline anchor for the article's s13. The phrase 'recompense to no man evil for evil' names exactly the in-kind disposition s13 refuses; 'avenge not yourselves' names the broader posture from which that refusal flows. The verse pairs prohibition with affirmative directive — feed the enemy, give drink — making clear that the refusal of retaliation is not passivity but active goodness directed toward the one who has wronged the disciple. The closing 'be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good' names the eschatological hope under which s13 is endurable: in-kind retaliation cedes the field to evil; affirmative goodness contests the field for Christ.

biblical.text: Ye have heard that it hath been said, An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth: But I say unto you, That ye resist not evil: but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also. And if any man will sue thee at the law, and take away thy coat, let him have thy cloak also. And whosoever shall compel thee to go a mile, go with him twain. Give to him that asketh thee, and from him that would borrow of thee turn not thou away.
biblical.comment: The dominical antithesis at its source, the Sermon-on-the-Mount instruction that grounds the entire NT non-retaliation tradition. The phrase 'ye have heard... but I say unto you' is Christ's most distinctive teaching pattern, and its application here marks non-retaliation as belonging to the same register as His other foundational antitheses (anger, lust, oaths, love-for-enemies). The article's s13 stands explicitly in this lineage — the triple is the disciple's working out of Christ's 'resist not evil' across the three currencies inter-Christian retaliation typically uses. The dominical original carries the article's most pointed claim that non-retaliation is not optional ethics but constitutive discipleship.

biblical.text: Not rendering evil for evil, or railing for railing; but contrariwise blessing; knowing that ye are thereunto called, that ye should inherit a blessing.
biblical.comment: Reasserted from Article 8 Span 10 in different rhetorical direction. At A8 s10 the verse anchored the general framing of non-retaliation as the disciple's standing posture toward defending the walls — the disposition. Here at A8 s13 the verse anchors the specific in-kind currencies the disciple refuses (railing for railing) as the article's triple makes them explicit — the operation. The two surfacings together carry the cluster's non-retaliation arc: s10 names the posture (we will not defend); s13 names the operation (we will not return). Same passage, two distinct rhetorical functions across adjacent A8 spans.

biblical.text: See that none render evil for evil unto any man; but ever follow that which is good, both among yourselves, and to all men.
biblical.comment: The closing biblical anchor with universality scope. The phrase 'unto any man' matches the article's 'we will not' in scope — the refusal is not selectively applied to certain offenders, certain traditions, or certain provocations but is the disciple's standing posture toward all. The pairing 'both among yourselves, and to all men' makes explicit the universality the article's s13 confesses: the disciple's posture toward fellow believers and toward all human beings is the same. Paul's 'see that none' is congregational and watchful — the church is to police the disposition collectively, not merely to instruct it individually.

restoration.text: And behold, it is written, an eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth; But I say unto you, that ye shall not resist evil, but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also; And whosoever shall compel thee to go a mile, go with him twain. Give to him that asketh thee, and from him that would borrow of thee turn thou not away.
restoration.comment: The resurrected Christ's Bountiful reaffirmation of Matthew 5:38–42. The verbal continuity between Matthew 5 and 3 Nephi 12 ratifies the dominical instruction across two sermons in two hemispheres — the same Christ teaching the same posture to two assemblies. The Restoration witness here is not novel content but confirming witness: what Christ taught on the Mount in Galilee, He reaffirmed at Bountiful in the New World, with the same antithesis structure ('ye have heard... but I say') and the same operational examples (the cheek, the cloak, the second mile). The article's s13 stands on this dual canonical witness — the disciple's refusal of in-kind response is not a culturally-bound first-century instruction but the dominical pattern Christ ratified across resurrection, hemisphere, and dispensation.

restoration.text: Now, I speak unto you concerning your families — if men will smite you, or your families, once, and ye bear it patiently and revile not against them, neither seek revenge, ye shall be rewarded; But if ye bear it not patiently, it shall be accounted unto you as being meted out as a just measure unto you. And again, if your enemy shall smite you the second time, and you revile not against your enemy, and bear it patiently, your reward shall be an hundredfold. And again, if he shall smite you the third time, and ye bear it patiently, your reward shall be an hundredfold.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's most extended anti-retaliation pericope, with the multi-bearing structure that no biblical passage matches in temporal extension. The verse names what the disciple does *across time* when the in-kind temptation is repeated: bears patiently the first time, the second time, the third time. The repetition is theologically significant — non-retaliation is not a single forgiveness-event but a sustained posture across iterations of provocation. The article's s13 'we will not return' carries this temporal weight: the refusal is not for one offense but for the long arc of inter-Christian relationship across decades of recurring suspicion, exclusion, and insult. The reward-structure ('an hundredfold' from the second time onward) names the accruing weight of patient bearing as itself spiritual capital.

restoration.text: For the natural man is an enemy to God, and has been from the fall of Adam, and will be, forever and ever, unless he yields to the enticings of the Holy Spirit, and putteth off the natural man and becometh a saint through the atonement of Christ the Lord, and becometh as a child, submissive, meek, humble, patient, full of love, willing to submit to all things which the Lord seeth fit to inflict upon him, even as a child doth submit to his father.
restoration.comment: The closing Restoration anchor at the dispositional level. King Benjamin names the very disposition that replaces the retaliatory instinct: submissive, meek, humble, patient, full of love, willing to submit. The article's s13 refusal is not suppression of native impulse but the natural-man-put-off and the saint-put-on through Christ's atonement. The grammatical structure 'putteth off... becometh' matches the article's structural movement: the disciple's refusal of in-kind response is the operation by which the natural-man impulse is laid down and the saint-disposition is taken up. The verse grounds s13 not in moral effort alone but in the atonement-mediated transformation that makes the disposition possible.

s14.text: We will sit at the table with every soul who has found Christ
s14.panel_comment: The article's affirmative table-fellowship claim, paired with s15's door-stayed-open claim to constitute the article's ecclesial center of gravity. Where s13 named what the disciple refuses to do, s14 names what the disciple actively does: sit, at the table, with every soul who has found Christ. Each element of the clause is editorially load-bearing. 'Sit' is the disciple's posture of unhurried presence — not visit, not pass through, not tolerate — but sit, with the implication of duration and shared meal. 'At the table' invokes the deepest biblical metaphor for fellowship across difference, from the patriarchs through the prophets through Christ's own table-ministry through the apostolic household-gatherings. 'With every soul who has found Christ' supplies the threshold: the article does not require the soul to share the disciple's denominational alignment, only to have found Christ. The biblical anchors carry the table-fellowship architecture at four registers. Luke 14:15–24 supplies the strongest single dominical anchor — the parable of the great supper, with its escalating pattern of inclusion (first the originally-invited, then the highways and hedges, then 'compel them to come in, that my house may be filled'). The parable is Christ's most direct teaching that the master's table is filled by the master's widening, not by the originally-invited's gatekeeping. Acts 2:42, 46 supplies the earliest apostolic table-pattern — the post-Pentecost church's 'breaking bread from house to house' as the daily texture of the body that had just been baptized. The verse grounds s14 in the apostolic original: the disciple's table-fellowship is not innovation but recovery of what the church was at its first morning. Galatians 2:11–14 supplies the strongest single biblical anchor for *refusing the withdrawal of the table* across in-group/out-group lines. Paul's public confrontation of Peter at Antioch — over Peter's withdrawal from Gentile table-fellowship under pressure from circumcision-party arrivals — is the apostolic precedent for the article's refusal. The article's s14 stands explicitly in this Antioch-rebuke lineage: the disciple does not withdraw the table under pressure from any party, however authoritative. Revelation 3:20 supplies the closing biblical anchor in dominical first-person: 'Behold, I stand at the door, and knock... I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me.' The verse names Christ's own table-fellowship offer as the pattern the disciple imitates — the disciple sits at the table because Christ first sat at the table, because Christ is even now standing at every door asking to sup. The Restoration anchors complete the architecture. D&C 27:5–14 supplies Christ's sweeping eschatological table-fellowship vision, the promise to drink the fruit of the vine 'with you on the earth' alongside named saints from across dispensations — Moroni, Elias, John, Elijah, Joseph, Adam, Peter, James, John. The verse names the article's table-fellowship not as accommodation but as participation in Christ's own promised table — the disciple's sitting now is rehearsal for Christ's sitting then. 3 Nephi 18:1–11 supplies the most pastoral table-discipline pericope in the Restoration canon, with the explicit instruction 'ye shall not suffer any one knowingly to partake of my flesh and blood unworthily... nevertheless, ye shall not cast him out from your synagogues, or your places of worship, for unto such shall ye continue to minister.' The Bountiful pattern is editorially significant for s14: it preserves the formal sacramental gateway as belonging to its own canonical territory while simultaneously refusing the casting-out of the unworthy from the worship community. The article's s14 honors precisely this distinction — the table of fellowship the article confesses is not the sacramental table (which belongs to A11 and to each tradition's own administration), but the table of pastoral hospitality that even the unworthy-by-formal-measure are not cast out from. Mosiah 25:17–24 supplies the Restoration's narrative anchor for table-across-communities: Alma's formation of seven churches across the land of Zarahemla, 'called the church of God, or the church of Christ, from that time forward... and they were called the people of God.' The verse names what name-bearing accomplishes when permitted to do its work across plural communities: many local churches, one named people. The article's s14 stands on this Zarahemla narrative — the table the disciple sits at today is filled across plural communities the disciple does not control, all confessing the same Christ.

biblical.text: And when one of them that sat at meat with him heard these things, he said unto him, Blessed is he that shall eat bread in the kingdom of God. Then said he unto him, A certain man made a great supper, and bade many: And sent his servant at supper time to say to them that were bidden, Come; for all things are now ready. And they all with one consent began to make excuse... Then the master of the house being angry said to his servant, Go out quickly into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in hither the poor, and the maimed, and the halt, and the blind. And the servant said, Lord, it is done as thou hast commanded, and yet there is room. And the lord said unto the servant, Go out into the highways and hedges, and compel them to come in, that my house may be filled.
biblical.comment: The strongest single dominical anchor for the article's s14 — the parable of the great supper, with its escalating pattern of inclusion. The pericope's structural movement is decisive: the originally-invited make excuse; the master sends out for the poor, maimed, halt, blind; there is yet room; the master sends out again to the highways and hedges. The article's s14 stands at the bottom of this escalation: the disciple sits at a table whose master is widening, not narrowing, the company. The closing 'compel them to come in, that my house may be filled' names the master's urgent intent — the table is for being-filled, and any disciple's gatekeeping at it works against the master's expressed will. The dominical pattern for s14: the table belongs to its master, and the master is widening it.

biblical.text: And they continued steadfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers... And they, continuing daily with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread from house to house, did eat their meat with gladness and singleness of heart.
biblical.comment: The earliest apostolic table-pattern — the post-Pentecost church's daily texture. The phrase 'breaking bread from house to house' names what the disciple's table-fellowship looks like at apostolic origin: not formal gathering only, but the daily-shared meal that constituted the body the apostles had just baptized into. The pairing of 'gladness and singleness of heart' with 'breaking bread' marks the table-fellowship as joyful and unified — the affective texture of the article's s14. The verse grounds s14 in apostolic recovery: the disciple's table-fellowship is not innovation but return to what the church was at its first morning, before the centuries of fragmentation made the table contestable.

biblical.text: But when Peter was come to Antioch, I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed. For before that certain came from James, he did eat with the Gentiles: but when they were come, he withdrew and separated himself, fearing them which were of the circumcision. And the other Jews dissembled likewise with him; insomuch that Barnabas also was carried away with their dissimulation. But when I saw that they walked not uprightly according to the truth of the gospel, I said unto Peter before them all, If thou, being a Jew, livest after the manner of Gentiles, and not as the Jews, why compellest thou the Gentiles to live as do the Jews?
biblical.comment: The strongest single biblical anchor for refusing the withdrawal of the table under in-group pressure. Paul's public confrontation of Peter at Antioch is the apostolic precedent for the article's s14 refusal — Peter, the chief apostle, withdrew from Gentile table-fellowship under pressure from circumcision-party arrivals, and Paul met him face to face for it. The pericope's claim is structurally extraordinary: even apostolic authority does not justify the withdrawal of the table from those Christ has received. The article's s14 stands explicitly in this Antioch-rebuke lineage. The disciple does not withdraw the table under pressure from any party — denominational, doctrinal, or institutional — however authoritative. The phrase 'walked not uprightly according to the truth of the gospel' names the gospel itself as the standard the table-withdrawal violated.

biblical.text: Behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any man hear my voice, and open the door, I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me.
biblical.comment: Christ's own table-fellowship offer in dominical first-person. The verse names the pattern the disciple imitates: the disciple sits at the table because Christ first sat at the table, because Christ is even now standing at every door asking to sup. The pairing of 'sup with him, and he with me' is mutual — the table is not Christ's alone or the disciple's alone but the place where the two are made present to each other. The article's s14 grounds the disciple's sitting in Christ's prior sitting; what the disciple does at the table is participation in what Christ has been doing all along. The reciprocity Christ offers ('with him... with me') is the deepest rebuttal to any disciple's gatekeeping: Christ does not gate the table where He Himself is the Host.

restoration.text: Behold, this is wisdom in me; wherefore, marvel not, for the hour cometh that I will drink of the fruit of the vine with you on the earth... with Moroni, whom I have sent unto you to reveal the Book of Mormon... and also with Elias, to whom I have committed the keys of bringing to pass the restoration of all things... and also John the son of Zacharias... and also Elijah... and also with Joseph and Jacob, and Isaac, and Abraham... and also with Michael, or Adam, the father of all... and also with Peter, and James, and John, whom I have sent unto you, by whom I have ordained you and confirmed you to be apostles, and especial witnesses of my name... wherefore, lift up your hearts and rejoice, and gird up your loins, and take upon you my whole armor.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's sweeping eschatological table-fellowship vision, given as Christ's direct first-person promise to drink the fruit of the vine 'with you on the earth' alongside named saints from across dispensations. The list — Moroni, Elias, John, Elijah, Joseph, Jacob, Isaac, Abraham, Michael/Adam, Peter, James, John — spans the entire arc of biblical and Restoration witness. The article's s14 stands at the foot of this promised future table: the disciple's sitting now is rehearsal for Christ's sitting then, and the company at the disciple's present table is the same company being gathered for the future one. The verse grounds s14's table-fellowship not as accommodation but as participation in Christ's own promised table — what the disciple does at the kitchen-table today is echo of what Christ has promised to do at the cosmic table at the day of His coming.

restoration.text: And it came to pass that Jesus commanded his disciples that they should bring forth some bread and wine unto him... And when the disciples had come with bread and wine, he took of the bread and brake and blessed it; and he gave unto the disciples and commanded that they should eat. And when they had eaten and were filled, he commanded that they should give unto the multitude... And he said unto them: He that eateth this bread eateth of my body to his soul; and he that drinketh of this wine drinketh of my blood to his soul; and his soul shall never hunger nor thirst, but shall be filled.
restoration.comment: The most pastoral table-discipline pericope in the Restoration canon, used here for its hospitality grammar specifically — not for sacramental gating. Bountiful establishes the pattern that the article's s14 honors: Christ Himself institutes the formal table (the sacrament) for those prepared to receive it, and yet within the same instruction (verses following the excerpt) commands the apostles 'ye shall not cast him out from your synagogues, or your places of worship, for unto such shall ye continue to minister.' The pattern is editorially decisive for the article's s14: the formal sacramental gateway belongs to its own canonical territory (each tradition's own administration of the sacrament, addressed elsewhere in the cluster at A11 Covenants and Commitments). The table of pastoral hospitality the article's s14 confesses is the wider table — the synagogue, the place of worship, the community of fellow believers — from which even the unworthy-by-formal-measure are not cast out. The article preserves both — the sacrament's formality belongs to A11; the hospitality of the wider table belongs to A8 s14.

restoration.text: And it came to pass that king Mosiah granted unto Alma that he might establish churches throughout all the land of Zarahemla; and gave him power to ordain priests and teachers over every church... And it came to pass that there were seven churches in the land of Zarahemla. And it came to pass that whosoever were desirous to take upon them the name of Christ, or of God, did join the churches of God; and they were called the people of God. And the Lord did pour out his Spirit upon them, and they were blessed, and prospered in the land.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's narrative anchor for table-across-communities. The verse names what name-bearing accomplishes when it is permitted to do its work across plural communities: seven local churches form across the land of Zarahemla, each ordained with priests and teachers, all together called 'the people of God.' The grammatical structure is decisive — many local churches, one named people, with the Lord pouring out His Spirit upon the whole. The article's s14 stands on this Zarahemla narrative: the table the disciple sits at today is filled across plural communities the disciple does not control, all confessing the same Christ. The verse refuses the false alternative between ecclesial unity and ecclesial plurality — the Restoration narrative shows that the people of God can be one in Spirit while gathered in seven separate churches, and the disciple's table-fellowship participates in that same one-in-many architecture.

s15.text: we will leave the door open to every soul still searching for Him
s15.panel_comment: The article's door-stayed-open claim, paired with s14's table-fellowship claim. Where s14 named what the disciple does for the soul who has found Christ — sit at the table — s15 names what the disciple does for the soul still searching for Him: leave the door open. The clause carries three editorial moves. 'We will leave' is the disciple's active posture — the door does not stay open by default but by the disciple's sustained refusal to close it. 'The door open' invokes the biblical metaphor of access (Christ-as-door, Christ-at-the-door, the disciples as door-keepers in the household of faith). 'To every soul still searching' supplies the universality scope — the door is not selectively open to seekers from particular backgrounds or with particular questions, but to every soul whose search has not yet found its end in Christ. The biblical anchors carry the door-imagery at four registers. Luke 15:11–24 supplies the strongest single dominical anchor — the parable of the prodigal son, with its decisive father-disposition: 'when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him.' The parable is Christ's most extended teaching that the Father's door is open even before the searching son arrives — open while the son is still in the far country, open while the son is yet a great way off, open as the natural disposition of the Father, not as a contingent reward for sufficient repentance. The article's s15 stands precisely in this prodigal-pattern: the door is open while the search continues, not after the search succeeds. John 10:9 supplies Christ's own first-person door-claim — 'I am the door: by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved, and shall go in and out, and find pasture.' The article's grammar is honored by Christ's own grammar: the door is not the disciple's to open or close; the door is Christ Himself, and the disciple's 'leaving open' is participation in Christ's perpetual opening. 2 Peter 3:9 supplies the apostolic anchor for God's own posture of waiting-with-door-open: 'the Lord is... not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance.' The verse names the door-stayed-open as God's own intent — Peter's 'not willing that any should perish' is the deepest theological ground for s15's claim. The disciple does not leave the door open as personal hospitality but as participation in God's own delay-of-judgment-for-the-sake-of-mercy. Hebrews 13:2 supplies the closing biblical anchor at the practical-disposition level: 'be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.' The verse names the disciple's door-keeping at the level of the unrecognized arrival — every soul still searching is a stranger of unknown status, and the disciple's leaving-open accommodates the possibility that the soul is more than appearance suggests. The Restoration anchors deepen the architecture. 3 Nephi 18:25 supplies Christ's own door-imagery in the Bountiful sermon: 'ye see that I have commanded that none of you should go away, but rather have commanded that ye should come unto me, that ye might feel and see; even so shall ye do unto the world; and whosoever breaketh this commandment suffereth himself to be led into temptation.' The verse names the article's s15 disposition as Christ's direct command — 'even so shall ye do unto the world' — making the door-stayed-open not optional generosity but commanded participation in Christ's own outreach to the searching. D&C 29:1–2 supplies the Restoration's gathering-imagery anchor: 'Listen to the voice of Jesus Christ, your Redeemer... who will gather his people even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, even as many as will hearken to my voice and humble themselves before me, and call upon me in mighty prayer.' The hen-gathering imagery names Christ's own sustained door-keeping disposition — protective, waiting, patient, inviting. The article's s15 stands on this image: the disciple's leaving-open is participation in Christ's gathering. (The verse's deeper theological work — divine pathos and the rejection of impassibility — belongs to the systematic theology of Volume 2; here the verse serves the article's ecclesial register specifically.) D&C 4:7 supplies the closing Restoration anchor with explicit door-language: 'Ask, and ye shall receive; knock, and it shall be opened unto you.' The verse names what the disciple's leaving-open accomplishes from the searching soul's side — the knock is met with opening, the asking with receiving. The article's s15 grammar is mirrored: the disciple keeps open the door that God Himself has promised to open in response to the searching soul's knock.

biblical.text: And he said, A certain man had two sons: And the younger of them said to his father, Father, give me the portion of goods that falleth to me. And he divided unto them his living. And not many days after the younger son gathered all together, and took his journey into a far country, and there wasted his substance with riotous living... And when he came to himself, he said... I will arise and go to my father, and will say unto him, Father, I have sinned against heaven, and before thee, And am no more worthy to be called thy son: make me as one of thy hired servants. And he arose, and came to his father. But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him.
biblical.comment: The strongest single dominical anchor for the article's s15 — Christ's most extended teaching on the Father's door-stayed-open disposition. The pericope's decisive moment is the father's seeing-while-yet-a-great-way-off: the door was open before the son arrived, open while the son was in the far country, open as the natural disposition of the Father rather than as contingent reward for sufficient repentance. The article's s15 stands precisely in this prodigal-pattern: the disciple keeps the door open while the search continues, not after the search succeeds. The father's running and falling-on-the-neck names the affective texture of door-stayed-open — not grudging tolerance but eager welcome, not waiting-to-see-if-they-deserve-it but running-to-meet-them. The article's s15 honors this grammar: the door is open as disposition, not as conditional permission.

biblical.text: I am the door: by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved, and shall go in and out, and find pasture.
biblical.comment: Christ's own first-person door-claim. The verse names the deepest theological ground for the article's s15: the door is not the disciple's to open or close; the door is Christ Himself. The disciple's 'leaving open' is participation in Christ's perpetual opening, not initiation of openness as if the disciple were the door-keeper of the kingdom. The grammatical structure 'I am the door' is dominical first-person — the same identity-claim register as 'I am the way, the truth, and the life' (deployed at A6 s8) and 'I am the bread of life.' The article's s15 grammar is corrected by this verse: the disciple does not leave open *a* door but participates in keeping unobstructed the door who is Christ. The closing 'shall go in and out, and find pasture' names the freedom the searching soul finds when the door is participated-in rather than gatekept.

biblical.text: The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance.
biblical.comment: The apostolic anchor for God's own posture of waiting-with-door-open. Peter's phrase 'not willing that any should perish' names the deepest theological ground for s15's claim — the door-stayed-open is God's own intent, not the disciple's contribution to mercy. The framing 'as some men count slackness' is editorially significant: what looks from the human side like delay or inaction is, from the divine side, longsuffering for the sake of the not-yet-arrived. The article's s15 honors this Petrine grammar: the disciple does not leave the door open as personal hospitality but as participation in God's own delay-of-judgment-for-the-sake-of-mercy. The disciple's patience with the still-searching soul is the disciple's participation in God's patience.

biblical.text: Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.
biblical.comment: The closing biblical anchor at the practical-disposition level. The verse names the disciple's door-keeping at the level of the unrecognized arrival — every soul still searching is a stranger of unknown status, and the disciple's leaving-open accommodates the possibility that the soul is more than appearance suggests. The phrase 'angels unawares' is editorially significant for the article's s15: the disciple cannot reliably identify which searching souls will turn out to have been bearing what the disciple did not initially recognize, and so the disciple's door-stayed-open is not selective recognition but uniform hospitality. Hebrews supplies the practical reason for the article's universality scope — the disciple cannot tell, in advance, who is whom.

restoration.text: For ye see that I have commanded that none of you should go away, but rather have commanded that ye should come unto me, that ye might feel and see; even so shall ye do unto the world; and whosoever breaketh this commandment suffereth himself to be led into temptation.
restoration.comment: Christ's own door-imagery in the Bountiful sermon, given as direct command. The phrase 'even so shall ye do unto the world' makes the article's s15 disposition not optional generosity but commanded participation in Christ's outreach to the searching. The verse establishes a structural parallel: as Christ commanded 'none of you should go away, but rather... come unto me, that ye might feel and see,' so the disciple is to enact toward the world the same posture Christ enacted toward His original gathering at Bountiful. The closing clause — 'whosoever breaketh this commandment suffereth himself to be led into temptation' — locates the door-closing impulse not as defensible caution but as the disciple's own susceptibility to the temptation of gatekeeping the searching out of Christ's reach.

restoration.text: Listen to the voice of Jesus Christ, your Redeemer, the Great I AM, whose arm of mercy hath atoned for your sins; Who will gather his people even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, even as many as will hearken to my voice and humble themselves before me, and call upon me in mighty prayer.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's gathering-imagery anchor. The hen-gathering metaphor names Christ's own sustained door-keeping disposition — protective, waiting, patient, inviting. The image is dominical first-person ('who will gather his people even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings'), and its texture is decisively maternal-protective rather than transactional or conditional. The article's s15 stands on this image: the disciple's leaving-open is participation in Christ's gathering. The verse's qualifier — 'even as many as will hearken to my voice and humble themselves before me, and call upon me in mighty prayer' — names the threshold of being-gathered without naming a credential beyond the searching itself, which is the article's s15 universality scope. The verse's deeper theological work in the cluster — divine pathos, the rejection of impassibility, the weeping God of Moses 7 — belongs to the systematic theology of Volume 2; here the verse serves the article's ecclesial register specifically.

restoration.text: Ask, and ye shall receive; knock, and it shall be opened unto you.
restoration.comment: The closing Restoration anchor with explicit door-language. The verse names what the disciple's leaving-open accomplishes from the searching soul's side: the knock is met with opening, the asking with receiving. The article's s15 grammar is mirrored — the disciple keeps open the door that God Himself has promised to open in response to the searching soul's knock. The verse pairs verbally with Matthew 7:7 (the Sermon-on-the-Mount original), but the modern-revelation deployment carries an additional weight: D&C 4 is a missionary commission, given to the disciple specifically as instruction for going out to those still searching. The article's s15 stands in this missionary-commission lineage — the disciple's door-stayed-open is not passive hospitality alone but active participation in God's own 'ask and receive, knock and it shall be opened' grammar.

s16.text: the fellowship He purchased with His blood
s16.panel_comment: The article's blood-purchase claim. Where s14 and s15 named the disciple's present-tense table-fellowship and door-stayed-open dispositions, s16 names what those dispositions are participating *in*: the fellowship Christ Himself purchased with His own blood. The clause shifts the article's grammar from ecclesial action (what the disciple does) to christological foundation (what Christ has done). Each element matters. 'Fellowship' (Greek koinonia) is the apostolic word for the deepest mode of shared participation — not mere association but corporate participation in the same reality. 'He purchased' (Greek peripoieo, agorazo) names the transaction Christ executed once for all; the disciple is not purchasing the fellowship now and is not contributing to its purchase price. 'With His blood' names the cost — the cost is paid in full, in Christ's own blood, with no remaining balance the disciple could be asked to add. The clause does not equate the article's ecclesial fellowship with Christ's atonement directly; it grounds the ecclesial fellowship in the atonement as its theological condition of possibility. The biblical anchors carry the blood-purchase architecture at four registers. Acts 20:28 supplies the strongest single biblical anchor — Paul's direct phrasing 'the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.' The verse is the verbatim source for the article's grammar; 'purchased with His blood' is the apostolic phrase the article reasserts. Paul's context is Ephesian elders' charge to 'feed the church of God' — the verse names the church's value (purchased with the blood of God Himself, in Paul's startling 'his own blood' construction) as the ground of the elders' care for it. 1 Peter 1:18–19 supplies the apostolic anchor for blood-redemption as the *value* of the fellowship: 'ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold... but with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot.' The verse names the cost-comparison explicitly: the fellowship the article confesses is not purchaseable by any human currency, however costly; the only currency that could purchase it is Christ's blood. 1 Corinthians 6:19–20 supplies the Pauline anchor at the individual level: 'ye are not your own? For ye are bought with a price.' The verse extends the purchase-claim from corporate fellowship to individual identity — each disciple's body belongs to the purchasing Christ, with the implication that the disciple's membership in the fellowship is grounded in the same purchase that grounds the fellowship itself. Revelation 5:9 supplies the closing biblical anchor at the eschatological-vision level: 'thou wast slain, and hast redeemed us to God by thy blood out of every kindred, and tongue, and people, and nation.' The verse is the article's most direct anchor for blood-purchased fellowship explicitly *across* the dividing markers of kindred, tongue, people, and nation — naming the article's fellowship not as a future hope but as the present reality the heavenly worship already names as accomplished. The Restoration anchors complete the architecture. Mosiah 3:7–11 supplies the Restoration's most direct narrative anchor for the blood Christ shed *for* the fellowship He purchased: 'behold, blood cometh from every pore, so great shall be his anguish for the wickedness and the abominations of his people.' King Benjamin's atonement pericope names the cost-side of the purchase with unflinching specificity — blood from every pore — and grounds the article's 'with His blood' in the Restoration canon's most extended atonement narrative. D&C 18:11–12 supplies the universality-scope anchor: 'the Son of God suffered death... to bring to pass the resurrection of the dead, that they might be brought back into the presence of God; yea, and to suffer the pains of all men, that all men might repent and come unto him.' The verse names the universal scope of the purchase — 'all men' — matching the article's 'every soul' opening at s1 and threading through s14/s15. The fellowship purchased with Christ's blood is purchased for all, not for a denominational subset. Alma 5:21–24 supplies the closing Restoration anchor at the cleansing-operation level: 'there can no man be saved except his garments are washed white; yea, his garments must be purified until they are cleansed from all stain, through the blood of him of whom it has been spoken.' The verse names the *operation* by which the blood-purchase is actualized in the disciple's life — the cleansing of the garments through the blood — distinguishing the article's s16 from a transactional-only reading. The fellowship Christ purchased is the fellowship into which the disciple is brought through the same blood that purchased it; the purchase and the cleansing are not two operations but one Christ-act in two grammars. Coordinates editorially with A6's atonement treatment: A6 s11 deploys Alma 7:11–12 for the broader atonement-mechanism (Christ taking upon Him the pains and afflictions of His people); s16 here deploys Alma 5:21–24 for the cleansing-operation specifically. Distinguishable rhetorical functions on the same theological floor.

biblical.text: Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
biblical.comment: The strongest single biblical anchor for the article's s16 — Paul's direct phrasing 'the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.' The verse is the verbatim source for the article's grammar; 'purchased with His blood' reasserts Paul's exact apostolic phrase, with the same theological weight Paul placed on it. The verse's startling construction 'his own blood' (Greek tou idiou haimatos) names the church's value at its highest theological register: the purchase price is the blood of God Himself in Christ. Paul's pastoral context (the Ephesian elders' charge to feed the church) supplies the application: the value of what was purchased grounds the care given to it. The article's s16 stands precisely at this Pauline apostolic anchor.

biblical.text: Forasmuch as ye know that ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold, from your vain conversation received by tradition from your fathers; But with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot.
biblical.comment: The apostolic anchor for blood-redemption as the *value* of the fellowship. Peter's explicit cost-comparison is editorially decisive: the fellowship the article confesses is not purchaseable by any human currency (silver, gold, traditional inheritance), however costly. The phrase 'vain conversation received by tradition from your fathers' is doubly apt for the article's s16 — the fellowship the disciple participates in cannot be purchased even by inherited tradition, however venerable; only Christ's blood is the currency adequate to the fellowship. The lamb-without-blemish image grounds the value of the blood in the perfection of the lamb whose blood it was — Christ Himself, without sin, without contradiction in His own person.

biblical.text: What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you, which ye have of God, and ye are not your own? For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body, and in your spirit, which are God's.
biblical.comment: The Pauline anchor at the individual level. Where Acts 20:28 names the corporate body purchased with blood, 1 Corinthians 6:19–20 extends the purchase-claim to individual identity — each disciple's body belongs to the purchasing Christ. The article's s16 implicit claim is structurally completed by this verse: the fellowship the disciple participates in is purchased, and the disciple's very person is purchased; the disciple's membership in the fellowship is grounded in the same purchase that grounds the fellowship itself. The closing 'glorify God in your body, and in your spirit' names the affirmative posture the purchase establishes — the disciple's life is response to a purchase already made, not contribution toward a purchase still being made.

biblical.text: And they sung a new song, saying, Thou art worthy to take the book, and to open the seals thereof: for thou wast slain, and hast redeemed us to God by thy blood out of every kindred, and tongue, and people, and nation.
biblical.comment: The closing biblical anchor at the eschatological-vision level. The verse is the article's most direct anchor for blood-purchased fellowship explicitly *across* the dividing markers of kindred, tongue, people, and nation — the very markers the article's s9–s12 named as walls Christ did not build. The heavenly-worship setting is editorially decisive: what the article's s16 confesses on earth as the disciple's present hope is what the heavenly worship already names as accomplished fact ('hast redeemed,' aorist tense). The fellowship purchased with His blood is not a future possibility but an already-done reality the heavenly worship is celebrating now. The article's s16 grammar is corrected by this eschatological grammar: the disciple's table-fellowship participates in a fellowship Christ has already purchased, not in one the disciple is still building.

restoration.text: And lo, he shall suffer temptations, and pain of body, hunger, thirst, and fatigue, even more than man can suffer, except it be unto death; for behold, blood cometh from every pore, so great shall be his anguish for the wickedness and the abominations of his people. And he shall be called Jesus Christ, the Son of God, the Father of heaven and earth, the Creator of all things from the beginning; and his mother shall be called Mary. And lo, he cometh unto his own, that salvation might come unto the children of men even through faith on his name; and even after all this they shall consider him a man, and say that he hath a devil, and shall scourge him, and shall crucify him.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's most direct narrative anchor for the blood Christ shed *for* the fellowship He purchased. King Benjamin's atonement pericope names the cost-side of the purchase with unflinching specificity: blood from every pore. The phrase grounds the article's 'with His blood' in the Restoration canon's most extended atonement narrative; the article's confession of a fellowship purchased with blood is supported here by the Restoration's confession of what that blood-cost involved at the body of Christ in Gethsemane. The pericope's broader sweep — the Christ being mistaken, scourged, crucified by the very humanity the blood was being shed for — is editorially significant: the article's s16 fellowship is one the recipients neither earned nor recognized at the moment of the purchase, which establishes the disciple's posture in s14/s15 (sit at the table with the unrecognizing, leave the door open to those still searching) as the only posture coherent with the gospel that purchased the fellowship.

restoration.text: For, behold, the Lord your Redeemer suffered death in the flesh; wherefore he suffered the pain of all men, that all men might repent and come unto him. And he hath risen again from the dead, that he might bring all men unto him, on conditions of repentance.
restoration.comment: The universality-scope anchor for the article's s16. The triple 'pain of all men... all men might repent... bring all men unto him' names the universal scope of the purchase explicitly — Christ's blood was not shed for a denominational subset, a doctrinal in-group, or a tradition-bound population. The article's s16 fellowship is purchased for all, matching the article's 'every soul' opening at s1 and the universality scope threading through s14/s15. The phrase 'on conditions of repentance' is editorially significant: the universality of the purchase does not collapse the threshold of receiving (repentance, name-bearing, walking with Christ); it does refuse the narrowing of the threshold to denominational alignment. Christ's blood purchased a fellowship that is wider than the disciple's tradition can deliver alone.

restoration.text: I say unto you, ye will know at that day that ye cannot be saved; for there can no man be saved except his garments are washed white; yea, his garments must be purified until they are cleansed from all stain, through the blood of him of whom it has been spoken by our fathers, who should come to redeem his people from their sins. And now I ask of you, my brethren, how will any of you feel, if ye shall stand before the bar of God, having your garments stained with blood and all manner of filthiness?
restoration.comment: The closing Restoration anchor at the cleansing-operation level. The verse names the *operation* by which the blood-purchase is actualized in the disciple's life — the cleansing of the garments through the blood — distinguishing the article's s16 from a transactional-only reading. The fellowship Christ purchased is the fellowship into which the disciple is brought through the same blood that purchased it; the purchase and the cleansing are not two operations but one Christ-act in two grammars. The verse coordinates editorially with A6's atonement treatment: A6 s11 deploys Alma 7:11–12 for the broader atonement-mechanism (Christ taking upon Him the pains and afflictions of His people); s16 here deploys Alma 5:21–24 for the cleansing-operation specifically. Distinguishable rhetorical functions on the same theological floor — A6 s11 names what Christ took on; A8 s16 names what Christ washes away. The closing Alma question ('how will any of you feel, if ye shall stand before the bar of God, having your garments stained with blood and all manner of filthiness?') is not for s16's rhetorical use — the article's register is ecclesial and confessional, not eschatological-warning. The verse's s16 deployment ends at the cleansing claim.
