s17.panel_comment: The article's closing triple — the texture of the fellowship s16 named. Where s16 named what Christ purchased, s17 names what the purchase produced: a fellowship that is free in cost, plain in access, and without price in mode. The triple is editorially deliberate. 'Free' names the gratuity — no purchase price the disciple must pay or contribute. 'Plain' names the access — no esoteric prerequisite, no specialized knowledge, no insider-language threshold; the fellowship is offered in plain language, on plain terms, to plain souls. 'Without price' names the mode — the fellowship is not transacted but given; the disciple does not negotiate terms or earn standing but simply receives. 'Plain' is the editorially load-bearing word for the cluster: it carries the cluster's entire title-thesis (Words of Plainness) and grounds the article's confession in the cluster's foundational claim that what is true is offered in language plain enough to be received. The biblical anchors carry the gratuity-claim at four registers. Isaiah 55:1 supplies the strongest single biblical anchor — the Old Testament's most direct pairing of 'free' with 'without price' in invitation language: 'Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price.' The verse is the prophetic original of the article's s17 triple, with the same paradoxical grammar (buy, but without money; without price, but real receiving) that the article's s17 reasserts. Ephesians 2:8–9 supplies the strongest single NT anchor for grace-not-purchase: 'by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: not of works, lest any man should boast.' The verse is editorially decisive for the article's s17 — the fellowship the disciple has received is gift, not purchase or merit, with the explicit closure of any boast that would credit the disciple. The pairing with s16 is theologically tight: the fellowship was purchased, but not by the disciple; the price was paid, but not by the disciple; what reaches the disciple is purely gift. (Note for cluster-development: this anchor will likely re-deploy at A10 Living by Grace as the anchor's natural primary home; the s17 surfacing here serves the article's ecclesial register specifically.) Matthew 10:8 supplies the dominical anchor for the gift-economy that grounds s17's 'without price': 'freely ye have received, freely give.' Christ's instruction to the apostles is the article's structural template — the disciple's offering of the fellowship to others must match the mode in which the disciple received it: freely received, freely given. The verse closes any temptation to charge for, gatekeep, or condition the fellowship the disciple has been given without charge or condition. Romans 3:23–24 supplies the closing biblical anchor at the theological-mechanism level: 'all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God; being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.' The phrase 'justified freely' (Greek dorean) names the theological mechanism by which the article's s17 'free' is possible — grace, not transaction, with the implicit ground that the disciple's prior sin makes any transactional grammar impossible. The Restoration anchors complete the architecture. 2 Nephi 26:25–28 supplies the strongest single Restoration anchor for 'free' as the article's verb: 'hath he commanded any that they should not partake of his salvation? Behold I say unto you, Nay; but he hath given it free for all men; and he hath commanded his people that they should persuade all men to repentance.' The verse is the Restoration's most direct anti-gatekeeping declaration in this exact register — the salvation Christ has given is free for all men, and the disciple's commission is to persuade-toward-repentance, not to ration the freely-given. 2 Nephi 31:3 supplies the cluster's foundational 'plain' anchor — Nephi's own first-person identification of plainness as the divine pedagogical mode: 'for my soul delighteth in plainness; for after this manner doth the Lord God work among the children of men.' The verse grounds the article's s17 'plain' in the cluster's title-thesis. The Words of Plainness ministry exists because plainness is what God does among the children of men; the article's s17 confesses that the fellowship Christ purchased is offered in the same plain mode that God characteristically uses, with no esoteric or specialized-language threshold. The verse echoes editorially across the entire cluster: A1 establishes plainness as the cluster's epistemic posture; A8 s17 surfaces plainness as the cluster's ecclesial offer. The same plainness that grounds knowing also grounds receiving. Alma 42:23–28 supplies the closing Restoration anchor at the theological-mechanism level: 'the plan of mercy... cometh by means of the atonement... and thus they are restored into his presence, to be judged according to their works, according to the law and justice.' The verse names the gratuity of the offer — Christ's atonement is the means by which 'free' is theologically possible. The article's s17 'without price' is grounded in the Restoration's atonement-as-the-condition-of-mercy claim: the fellowship is free to the disciple because it was costly to Christ, and the means of mercy is precisely the atonement that paid that cost. The article ends where the Restoration's atonement theology grounds it — in the gratuity that flows from the costly love of Christ.

biblical.text: Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price.
biblical.comment: The strongest single biblical anchor for the article's s17 — the Old Testament's most direct pairing of 'free' with 'without price' in invitation language. The verse is the prophetic original of the article's s17 triple, with the same paradoxical grammar (buy, but without money; without price, but real receiving) that s17 reasserts. The opening 'Ho, every one that thirsteth' names the universality scope of the invitation — the threshold is thirst, not credential. The phrase 'he that hath no money' is editorially decisive: the offer is precisely for those who have no purchase-power, with the implication that those who imagine themselves possessed of purchase-power are the very ones the offer is hardest for. The article's s17 stands in this prophetic invitation lineage.

biblical.text: For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: not of works, lest any man should boast.
biblical.comment: The strongest single NT anchor for grace-not-purchase. The verse is editorially decisive for the article's s17 — the fellowship the disciple has received is gift, not purchase or merit, with the explicit closure of any boast that would credit the disciple. The pairing with s16 is theologically tight: the fellowship was purchased (s16 anchored at Acts 20:28), but not by the disciple; the price was paid (1 Peter 1:18–19), but not by the disciple; what reaches the disciple is purely gift (Eph 2:8–9). The closing 'lest any man should boast' names the disposition s17 deliberately forecloses — the disciple's confession of free, plain, without-price fellowship is incompatible with any boast about contribution to the fellowship's ground. The verse will likely re-deploy at A10 Living by Grace as the anchor's natural primary home; here at A8 s17 it serves the article's ecclesial register specifically.

biblical.text: Heal the sick, cleanse the lepers, raise the dead, cast out devils: freely ye have received, freely give.
biblical.comment: The dominical anchor for the gift-economy that grounds s17's 'without price.' Christ's instruction to the apostles is the article's structural template: the disciple's offering of the fellowship to others must match the mode in which the disciple received it. 'Freely ye have received, freely give' is grammatically symmetrical, with the 'freely' (Greek dorean — gift-as-mode) governing both verbs equally. The verse closes any temptation to charge for, gatekeep, or condition the fellowship the disciple has been given without charge or condition. The article's s17 honors this dominical symmetry: what we received free and plain we offer free and plain.

biblical.text: For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God; Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.
biblical.comment: The closing biblical anchor at the theological-mechanism level. The phrase 'justified freely' (Greek dorean — the same word as Matthew 10:8's 'freely give') names the theological mechanism by which the article's s17 'free' is possible: grace, not transaction. The pairing with the prior verse — 'all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God' — names the implicit ground that the disciple's prior sin makes any transactional grammar impossible. There is no purchase-price the disciple could supply that would meet the cost; only grace through redemption can deliver justification. The article's s17 'without price' is the article's ecclesial expression of Romans 3's soteriological claim.

restoration.text: Behold, doth he cry unto any, saying: Depart from me? Behold, I say unto you, Nay; but he saith: Come unto me all ye ends of the earth, buy milk and honey, without money and without price... Hath he commanded any that they should not partake of his salvation? Behold I say unto you, Nay; but he hath given it free for all men; and he hath commanded his people that they should persuade all men to repentance.
restoration.comment: The strongest single Restoration anchor for 'free' as the article's verb. The verse is the Restoration's most direct anti-gatekeeping declaration in this exact register: the salvation Christ has given is free for all men, and the disciple's commission is to persuade-toward-repentance, not to ration the freely-given. The verbal echo of Isaiah 55:1 ('without money and without price') is editorially decisive — Nephi is reading Isaiah and reasserting the prophetic original in the Restoration canon, with the same gratuity-grammar made explicit. The closing instruction ('persuade all men to repentance') names the disciple's right activity given the gratuity: persuading, not gatekeeping. The article's s17 stands on Nephi's reading of Isaiah, with the article's 'free, plain, and without price' explicitly echoing the prophet's 'without money and without price.'

restoration.text: For my soul delighteth in plainness; for after this manner doth the Lord God work among the children of men. For the Lord God giveth light unto the understanding; for he speaketh unto men according to their language, unto their understanding.
restoration.comment: The cluster's foundational 'plain' anchor — Nephi's own first-person identification of plainness as the divine pedagogical mode. The verse grounds the article's s17 'plain' in the cluster's title-thesis: the Words of Plainness ministry exists because plainness is what God does among the children of men. The article's s17 confesses that the fellowship Christ purchased is offered in the same plain mode that God characteristically uses, with no esoteric or specialized-language threshold. The verse echoes editorially across the entire cluster: A1 establishes plainness as the cluster's epistemic posture (what the disciple may legitimately claim to know); A8 s17 surfaces plainness as the cluster's ecclesial offer (how the disciple holds out the fellowship to others). The same plainness that grounds knowing also grounds receiving. The Lord's 'speaketh unto men according to their language, unto their understanding' is the divine pattern the article's s17 honors: the fellowship is offered in plain language because that is the language God Himself uses to give it.

restoration.text: But God ceaseth not to be God, and mercy claimeth the penitent, and mercy cometh because of the atonement; and the atonement bringeth to pass the resurrection of the dead; and the resurrection of the dead bringeth back men into the presence of God; and thus they are restored into his presence, to be judged according to their works, according to the law and justice. For behold, justice exerciseth all his demands, and also mercy claimeth all which is her own; and thus, none but the truly penitent are saved.
restoration.comment: The closing Restoration anchor at the theological-mechanism level. The verse names the gratuity of the offer at its theological foundation: 'mercy cometh because of the atonement.' Christ's atonement is the means by which 'free' is theologically possible — the article's s17 'without price' is grounded in the Restoration's atonement-as-the-condition-of-mercy claim. The article's s17 fellowship is free to the disciple because it was costly to Christ, and the means of mercy is precisely the atonement that paid that cost. The verse's closing — 'justice exerciseth all his demands, and also mercy claimeth all which is her own' — names the cost-and-gift architecture that makes the article's s17 coherent: the cost was real and was paid in full at the atonement; what flows to the disciple from that paid cost is pure mercy. The article ends where the Restoration's atonement theology grounds it — in the gratuity that flows from the costly love of Christ.

s1.text: Jesus the Christ as the fixed point by whom every soul may find the way to God
s1.panel_comment: The article's thesis statement and the foundation of the navigational architecture. 'Fixed point' is the spatial-relational claim — Christ does not move; every other reference is calibrated to Him. The biblical anchors carry the way-to-God witness in three registers: Hebrews 12:2 names Christ as the standing point on whom the disciple's gaze is fixed (the navigational version of the same load-bearing claim that grounds the hermeneutic at A4 s13 and the standard for measurement at A5 s16 — distinct here as the navigational orientation by which the soul finds its course); and Acts 4:12 grounds the exclusive way-claim — there is no other name under heaven by which souls find God (distinct from A6 s2, where the verse grounded faith in the name as receiving instrument, and from A6 s8, where it grounded the proclamation of the person who bears the name; here it grounds the navigational exclusivity of the way itself). The Restoration anchors cluster the universal access claim: 2 Nephi 25:29 grounds the all-soul-may-come promise ('ye shall in nowise be cast out'); and Helaman 5:9 grounds the way-foundation specifically — 'there is no other way nor means whereby man can be saved, only through the atoning blood of Jesus Christ' (distinct from A5 s7, where it grounded the titles cluster, and from A6 s8, where it grounded the proclamation cluster; here it grounds the foundational way-claim that the entire article rests on). Together the cluster establishes the article's premise: Christ is the navigational fixed point for every soul, and there is no other.

biblical.text: Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God.
biblical.comment: Christ as the standing reference on whom the disciple's gaze is fixed. (Reasserted from Article 4 Span 13 and Article 5 Span 16 in different rhetorical direction: at A4 s13 closes the Christological-hermeneutic exhortation; at A5 s16 names Christ as the standing reference for measurement; here at A9 s1 names Christ as the standing reference for the soul's navigation to God.)

biblical.text: Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved.
biblical.comment: The biblical anchor for navigational exclusivity — there is no other name by whom souls find their way to God. (Reasserted from Article 6 Span 2 and Article 6 Span 8 in different rhetorical direction: at A6 s2 the verse grounds faith in the name as the receiving instrument; at A6 s8 it grounds the proclamation of the person who bears that name; here at A9 s1 it grounds the navigational exclusivity of the way itself.)

restoration.text: And now behold, I say unto you that the right way is to believe in Christ, and deny him not; and Christ is the Holy One of Israel; wherefore ye must bow down before him, and worship him with all your might, mind, and strength, and your whole soul; and if ye do this ye shall in nowise be cast out.
restoration.comment: Nephi's plain promise that every soul who comes to Christ will in nowise be cast out — the universal-access foundation grounding the article's opening claim that the way is open to every soul.

restoration.text: O remember, remember, my sons, the words which king Benjamin spake unto his people; yea, remember that there is no other way nor means whereby man can be saved, only through the atoning blood of Jesus Christ, who shall come; yea, remember that he cometh to redeem the world.
restoration.comment: Helaman's recollection of King Benjamin's no-other-way claim — the most direct Restoration anchor for the navigational way-foundation. (Reasserted from Article 5 Span 7 and Article 6 Span 8 in different rhetorical direction: at A5 s7 it grounds the titles cluster; at A6 s8 it grounds the proclamation cluster; here at A9 s1 it grounds the foundational way-claim on which the entire article's navigational architecture rests.)

s2.text: He is the way and the life
s2.panel_comment: The verbatim Christological self-claim. 'He is the way and the life' compresses Christ's own 'I am the way, the truth, and the life' (John 14:6) into the article's confessional grammar — the source paragraph drops 'the truth' not because the article denies the truth-claim but because the article is concerned specifically with navigation (the way) and with life as the destination (eternal life as relationship with God, the same Hebraic-relational shape that grounds A7 s6). The biblical anchor is John 14:6 itself, here making its first deployment in the cluster after appearing as a proof-text in restoration-side reuse-network commentary at A5 s16 and A6 s8 — at A5 s16 the verse named Christ as the way for the disciple's path of measurement; at A6 s8 it named Christ as the way of salvation specifically; here at A9 s2 it functions as the source-paragraph's direct verbatim claim, the article's Christological landing. The Restoration anchors carry Christ's own self-naming in two registers: Ether 12:41 commends seeking 'this Jesus' as the relational object of the disciple's pursuit; and 3 Nephi 11:11 carries the I-am self-introduction at the New World theophany, where Christ identifies Himself directly to His disciples (distinct from A5 s8, where the same passage grounded divine sonship and self-introduction at His descent, and from A5 s15, where it grounded willed obedience to the Father; here at A9 s2 it grounds the verbatim self-naming Christ undertakes when His disciples first encounter Him in person — the dominical shape of the article's own 'He is the way and the life'). Together the cluster grounds the source paragraph's direct claim in Christ's own first-person witness to Himself.

biblical.text: Jesus saith unto him, I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.
biblical.comment: Christ's own first-person Christological self-claim — the direct biblical anchor for the source paragraph's verbatim 'He is the way and the life.' The article compresses 'the way, the truth, and the life' to 'the way and the life' because the source paragraph is concerned specifically with navigation and life-as-destination; the truth-claim is not denied but is carried elsewhere in the cluster.

restoration.text: And now, I would commend you to seek this Jesus of whom the prophets and apostles have written, that the grace of God the Father, and also the Lord Jesus Christ, and the Holy Ghost, which beareth record of them, may be and abide in you forever. Amen.
restoration.comment: Moroni's closing commendation to seek 'this Jesus' as the relational object of every disciple's pursuit — the Restoration's direct echo of John 14:6's relational claim that Christ is the way to the Father.

restoration.text: And behold, I am the light and the life of the world; and I have drunk out of that bitter cup which the Father hath given me, and I have glorified the Father in taking upon me the sins of the world, in the which I have suffered the will of the Father in all things from the beginning.
restoration.comment: Christ's own self-naming at the New World theophany — 'I am the light and the life of the world.' (Reasserted from Article 5 Span 8 and Article 5 Span 15 in different rhetorical direction: at A5 s8 the passage grounded divine sonship and self-introduction at the descent; at A5 s15 it grounded willed obedience to the Father; here at A9 s2 it grounds Christ's verbatim self-naming as the way and the life — the dominical shape of the source paragraph's own claim.)

s3.text: He does not move. He does not change with the seasons, the pressures of an age, or the shifting claims of men
s3.panel_comment: The cosmic-immutability claim that grounds the navigational architecture. If the fixed point itself moved, every reference calibrated to it would lose its bearing; the article's entire scheme rests on the immutability of the One being navigated to. The biblical anchors carry the immutability witness in three registers: Hebrews 13:8 names Christ Himself as the same yesterday, today, and forever — the New Testament locus classicus for personal Christological immutability (here making its first biblical-side deployment in the cluster, distinct from the restoration-side cross-canon reuse at A4 s6, where the verse functioned as both biblical and Restoration-claimed witness for revelation continuity; here at A9 s3 the same verse grounds personal-immutability-of-Christ specifically, the navigational fixed-point claim rather than the revelation-continuity claim); Malachi 3:6 grounds the Old Testament side of the immutability bracket — 'I am the LORD, I change not' — the divine self-identification that establishes immutability as a defining attribute of God; and James 1:17 carries the no-variableness, no-shadow-of-turning claim, naming the absence of any astronomical-pressure-of-rotation in the Father of lights. The Restoration anchors cluster the same witness across canon: Mormon 9:9 names the doctrinal continuity of God's nature across all scripture ('the same yesterday, today, and forever, and in him there is no variableness neither shadow of changing'); 3 Nephi 27:21 grounds the gospel's doctrinal stability in Christ's own first-person voice ('this is my gospel') — the gospel does not shift with the age because Christ Himself does not; and D&C 35:1 names Christ as 'Alpha and Omega ... whose course is one eternal round, the same today as yesterday, and forever' — the cosmic-temporal immutability that grounds the navigational fixed-point. Together the cluster establishes that the fixed point of the article's thesis is not a metaphor for stability but the literal condition of the One to whom every soul navigates.

biblical.text: Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever.
biblical.comment: The New Testament locus classicus for personal Christological immutability — the most concentrated single-verse anchor for 'He does not move.' (Reasserted from Article 4 Span 6 in different rhetorical direction: at A4 s6 the verse functioned as both biblical witness and Restoration-claimed witness for revelation continuity through Christ; here at A9 s3 the same verse grounds the personal immutability of Christ Himself as the navigational fixed point — distinct as the personal-immutability claim rather than the revelation-continuity claim.)

biblical.text: For I am the LORD, I change not; therefore ye sons of Jacob are not consumed.
biblical.comment: The Old Testament divine self-identification that establishes immutability as a defining attribute of God — the OT-side of the immutability bracket whose NT-side is Hebrews 13:8.

biblical.text: Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning.
biblical.comment: The no-variableness, no-shadow-of-turning claim — names the absence of any astronomical-pressure-of-rotation in the Father of lights, and grounds the article's specific refusal of 'the seasons, the pressures of an age, or the shifting claims of men' as forces that could alter Him.

restoration.text: For do we not read that God is the same yesterday, today, and forever, and in him there is no variableness neither shadow of changing?
restoration.comment: Moroni's direct echo of Hebrews 13:8 and James 1:17 in compressed form — the doctrinal continuity of God's nature across all scripture, named explicitly as a question whose answer is self-evident from the canon.

restoration.text: Verily, verily, I say unto you, this is my gospel; and ye know the things that ye must do in my church; for the works which ye have seen me do that shall ye also do; for that which ye have seen me do even that shall ye do.
restoration.comment: Christ's own first-person voice grounding the gospel's doctrinal stability — 'this is my gospel.' The gospel does not shift with the age because Christ Himself does not; the works His disciples are to do are the same works He has shown them, across every generation.

restoration.text: Listen to the voice of the Lord your God, even Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end, whose course is one eternal round, the same today as yesterday, and forever.
restoration.comment: Christ's self-identification as Alpha and Omega whose course is one eternal round — the cosmic-temporal immutability that grounds the navigational fixed-point claim. The 'eternal round' is not a circle of repetition but the Restoration's image of unchanging completeness across time.

s4.text: What He taught is what He taught. What He was is what He was.
s4.panel_comment: Where s3 carried the cosmic-immutability claim in the language of being ('He does not move'), s4 specifies that immutability for the two faces by which Christ is most often pressured to bend: His teaching and His character. The two sentences are deliberately tautological because the rhetorical work is refusal — refusal to revise the teaching to fit the present age, and refusal to recast the character to fit a more comfortable Christ. The biblical anchors cluster the teaching-and-character-immutability witness in three registers: Matthew 24:35 names the permanence of Christ's words against the passing of heaven and earth themselves — the strongest anchor for 'what He taught is what He taught'; Galatians 1:8–9 names the apostolic refusal of any revised gospel, including from an angel from heaven, as the ecclesial form of the same claim — what He taught is not subject to amendment by any later authority; and John 8:25 carries Christ's own response to the questioning crowd that pressed Him to explain Himself otherwise — 'Even the same that I said unto you from the beginning' — the dominical anchor for 'what He was is what He was' against the pressure of those who wanted Him to be someone else. The Restoration anchors deepen the witness in Christ's first-person voice: 3 Nephi 24:6 records Christ's own quotation of Malachi 3:6 to the New World disciples — the canonical pairing that grounds the s3/s4 architecture (cosmic immutability at s3, applied here at s4 to His personal teaching and being); D&C 6:21 carries Christ's direct self-identification across dispensations — 'I am the same that came unto mine own, and mine own received me not. I am the light which shineth in darkness' — the latter-day declaration that what He was at the first advent is what He still is in the present age; and D&C 35:17–18 names the continuity of His mission and message in the latter-day commission — 'these signs shall follow them that believe' — the same signs, the same gospel, the same Christ. Together the cluster establishes that Aaron's tautology is not stylistic but doctrinal: the sentences refuse to grant any ground on which Christ's teaching or person could be culturally renegotiated.

biblical.text: Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away.
biblical.comment: Christ's own claim that His words outlast the cosmos itself — the strongest single-verse anchor for the immutability of what He taught. Heaven and earth shifting do not move His words; no lesser pressure can.

biblical.text: But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed. As we said before, so say I now again, If any man preach any other gospel unto you than that which ye have received, let him be accursed.
biblical.comment: The Pauline refusal of any revised gospel — even from an angel from heaven — as the ecclesial form of the teaching-immutability claim. What Christ taught is not subject to amendment by any later messenger, however exalted.

biblical.text: Then said they unto him, Who art thou? And Jesus said unto them, Even the same that I said unto you from the beginning.
biblical.comment: Christ's direct response to the questioning crowd that pressed Him to explain Himself otherwise — the dominical anchor for 'what He was is what He was' against the pressure of those who wanted Him to be someone else. He does not adjust His self-presentation to satisfy His questioners.

restoration.text: For I am the Lord, I change not; therefore ye sons of Jacob are not consumed.
restoration.comment: Christ's own quotation of Malachi 3:6 to the New World disciples — the canonical pairing that grounds the s3/s4 architecture by setting the cosmic-immutability claim of s3 in the dominical voice and applying it here at s4 to His personal teaching and being. The Lord does not change; therefore what He taught is what He taught and what He was is what He was.

restoration.text: Behold, I am Jesus Christ, the Son of God. I am the same that came unto mine own, and mine own received me not. I am the light which shineth in darkness, and the darkness comprehendeth it not.
restoration.comment: Christ's first-person self-identification across dispensations — 'I am the same that came unto mine own.' The latter-day declaration that what He was at the first advent is what He still is in the present age; the rejection then and the rejection now do not alter the Christ being rejected.

restoration.text: And he hath received a fulness of my gospel ... that ye may bear record of him whom I have sent ... and these signs shall follow them that believe — In my name they shall do many wonderful works.
restoration.comment: The latter-day commission carrying the same gospel, the same signs, and the same Christ as in the first century — naming the continuity of mission and message that grounds the teaching-and-character-immutability claim across all dispensations.

crossref.label: Within this article
crossref.title: Span 3: He does not move. He does not change with the seasons, the pressures of an age, or the shifting claims of men

s5.text: He stands as the unchanging North Star above every traveler’s path
s5.definition: The fixed Christological reference point — the unchanging Person of Jesus Christ Himself, by whom every other navigational instrument (the inward Spirit, the written witness) is calibrated. The first of three named-concept instruments in the article's triangulation architecture (North Star, Compass, Map).
s5.panel_comment: The named-concept landing of the article's triangulation architecture and the first of its three navigational instruments. 'North Star' is the fixed Christological reference point — the unchanging Person of Christ Himself, by whom every other instrument (the inward Spirit at s10, the written witness at s14) is calibrated. The metaphor is chosen with care: the North Star does not lead the traveler; it orients the traveler's lesser instruments to true north. Christ does not function in the article as a guide who walks ahead but as the standing reference whose immutability makes navigation possible at all. The biblical anchors carry the celestial-witness-of-Christ in three registers: 2 Peter 1:19 names the day star arising in the disciple's heart as the most direct biblical cognate to the navigational-light claim — Peter's 'light that shineth in a dark place' is the precise scriptural shape of the metaphor's dark-wilderness-with-fixed-light architecture; Revelation 22:16 grounds Christ's own self-identification as the bright and morning star — the Christological direct anchor for the named concept (Christ is not like a star; He says He is one); and Numbers 24:17 carries the Old Testament Messianic star-prophecy ('There shall come a Star out of Jacob'), the prophetic anchor for the celestial-image of Christ that the New Testament fulfills. The Restoration anchors deepen the witness with characteristic specificity: 3 Nephi 1:21 records the appearing of the new star at Christ's birth — the Restoration's witness that the celestial sign was not metaphor but historical fact; and D&C 88:7–10 grounds the deepest theological warrant for the metaphor — 'he is in the sun, and the light of the sun ... as also the light of the stars, and the power thereof by which they were made.' Christ is not merely *like* the North Star; He is the light in the celestial reference points themselves. The metaphor lands with full theological weight because the Restoration grounds it in the doctrine of the light of Christ as the actual luminous principle of the cosmos. Together the cluster establishes the named concept 'North Star' as the article's fixed Christological reference point — the first instrument of triangulation, by which every other instrument is calibrated.

biblical.text: We have also a more sure word of prophecy; whereunto ye do well that ye take heed, as unto a light that shineth in a dark place, until the day dawn, and the day star arise in your hearts.
biblical.comment: The biblical cognate closest to the article's North Star metaphor — Peter's 'light that shineth in a dark place, until ... the day star arise.' The dark-wilderness-with-fixed-light architecture of the source paragraph echoes Peter's exact image; the day star arising in the heart names the Christological orientation by which the disciple navigates.

biblical.text: I Jesus have sent mine angel to testify unto you these things in the churches. I am the root and the offspring of David, and the bright and morning star.
biblical.comment: Christ's own self-identification as the bright and morning star — the Christological direct anchor for the named concept. He does not say He is like a star; He says He is one. The metaphor of the article is grounded in Christ's own self-naming.

biblical.text: I shall see him, but not now: I shall behold him, but not nigh: there shall come a Star out of Jacob, and a Sceptre shall rise out of Israel.
biblical.comment: Balaam's Old Testament Messianic star-prophecy — the prophetic anchor for the celestial image of Christ that the New Testament fulfills at His birth and that He claims for Himself in Revelation 22:16.

restoration.text: And it came to pass also that a new star did appear, according to the word.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's witness that the celestial sign of Christ's coming was not metaphor but historical fact — a new star did appear at His birth, fulfilling Samuel the Lamanite's prophecy and grounding the named concept in the actual celestial witness of the Restoration's record.

restoration.text: Which truth shineth. This is the light of Christ. As also he is in the sun, and the light of the sun, and the power thereof by which it was made. As also he is in the moon, and is the light of the moon, and the power thereof by which it was made; as also the light of the stars, and the power thereof by which they were made.
restoration.comment: The deepest Restoration anchor for the North Star metaphor — Christ is not merely *like* the North Star; He is the light in the celestial reference points themselves. The doctrine of the light of Christ as the actual luminous principle of the cosmos grounds the metaphor in metaphysical reality, not poetic imagination.

s6.text: Trusting Him is more important than understanding Him
s6.panel_comment: The first claim of the paragraph and the floor of its three-clause architecture. Where Article 1 carried the restraint of merognosis as a negative discipline — knowing only in part, refusing to overclaim — A9 paragraph 2 carries the positive doctrine that grounds the restraint: trust is the primary disposition of the disciple, and understanding is welcomed without being required as its precondition. The biblical anchors carry the trust-supremacy witness in two registers: Proverbs 3:5–6 names the disciple's posture directly — 'trust in the Lord with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding' — the locus classicus for the s6 claim, here grounding the disciple's trust-posture clause specifically (the same passage will return at s9 to ground the divine-response clause 'make our paths straight,' with the two deployments dividing the proverb's two halves across the paragraph's architecture); and Isaiah 55:8–9 grounds the asymmetry that makes trust the proper posture — 'my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways' — the divine-human cognitive gap that cannot be closed by understanding and that therefore requires trust if the soul is to navigate at all. The Restoration anchors deepen the witness with pastoral specificity: Mosiah 4:9 carries King Benjamin's most direct pairing of belief and frank acknowledgment of incomprehension — 'believe in God; believe that he is, and that he created all things ... believe that man doth not comprehend all the things which the Lord can comprehend' — naming belief itself as the proper posture toward what cannot be comprehended; and 2 Nephi 9:28–29 grounds Jacob's classic subordination of learning to trust — 'to be learned is good if they hearken unto the counsels of God' — preserving learning as good while subordinating it to the trust-posture that hearkens. Together the cluster establishes that the precedence of trust over understanding is not anti-intellectual but architectural: trust is the disposition by which the disciple navigates the asymmetry that understanding alone cannot resolve.

biblical.text: Trust in the Lord with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding. In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths.
biblical.comment: The locus classicus for the s6 claim. The disciple's posture is trust; understanding is not the foundation of the relationship with God, trust is. (Reasserted at A9 s9 in different rhetorical direction: here at s6 the proverb grounds the disciple's trust-posture clause 'lean not unto thine own understanding'; at s9 the same passage grounds the divine-response clause 'he shall direct thy paths.' The two halves of the proverb divide across the paragraph's two-clause architecture — disciple's posture, divine response.)

biblical.text: For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, saith the Lord. For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways, and my thoughts than your thoughts.
biblical.comment: The divine-human cognitive asymmetry that makes trust the proper posture. The gap between God's thoughts and the disciple's cannot be closed by greater understanding; it can only be navigated by trust in the One whose thoughts exceed the disciple's reach.

restoration.text: Believe in God; believe that he is, and that he created all things, both in heaven and in earth; believe that he has all wisdom, and all power, both in heaven and in earth; believe that man doth not comprehend all the things which the Lord can comprehend.
restoration.comment: King Benjamin's most direct pastoral pairing of belief with frank acknowledgment of incomprehension. Belief is the proper posture toward what cannot be comprehended; incomprehension does not bar belief, it is the very ground on which belief is asked.

restoration.text: O the vainness, and the frailties, and the foolishness of men! When they are learned they think they are wise, and they hearken not unto the counsel of God, for they set it aside, supposing they know of themselves, wherefore, their wisdom is foolishness and it profiteth them not. And they shall perish. But to be learned is good if they hearken unto the counsels of God.
restoration.comment: Jacob's classic subordination of learning to trust. Learning is preserved as good; it is the trust-posture that determines whether learning becomes wisdom or vanity. The s6 claim does not dismiss understanding; it names what understanding must be ordered to.

s7.text: One’s relationship with the Divine takes precedence over the accuracy of their doctrine
s7.panel_comment: The article's positive expression of the merognosis floor first named negatively at Article 1 s7. Where Article 1's restraint refuses to make doctrinal precision the gate of fellowship, A9 s7 names the precedence that grounds the refusal: the relationship with God is prior to the accuracy of the disciple's doctrine about Him. The claim must be heard precisely — it is precedence, not replacement. Doctrine is not dismissed; it is honored as good (s8 names this explicitly) and then ordered beneath the relational ground that gives it meaning. The biblical anchors carry the precedence witness in two registers: 1 Corinthians 8:1–3 grounds the Pauline locus — 'knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth ... if any man think that he knoweth any thing, he knoweth nothing yet as he ought to know. But if any man love God, the same is known of him' — the apostolic refusal of doctrinal mastery as the measure of the disciple, replaced by the relational claim of being known by God; and John 17:3 carries the Hebraic-relational know that grounds eternal life itself — 'this is life eternal, that they might know thee' — where the verb is not propositional cognition but relational fellowship (the same Hebraic shape Article 7 establishes for eternal life now; here at A9 s7 the verse grounds not the eternal-life-as-knowing claim but the relational priority specifically — the disciple's relationship to God is the knowing that matters, in distinction from the propositional accuracy of doctrine about God). The Restoration anchors deepen the witness in Christ's own voice: Moroni 7:33 carries Christ's promise to those who have faith in me — the relational disposition, not doctrinal mastery, as the ground of the promise — 'whatsoever thing is expedient in me'; and Alma 32:27–28 grounds the pastoral allowance for minimal relational movement — 'even if ye can no more than desire to believe, let this desire work in you, even until ye believe' — naming the smallest motion toward Christ as already sufficient relational ground, independent of doctrinal precision (distinct from A3 s11, where the same passage grounded Alma's experiment-upon-the-word seed-faith mechanism; here at A9 s7 the same verses ground the pastoral allowance for minimal belief as fully counted, regardless of how unformed the disciple's doctrine remains). Together the cluster establishes the s7 claim as a refusal to make doctrinal accuracy the gate of fellowship with God — the relational priority that makes the entire article's interfaith register possible.

biblical.text: Now as touching things offered unto idols, we know that we all have knowledge. Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth. And if any man think that he knoweth any thing, he knoweth nothing yet as he ought to know. But if any man love God, the same is known of him.
biblical.comment: The Pauline locus for the s7 claim. Doctrinal knowledge is subordinated to love; the operative measure is not whether the disciple knows rightly but whether the disciple is known by God. The relational ground precedes and exceeds the doctrinal one.

biblical.text: And this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent.
biblical.comment: The Hebraic-relational know — yada‘ / ginōskō — naming the relational fellowship that constitutes eternal life. (Reasserted from Article 7 Span 6 in different rhetorical direction: at A7 s6 the verse grounded the eternal-life-as-knowing-God claim that defines Christ's kingdom-life-now; here at A9 s7 the same verse grounds the relational priority over propositional accuracy specifically — the disciple's relational knowing of God is the knowing that matters, in distinction from doctrinal precision about Him.)

restoration.text: And Christ hath said: If ye will have faith in me ye shall have power to do whatsoever thing is expedient in me.
restoration.comment: Christ's promise predicated on the relational disposition — faith in Him — rather than on doctrinal mastery. The condition of the promise is relational, not propositional; the disciple is invited into power on the basis of who they trust, not on the basis of what they know.

restoration.text: But behold, if ye will awake and arouse your faculties, even to an experiment upon my words, and exercise a particle of faith, yea, even if ye can no more than desire to believe, let this desire work in you, even until ye believe in a manner that ye can give place for a portion of my words.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's most direct pastoral allowance for minimal relational movement — desire to believe counted as already sufficient ground. (Reasserted from Article 3 Span 11 in different rhetorical direction: at A3 s11 the passage grounded Alma's experiment-upon-the-word seed-faith mechanism — the active process of testing; here at A9 s7 the same passage grounds the pastoral allowance for minimal belief regardless of doctrinal precision — the smallest motion toward Christ as already sufficient relational ground, independent of how unformed the disciple's doctrine remains.)

s8.text: Correct doctrines and personal knowledge are good, but faith in Him is better
s8.panel_comment: The mechanism-clause of the relational priority. Where s7 names the precedence (relationship over doctrinal accuracy), s8 names the operational mechanism by which the relationship is carried — faith in Christ. The 'good ... but better' construction is deliberate and load-bearing: doctrine and knowledge are not dismissed but preserved as good, and then subordinated to the better thing without which they cannot save. The gradient guards both flanks at once — against doctrinal indifference on one side, against anti-doctrinal antinomianism on the other. The biblical anchors carry the faith-as-mechanism witness in two registers: Hebrews 11:6 is the New Testament locus classicus for faith as the indispensable approach to God — 'without faith it is impossible to please him: for he that cometh to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him' — naming faith not as one option among several but as the necessary mechanism by which the soul approaches God at all; and James 2:14–17 guards the s8 gradient against the antinomian misreading — 'faith, if it hath not works, is dead' — preventing the 'good ... but better' of s8 from collapsing into 'faith alone, doctrine and works do not matter.' The Restoration anchors deepen the witness with characteristic precision: Alma 32:21 grounds Alma's working definition of faith — 'faith is not to have a perfect knowledge of things; therefore if ye have faith ye hope for things which are not seen, which are true' — explicitly separating faith from perfect knowledge as its distinguishing feature, the same distinction Aaron's s8 names (faith is the better mechanism precisely because it operates without the perfect knowledge that would otherwise be required). The same passage was deployed at s6 in different rhetorical direction (at s6 it grounded the cognitive-humility companion to trust-supremacy — the epistemic-posture claim; here at s8 it grounds the explicit faith > knowledge claim — the operational mechanism). Ether 12:6 carries Moroni's foundational anchor for faith's operation precisely in the absence of seeing — 'faith is things which are hoped for and not seen; wherefore, dispute not because ye see not, for ye receive no witness until after the trial of your faith' — naming the temporal order: faith first, witness afterward, never the reverse. Together the cluster establishes that the 'better' of s8 is not better as competition but better as mechanism — faith is what the relationship runs on, while doctrine and knowledge are honored servants of the relational ground.

biblical.text: But without faith it is impossible to please him: for he that cometh to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him.
biblical.comment: The NT locus classicus for faith as the mechanism of approach to God. Faith is not one approach among several; it is the indispensable disposition without which the soul cannot please God or come to Him at all. The s8 claim names this directly: faith is better not as a competitor to doctrine but as the mechanism without which the relationship does not run.

biblical.text: What doth it profit, my brethren, though a man say he hath faith, and have not works? can faith save him? ... Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone.
biblical.comment: Guards the s8 gradient against antinomian misreading. The 'good ... but better' of s8 does not collapse into 'faith alone, doctrine and works do not matter.' James preserves works as the necessary evidence that faith is alive; the gradient orders faith above doctrine without dismissing the works in which the relationship is lived out.

restoration.text: And now as I said concerning faith — faith is not to have a perfect knowledge of things; therefore if ye have faith ye hope for things which are not seen, which are true.
restoration.comment: Alma's working definition of faith that explicitly separates it from perfect knowledge. The s8 claim names this directly: faith is the better mechanism because it operates without the perfect knowledge that would otherwise be required. (Reasserted from A9 s6 in different rhetorical direction: at s6 the verse grounds the cognitive-humility companion to trust-supremacy — the epistemic-posture claim that faith does not require perfect knowledge; here at s8 the same verse grounds the explicit faith > knowledge claim — the operational mechanism by which the relational priority of s7 is carried.)

restoration.text: And now, I, Moroni, would speak somewhat concerning these things; I would show unto the world that faith is things which are hoped for and not seen; wherefore, dispute not because ye see not, for ye receive no witness until after the trial of your faith.
restoration.comment: Moroni's foundational anchor for faith's operation precisely in the absence of seeing. The temporal order is fixed: faith first, witness afterward, never the reverse. The s8 claim's 'but faith in Him is better' names this temporal priority — faith is the operative mechanism before knowledge is granted.

s9.text: Our hope is that, as we submit to Him, God will make our paths straight
s9.panel_comment: The paragraph's pastoral closer and the resolution of the trust/relationship/faith priority into a single divine-response claim. The span is a direct paraphrase of Proverbs 3:6, and the article's added word submit names the disciple's posture; make our paths straight names the divine action that responds to it. The biblical anchors carry the submission-with-divine-response witness in two registers: Proverbs 3:5–6 returns here as the direct paraphrase anchor, with the second half of the proverb — 'in all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths' — grounding the verbatim paraphrase that the span's text reworks (the same passage was deployed at s6 in different rhetorical direction; at s6 the first half of the proverb grounded the disciple's trust-posture clause; here at s9 the second half grounds the divine-response clause, the two deployments dividing the proverb's two halves across the paragraph's two-clause architecture); and James 4:7–10 carries the NT amplification of the same posture — 'submit yourselves therefore to God ... humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he shall lift you up' — naming the same submission-and-divine-response shape that s9 carries in its closing form. The Restoration anchors deepen the witness with characteristic personal weight: 2 Nephi 4:34–35 carries Nephi's psalm of personal trust — 'O Lord, I have trusted in thee, and I will trust in thee forever. I will not put my trust in the arm of flesh ... yea, I know that God will give liberally to him that asketh' — grounding the submission-and-divine-response shape in personal witness rather than abstract principle; and D&C 112:10 grounds the most direct latter-day pairing — 'be thou humble; and the Lord thy God shall lead thee by the hand, and give thee answer to thy prayers' — naming hand-leading as the latter-day form of path-straightening, and prayer-answering as the latter-day form of divine response. Together the cluster establishes the paragraph's closing hope: trust is the disposition (s6), relationship the priority (s7), faith the mechanism (s8), and submission-with-divine-response the ongoing pattern by which the disciple's path is straightened over a lifetime of walking with God.

biblical.text: Trust in the Lord with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding. In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths.
biblical.comment: The direct paraphrase anchor for the source span. The second half of the proverb — 'in all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths' — grounds the verbatim 'make our paths straight' that the article reworks. (Reasserted from A9 s6 in different rhetorical direction: at s6 the first half of the proverb grounds the disciple's trust-posture clause; here at s9 the second half grounds the divine-response clause. The two deployments divide the proverb's two halves across the paragraph's two-clause architecture — disciple's posture at s6, divine response at s9.)

biblical.text: Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you. Draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you ... Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he shall lift you up.
biblical.comment: The NT amplification of the submission-with-divine-response shape. Submission is met by drawing nigh; humility is met by lifting up. The same shape that s9 carries in its closing form — submission produces divine response, every time.

restoration.text: O Lord, I have trusted in thee, and I will trust in thee forever. I will not put my trust in the arm of flesh; for I know that cursed is he that putteth his trust in the arm of flesh. Yea, cursed is he that putteth his trust in man or maketh flesh his arm. Yea, I know that God will give liberally to him that asketh.
restoration.comment: Nephi's psalm of personal trust, grounding the submission-and-divine-response shape in personal witness rather than abstract principle. The s9 paraphrase carries Nephi's same confidence: the disciple who trusts and asks rightly will not be disappointed.

restoration.text: Be thou humble; and the Lord thy God shall lead thee by the hand, and give thee answer to thy prayers.
restoration.comment: The most direct latter-day pairing of submission and divine guidance. Hand-leading is the latter-day form of path-straightening; prayer-answering is the latter-day form of divine response. The s9 hope is grounded in this precise latter-day promise: humility produces hand-leading, every time.

s10.text: the Spirit of God is given to each honest conscience as a compass within — a witness that responds to divine reality, drawing us toward what is true and warning us away from what would destroy us
s10.definition: The inward navigational instrument — the Spirit of God given to each honest conscience as a witness that responds to divine reality, drawing the disciple toward what is true and warning her away from what would destroy her. The second of three named-concept instruments in the article's triangulation architecture (North Star, Compass, Map), and the only one housed within the disciple herself; therefore the only one subject to the disturbing magnetism of mortal flesh and requiring constant calibration to the unmoving Christological reference of the North Star.
s10.panel_comment: The named-concept landing of the article's second navigational instrument and the inward complement to the fixed external reference of s5. Where the North Star stands above the traveler and does not move, the Compass is housed within the traveler and is therefore the only instrument of the three that the disciple carries inside her own mortal flesh. This anatomical fact — that the Compass is the inward instrument — is what makes the calibration architecture of ¶3 necessary in the first place: a perfectly working compass still needs calibration to a fixed external reference when the housing it sits in carries its own magnetic field. The biblical anchors carry the universal Spirit-given witness in two registers: John 16:13 names the Spirit of truth as the One who guides the disciple into all truth — the navigational verb *guide* the most direct biblical anchor for the named concept (here making its first cluster deployment, distinct from the Comforter-as-teacher claim of John 14:26 in restraint-of-merognosis registers elsewhere; here at A9 s10 the verse grounds the Spirit's specifically navigational operation as the article's inward Compass); and John 1:9 grounds the universal scope of the gift — the true Light that lighteth every man that cometh into the world — the locus classicus for the universal-conscience claim that supports the source paragraph's phrase 'given to each honest conscience' without restricting the Compass to those inside any specific covenant boundary. The Restoration anchors deepen the witness with characteristic precision and pair the universality with a conditional clause: Moroni 7:16 carries the most direct Restoration anchor for the universal-Spirit-given claim — 'the Spirit of Christ is given to every man, that he may know good from evil' — naming both the universality (every man) and the discriminative function (know good from evil) that the Compass performs (verse-scope distinct from Moroni 7:16–17 at s12, where the expanded passage grounds the calibration test specifically; here at s10 verse 16 alone grounds the universal-given operation); and D&C 84:46 pairs the universal scope with the conditional response — 'the Spirit enlighteneth every man through the world, that hearkeneth to the voice of the Spirit' — naming hearkening as the condition that activates the Compass and grounding the source paragraph's 'honest conscience' qualifier in the Spirit's operational logic (the gift is universal; its enlightening is conditional on hearkening). Together the cluster establishes the named concept as the inward complement of the North Star: every soul carries it, every honest conscience receives its witness, and the witness draws the disciple toward what is true precisely because the Spirit Himself is oriented toward the truth that Christ Himself is.

biblical.text: Howbeit when he, the Spirit of truth, is come, he will guide you into all truth: for he shall not speak of himself; but whatsoever he shall hear, that shall he speak: and he will shew you things to come.
biblical.comment: Christ's own promise of the Spirit's navigational operation. The verb 'guide' is the most direct biblical anchor for the named-concept Compass; the Spirit does not speak of Himself but speaks what He hears — the calibration relationship of s12 is grounded in this dominical claim that the Spirit's native direction is not autonomous but Christ-relational from the outset.

biblical.text: That was the true Light, which lighteth every man that cometh into the world.
biblical.comment: The Johannine locus classicus for the universal-conscience claim. The true Light lights every man — the universality that grounds the source paragraph's 'each honest conscience' against any restriction of the Compass to a covenant boundary. The Compass is given before any tradition's claim about who has it.

restoration.text: For behold, the Spirit of Christ is given to every man, that he may know good from evil; wherefore, I show unto you the way to judge; for every thing which inviteth to do good, and to persuade to believe in Christ, is sent forth by the power and gift of Christ; wherefore ye may know with a perfect knowledge it is of God.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's most direct universal-Spirit-given claim. Verse 16 alone here at s10 grounds the universality of the gift and the discriminative function the Compass performs; the expanded passage (verses 16–17) returns at s12 to ground the calibration test mechanism. Verse-scope split is deliberate: the universal-given claim and the calibration test are theologically distinct operations, and Moroni's text supports the distinction.

restoration.text: And the Spirit giveth light to every man that cometh into the world; and the Spirit enlighteneth every man through the world, that hearkeneth to the voice of the Spirit.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's pairing of universal-scope with conditional-response. The gift is given to every man; the enlightening is to every man that hearkeneth. The source paragraph's 'honest conscience' qualifier is grounded in this operational logic — the Compass is given universally, but its witness is activated by the disciple's hearkening posture.

s11.text: the compass in our own hearts is housed in mortal flesh, and mortal flesh carries its own magnetism — our wounds, our fears, our desires, the pull of those we love and of those we resent
s11.panel_comment: The article's diagnostic claim for why the Compass requires calibration in the first place. The source paragraph's image is technical: every magnetic compass on earth is housed in a body that carries its own iron, and the iron in the housing creates a magnetic field that pulls the needle off true north unless corrected. The disciple's compass — the inward Spirit-witness — is housed in mortal flesh, and mortal flesh carries its own magnetism. The article names the magnetism specifically: wounds, fears, desires, the pull of those we love and of those we resent. The list is pastoral and exact — these are the four most common sources of false bearing in the disciple's inward witness, and naming them is the diagnostic discipline. The biblical anchors carry the inward-distortion witness in two registers: Jeremiah 17:9 is the locus classicus — 'the heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked; who can know it?' — naming the heart's distorting power as a defining feature of mortal existence, not an exceptional condition; and 1 John 4:1 grounds the apostolic discipline that responds to the diagnostic — 'believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God' — naming testing as the standing posture, not paranoia but discipline. The Restoration anchors deepen the witness with characteristic personal weight: 2 Nephi 4:17–18 carries Nephi's psalm of personal lament — 'O wretched man that I am! Yea, my heart sorroweth because of my flesh ... I am encompassed about, because of the temptations and the sins which do so easily beset me' — grounding the magnetism-of-mortal-flesh claim in the Restoration's most personal first-person witness (Nephi, the prophet whose every action the reader has seen, naming his own flesh as the field of struggle); and Mosiah 3:19 names the magnetism doctrinally — 'the natural man is an enemy to God ... and will be, forever and ever, unless he yields to the enticings of the Holy Spirit' — naming the magnetism as the natural-man's standing posture (here the diagnostic operation; the same passage returns at s12 to ground the yielding-mechanism that calibrates the Compass against the magnetism — the intra-batch divergence is the architectural pivot of the paragraph, diagnostic at s11 / mechanism at s12). Together the cluster establishes ¶3's diagnostic floor: the Compass is real and is given to every honest conscience (s10), and the housing is real and pulls the needle off true (s11), and both are facts about the disciple's situation that the article refuses to soften — without which the calibration claim of s12 would be sentimental rather than necessary.

biblical.text: The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?
biblical.comment: The locus classicus for the heart's distorting power. The article names wounds, fears, desires, and the pull of love and resentment as the magnetism's specific forms; Jeremiah grounds the general claim that the heart's distortion is a defining feature of mortal existence, not an exceptional condition.

biblical.text: Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world.
biblical.comment: The apostolic discipline of testing inward witnesses. The s11 diagnostic posture is grounded in John's command — testing is the standing posture, not paranoia. The verse names the magnetism's external source (many false prophets) without exhausting it; the article's pastoral specificity (wounds, fears, desires, pulls of love and resentment) names the magnetism's internal forms.

restoration.text: O wretched man that I am! Yea, my heart sorroweth because of my flesh; my soul grieveth because of mine iniquities. I am encompassed about, because of the temptations and the sins which do so easily beset me.
restoration.comment: Nephi's psalm of personal lament — the Restoration's most pastoral first-person witness to the magnetism of mortal flesh. The prophet whose every action the reader has seen names his own flesh as the field of his struggle; the diagnostic is not abstract doctrine but lived testimony from inside the Restoration's most exemplary disciple.

restoration.text: For the natural man is an enemy to God, and has been from the fall of Adam, and will be, forever and ever, unless he yields to the enticings of the Holy Spirit, and putteth off the natural man, and becometh a saint through the atonement of Christ the Lord.
restoration.comment: King Benjamin's doctrinal naming of the magnetism as the natural-man's standing posture. Here at s11 the passage grounds the *diagnostic* — the magnetism is real, doctrinally named, and not a feature of weakness but of the mortal condition itself. (Reasserted at A9 s12 in different rhetorical direction: at s11 the passage grounds the magnetism diagnostic; at s12 the same passage grounds the yielding-as-calibration mechanism — the natural man's only response to the magnetism is the yielding the verse names, and that yielding is the operational calibration of the Compass to the North Star of Christ Himself.)

s12.text: the compass of the Spirit in us must be calibrated always to the North Star of Christ Himself
s12.panel_comment: The article's central calibration claim and the architectural pivot of the paragraph. Where s11 diagnoses the magnetism, s12 names the mechanism — the inward Compass must be calibrated always to the unmoving Christological reference of s5. The word *calibrated* carries the technical weight of the navigational metaphor: it is not a one-time alignment but an ongoing operation, the disciple's standing relationship between her inward witness and the fixed Person of Christ. The biblical anchors carry the Christological-calibration witness in two registers: 1 John 4:2–3 names the most direct biblical calibration test — 'every spirit that confesseth that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh is of God; and every spirit that confesseth not that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh is not of God' — the Christological discrimination that John gives the church for testing the spirits of 1 John 4:1 (the testing posture of s11), here functioning as the operational calibration mechanism (the test produces the calibration: spirits that confess Christ are of God; spirits that do not are not); and John 15:26 grounds the deeper claim that calibration is not a foreign discipline imposed on the Spirit from outside but the Spirit's own native direction — 'even the Spirit of truth ... he shall testify of me' — the Spirit's own work is to point to Christ, so calibrating the Compass to Christ is calibrating the Compass to its own truest motion. The Restoration anchors deepen the witness with characteristic specificity and complete the intra-batch divergences: Moroni 7:16–17 (here in expanded verse-scope from s10's verse 16 alone) carries the Restoration's most direct calibration test — 'every thing which inviteth to do good, and to persuade to believe in Christ, is sent forth by the power and gift of Christ ... but whatsoever thing persuadeth men to do evil, and believe not in Christ, and deny him, and serve not God, then ye may know with a perfect knowledge it is of the devil' — naming the precise discrimination the Compass performs when calibrated: inviting-to-Christ is the Spirit's signature, and persuading-against-Christ is the counterfeit's. Verse-scope split from s10 is the architectural point: at s10 verse 16 alone grounds the universal-Spirit-given claim; here at s12 verses 16–17 together ground the calibration test specifically. And Mosiah 3:19 returns from s11 in different rhetorical direction — at s11 the passage grounds the *diagnostic* (the natural man's enemy-to-God magnetism); here at s12 the same passage grounds the *mechanism* (the yielding to the enticings of the Holy Spirit that calibrates the Compass against the magnetism). The natural man's only response to the magnetism is the yielding King Benjamin names, and that yielding is the operational calibration. Together the cluster establishes ¶3's central claim: the Compass works, the housing distorts, and the disciple's standing discipline is to calibrate the Compass to the North Star — and the calibration mechanism is not foreign discipline but yielded fellowship with the Spirit whose own native direction is back toward Christ.

biblical.text: Hereby know ye the Spirit of God: Every spirit that confesseth that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh is of God: And every spirit that confesseth not that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh is not of God: and this is that spirit of antichrist.
biblical.comment: The most direct biblical calibration test. John gives the church the Christological discrimination that operationalizes the testing posture of 1 John 4:1 (deployed at s11); here the same epistle's test functions as the calibration mechanism. The criterion is Christological — confession of Christ come in the flesh — and any spirit that fails the test is not of God, however inward or feeling-laden its whisper.

biblical.text: But when the Comforter is come, whom I will send unto you from the Father, even the Spirit of truth, which proceedeth from the Father, he shall testify of me.
biblical.comment: Christ's own claim that the Spirit's native direction is back toward Him. Calibration is not foreign discipline imposed on the Spirit from outside; calibrating the Compass to Christ is calibrating the Compass to its own truest motion. The Spirit's own work is to testify of Christ, so the disciple's calibration is fellowship with what the Spirit was already doing.

restoration.text: For behold, the Spirit of Christ is given to every man, that he may know good from evil; wherefore, I show unto you the way to judge; for every thing which inviteth to do good, and to persuade to believe in Christ, is sent forth by the power and gift of Christ; wherefore ye may know with a perfect knowledge it is of God. But whatsoever thing persuadeth men to do evil, and believe not in Christ, and deny him, and serve not God, then ye may know with a perfect knowledge it is of the devil.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's most direct calibration test. (Reasserted from A9 s10 in different rhetorical direction: at s10 verse 16 alone grounds the universal-Spirit-given claim — the gift; here at s12 verses 16–17 together ground the calibration test mechanism — the operation by which the gift is discriminated from the counterfeit. The verse-scope split is deliberate: Moroni's text supports the distinction between the gift and the test, and the article's apparatus honors the distinction at the architectural level.)

restoration.text: For the natural man is an enemy to God, and has been from the fall of Adam, and will be, forever and ever, unless he yields to the enticings of the Holy Spirit, and putteth off the natural man, and becometh a saint through the atonement of Christ the Lord.
restoration.comment: King Benjamin's doctrinal naming of the yielding mechanism. (Reasserted from A9 s11 in different rhetorical direction: at s11 the passage grounds the *diagnostic* — the natural man's enemy-to-God magnetism is real; here at s12 the same passage grounds the *mechanism* — yielding to the enticings of the Holy Spirit is the operational calibration. The natural man's only response to the magnetism is the yielding; the yielding is calibration. The diagnostic at s11 and the mechanism at s12 are the architectural pivot of the paragraph, and the same passage carries both nodes — a single doctrinal foundation under both halves of ¶3's central architectural move.)
