crossref.title: Span 13: When the inward whisper points us away from what Christ taught and what Christ was

s13.text: When the inward whisper points us away from what Christ taught and what Christ was, we know the compass has been disturbed, and we return our sighting to Him
s13.panel_comment: The corrective claim that follows from s12's calibration mechanism: when the calibrated Compass and the disciple's inward whisper diverge — when the whisper points away from what Christ taught (s4's teaching-immutability) and what Christ was (s4's character-immutability) — the disciple's discipline is not to trust the whisper but to know the compass has been disturbed and return the sighting to Christ Himself. The intra-article crossref to s4 is load-bearing: s4 named what Christ taught and what Christ was as the two faces of His immutability that culture pressures to bend; s13 names those same two faces as the calibration test for the disciple's own whispers. The same standard that refused cultural revision in s4 refuses inward revision here. The biblical anchors carry the inward-refusal witness in two registers: Galatians 1:8 returns from s4 in different rhetorical direction — at s4 the apostolic refusal of any other gospel governed ecclesial teaching ('though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel'); here at s13 the same anchor governs the disciple's personal calibration ('though we' — Paul includes himself — and 'an angel from heaven' — the most exalted possible inward messenger). The Pauline refusal is doubly applied: ecclesially at s4, personally at s13. The intra-article reuse is the structural payoff of placing Galatians 1:8 at s4 in Batch 1: the same apostolic floor governs both registers, and the article's architecture surfaces the unity. And Matthew 7:15 carries Christ's own warning that grounds the diagnostic image — 'Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves' — the sheep's clothing is the precise image of a disturbed compass: the messenger feels and looks right but is inwardly off, and the discriminating mark is fruit (Matthew 7:16) which is conformity to what Christ taught and what Christ was. The Restoration anchors deepen the witness with the explicit detection-and-rejection mechanism: D&C 50:31–32 grounds the most direct operational pair — 'if it be by some other way it is not of God ... wherefore, by this ye may know the spirits in all cases under the whole heavens' — naming the detection (some-other-way is not of God) and the universal scope of the test (all cases under the whole heavens), which together ground the disciple's confidence that the return-sighting motion is always available; and Alma 5:40 carries the Christological-source discrimination that completes the cluster — 'for I say unto you that whatsoever is good cometh from God, and whatsoever is evil cometh from the devil' — naming the source-attribution test that grounds the return-sighting: a whisper that bears bad fruit cannot be from God, and the disciple's response is to return her sighting to the One from whom good comes. Together the cluster establishes the s13 corrective: the disciple does not flatter herself that her inward whispers are infallible, does not panic when a disturbance is detected, and does not abandon the Compass when the housing's magnetism is named; she returns her sighting to Christ Himself, and the calibration of s12 resumes.

biblical.text: But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.
biblical.comment: The Pauline refusal of any revised gospel, including from the most exalted possible inward messenger. (Reasserted from A9 s4 in different rhetorical direction: at s4 the apostolic refusal governs ecclesial teaching — the Pauline floor against cultural revision of the gospel's content; here at s13 the same apostolic floor governs the disciple's personal calibration — the Pauline floor against inward revision of the gospel's content. The same standard refuses both forms of revision; the intra-article reuse surfaces the architectural unity. Paul includes himself in the 'though we'; the disciple includes her own inward whispers in the same accountability.)

biblical.text: Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves.
biblical.comment: Christ's own warning grounding the diagnostic image. The sheep's clothing is the precise image of a disturbed compass — the messenger feels and looks right but is inwardly off. The verse's surrounding context (Matthew 7:16) names the discriminating mark as fruit, which is conformity to what Christ taught and what Christ was — the same calibration standard the article has carried since s4.

restoration.text: Wherefore, it shall come to pass, that if you behold a spirit manifested that you cannot understand, and you receive not that spirit, ye shall ask of the Father in the name of Jesus; and if he give not unto you that spirit, then you may know that it is not of God. And it shall be given unto you, power over that spirit; and you shall proclaim against that spirit with a loud voice that it is not of God.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's most direct detection-and-rejection mechanism. Naming both the detection (asking the Father in the name of Jesus and receiving no confirmation means the spirit is not of God) and the rejection (power to proclaim against the spirit). The s13 return-sighting motion is grounded in this operational pair: detection by Christological referral, rejection by the disciple's authorized refusal.

restoration.text: For I say unto you that whatsoever is good cometh from God, and whatsoever is evil cometh from the devil.
restoration.comment: Alma's source-attribution test that completes the s13 cluster. The Christological-source discrimination is the floor of the return-sighting motion: a whisper that bears bad fruit cannot be from God, and the disciple's response is to return her sighting to the One from whom good comes. The s13 corrective is grounded in the most basic source-attribution claim of the Restoration's pastoral ethics.

s14.text: the scriptures are given as the sure map — the testimony of those who have traveled before us, marking the way and pointing always to the same North Star
s14.definition: The inherited navigational instrument — the testimony of witnesses who have wrestled with God before us, recorded as the canonical text and marking the way for those who travel after. The third of three named-concept instruments in the article's triangulation architecture (North Star, Compass, Map). The Map is not the territory and the witness is not the destination; it is the chart of the way that points always to the same North Star, naming the pathways and hazards that the inward Compass alone cannot tell the traveler about.
s14.panel_comment: The named-concept landing of the article's third and final navigational instrument and the completion of the triangulation architecture. Where the North Star (s5) is fixed external and the Compass (s10) is inward and calibration-dependent, the Map is inherited — given to the disciple as the testimony of witnesses who have traveled before her. The metaphor is chosen with care: maps are not the territory, and a map is only as useful as the wrestler-witnesses who produced it (s15 will name them; s16 will name the Spirit who spoke through them). The Map honors the limits of its own image — it marks the way, but the traveler still walks; it names the hazards, but the traveler still discerns; it points always to the same North Star, but the orientation work is the disciple's. The biblical anchors carry the scripture-as-navigational-instrument witness in two registers: 2 Peter 1:19 returns from s5 in different rhetorical direction — at s5 the verse grounded the day-star-arising-in-the-heart claim (the Christological celestial reference of the North Star); here at s14 the same verse grounds the *more sure word of prophecy* + *a light that shineth in a dark place* claim (the scripture-as-navigational-instrument register). The verse contains both metaphors and grounds both named concepts; the architectural split is the strongest intra-article scaffolding instance in the article, and the April 22 finalization document names the pairing explicitly — Peter's *prophetic word* and *day-star* work together because scripture's purpose is to orient the traveler to Christ. Psalm 119:105 grounds the locus classicus of the metaphor — 'thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path' — the most direct biblical pairing of scripture with navigational illumination, and the explicit echo Aaron's source paragraph carries when it shifts metaphor from nautical to wilderness travel at s16 ('when the wilderness grows dark'). The Restoration anchors complete the witness with characteristic specificity: D&C 33:16 grounds the foundation-claim — 'the scriptures ... are given by my Spirit unto you, and ... in them are all things written concerning the foundation of my church, my gospel, and my rock' — naming the scriptures themselves as the foundational record by which the disciple knows what Christ has built; and 2 Nephi 32:3 grounds the pastoral sufficiency claim — 'feast upon the words of Christ; for behold, the words of Christ will tell you all things what ye should do' — the Restoration's most direct promise that the Map is sufficient for the disciple's navigation (without claiming it is everything; the Compass at s10 and the North Star at s5 remain). Together the cluster establishes the third named concept as the inherited complement of the fixed external reference and the inward witness: the chart of the way, drawn by wrestlers, given by the Spirit, pointing always to Christ.

biblical.text: We have also a more sure word of prophecy; whereunto ye do well that ye take heed, as unto a light that shineth in a dark place, until the day dawn, and the day star arise in your hearts.
biblical.comment: The architectural-split anchor for the article's named-concept triangulation. (Reasserted from A9 s5 in different rhetorical direction: at s5 the verse grounded the day-star-arising-in-the-heart claim — the Christological celestial reference of the North Star; here at A9 s14 the same verse grounds the more-sure-word-of-prophecy and light-in-dark-place halves — the scripture-as-navigational-instrument claim of the Map. The verse contains both metaphors and grounds both named concepts; Peter's pairing of prophetic word with day-star arising in the heart anticipates the article's triangulation architecture by naming the scripture and the celestial reference as instruments working together in the disciple's dark-place navigation.)

biblical.text: Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path.
biblical.comment: The locus classicus pairing scripture with navigational illumination. The most direct biblical anchor for the source paragraph's Map metaphor and the explicit echo audible when the article shifts at s16 from nautical to wilderness travel. The Psalmist names scripture's two operations: lamp (immediate guidance, near-field illumination) and light (path-revealing, far-field orientation) — the same two functions Aaron's Map performs.

restoration.text: And the scriptures shall be given, even as they are in mine own bosom, for the salvation of mine own elect; for they will hear my voice, and shall see me, and shall not be asleep, and shall abide the day of my coming; for they shall be purified, even as I am pure.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's most direct foundation-claim for scripture as the inherited record of Christ's voice. The scriptures are given as Christ's own bosom-testimony; the Map is not the disciple's own construction but Christ's gift, drawn from His own witness through His servants.

restoration.text: Wherefore, I said unto you, feast upon the words of Christ; for behold, the words of Christ will tell you all things what ye should do.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's pastoral sufficiency-promise for scripture-as-Map. Nephi's claim is not that the words of Christ are everything — the Compass at s10 and the North Star at s5 remain — but that the Map is sufficient for the disciple's navigation when read in fellowship with the other two instruments. The word 'feast' names the posture: not consultation but sustenance.

crossref.title: Span 15: They experienced their own wrestles with God

s15.text: They experienced their own wrestles with God
s15.panel_comment: The article's pastoral claim about the human texture of scripture's production — and one of A9's most theologically distinctive moves. Where the previous span (s14) named scripture as the inherited Map, this span names the *humanity of the cartographers*: scripture was not dictated from a serene divine elsewhere but written by wrestlers, men and women who struggled with God before they wrote, and whose struggling is itself part of the witness their writing carries. The choice of verb is deliberate and load-bearing: *wrestles* is Jacob's verb at Peniel (Genesis 32), and Aaron extends it into a general name for the prophetic life. The pastoral consequence is large — it forecloses the reading of scripture as oracle-dictation that produces inerrant transcripts, and instead names scripture as the testimony of fellow strugglers whose witness gained its weight precisely *through* their wrestling. The biblical anchors carry the wrestlers cluster in three registers: Genesis 32:24–28 is the locus classicus and the verbal source — Jacob's all-night struggle with the divine adversary at the Jabbok ford, ending with the limp, the new name (Israel = 'he strives with God'), and the blessing only the wrestler receives; Jeremiah 20:7–9 carries the prophet's most agonized confession — 'O LORD, thou hast deceived me, and I was deceived ... his word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones' — the wrestler who could not stop prophesying *and* could not stop complaining about prophesying, and whose tortured witness became the Book of Jeremiah; and Psalm 22:1 carries David's wrestle — 'My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?' — the canonical opener of lament psalmody, and the verse Christ Himself would later quote at Golgotha, binding the wrestler's cry across the canon into the Master's own dereliction. The Restoration anchors deepen the witness with characteristic specificity and verbal directness: Enos 1:2–4 uses Aaron's exact verb — 'I will tell you of the wrestle which I had before God, before I received a remission of my sins' — making the Book of Mormon's most direct verbal anchor for the source paragraph's framing (and naming the wrestle as the precondition of the spiritual gift, not its absence); D&C 121:1–6 carries Joseph Smith's wrestle at Liberty Jail — 'O God, where art thou? And where is the pavilion that covereth thy hiding place?' — explicitly named in Restoration scholarship as comparable to Jacob's wrestle, and the latter-day locus classicus of the prophet-as-wrestler whose breakthrough revelations followed the wrestle's intensity; and Joseph Smith—History 1:14–17 grounds the wrestle that opened the Restoration itself — 'thick darkness gathered around me, and it seemed to me for a time as if I were doomed to sudden destruction' — the wrestle preceding the First Vision, naming the wrestler-pattern at the foundational moment of the latter-day work. Together the cluster establishes that scripture's authority does not rest on the wrestlers' perfection but on the Spirit's faithfulness in speaking through their wrestling (which s16 will name explicitly); and that the disciple who reads the Map is also a wrestler, reaching for the same God who never let any of these go.

biblical.text: And Jacob was left alone; and there wrestled a man with him until the breaking of the day. And when he saw that he prevailed not against him, he touched the hollow of his thigh; and the hollow of Jacob's thigh was out of joint, as he wrestled with him. And he said, Let me go, for the day breaketh. And he said, I will not let thee go, except thou bless me. And he said unto him, What is thy name? And he said, Jacob. And he said, Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel: for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men, and hast prevailed.
biblical.comment: The locus classicus and the verbal source for Aaron's claim. Jacob's all-night wrestle at the Jabbok is the canonical foundation of the wrestler-prophet pattern; the limp, the new name, and the blessing only the wrestler receives establish the architecture the article's claim rests on. The verb itself comes from this passage — Aaron extends Jacob's verb into a general name for the prophetic life.

biblical.text: O LORD, thou hast deceived me, and I was deceived: thou art stronger than I, and hast prevailed: I am in derision daily, every one mocketh me ... Then I said, I will not make mention of him, nor speak any more in his name. But his word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I was weary with forbearing, and I could not stay.
biblical.comment: The most agonized prophetic confession in the Tanakh — Jeremiah unable to stop prophesying and unable to stop complaining about prophesying. The wrestler whose tortured witness became the Book of Jeremiah, naming explicitly that the prophetic word came through wrestling, not despite it.

biblical.text: My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? why art thou so far from helping me, and from the words of my roaring?
biblical.comment: The canonical opener of lament psalmody and David's wrestle made canonical. Christ Himself would later quote this verse from the cross (Matthew 27:46), binding David's wrestler-cry across the canon into the Master's own dereliction at Golgotha — the wrestlers' cry taken up by the One who entered every wrestler's darkness.

restoration.text: And I will tell you of the wrestle which I had before God, before I received a remission of my sins. Behold, I went to hunt beasts in the forests; and the words which I had often heard my father speak concerning eternal life, and the joy of the saints, sunk deep into my heart. And my soul hungered; and I kneeled down before my Maker, and I cried unto him in mighty prayer and supplication for mine own soul; and all the day long did I cry unto him; yea, and when the night came I did still raise my voice high that it reached the heavens.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's most direct verbal anchor for the source paragraph's framing. Enos uses Aaron's exact verb — 'the wrestle which I had before God' — and names the wrestle as the precondition of the spiritual gift (the remission of sins he sought), not its absence. The Book of Mormon's wrestler-witness in his own first-person voice.

restoration.text: O God, where art thou? And where is the pavilion that covereth thy hiding place? How long shall thy hand be stayed, and thine eye, yea thy pure eye, behold from the eternal heavens the wrongs of thy people and of thy servants, and thine ear be penetrated with their cries? Yea, O Lord, how long shall they suffer these wrongs and unlawful oppressions, before thine heart shall be softened toward them, and thy bowels be moved with compassion toward them?
restoration.comment: Joseph Smith's wrestle at Liberty Jail — the latter-day locus classicus of the prophet-as-wrestler. The cry 'O God, where art thou?' parallels Jacob's all-night struggle and David's 'why hast thou forsaken me?'; the revelations that followed the wrestle (D&C 121–123) contain some of the Restoration's most expansive theological content. The wrestle did not disqualify the prophet; it qualified the revelation.

restoration.text: After I had retired to the place where I had previously designed to go, having looked around me, and finding myself alone, I kneeled down and began to offer up the desires of my heart to God. I had scarcely done so, when immediately I was seized upon by some power which entirely overcame me, and had such an astonishing influence over me as to bind my tongue so that I could not speak. Thick darkness gathered around me, and it seemed to me for a time as if I were doomed to sudden destruction ... I saw a pillar of light exactly over my head, above the brightness of the sun, which descended gradually until it fell upon me.
restoration.comment: The wrestle that opened the Restoration itself. Joseph Smith's First Vision was preceded by a wrestle so severe that it seemed to threaten his destruction; the breakthrough vision came only after the wrestle. The wrestler-pattern names the foundational moment of the latter-day work and grounds the article's claim that the wrestlers' wrestles are themselves part of the Map's witness.

crossref.label: Within this article
crossref.title: Span 16: through them the Spirit spoke truth that still lights the way when the wilderness grows dark

s16.text: through them the Spirit spoke truth that still lights the way when the wilderness grows dark
s16.panel_comment: The pneumatological claim that grounds the Map's authority despite the wrestlers' imperfection. Where s15 names the human texture of scripture's production, s16 names how the testimony of imperfect wrestlers became trustworthy witness: the Spirit spoke through them, and the Spirit's truth survives across centuries as the lamp that still lights the way when the wilderness grows dark. The metaphorical shift from nautical to wilderness travel is deliberate and consistent with the article's broader frame — every traveler's path from the opening paragraph — and the wilderness is the biblical traveler's standard context (Exodus, the prophets, John the Baptist, Christ's forty days). Psalm 119:105's lamp-and-light is audible in the new sentence, and the shift extends the chart image toward the illumination image without losing the navigational logic. The biblical anchors carry the Spirit-through-imperfect-vessels witness in two registers: 2 Peter 1:21 returns from A4 in different rhetorical direction — at A4 s1 the verse grounded the revelation-origin claim (Spirit-moved authors, the article's directly-paraphrased anchor at A4 s3); here at A9 s16 the same verse grounds the *enduring* witness claim — the Spirit who moved the wrestlers to speak still speaks through their record across centuries, and the truth they bore still lights the way. The temporal-endurance register is distinct from the origin-and-substance registers A4 carried. And 2 Timothy 3:16–17 grounds the operational sufficiency of the inherited witness — 'all scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness: that the man of God may be perfect, throughly furnished unto all good works' — here at A9 s16 the verse functions in its third use across the cluster (A4 s2: survival-through-imperfection / transmission integrity; A4 s9: substance-of-what-is-received / reception-posture; here at A9 s16: operational sufficiency for the wilderness traveler — the Map works in the dark wilderness because the Spirit's truth in it works). The Restoration anchors deepen the witness with characteristic personal weight: Mormon 8:12, 17 carries Moroni's most direct first-person plea about prophetic imperfection — 'And whoso receiveth this record, and shall not condemn it because of the imperfections which are in it, the same shall know of greater things than these ... And if there be faults they be the faults of a man. But behold, we know no fault; nevertheless God knoweth all things; therefore, he that condemneth, let him be aware lest he shall be in danger of hell fire' — the precise theological frame Aaron's s16 carries: the Spirit speaks through wrestler-witnesses despite their imperfections, and the record endures because the Spirit endures behind it; and D&C 1:24–28 grounds the latter-day locus classicus of survival-through-weakness — 'these commandments are of me, and were given unto my servants in their weakness, after the manner of their language, that they might come to understanding ... and inasmuch as they erred it might be made known; and inasmuch as they sought wisdom they might be instructed' — naming weakness-of-the-vessel and after-the-manner-of-their-language as features (not failures) of how the Spirit's truth reaches the disciple. Together the cluster establishes that the Map's authority rests on the Spirit's faithfulness through wrestler-witnesses, not on the witnesses' own perfection — and the lamp still lights the way for the disciple in the wilderness because the Spirit who lit it is the same Spirit who now illuminates the disciple's reading.

s17.text: Without the map, the compass alone cannot tell us which pathways we have entered or which perils lie ahead
s17.panel_comment: The paragraph's closing synthesis claim and the sufficiency-triad assertion that prepares the article's final two paragraphs. Where s14 names the Map, s15 names the wrestlers, and s16 names the Spirit who spoke through them, s17 names what the Map *does* for the disciple — and what its absence would mean. The claim is doubly load-bearing: it asserts the Map's navigational necessity (the Compass alone is insufficient) without claiming the Map's totalizing sufficiency (the Compass and the North Star remain). The triangulation architecture lands here as architectural completion: three instruments, each with distinct work, each insufficient alone, each necessary to the others. The biblical anchors carry the navigational-necessity witness in two registers: Acts 17:11 returns from A4 in different rhetorical direction — at A4 s8 the verse grounded the noble-Berean confirmation pattern (searching the scriptures to verify revelation); at A4 s12 it grounded the testing-of-doctrinal-claims register (the apostolic discipline of measurement against scripture); here at A9 s17 the same verse grounds *navigational necessity* specifically — the Bereans did not consult the scriptures as an optional confirmation but as the necessary instrument by which they could discriminate at all; without the Map, the discrimination cannot happen. And Hosea 4:6 grounds the most direct biblical anchor for the 'perils lie ahead' register — 'my people are destroyed for lack of knowledge' — naming the operational consequence of the absent Map: not error of intellect but destruction of life. Hosea's prophetic indictment is precisely what s17 names in pastoral register — without the inherited witness, the disciple cannot know which waters she has entered or which shoals have wrecked others before her, and the cost is real. The Restoration anchors complete the witness with characteristic specificity: Mosiah 1:3–5 carries King Benjamin's most direct claim — 'were it not for these plates ... we should have suffered in ignorance ... not knowing the mysteries of God' — the absence-of-Map claim made in Restoration scripture's own first-person voice (Benjamin to his sons; the plates are the Map; the absence is the suffering); and Alma 37:8 grounds the operational claim of what the Map accomplishes — 'they have enlarged the memory of this people, yea, and convinced many of the error of their ways, and brought them to the knowledge of their God unto the salvation of their souls' — naming three Map-operations the Compass alone cannot perform (memory enlargement, error correction, salvation knowledge). Together the cluster establishes ¶4's closing sufficiency-triad: the Map is necessary, the Map is not everything, the three instruments together give the disciple what she needs to navigate. The article will return to this triad at s20 to name it as the disciple's standing pattern — 'We do not walk by the inward whisper alone. We do not walk by written word alone. We walk by Christ, who is the living reference, and by His Spirit, who leads us toward Him and never away.'

s18.text: Each time we find ourselves lost or uncertain, we have the navigational tools to reorient and find our way again
s18.panel_comment: The pastoral payoff of the triangulation architecture established in ¶2–¶4. Where s5, s10, and s14 named the three navigational instruments (North Star, Compass, Map) and s17 named their integrated sufficiency, s18 names the iterative-temporal claim that the triad serves the disciple at *every* point of lostness, not as a one-time deliverance from confusion but as the standing pastoral provision for the disciple's recurring need. The article's only iterative-temporal phrase — 'Each time' — does load-bearing work here: it forecloses the perfectionist reading in which the navigational tools are reserved for the spiritually settled, and instead names recovery as the disciple's standing inheritance. The secondary register — universal access to spiritual guidance through conscience — names the scope: the tools are accessible to every soul, not reserved to an elect or a credentialed class. The biblical anchors cluster the recovery-and-restoration witness in two registers: Psalm 23:3 grounds the Shepherd-Psalm's soul-restoration claim — 'he restoreth my soul; he leadeth me in the paths of righteousness for his name's sake.' The verse is the canonical anchor for *each-time recoverability*: restoration is the Shepherd's standing pastoral promise, not a one-time event, and the paths of righteousness are reentered through the Shepherd's leading rather than the sheep's own discernment. The Psalmist names the asymmetry that grounds the disciple's confidence — when the soul is lost, the restorer is the Shepherd Himself. And Luke 15:4–6 carries Christ's own pastoral teaching on the same claim in parable form — 'what man of you, having an hundred sheep, if he lose one of them, doth not leave the ninety and nine in the wilderness, and go after that which is lost, until he find it?' The dominical anchor names the asymmetry of grace: the Shepherd's seeking outlasts the sheep's lostness, and the parable's closing — 'rejoice with me; for I have found my sheep which was lost' — names the Shepherd's joy as the disciple's recovered standing. Luke 15 places s18's claim in Christ's own first-person voice. The Restoration anchors deepen the witness with characteristic operational specificity: Mormon's narration of Alma and the sons of Mosiah at Mosiah 27:25–26 carries the *be-made-new* register here applied to the disciple's recurring reorientation — 'marvel not that all mankind, yea, men and women, all nations, kindreds, tongues and people, must be born again; yea, born of God, changed from their carnal and fallen state, to a state of righteousness, being redeemed of God, becoming his sons and daughters' — the verses ground the recurring-renewal claim that grounds s18's 'each time we find ourselves lost' temporal repetition (distinct from prior uses; the third deployment carries the iterative-restoration register specifically); and 2 Nephi 32:5 grounds the Spirit-will-show-you-all-things promise applied to recovery navigation — 'for behold, the Holy Ghost will show unto you all things what ye should do' — when the disciple is lost, the Compass (s10) and the Map (s14) remain accessible *because the Holy Ghost remains accessible*; the secondary universal-access register is grounded in the Spirit's standing availability rather than in any human credential. Together the cluster establishes s18's pastoral payoff: the triangulation architecture is not a possession to be guarded but a provision to be returned to, and the Shepherd who restores the soul is the same Shepherd who gave the instruments.

s19.text: the disciple’s walk does not require the approval of any person, tradition, or institution beyond the approval of Christ Himself, who is the only righteous and eternal Judge of human souls
s19.panel_comment: The article's most explicit pastoral statement of the disciple-direct-to-Christ confession, made in positive Christological register. The source-paragraph clause makes two welded claims: (a) the disciple's standing before Christ is not mediated by human approval — no person, no tradition, no institution can finally validate or invalidate the disciple's walk; and (b) Christ alone holds eternal judicial standing over human souls. The two claims are mutually grounded: the first follows from the second. Because Christ alone judges, no human approval can finally settle what is settled by Him. The discipline of this panel_comment is to name the claim positively — as Christological assertion about Christ's sole judicial standing — rather than negatively as polemic against human authority. The container-words 'person,' 'tradition,' and 'institution' function as biblical containers each reader fills from her own context; the article is not naming any human authority as illegitimate, only as non-final. The unilateral-fellowship discipline of the broader cluster (A8 s1–s17) governs here: s19 does not withdraw the disciple from legitimate fellowship or right tradition; it names where the disciple's *final* standing rests, and the final standing is before Christ alone. The biblical anchors cluster the witness in three registers: Romans 14:4 grounds the Pauline locus classicus for the no-human-approval claim — 'who art thou that judgest another man's servant? to his own master he standeth or falleth. Yea, he shall be holden up: for God is able to make him stand.' The verse names the disciple as Christ's servant whose standing or falling is *to his own master*, and the rhetorical question 'who art thou' is the apostolic refusal of any human positioning as the disciple's judge. Notable: Romans 14:1 and 14:13 already appear in the cluster at A1 s2 and s11, A2 s7, and A3 s6 — the chapter is foundational ground for the disciple-direct theology; verse 4 is the master-servant judicial claim that grounds s19's positive Christological register. James 4:12 carries the most concentrated single-verse anchor for Christ-as-sole-Judge with the same 'who art thou' rhetorical refusal — 'there is one lawgiver, who is able to save and to destroy: who art thou that judgest another?' The two apostolic verses form the biblical bracket for s19's twin claims: Paul on the no-human-approval direction, James on the Christ-as-sole-Judge direction, both closing with the same rhetorical refusal. And 2 Timothy 4:1, 8 grounds the Pauline confession of Christ-as-eschatological-Judge in Paul's own farewell voice — 'the Lord Jesus Christ, who shall judge the quick and the dead at his appearing and his kingdom ... the righteous judge, shall give me at that day.' The verse carries the verbatim register Aaron's source paragraph names — 'the only righteous and eternal Judge of human souls' — and grounds the *righteous Judge* claim in the apostolic farewell where Paul submits his own standing to Christ's judgment rather than to any human court. The Restoration anchors deepen the witness with characteristic specificity: 2 Nephi 9:41 grounds Jacob's most direct no-mediator claim — 'the keeper of the gate is the Holy One of Israel; and he employeth no servant there.' The gate of the way is kept by Christ Himself, and Jacob names explicitly that Christ employs *no servant* at that gate — the cleanest Restoration anchor for the no-human-approval claim, made in Jacob's pastoral voice and grounded in the gate-keeping image that the article's navigational architecture echoes. 3 Nephi 27:13–14 carries Christ's own first-person voice on His judicial mission — 'I came into the world to do the will of my Father ... that I might draw all men unto me, that as I have been lifted up by men even so should men be lifted up by the Father, to stand before me, to be judged of their works.' The dominical anchor names the Father's purpose as lifting all souls to stand *before Christ* for judgment — the most direct verba Christi anchor for Christ-as-sole-Judge, in Christ's own self-disclosure. And Mosiah 4:13 grounds the peaceable-disposition register that the interfaith register quietly carries — 'ye will not have a mind to injure one another, but to live peaceably, and to render to every man according to that which is his due' — the verse names the disciple's positive ethical posture toward person, tradition, and institution, grounding the freedom from human approval not as license for human disregard but as the standing for peaceable engagement. King Benjamin's instruction closes the cluster by naming the disciple's positive ethical posture in Restoration scripture's own pastoral grammar. Together the cluster establishes s19's positive Christological assertion: the disciple's walk rests on Christ's sole judicial standing, and the freedom from human approval is the consequence of that standing, not the assertion of any human prerogative against tradition or institution. The article preserves the legitimate good of fellowship and tradition (A8's territory) while naming where the disciple's final standing rests.

The disciple is Christ's servant whose standing or falling is *to his own master*, and the rhetorical question 'who art thou' is the apostolic refusal of any human positioning as the disciple's judge. Romans 14:1 and 14:13 already ground other claims in the cluster (A1 s2 and s11, A2 s7, A3 s6); verse 4 is the master-servant judicial claim that grounds s19's positive Christological register.

The two apostolic verses form the biblical bracket for s19's twin claims: Paul on the no-human-approval direction, James on the Christ-as-sole-Judge direction, both closing with the same rhetorical refusal of any human assumption of the judicial position Christ alone occupies.

The verse grounds the interfaith register that s19 quietly carries — the disciple's direct-to-Christ standing does not authorize injury toward those whose tradition differs, but the opposite: it grounds the peaceable disposition toward every soul, rendering to each what is due. The verse closes the cluster by naming the disciple's positive ethical posture toward person, tradition, and institution — the freedom from human approval as the final judicial standard does not become license for human disregard. s20.text: We do not walk by the inward whisper alone. We do not walk by written word alone. We walk by Christ, who is the living reference, and by His Spirit, who leads us toward Him and never away
s20.panel_comment: The article's synthesis confession and the load-bearing integration claim that closes the triangulation architecture. Where ¶3 named the Compass (s10) and ¶4 named the Map (s14), ¶6 returns to the triad and names what the disciple's standing walk actually rests on: not the Compass alone, not the Map alone, but Christ Himself — the living reference — with His Spirit doing the directional work of leading the disciple toward Him. The discipline of the span is to refuse two errors at once: the error of subjective immediacy that walks by inward whisper without the corrective witness of the written word, and the error of textualism that walks by the written word without the inward witness of the Spirit. Both errors are refused by the same positive confession — Christ is the Person to whom both instruments point, and the Spirit is the One whose work is always to lead the disciple toward Him and never away. The biblical anchors carry the synthesis in three registers: John 14:6 returns from prior cluster deployments in different rhetorical direction — at A5 s16 the verse anchored Christ as the measuring reference of the disciple's path, and at A6 s8 it anchored Christ as the way of salvation specifically (the Person by whom salvation comes); here at A9 s20 the same verse anchors Christ as the integrating reference of the triangulation architecture — the Person under whom both the inward Compass and the inherited Map find their true orientation. The three deployments together form a Christological progression: measurement, salvation, navigation — each a distinct rhetorical function of the same verba Christi. Romans 8:14 grounds the Spirit's specifically leading operation — 'as many as are led by the Spirit of God, they are the sons of God' — the locus classicus for the verb that distinguishes the Spirit's work in the triad from any merely informational role; the Spirit does not only witness or only teach but actively leads, and the leading is the substance of the s20 claim about His operation. And 2 Corinthians 3:17–18 grounds the Pauline confession of Christ-and-Spirit working together upon the disciple — 'we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image, from glory to glory, even as by the Spirit of the Lord' — the verse names the Spirit's directional work as transformation toward Christ Himself ('changed into the same image'), grounding the source paragraph's 'toward Him and never away' claim in Paul's most direct Christ-and-Spirit synthesis. The Restoration anchors deepen the witness with characteristic specificity. 2 Nephi 31:20 grounds the most direct Restoration synthesis of the triad in a single verse — 'ye must press forward with a steadfastness in Christ, having a perfect brightness of hope, and a love of God and of all men. Wherefore, if ye shall press forward, feasting upon the word of Christ, and endure to the end, behold, thus saith the Father: Ye shall have eternal life.' Nephi names Christ as the destination of the disciple's pressing forward and the word of Christ as the means of the feasting; the inward steadfastness and the written word are joined in a single navigational pattern, and the Father's promise seals the synthesis. D&C 50:23–24 grounds the Spirit's specifically toward-Christ-and-never-away operation — 'that which doth not edify is not of God, and is darkness ... that which is of God is light; and he that receiveth light, and continueth in God, receiveth more light; and that light groweth brighter and brighter until the perfect day' — the most direct Restoration anchor for the directional claim that the source paragraph carries; the Spirit's work is always toward more light, always toward the perfect day (which Peter at s5 named as the day star arising in the heart), never toward darkness or away from Christ. And D&C 93:1 grounds the Christological destination of the disciple's walk — 'every soul who forsaketh his sins and cometh unto me, and calleth on my name, and obeyeth my voice, and keepeth my commandments, shall see my face and know that I am' — naming Christ Himself as the end toward which the Spirit leads and the written word points. Together the cluster establishes the article's closing synthesis: the disciple does not walk by inward witness alone, does not walk by written word alone, but walks by Christ — the living reference — with the Spirit doing the directional work of leading her toward Him, the Map showing the way that prior wrestlers have walked, and Christ Himself the standing reference by which everything else is calibrated.

biblical.text: Jesus saith unto him, I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.
biblical.comment: Reasserted from Article 5 Span 16 and Article 6 Span 8 in different rhetorical direction: at A5 s16 the verse anchored Christ as the measuring reference of the disciple's path of measurement; at A6 s8 it anchored Christ as the way of salvation specifically — the Person by whom salvation comes; here at A9 s20 the same verse anchors Christ as the integrating reference of the triangulation architecture — the Person under whom both the inward Compass and the inherited Map find their true orientation. The three deployments form a Christological progression: measurement, salvation, navigation.

biblical.text: For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, they are the sons of God.
biblical.comment: The Pauline locus classicus for the Spirit's specifically leading operation. The verb is the substance — the Spirit does not only witness or only teach but actively leads, and the leading is what distinguishes the Spirit's work in the triad from any merely informational role. Grounds the source paragraph's 'leads us toward Him' clause directly.

biblical.text: Now the Lord is that Spirit: and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty. But we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image, from glory to glory, even as by the Spirit of the Lord.
biblical.comment: The Pauline confession of Christ-and-Spirit working together upon the disciple. The Spirit's directional work is transformation toward Christ Himself ('changed into the same image'), grounding the source paragraph's 'toward Him and never away' in Paul's most direct Christ-and-Spirit synthesis.

restoration.text: Wherefore, ye must press forward with a steadfastness in Christ, having a perfect brightness of hope, and a love of God and of all men. Wherefore, if ye shall press forward, feasting upon the word of Christ, and endure to the end, behold, thus saith the Father: Ye shall have eternal life.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's most direct synthesis of the triad in a single verse. Nephi names Christ as the destination of the disciple's pressing forward and the word of Christ as the means of the feasting; the inward steadfastness and the written word are joined in a single navigational pattern, and the Father's promise seals the synthesis.

restoration.text: That which doth not edify is not of God, and is darkness. That which is of God is light; and he that receiveth light, and continueth in God, receiveth more light; and that light groweth brighter and brighter until the perfect day.
restoration.comment: The most direct Restoration anchor for the directional claim the source paragraph carries — 'leads us toward Him and never away.' The Spirit's work is always toward more light, always toward the perfect day, never toward darkness or away from Christ. Pairs with Peter's day-star (at A9 s5) as the cluster's Christological-destination image.

restoration.text: Verily, thus saith the Lord: It shall come to pass that every soul who forsaketh his sins and cometh unto me, and calleth on my name, and obeyeth my voice, and keepeth my commandments, shall see my face and know that I am.
restoration.comment: Christ's first-person voice naming Himself as the end toward which the Spirit leads and the written word points. The verse carries the verbatim Christological destination of the disciple's walk and grounds the s20 synthesis in dominical scripture.

s21.text: The Father who knows our hearts will guide every soul who comes to Him in sincerity
s21.panel_comment: The article's pastoral close in Trinitarian symmetry with s22 — the Father's promise to the sincere seeker, paired with the Son's promise to the honest disciple. The source paragraph clause makes three welded claims: (a) the Father knows the disciple's heart, (b) the Father guides every soul who comes to Him, and (c) the sufficient condition for the guidance is sincerity — not orthodoxy, not membership, not mastery, but the honest movement of the heart toward Him. The discipline of the span is to name the universal scope of the promise without softening the qualifier. Sincerity is the condition; the condition is real. But the condition is one no sincere seeker fails to meet by definition, and the article's reach to the doubter, the wanderer, the believer outside the writer's own covenant boundary rests on this. The biblical anchors carry the promise in two registers. Jeremiah 29:13 grounds the locus classicus for sincere-seeking-finds-God — 'and ye shall seek me, and find me, when ye shall search for me with all your heart' — the prophetic promise in YHWH's own first-person voice that the wholehearted seeking finds the One sought. The verse stands as the Old Testament bedrock for s21's claim, and the with-all-your-heart register is the precise biblical idiom for what Aaron's source paragraph names as sincerity. And 1 Samuel 16:7 grounds the source paragraph's specific 'who knows our hearts' register — 'for the Lord seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the Lord looketh on the heart.' The verse names the Father's discernment as distinct from human evaluation; the disciple's appearance, station, articulation, or doctrinal precision are not what the Lord is reading. He reads the heart, and the heart is what He responds to. The pairing of Jeremiah and 1 Samuel gives s21 the biblical bracket it needs: the Lord knows the heart (1 Sam 16:7) and responds to the heart's seeking (Jer 29:13). The Restoration anchors deepen the witness with the Lord's first-person voice repeating the same promise in latter-day register. D&C 88:63 carries the Restoration's most direct echo of Jeremiah 29:13 in the Lord's own first-person voice — 'Draw near unto me and I will draw near unto you; seek me diligently and ye shall find me; ask, and ye shall receive; knock, and it shall be opened unto you' — confirming the prophetic promise in dispensational immediacy and grounding the source paragraph's 'comes to Him in sincerity' in the Lord's standing offer. The pattern is reciprocal: the disciple draws near, and the Lord draws near in response; the seeking is met by being found. And Alma 26:37 grounds the Father's universal mindfulness — 'now my brethren, we see that God is mindful of every people, whatsoever land they may be in; yea, he numbereth his people, and his bowels of mercy are over all the earth' — naming the Father's knowledge as extending to every people in every land, and grounding the source paragraph's 'every soul' in Ammon's pastoral confession after the Lamanite conversions. The Restoration scripture here makes explicit what the biblical anchors imply: the Father's pastoral knowledge is not restricted by covenant boundary, geography, or prior tradition. Every soul is numbered, every people is mindful to Him, and the seeker who comes to Him in sincerity is met by a Father who already knew her heart before she came. Together the cluster establishes s21 as the article's pastoral close on the Father's side of the Trinitarian confession: the Father knows hearts, responds to the wholehearted seeking, and turns away no sincere seeker.

biblical.text: And ye shall seek me, and find me, when ye shall search for me with all your heart.
biblical.comment: The Old Testament locus classicus for sincere-seeking-finds-God, in YHWH's own first-person voice. The with-all-your-heart register is the precise biblical idiom for what the source paragraph names as sincerity, and the verse stands as the bedrock for s21's promise.

biblical.text: But the LORD said unto Samuel, Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.
biblical.comment: Grounds the source paragraph's 'who knows our hearts' directly. The Lord's discernment is distinct from human evaluation: the disciple's appearance, station, articulation, or doctrinal precision are not what He is reading. He reads the heart, and the heart is what He responds to.

restoration.text: Draw near unto me and I will draw near unto you; seek me diligently and ye shall find me; ask, and ye shall receive; knock, and it shall be opened unto you.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's most direct echo of Jeremiah 29:13 and Matthew 7:7–8 in the Lord's own first-person voice. The pattern is reciprocal — the disciple draws near, and the Lord draws near in response; the seeking is met by being found. Grounds the source paragraph's 'comes to Him in sincerity' in the Lord's standing offer.

restoration.text: Now my brethren, we see that God is mindful of every people, whatsoever land they may be in; yea, he numbereth his people, and his bowels of mercy are over all the earth. Now this is my joy, and my great thanksgiving; yea, and I will give thanks unto my God forever. Amen.
restoration.comment: Ammon's pastoral confession after the Lamanite conversions grounds the source paragraph's 'every soul' in Restoration scripture's own universalizing voice. The Father's pastoral knowledge is not restricted by covenant boundary, geography, or prior tradition — every soul is numbered, every people is mindful to Him.

s22.text: the Son who bids us follow has never led any honest disciple astray
s22.panel_comment: The article's final claim and the structural benediction that closes the triangulation architecture. In Trinitarian symmetry with s21's Father-promise, s22 carries the Son's promise: He bids the disciple follow, and His record of faithful leading is perfect. The source paragraph clause makes two welded claims: (a) the Son invites — the disciple's walk begins in His bidding, not in her self-starting; and (b) the Son has never led any honest disciple astray — His record across every honest following is unbroken. The 'honest' qualifier carries the same weight in s22 that 'sincere' carries in s21: it is a real condition, not a softening, but the condition is one no honest disciple fails to meet by definition. The discipline of the span is to land the article's benediction in Christ's pastoral faithfulness — not as comfort against any particular fear, but as the standing ground on which the triangulation rests. If Christ Himself is the integrating reference (s20), then Christ's record as the One who leads is what makes the integration trustworthy. The biblical anchors cluster the promise in three registers. John 10:27–28 grounds the verba Christi on faithful following and no loss — 'my sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me: and I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand.' The verses contain three claims s22 carries verbatim: the disciple hears (the bidding), the disciple follows (the walking), and the Son holds her so that no one plucks her from His hand (the never-astray promise). Christ's self-disclosure as the good shepherd in His own first-person voice grounds the s22 claim in the strongest biblical anchor available. Matthew 11:28–30 grounds the source paragraph's 'bids us follow' register specifically — 'Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.' The verba Christi name the Son's invitation as universal ('all ye that labour'), the Son's pastoral character as the ground of trust ('meek and lowly in heart'), and the disciple's yoke as one that fits ('easy ... light'). The Son does not bid the disciple to a burden she cannot carry; the leading is calibrated to the follower. And Hebrews 13:5 grounds the never-forsaking promise in the Lord's most concentrated single-verse anchor — 'I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee' — the apostolic confession that the Son's leading is not occasional, conditional, or vulnerable to failure. The verb stands at the center of s22's never-astray claim. The Restoration anchors deepen the witness with the Lord's own first-person voice in three further registers. Alma 5:38–39 grounds the shepherd's standing call after every wandering disciple — 'behold, the good shepherd doth call after you; and if ye will hear his voice it shall be the voice of the good shepherd' — naming both the universality of the call (after every wanderer) and the recognizable character of the voice (the disciple knows the Shepherd's voice when she hears it). D&C 50:44 grounds the never-fall promise in the Lord's first-person voice in latter-day register — 'I am the good shepherd, and the stone of Israel. He that buildeth upon this rock shall never fall' — pairing with Hebrews 13:5 in the biblical column to give s22 the cross-canon bracket on the never-astray claim. And 3 Nephi 27:33 holds the article's closing benediction against universalist misreading — 'strait is the gate, and narrow is the way that leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it' — naming Christ's own dominical claim that the way is narrow and not all who walk arrive. The verse does not soften s22's promise; it qualifies the promise's reach. The Son who bids us follow has never led any honest disciple astray, but the way the Son bids us walk is strait, and dishonest disciples — those who name His name but refuse His voice — are not the disciples the promise covers. The pastoral assurance is real; the assurance is for honest disciples who hear and follow. Together the cluster establishes the article's Trinitarian close: the Father knows hearts and guides sincere seekers (s21), the Son bids the disciple follow and has never led any honest disciple astray (s22), the Spirit leads always toward Christ and never away (s20). The triangulation architecture rests, finally, on the pastoral faithfulness of the One to whom every instrument points.

The verses contain three claims s22 carries verbatim — the disciple hears (the bidding), the disciple follows (the walking), and the Son holds her so no one plucks her from His hand (the never-astray promise). The strongest biblical anchor available for the source paragraph's claim.

biblical.text: Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.

Names the Son's invitation as universal ('all ye that labour'), the Son's pastoral character as the ground of trust ('meek and lowly in heart'), and the disciple's yoke as one that fits. The Son does not bid the disciple to a burden she cannot carry; the leading is calibrated to the follower.

biblical.text: Let your conversation be without covetousness; and be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.
biblical.comment: The apostolic confession that the Son's leading is not occasional, conditional, or vulnerable to failure. The never-forsaking verb stands at the center of s22's never-astray claim and pairs with John 10:28's no-plucking-from-hand in the same biblical column.

restoration.text: Behold, I say unto you, that the good shepherd doth call you; yea, and in his own name he doth call you, which is the name of Christ; and if ye will not hearken unto the voice of the good shepherd, to the name by which ye are called, behold, ye are not the sheep of the good shepherd. And now if ye are not the sheep of the good shepherd, of what fold are ye?
restoration.comment: Alma's most direct Restoration anchor for the shepherd's standing call after every wandering disciple. Names both the universality of the call (after every wanderer) and the recognizable character of the voice — the disciple knows the Shepherd's voice when she hears it.

restoration.text: For I am the good shepherd, and the stone of Israel. He that buildeth upon this rock shall never fall.
restoration.comment: The Lord's first-person voice in latter-day register on the never-fall promise. Pairs with Hebrews 13:5 in the biblical column to give s22 the cross-canon bracket on the never-astray claim.

restoration.text: And it came to pass that when Jesus had ended these sayings he said unto his disciples: Enter ye in at the strait gate; for strait is the gate, and narrow is the way that leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it; but wide is the gate, and broad the way which leadeth to death, and many there be that travel therein, until the time is past, that they may no more enter in, because of the iniquity of which they aboundeth.
restoration.comment: Christ's own dominical claim that the way is narrow and not all who walk arrive. The verse does not soften s22's promise but qualifies its reach: the Son who bids us follow has never led any honest disciple astray, but the way is strait, and dishonest disciples — those who name His name but refuse His voice — are not the disciples the promise covers. The pastoral assurance is real; the assurance is for honest disciples who hear and follow.

s1.text: God speaks to every conscience open to hearing Him, whether we feel worthy or not
s1.panel_comment: The article's opening move: before the mechanics of grace are named, this span establishes the universality and worthiness-independence of God's communication. The claim does not say "God speaks to believers" or "God speaks to the morally prepared" — it says "every conscience open to hearing Him," placing the condition on receptivity, not on worthiness. This distinction is load-bearing: grace begins not with the soul's qualification but with God's uncoerced speaking. The biblical anchors carry the claim in two registers. Romans 2:14–15 is the locus classicus for universal moral conscience — the law written in every human heart, conscience bearing witness even to those who have not received covenant instruction. The verse grounds the "every conscience" universality: God speaks to all, not only the already-converted. Isaiah 30:21 carries the guiding-voice claim in its most direct form: God's voice behind the soul saying "This is the way, walk ye in it" — the ongoing, directional, quotidian character of divine speaking that s2 will develop as daily paths and circumstances. The Restoration anchor grounds the worthiness-independence of the source span's qualifying clause. D&C 18:10's "the worth of souls is great in the sight of God" establishes the theological basis for God's unconditional speaking: if every soul carries great worth regardless of its state, God speaks not because the soul has earned hearing but because the soul's worth precedes its worthiness. The "whether we feel worthy or not" qualifier rests on this prior claim.

biblical.text: For when the Gentiles, which have not the law, do by nature the things contained in the law, these, having not the law, are a law unto themselves: Which shew the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience also bearing witness, and their thoughts the mean while accusing or else excusing one another;
biblical.comment: The locus classicus for universal moral conscience. God's law written in every human heart, conscience bearing witness regardless of covenant status. Grounds the "every conscience" universality of the source span: God speaks to all, not only the already-instructed.

biblical.text: And thine ears shall hear a word behind thee, saying, This is the way, walk ye in it, when ye turn to the right hand, and when ye turn to the left.
biblical.comment: The guiding-voice claim in its most direct form — God's voice actively directing the soul's daily path. Grounds "God speaks" as an ongoing directional address, and anticipates s2's "daily paths He knows."

restoration.text: Remember the worth of souls is great in the sight of God;
restoration.comment: The worth-of-souls anchor that grounds the worthiness-independence of God's speaking. God addresses every conscience not because the soul has qualified itself but because its worth before God precedes and exceeds its felt worthiness.

s2.text: He subtly guides each of us through the daily paths He knows, through circumstances He sees, toward a character He is shaping
s2.panel_comment: Where s1 names God's speaking to conscience, s2 names God's active-formation work through the ordinary material of daily life: not crisis intervention but the "subtle" ongoing guidance through paths and circumstances that have been known and seen from God's vantage. The word "subtle" carries theological weight — it names the character of divine guidance as quiet, threading through circumstance rather than overriding it, visible often only in retrospect. "Toward a character He is shaping" adds the teleological claim: God's guidance through circumstances has a destination, and that destination is character. This is the article's sanctification thesis in its most compressed form, naming the Christian life from God's side before s5 names it from the disciple's. The biblical anchors carry the claim in two registers. Jeremiah 29:11 is the Old Testament anchor for the providential-knowledge direction: "I know the thoughts that I think toward you… to give you an expected end" — the personal knowing that grounds "the daily paths He knows, through circumstances He sees." God's guidance is not generic but particular; the prophet's word confirms that the knowing is already active before the disciple perceives it. Philippians 1:6 carries the performing-in-progress claim: God "which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ" — the active continuing grounds "toward a character He is shaping" as God's own ongoing motion in the disciple's life, not a completed state. The Restoration anchor names the specific instrument by which God shapes character through circumstances: Ether 12:27 records God's own words — "I give unto men weakness that they may be humble… then will I make weak things become strong." The circumstance (given weakness) is the appointed shaping instrument; the humility it occasions is the formation mechanism; the strength that follows is the character God is shaping toward. The character-formation is not despite the difficult circumstances but through them.

biblical.text: For I know the thoughts that I think toward you, saith the LORD, thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you an expected end.
biblical.comment: The providential-personal-knowing anchor. God's thoughts toward each soul are particular, peaceful-intentioned, and already active toward a specific end — the "paths He knows, through circumstances He sees" direction in its Old Testament form.

biblical.text: Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ:
biblical.comment: The performing-in-progress anchor. God does not initiate formation and withdraw; He performs it to the end. Grounds "toward a character He is shaping" as God's own continuing, ongoing work.

restoration.text: And if men come unto me I will show unto them their weakness. I give unto men weakness that they may be humble; and my grace is sufficient for all men that humble themselves before me; for if they humble themselves before me, and have faith in me, then will I make weak things become strong unto them.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's most direct anchor for circumstance-as-shaping-instrument. God gives weakness — names the circumstance as divinely appointed — so that the disciple may be humble and then made strong. The character-formation is not despite the difficult circumstances but through them as the appointed instruments.

s3.panel_comment: The article's agency-within-grace affirmation. Coming immediately after s2's providential-formation claim, this three-word sentence guards against a quietism that God's guiding care could otherwise license. The short declarative form is itself the argument: no qualifying clause, no softening. Daily choices matter — not ultimately (grace is not predicated on aggregate performance), but really. The sentence refuses the misreading of s2 that would render the disciple passive because God is already shaping the character. The biblical anchors carry the consequence-weight of moral choice in two registers. Matthew 7:24–25 grounds the doing/not-doing distinction as the decisive variable: the wise man and the foolish man are differentiated by whether they do Christ's sayings — the doing or not-doing determines whether the house stands or falls. Daily choices are the building material. Galatians 6:7–8 establishes the sowing-and-reaping grammar that makes grace not a suspension of moral consequence: "God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap." The verse guards both flanks — against the presumption that sin has no consequence and against the passivism that choice is irrelevant. The Restoration anchor names the same logic in its most direct form of mortal agency: 2 Nephi 2:27 places before every soul the choice between liberty and eternal life or captivity and death. The freedom to choose is the gift the great Mediator's Atonement restored; that choosing is real, ongoing, and consequential.

biblical.text: Therefore whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock: And the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house; and it fell not: for it was founded upon a rock.
biblical.comment: The doing/not-doing contrast that names daily choices as the building material. What the disciple does or fails to do with Christ's words determines the foundation; choices are the construction, and the construction is real.

biblical.text: Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap. For he that soweth to his flesh shall of the flesh reap corruption; but he that soweth to the Spirit shall of the Spirit reap life everlasting.
biblical.comment: The sowing-and-reaping anchor for moral consequence within a grace framework. Daily choices carry genuine consequence; the harvest follows the planting. Guards s3 against the quietism s2's providential care could otherwise license.

restoration.text: Wherefore, men are free according to the flesh; and all things are given them which are expedient unto man. And they are free to choose liberty and eternal life, through the great Mediator of all men, or to choose captivity and death, according to the captivity and power of the devil; for he seeketh that all men might be miserable like unto himself.
restoration.comment: Lehi's most direct teaching on the reality and weight of mortal agency. The freedom to choose is the gift the great Mediator's Atonement restored; that choosing is real, ongoing, and consequential — the Restoration ground for "Our daily choices matter."

s4.text: Grace is not a license to sin; it is a divine trait and power
s4.definition: Grace as the character-attribute and operative power of God — not the suspension of moral accountability, but the divine capacity actively shaping the disciple toward Christ's likeness.
s4.panel_comment: The article's theological centerpiece and its named concept. The sentence moves in two clauses: a negation that clears the most common misreading of grace, and a positive definition that replaces it with a claim of much greater scope. The positive clause carries two nouns — "trait" and "power" — that together name what grace is at two levels: the level of God's character (a trait, something God is) and the level of God's operative work in the disciple's life (a power, something God does). Neither noun alone is sufficient: "trait" without "power" would make grace merely descriptive; "power" without "trait" would make grace a mechanism without a personal source. Together they name grace as what God is and what God does. The negation is grounded in the biblical cluster's direct refutation of antinomianism. Romans 6:1–2 is the apostolic locus classicus: Paul's imagined objector raises the license-to-sin misreading explicitly, and Paul's answer is an unqualified "God forbid." Titus 2:11–12 develops the positive definition — the grace of God "teaching us that, denying ungodliness… we should live soberly, righteously, and godly" — naming grace as itself an active teacher and the ground for the "power" noun of the named concept. Exodus 34:6 grounds the "divine trait" direction with the most direct available anchor: the theophany in which God names His own character attributes — "merciful and gracious" — the Hebrew hannun naming grace as what God is, not merely what God gives. The Restoration anchors carry both directions with characteristic precision. 2 Nephi 25:23 grounds the enabling-power direction distinct from the salvific-source direction at which the same verse was deployed at Article 6 Span 1. Where A6 s1 named grace as the source of salvation's offer, here at A10 s4 the verse grounds the power-direction specifically: grace is the operating capacity that empowers the daily walk, making "after all we can do" a location-clause rather than a merit-threshold. (Reasserted from Article 6 Span 1 in different rhetorical direction. At A6 s1 the verse grounds grace-as-salvific-source — the offer by which salvation comes. Here at A10 s4 the verse grounds grace-as-enabling-power — the operative capacity the daily walk of discipleship runs on.) Moroni 10:32–33 carries both noun-directions: "then is his grace sufficient for you, that by his grace ye may be perfect in Christ" names grace as the sufficient operative power (the "power" noun) while the "by his grace" formulation presupposes grace as God's operative character-trait extended toward the disciple (the "trait" noun). (Reasserted from Article 3 Span 14, Article 6 Span 1, and Article 6 Span 12 in different rhetorical direction. At A3 s14 the passage closed the formation-affirmation; at A6 s1 it grounded grace-as-salvific-source; at A6 s12 it grounded the Spirit's transformative completion of grace. Here at A10 s4 the same passage grounds the named concept's positive definition — the sufficient-and-operative divine power that the "divine trait and power" definition names, foregrounding the power-claim that all prior deployments presupposed but none named as the definition.)

biblical.text: What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid. How shall we, that are dead to sin, live any longer therein?
biblical.comment: The apostolic locus classicus for the grace-not-license negation. Paul's own imagined interlocutor raises exactly the misreading this span refuses; the "God forbid" is the cleanest biblical anchor for the source clause's first half. The passage establishes that death to sin — not continued living in it — is the natural state of the person who has received grace.

biblical.text: For the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men, Teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world;
biblical.comment: Grace as active teacher and formative power — the positive content of the named concept's "power" noun. Grace does not merely acquit; it teaches, denying ungodliness and redirecting toward righteous living. The "teaching us" participle names grace as the operative agent of the disciple's formation.

biblical.text: And the LORD passed by before him, and proclaimed, The LORD, The LORD God, merciful and gracious, longsuffering, and abundant in goodness and truth,
biblical.comment: The theophanic naming of God's own character. "Gracious" (Hebrew hannun) is here a descriptor of what God IS — a divine character-attribute proclaimed by God Himself in self-revelation. The primary biblical anchor for the named concept's "divine trait" noun: grace belongs first to the ontology of God's character.

restoration.text: For we labor diligently to write, to persuade our children, and also our brethren, to believe in Christ, and to be reconciled to God; for we know that it is by grace that we are saved, after all we can do.
restoration.comment: (Reasserted from Article 6 Span 1 in different rhetorical direction. At A6 s1 the verse grounds grace-as-salvific-source — the offer by which salvation comes. Here at A10 s4 the verse grounds grace-as-enabling-power — the operative capacity the daily walk of discipleship runs on, naming "after all we can do" as the location of grace's operation rather than a merit-threshold before grace applies.)

restoration.text: Yea, come unto Christ, and be perfected in him, and deny yourselves of all ungodliness; and if ye shall deny yourselves of all ungodliness, and love God with all your might, mind and strength, then is his grace sufficient for you, that by his grace ye may be perfect in Christ; and if by the grace of God ye are perfect in Christ, ye can in nowise deny the power of God.
restoration.comment: (Reasserted from Article 3 Span 14, Article 6 Span 1, and Article 6 Span 12 in different rhetorical direction. At A3 s14 the passage closed the formation-affirmation; at A6 s1 it grounded grace-as-salvific-source; at A6 s12 it grounded the Spirit's transformative completion of grace. Here at A10 s4 the same passage grounds the named concept's positive definition — the sufficient-and-operative divine power that the "divine trait and power" definition names, foregrounding the power-claim that all prior deployments presupposed but none named as the definition.)
