s5.text: The Christian life is a walk, a maturing, a becoming
s5.panel_comment: The sanctification-as-process affirmation. The three-beat rhythm "a walk, a maturing, a becoming" names the Christian life through its motion rather than its destination. Each noun adds a dimension: "walk" names the directional ongoing nature of the life; "maturing" names the developmental character of the growth — organic, not instantaneous; "becoming" names the unfinished quality — the disciple is not yet what she will be, but is in active motion toward it. The rhythm is itself theological: three nouns of pure process, no static noun of arrival. The biblical anchors carry the process-claim in two forms. Philippians 3:12–14 is the apostolic model: Paul explicitly disavows arrival ("not as though I had already attained, either were already perfect"), names the ongoing press ("I press toward the mark"), and does so from within his mature apostolic experience — not as an excuse for spiritual infancy but as the honest permanent posture of the disciple before Christ. The span's three nouns are Paul's own posture: still walking, still maturing, still becoming. 2 Peter 1:5–8 carries the additive-grace pattern: "add to your faith virtue; and to virtue knowledge… and to knowledge temperance… and to temperance patience" — each addition is a maturing; the whole sequence is the becoming the source span names. The fruitfulness promised in verse 8 is itself a process-claim: it comes through the adding, not despite it. The Restoration anchor carries the same process-pattern in luminous spatial language: D&C 50:24's "that light groweth brighter and brighter until the perfect day" names the Christian life as incremental brightening toward a destination that remains, throughout the journey, a perfect day still coming. The growing brighter is the walk; the brighter and brighter is the maturing; the "until the perfect day" is the becoming's destination. The span's three nouns are the same arc in luminous Restoration language.

biblical.text: Not as though I had already attained, either were already perfect: but I follow after, if that I may apprehend that for which also I am apprehended of Christ Jesus. Brethren, I count not myself to have apprehended: but this one thing I do, forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before, I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.
biblical.comment: The apostolic model of the Christian life as ongoing press rather than arrived state. Paul's explicit disavowal of attainment grounds "a walk, a maturing, a becoming" in the posture of the most mature apostle: the walk is still walking, the becoming is still becoming.

biblical.text: And beside this, giving all diligence, add to your faith virtue; and to virtue knowledge; And to knowledge temperance; and to temperance patience; and to patience godliness; And to godliness brotherly kindness; and to brotherly kindness charity. For if these things be in you, and abound, they make you that ye shall neither be barren nor unfruitful in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ.
biblical.comment: The additive-grace pattern. Each virtue layered on the previous names "a maturing" in its most concrete form; the whole sequence is the becoming. Fruitfulness is the result of the adding — itself a process-claim.

restoration.text: That which is of God is light; and he that receiveth light, and continueth in God, receiveth more light; and that light groweth brighter and brighter until the perfect day.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's most direct image of the Christian life as progressive brightening. Growing brighter is the walk; brighter and brighter is the maturing; "until the perfect day" is the becoming's destination. The span's three nouns are the same arc in luminous Restoration language.

s6.text: We follow the example of our Savior, who went about doing good, and we continue to go about doing good
s6.panel_comment:
The span is the article’s imitatio Christi declaration—named explicitly as following an example, not merely as continuing a tradition or fulfilling an assignment. The phrase “who went about doing good” is drawn verbatim from Acts 10:38, and the span’s structure folds that verbatim phrase into the “We follow the example” frame. The two clauses are parallel in purpose: “We follow the example of our Savior” names the commitment; “we continue to go about doing good” names the ongoing practice. The word “continue” carries the article’s sanctification-as-process register—this is not a one-time resolution but a sustained posture across time, linking forward to s8 (“No soul finishes in a day”) and backward to s5’s walk/maturing/becoming arc.

Acts 10:38’s prior deployments in the cluster trace a Christological arc: at A5 s11 the verse anchors Christ’s own mortal ministry—Peter’s apostolic testimony naming what Christ did, type direct. At A7 s10 the same verse anchors the Holy-Ghost-and-power compound the disciple herself experiences in her daily life—the Spirit enabling the disciple’s conduct in a parallel register to Christ’s. Here at A10 s6 the verse carries its third distinct function: volitional emulation—“We follow the example.” The span does not describe what Christ did (A5) or name what the Spirit enables (A7) but declares the disciple’s conscious choice to adopt Christ’s conduct as her own explicit pattern. (Reasserted from Article 5 Span 11 and Article 7 Span 10 in different rhetorical direction. At A5 s11 the verse anchors the apostolic description of Christ’s own mortal doing-good—the source; at A7 s10 the verse anchors the Spirit’s enabling the disciple’s parallel conduct—the power; here at A10 s6 the verse anchors the disciple’s volitional adoption of Christ’s conduct as her template—the imitation.)

1 Peter 2:21 carries the explicit imitatio Christi imperative that Acts 10:38 implies by example. Peter names both the grounds (“Christ also suffered for us”) and the call (“leaving us an example, that ye should follow his steps”)—the command to imitate is distinct from the act of doing-good, and its presence here completes the span’s logic: not only did Christ go about doing good, but we are called to follow in those steps. 3 Nephi 27:27 grounds the span at the deepest theological level—Christ’s own rhetorical question and answer in Restoration form: “what manner of men ought ye to be? even as I am.” The imitatio is named as the disciple’s telos, not merely her practice.

biblical.text: How God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Ghost and with power: who went about doing good, and healing all that were oppressed of the devil; for God was with him.
biblical.comment: The verbatim source of “who went about doing good” embedded in the source paragraph. (Reasserted from Article 5 Span 11 and Article 7 Span 10 in different rhetorical direction—see panel_comment above. Here the function is volitional emulation: the disciple explicitly naming Christ’s conduct as her adopted pattern.)

biblical.text: For even hereunto were ye called: because Christ also suffered for us, leaving us an example, that ye should follow his steps:
biblical.comment: The explicit imitatio Christi imperative—“leaving us an example, that ye should follow his steps.” Names both the grounds of the call (Christ’s own suffering) and the call itself (follow). First-time cluster deployment.

restoration.text: Therefore, what manner of men ought ye to be? Verily I say unto you, even as I am.
restoration.comment: Christ’s own dominical answer to the imitatio question—the disciple’s pattern is Christ Himself in person. The rhetorical question and answer together name the imitation as the disciple’s telos, not merely her ethical obligation. First-time cluster deployment.

s7.text: whether or not our efforts are authorized, recognized, or rewarded by any institutions or traditions of mortals
s7.panel_comment:
The span is the article’s institutional-independence declaration—the disciple’s service is not predicated on the approval, recognition, or credentialing of any human institution or tradition. The triple structure (“authorized, recognized, or rewarded”) names three distinct institutional functions that the span refuses to make prerequisite: authorization (whether the institution permits the effort), recognition (whether the institution acknowledges it), and reward (whether the institution compensates or validates it). The span does not merely say “we do not need permission”; it refuses all three institutional dependencies simultaneously and in that order—from the most foundational to the most residual.

This claim operates within the article’s theological architecture, not against it. “Institutions or traditions of mortals” names human credentialing and gatekeeping systems specifically; it does not reach God’s own covenants and ordinances, which are A11’s domain. The independence the span names is from human institutional mediation; the disciple’s covenant obligations to God stand on a different and higher footing.

Colossians 3:23–24 carries the “not recognized or rewarded by mortals” direction at the sentence’s theological ground: “as to the Lord, and not unto men.” The service’s address is God; therefore the institution’s non-recognition carries no theological weight. “Of the Lord ye shall receive the reward of the inheritance” names where recognition actually comes from—and it is not from a mortal institution. D&C 58:26–27 grounds the “not authorized” direction with precision: God specifically does not command in all things, and He names self-directed, uninstructed service as the mature expression of agency—“do many things of their own free will, and bring to pass much righteousness; for the power is in them, wherein they are agents unto themselves.” Uninstructed, institutionally-uncredentialed service is not a deficiency to be remedied by authorization; it is precisely what God values in an agent-unto-themselves disciple. Mosiah 2:17 grounds the theological basis that makes institutional mediation irrelevant at the root: service to one’s fellow beings is—already, regardless of institutional framing—service to God directly. No institution adds to this reality; no institution’s non-recognition subtracts from it.

biblical.text: And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men; Knowing that of the Lord ye shall receive the reward of the inheritance: for ye serve the Lord Christ.
biblical.comment: The “not unto men” anchor. The service’s address is God; institutional non-recognition carries no weight because the reward comes from the one whose recognition matters—and that one is not a mortal institution. First-time cluster deployment.

restoration.text: For behold, it is not meet that I should command in all things; for he that is compelled in all things, the same is a slothful and not a wise servant; wherefore he receiveth no reward. Verily I say, men should be earnestly engaged in a good cause, and do many things of their own free will, and bring to pass much righteousness; For the power is in them, wherein they are agents unto themselves.
restoration.comment: The “not authorized” anchor. God specifically values uninstructed, self-directed service—the agent-unto-themselves frame makes doing-good without institutional authorization not merely tolerated but the mature expression of agency that God commends. First-time cluster deployment.

restoration.text: And behold, I tell you these things that ye may learn wisdom; that ye may learn that when ye are in the service of your fellow beings ye are only in the service of your God.
restoration.comment: The theological ground that makes institutional mediation irrelevant at the root: the service is rendered directly to God regardless of which human channel it flows through. No institution adds to or subtracts from this reality. First-time cluster deployment.

s8.text: No soul finishes in a day
s8.panel_comment:
The span is the article’s pastoral patience word—an unconditional declaration directed at the soul who measures her standing by whether her formation is complete. The sentence’s brevity is its argument: no qualifying clause, no condition, no exhortation. It simply names the reality of mortal becoming as an article of grace. Positioned between s7’s service-independence declaration and s9’s reach-of-grace assurance, s8 occupies the pastoral fulcrum of ¶1’s closing movement—the soul who has not finished (s8) is the soul who remains within His reach (s9). The two sentences are the article’s paired pastoral couplet.

The claim links structurally to s2’s “toward a character He is shaping” (God is still shaping) and to s5’s “a walk, a maturing, a becoming” (the Christian life is constitutively incomplete). What s2 names from God’s side and s5 names from the disciple’s side, s8 names as pastoral permission: the formation is not yet done, and that is not a failure.

Ephesians 4:13–15 names the destination-still-ahead through Paul’s “till we all come” frame—maturity defined as a future arrival, with the present stage of the journey being one of active growth (“may grow up into him in all things”). The risk Paul names in verse 14—being “tossed to and fro”—identifies what happens when the incompleteness of the journey is exploited as vulnerability. S8’s pastoral word guards this vulnerability not by accelerating the completion but by normalizing the incompleteness: the journey is not yet finished, and that is the nature of the journey. Alma 32:42 carries the temporal-patience idiom directly and specifically: “by and by ye shall pluck the fruit thereof.” The fruit is certain and precious, but it comes in its own time—diligence, faith, and patience are the present-tense posture, not the fruit itself. “By and by” is the Restoration’s patience idiom for this same pastoral claim: not yet, but surely, and the not-yet is not condemnation.

biblical.text: Till we all come in the unity of the faith, and of the knowledge of the Son of God, unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ: That we henceforth be no more children, tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the sleight of men, and cunning craftiness, whereby they lie in wait to deceive; But speaking the truth in love, may grow up into him in all things, which is the head, even Christ:
biblical.comment: Maturity named as a future “till we all come” arrival—the destination is ahead, the present stage is growth. The incompleteness is structural, not pathological; Paul’s “tossed to and fro” risk names what happens when incompleteness becomes vulnerability rather than pastoral permission. First-time cluster deployment.

restoration.text: And because of your diligence and your faith and your patience with the word in nourishing it, that it may take root in you, behold, by and by ye shall pluck the fruit thereof, which is most precious, which is sweet above all that is sweet, and which is white above all that is white, yea, and pure above all that is pure; and ye shall feast upon this fruit even until ye are filled, that ye hunger not, neither shall ye thirst.
restoration.comment: The Restoration’s patience idiom for formation-incompleteness: “by and by ye shall pluck the fruit.” The fruit is coming and is precious; the present tense is diligence, faith, and patience in nourishing—not yet the fruit. “By and by” names the same temporal claim s8 makes without apology. First-time cluster deployment.

s9.text: No soul is beyond His reach
s9.panel_comment:
The span is the article’s closing pastoral assurance—the declaration that no soul, however distant, however self-disqualifying, lies outside the range of God’s reaching toward her. It pairs with s8 as ¶1’s closing couplet: the soul who has not finished (s8) is the soul who is still within His reach (s9). Together the two sentences address the discouraged soul at the point where discouragement most commonly calcifies into despair—the conviction that one’s own incompleteness or unworthiness has finally exceeded what grace can cover.

The “reach” language names an active direction: God reaching toward the soul, not merely waiting for the soul to arrive. This active movement distinguishes the span from the cluster’s prior grace-assurance language, which has generally operated in the passive register of reception.

Isaiah 59:1 carries the capability claim from the divine side in negation form: the LORD’s hand is not shortened, His ear not too heavy. The verse refutes the self-disqualifying logic at its premise—the soul’s typical fear is that God’s patience has run out, that His reach no longer extends to where she is. Isaiah’s double negation answers that fear directly: not shortened, not heavy. The rhetorical form mirrors the span’s own negation, “No soul is beyond His reach,” giving the verse a structural fit that exceeds proof-text deployment. Romans 8:38–39 grounds the separability-impossibility from the other direction: nothing can separate the soul from the love of God in Christ Jesus. Paul’s exhaustive catalog—death, life, angels, principalities, powers, present things, future things, height, depth—names every force the soul might invoke as the barrier that placed her beyond reach, and refuses each one. The soul who fears herself beyond His reach typically has one of Paul’s listed forces in mind; the list names them all and refuses them all.

2 Nephi 26:33 has appeared three times in the cluster before this deployment. At A1 s12, the verse anchored the soteriological negation against gatekeeping—no soul barred from salvation for lacking perfect understanding. At A8 s1 and A8 s2, the same verse anchored two ecclesial-universality directions within A8’s body-of-Christ architecture. All three prior uses operated in corporate registers: the soteriological claim (A1), the ecclesial-scope claim (A8 s1), the ecclesial-reception claim (A8 s2). Here at A10 s9 the verse carries its fourth distinct function: the pastoral-personal reach-of-grace word—not a corporate or institutional claim but a declaration addressed to the individual soul who has placed herself, in her own estimation, beyond what God’s reach covers. “He denieth none that come unto him” and “all are alike unto God” together ground the pastoral assurance that the self-disqualifying soul’s own estimation is not the measure. (Reasserted from Article 1 Span 12, Article 8 Span 1, and Article 8 Span 2 in different rhetorical direction. At A1 s12 the verse anchors the soteriological negation against gatekeeping; at A8 s1 and A8 s2 the verse grounds ecclesial-universality scope within A8’s body-of-Christ architecture. Here at A10 s9 the verse grounds the pastoral-personal assurance directed at the self-disqualifying individual soul—the reader whose own conscience has placed her beyond what she believes His reach covers.)

biblical.text: Behold, the LORD’S hand is not shortened, that it cannot save; neither his ear heavy, that it cannot hear:
biblical.comment: The capability-negation anchor—God’s hand is not too short, His ear not too heavy. Refutes the self-disqualifying premise that God’s reach no longer extends to where the soul is. The double negation mirrors the span’s own negation form. First-time cluster deployment.

biblical.text: For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, Nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.
biblical.comment: The exhaustive separability-impossibility anchor. Every force the soul might name as the barrier that placed her beyond reach is listed and refused. The comprehensiveness of Paul’s catalog is itself the pastoral argument—no exception remains. First-time cluster deployment.

restoration.text: For none of these iniquities come of the Lord; for he doeth that which is good among the children of men; and he doeth nothing save it be plain unto the children of men; and he inviteth all to come unto him and partake of his goodness; and he denieth none that come unto him, black and white, bond and free, male and female; and he remembereth the heathen; and all are alike unto God, both Jew and Gentile.
restoration.comment: (Reasserted from Article 1 Span 12, Article 8 Span 1, and Article 8 Span 2 in different rhetorical direction. At A1 s12 the verse anchors the soteriological negation against gatekeeping; at A8 s1 and A8 s2 the verse grounds ecclesial-universality scope. Here at A10 s9 the verse grounds the pastoral-personal assurance directed at the self-disqualifying individual soul: “he denieth none that come unto him” and “all are alike unto God” together name that the soul’s own estimation is not the measure of His reach.)

s10.text: We call to repentance anyone who would think to manage or restrict the grace of God toward any of His children
s10.panel_comment: The paragraph opens with a prophetic summons to repentance — not addressed to unbelievers or outsiders but to those within religious communities who have appointed themselves gatekeepers of divine grace. “Manage or restrict the grace of God” names the sin with theological precision: to restrict grace is to assert a position God has never granted to any mortal. The two biblical anchors carry the refusal in different registers. Galatians 2:21’s “I do not frustrate the grace of God” (Greek: atheteo — to set aside, render void) grounds the impossibility of the gatekeeper’s claim: the one who restricts grace has placed herself in the position of voiding what God extends — the theological absurdity of the project is Paul’s point. Matthew 23:13 names the action’s practical consequence: “ye shut up the kingdom of heaven against men.” The Pharisee is not merely wrong in doctrine; she has made herself the door and locked it. The Restoration anchor grounds the scope of “any of His children” with doctrinal precision. Moroni 8:9 and 8:12 establish that grace extends to all God’s children without prerequisite — denying this is explicitly named “solemn mockery before God” and implies “a partial God.” The one who restricts grace has not only presumed to manage God; she has attributed to Him a partiality He disowns.

biblical.text: But woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye shut up the kingdom of heaven against men: for ye neither go in yourselves, neither suffer ye them that are entering to go in.
biblical.comment: The paradigmatic gatekeeping image — the gatekeeper has made herself the door and locked it. Christ’s own first woe: she shuts up the kingdom not only to others but enters not herself. First-time cluster deployment.

biblical.text: I do not frustrate the grace of God: for if righteousness come by the law, then Christ is dead in vain.
biblical.comment: The theological absurdity of restricting grace: atheteo — to set aside, render void — names the gatekeeper’s action as attempting to void what God extends. “Then Christ is dead in vain” names the implication of her project. First-time cluster deployment.

restoration.text: And after this manner did the Holy Ghost manifest the word of God unto me; wherefore, my beloved son, I know that it is solemn mockery before God, that ye should baptize little children.
restoration.comment: “Solemn mockery before God” — the gravity of restricting grace from God’s children without warrant. First-time cluster deployment.

restoration.text: But little children are alive in Christ, even from the foundation of the world; if not so, God is a partial God, and also a changeable God, and a respecter to persons; for how many little children have died without baptism!
restoration.comment: The doctrinal consequence of grace-restriction named directly: to limit grace to the credentialed is to attribute partiality to God. “Any of His children” in the source span rests on this ground — grace extends to all because any other position makes God a respecter of persons. First-time cluster deployment.

s11.text: Gatekeeping of salvation and other modern woes of the Pharisees will not be tolerated within this interfaith community
s11.panel_comment: The source paragraph’s second sentence names the pattern and makes the community standard explicit. The word “woes” is deliberate allusion to Matthew 23’s woe-oracles — the source paragraph consciously inhabits that prophetic register, naming gatekeeping not as mere disagreement but as a sin Christ addressed in its harshest form. “Will not be tolerated” is the institutional correlate: not only is the practice rebuked prophetically at s10, but it is named as incompatible with membership in this community. The two biblical anchors carry the Pharisee-woes framing from within. Matthew 23:4 names the weight the gatekeeper imposes — grievous burdens laid on others that she does not herself bear — the burden-making direction. Matthew 23:23 names the priority inversion: meticulous enforcement of secondary matters while “omitting the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy, and faith” — the priority-inverting direction. Both patterns are recognizable in “gatekeeping of salvation”: the burden-imposing and priority-inverting directions together constitute the Pharisee signature being named. The Restoration anchor carries the institutional consequence of the gatekeeping disposition. D&C 121:37’s “exercise control or dominion or compulsion upon the souls of the children of men, in any degree of unrighteousness” names the precise mechanism by which salvific gatekeeping operates — compulsion and control — and names God’s response: “the heavens withdraw themselves; the Spirit of the Lord is grieved.” The gatekeeper does not merely harm the souls she restricts; she extinguishes her own spiritual authority in the act.

biblical.text: For they bind heavy burdens and grievous to be borne, and lay them on men's shoulders; but they themselves will not move them with one of their fingers.
biblical.comment: The burden-making direction: grievous requirements imposed on others that the imposer does not carry. The asymmetry of burden is the sign of gatekeeping’s structural injustice. First-time cluster deployment.

biblical.text: Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye pay tithe of mint and anise and cummin, and have omitted the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy, and faith: these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone.
biblical.comment: The priority-inversion direction: minor matters enforced with precision while judgment, mercy, and faith are omitted. Secondary doctrinal criteria replacing mercy and faith as the test of belonging is precisely the “gatekeeping of salvation” pattern. First-time cluster deployment.

restoration.text: That they may be conferred upon us, it is true; but when we undertake to cover our sins, or to gratify our pride, our vain ambition, or to exercise control or dominion or compulsion upon the souls of the children of men, in any degree of unrighteousness, behold, the heavens withdraw themselves; the Spirit of the Lord is grieved; and when it is withdrawn, Amen to the priesthood or the authority of that man.
restoration.comment: “Exercise control or dominion or compulsion upon the souls of the children of men” — the precise language for what salvific gatekeeping performs. God’s response is categorical: the heavens withdraw, the Spirit is grieved, the authority of the gatekeeper ends. First-time cluster deployment.

s12.text: do not dare to condemn anyone over differences in doctrine or theology
s12.panel_comment: The exhortation “do not dare to condemn” narrows the general gatekeeping refusal of s10–s11 into a specific community practice: condemnation directed at persons whose doctrinal conclusions differ from one’s own. The word “dare” carries prophetic weight — not a measured request but a warning, the same register as s10’s summons to repentance. Romans 2:1 is the apostolic locus classicus for the self-condemnation logic: “wherein thou judgest another, thou condemnest thyself; for thou that judgest doest the same things.” The doctrinal condemner has not escaped the scrutiny she has turned on another — she has placed herself under it. The “dare” is a dare because the one who condemns takes the greater risk. First-time cluster deployment. 1 Corinthians 4:3–4 carries the argument from a different direction — not the condemnation’s irony but its improper jurisdiction: “with me it is a very small thing that I should be judged of you, or of man’s judgment... he that judgeth me is the Lord.” Human condemnation over doctrinal difference is not merely harsh; it is a category error. The judgment seat belongs to the Lord; the community member who condemns over doctrine has presumed a position she has not been given. First-time cluster deployment. D&C 64:9–10 grounds the self-condemnation logic in explicit community terms: “he that forgiveth not his brother his trespasses standeth condemned before the Lord; for there remaineth in him the greater sin.” The community member who withholds forgiveness of doctrinal difference does not occupy the position of the righteous judge; she occupies the position of the one in whom the greater sin remains. “Of you it is required to forgive all men” names the community practice as unconditional. First-time cluster deployment.

biblical.text: Therefore thou art inexcusable, O man, whosoever thou art that judgest: for wherein thou judgest another, thou condemnest thyself; for thou that judgest doest the same things.
biblical.comment: The self-condemnation irony: the doctrinal condemner places herself under the very scrutiny she exercises. The “dare” register of the source span rests on this Pauline logic — condemning is a dare because the condemner takes the greater risk. First-time cluster deployment.

biblical.text: But with me it is a very small thing that I should be judged of you, or of man's judgment: yea, I judge not mine own self. For I know nothing by myself; yet am I not hereby justified: but he that judgeth me is the Lord.
biblical.comment: The improper-jurisdiction argument: human doctrinal condemnation is a category error. The judgment seat belongs to the Lord; the community member who condemns over doctrine has presumed a position she has not been given. First-time cluster deployment.

restoration.text: Wherefore, I say unto you, that ye ought to forgive one another; for he that forgiveth not his brother his trespasses standeth condemned before the Lord; for there remaineth in him the greater sin. I, the Lord, will forgive whom I will forgive, but of you it is required to forgive all men.
restoration.comment: The community-practice correlate of s12’s self-condemnation logic: withholding forgiveness of doctrinal difference places the withholder in the position of the condemned, in whom the greater sin remains. First-time cluster deployment.

s13.text: Every soul who seeks Christ is under His protection. Every one of them is precious to Him.
s13.panel_comment: The two sentences form the theological ground for the millstone warning at s14. The first sentence (“under His protection”) explains the severity of the warning before it is quoted: Christ’s fierce response is rooted here. The second sentence (“precious to Him”) names the affective reality beneath the protective claim — Christ does not guard what is merely useful but what is precious. The two sentences are inseparable: the protection issues from the preciousness. Matthew 18:12–14 anchors “under His protection” in the Father’s own declared will — “it is not the will of your Father which is in heaven, that one of these little ones should perish.” The protection is not conditional on doctrinal accuracy or institutional standing; the Father’s will is that none be lost. The verse immediately precedes Matthew 18:6 in the same discourse, making s13 and s14 a sequential anchoring of the same Matthean movement. Isaiah 43:4 grounds “precious to Him” in its most direct Old Testament form: “thou wast precious in my sight... and I have loved thee.” The preciousness is prior to the seeking — a condition that has always been true — which is why even the soul who barely turns toward Christ falls under the protection s13 names. D&C 18:10 grounds the “precious to Him” claim in the Restoration’s root statement of soul-worth. (Reasserted from A10 s1 in different rhetorical direction. At s1 the verse grounds the worthiness-independence of God’s speaking — God addresses every conscience because its worth precedes its felt worthiness. Here at s13 the same anchor grounds the intrinsic worth that makes every seeking soul precious to Christ — the preciousness that explains both the Shepherd’s protective response of s13 and the severity of the millstone warning at s14.) D&C 18:13’s “how great is his joy in the soul that repenteth” adds the affective register the “precious” noun carries: joy is the measure of preciousness, and it is great. First-time cluster deployment.

biblical.text: How think ye? if a man have an hundred sheep, and one of them be gone astray, doth he not leave the ninety and nine, and goeth into the mountains, and seeketh that which is gone astray? And if so be that he find it, verily I say unto you, he rejoiceth more of that sheep, than of the ninety and nine which went not astray. Even so it is not the will of your Father which is in heaven, that one of these little ones should perish.
biblical.comment: The Father’s own will made explicit: not one of these little ones should perish. The protection of s13 is a declared divine will, not a disposition. Immediately precedes Matthew 18:6 in the same discourse — s13 and s14 anchor sequential verses of the same Matthean movement. First-time cluster deployment.

biblical.text: Since thou wast precious in my sight, thou hast been honourable, and I have loved thee: therefore will I give men for thee, and people for thy life.
biblical.comment: “Since thou wast precious” — the preciousness as a prior, durable condition, not an earned status. Every seeking soul carries this prior preciousness that explains why the Shepherd leaves the ninety-nine. First-time cluster deployment.

restoration.text: Remember the worth of souls is great in the sight of God;
restoration.comment: (Reasserted from A10 s1 in different rhetorical direction. At s1 the verse grounds the worthiness-independence of God’s speaking — God addresses every conscience because its worth precedes its felt worthiness. Here at s13 the same anchor grounds the intrinsic worth that makes every seeking soul “precious to Him” — the preciousness that explains both the Shepherd’s protective response of s13 and the severity of the millstone warning at s14.)

restoration.text: And how great is his joy in the soul that repenteth!
restoration.comment: The affective register of “precious to Him” — joy as the measure of preciousness. The greatness of Christ’s joy names the depth of relational investment that makes the protection of s13 intelligible. First-time cluster deployment.

s14.text: Whoso shall offend one of these little ones which believe in me, it were better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck, and that he were drowned in the depth of the sea
s14.panel_comment: The span anchors the longest direct quotation in the apparatus — the millstone warning in its verbatim form. The source paragraph names Christ’s action in speaking this as an expression of “His fierce protective nature over all who seek Him.” The word “fierce” is the source paragraph’s own interpretive frame: not a correction only, but a fierce expression of the same protective love that made every seeking soul precious to Him at s13. The two clauses carry distinct weight. “It were better for him” is a comparative: physical death is preferable to becoming the obstacle between a seeking soul and her Shepherd. “Drowned in the depth of the sea” is the absolute: the depth of the sea is not a recoverable position — it names the gravity of the harm in spatial and final terms. Together the clauses name the warning as the proportional consequence of making oneself the instrument by which a seeking soul is turned from Christ. Matthew 18:10 is the companion verse in the same discourse: “Take heed that ye despise not one of these little ones; for I say unto you, That in heaven their angels do always behold the face of my Father.” The angelic-beholding clause names the status of the little ones before God — they are represented at the Father’s face — which is why to offend them is to offend what the Father holds. The Restoration anchor grounds Christ’s fierce protection in its most direct narrative form. 3 Nephi 17:21–22 records Christ’s weeping over and blessing of the little children — the scene in which His own emotional response to the vulnerable is most fully visible. “He wept... Behold your little ones.” The source paragraph’s “fierce protective nature” is not contradiction to this tenderness; it is its consequence. What Christ weeps over, He will protect at the cost named in the warning.

biblical.text: But whoso shall offend one of these little ones which believe in me, it were better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck, and that he were drowned in the depth of the sea.
biblical.comment: The primary direct-type anchor — the verbatim quotation in the source paragraph. Christ’s own words in the discourse on the little ones (Matthew 18:1–14). First-time cluster deployment.

biblical.text: Take heed that ye despise not one of these little ones; for I say unto you, That in heaven their angels do always behold the face of my Father which is in heaven.
biblical.comment: The companion verse: “despise not” as the positive counterpart to the millstone warning’s negative. The angelic representation at the Father’s face names the standing of the little ones — they are not negligible but represented at the highest court. First-time cluster deployment.

restoration.text: And when he had done this he wept again; And he spake unto the multitude, and said unto them: Behold your little ones. And as they looked to behold they cast their eyes towards heaven, and they saw the heavens open, and they saw angels descending out of heaven as it were in the midst of fire; and they came down and encircled those little ones about, and they were encircled about with fire; and the angels did minister unto them.
restoration.comment: Christ’s weeping, His command to behold the little ones, and the angelic encircling that follows — the Restoration’s most concentrated image of fierce protective tenderness toward the vulnerable. What He weeps over, heaven confirms with fire. First-time cluster deployment.

s15.text: Deal gently with the ignorant and misguided
s15.panel_comment: The span covers the first of two direct-quotation community standards named in ¶2’s closing movement. The source paragraph introduces both with “The standards for this interfaith community?” — distinguishing them from the warning of s14 as governing norms rather than prophetic rebukes. Translation note: the source paragraph’s rendering (“deal gently with the ignorant and misguided”) follows a modern translation (ESV/NRSV); the KJV text of Hebrews 5:2 reads “Who can have compassion on the ignorant, and on them that are out of the way.” Both carry the same theological content. This is the first instance in the apparatus of the source paragraph quoting non-KJV translation; the KJV text is carried in the anchor’s text field. Hebrews 5:2’s original context is the high priest who “can have compassion on the ignorant, and on them that are out of the way; for that he himself also is compassed with infirmity” — the basis of gentleness is shared vulnerability, not superiority. The source paragraph lifts the standard from the high priest’s own character and applies it as the community’s governing norm: the same compassion the high priest is called to exercise toward the doctrinally ignorant and morally wandering is the community’s posture toward every soul in those conditions. 2 Timothy 2:24–25 carries the standard in its directive form: “the servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient, In meekness instructing those that oppose themselves.” The “not strive” qualifier anticipates s16’s “without quarreling” — the two Pauline passages form the governing complementary pair. D&C 121:41–42 makes the gentleness standard institutional in Restoration theology: “No power or influence can or ought to be maintained... only by persuasion, by long-suffering, by gentleness and meekness, and by love unfeigned; By kindness, and pure knowledge.” These are not pastoral recommendations; they are the constitutional constraints on all legitimate spiritual authority. First-time cluster deployment.

biblical.text: Who can have compassion on the ignorant, and on them that are out of the way; for that he himself also is compassed with infirmity;
biblical.comment: The direct-type anchor for the quoted phrase. Compassion grounded in shared vulnerability — the high priest’s own compassed infirmity, not superiority, is the basis of gentleness. Note: source paragraph quotes ESV/NRSV; KJV text carried here. First-time cluster deployment.

biblical.text: And the servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient, In meekness instructing those that oppose themselves; if God peradventure will give them repentance to the acknowledging of the truth;
biblical.comment: “Must not strive... gentle... patient... in meekness” as the directive form of the community standard. The “not strive” qualifier links forward to s16’s “without quarreling.” First-time cluster deployment.

restoration.text: No power or influence can or ought to be maintained by virtue of the priesthood, only by persuasion, by long-suffering, by gentleness and meekness, and by love unfeigned; By kindness, and pure knowledge, which shall greatly enlarge the soul without hypocrisy, and without guile—
restoration.comment: The constitutional constraint on spiritual authority in Restoration theology: gentleness and meekness are the only legitimate instruments. The community standard of s15 is D&C 121’s governance discipline applied to interfaith reception. First-time cluster deployment.

s16.text: accept the one whose faith is weak, without quarreling over disputable matters
s16.panel_comment: The span covers the paragraph’s second community standard — a direct quotation of Romans 14:1 named explicitly as the governing norm of reception within this interfaith community. As a direct-type anchor on a verbatim quotation in the source paragraph, Romans 14:1 cannot be substituted; the verse is the source. This is the verse’s fifth deployment in the cluster; the rhetorical-divergence audit is accordingly rigorous. The four prior functions: at A1 s2 the verse grounded the epistemic-welcome posture — receiving the believer whose understanding is incomplete, as the behavioral implication of merognosis; at A1 s11 the same direction recurred in the article’s second merognosis-application context; at A2 s7 the verse carried the doctrinal-restraint direction within the corporate-restraint architecture; at A3 s6 the verse was reasserted in the merognosis-in-context pattern. All four prior deployments operated in the epistemic-posture register: Romans 14:1 as the behavioral implication of recognizing that we all see through a glass darkly. Here at A10 s16 the verse functions in a distinct register: community-rule application. The source paragraph does not deploy Romans 14:1 as an epistemic-posture implication; it quotes it as a governing norm — “the standards for this interfaith community.” The shift is from posture to law, from implication to explicit standard. The verse is no longer evidence for epistemic humility; it is the rule the community is announced to operate by. (Reasserted from Article 1 Spans 2 and 11, Article 2 Span 7, and Article 3 Span 6, in different rhetorical direction. At A1 s2 and s11 the verse grounds the epistemic-welcome posture as the behavioral implication of merognosis; at A2 s7 and A3 s6 the same posture is carried in doctrinal-restraint register. Here at A10 s16 the verse functions as an explicit community standard — not as the implication of an epistemic posture but as the rule the article announces the interfaith community to operate by. The same Pauline instruction shifts from epistemology to governance.) Moroni 6:4 grounds the receiving-and-nurturing practice that s16’s acceptance standard makes concrete in Restoration ecclesial form — the community’s ongoing nourishment of members “by the good word of God,” regardless of their present stage, “relying alone upon the merits of Christ.” First-time cluster deployment.

biblical.text: Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations.
biblical.comment: (Reasserted from Article 1 Spans 2 and 11, Article 2 Span 7, and Article 3 Span 6, in different rhetorical direction — see panel_comment. Here the verse is directly quoted in the source paragraph as an explicit community standard, not deployed as the implication of an epistemic posture. The shift is from posture to governance.)

restoration.text: And after they had been received unto baptism, and were wrought upon and cleansed by the power of the Holy Ghost, they were numbered among the people of the church of Christ; and their names were taken, that they might be remembered and nourished by the good word of God, to keep them in the right way, to keep them continually watchful unto prayer, relying alone upon the merits of Christ, who was the author and the finisher of their faith.
restoration.comment: The Restoration’s own reception practice: those received are remembered, nourished by the word of God, and supported in relying on the merits of Christ — not subjected to doctrinal inspection. First-time cluster deployment.

s17.text: do not stand between the Shepherd and His lambs
s17.panel_comment: The paragraph’s closing sentence is the article’s prophetic warning in its most compressed spatial form — five words that name the sin by what it does to the space between the Shepherd and those He moves toward. The image does not name the gatekeeper’s motive or doctrinal position; it names her location. She has placed herself between. John 10:11–15 provides the Good Shepherd teaching that gives s17 its Christological ground: the shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep, in contrast to the hireling who flees when the wolf comes because the sheep are not his own. The gatekeeper of ¶2 occupies a third position — she has not merely abandoned the sheep to the wolf but has positioned herself as the door the sheep must pass through and is refusing passage. Ezekiel 34:10 grounds the divine response: “I will require my flock at their hand... for I will deliver my flock from their mouth.” God does not petition those who stand between Him and His lambs; He delivers the flock from them. The judgment is categorical and terminal. Jacob 1:19’s Restoration anchor names the accountability of the shepherd-role from the faithful side, which inverts exactly to the gatekeeper’s situation: “taking upon us the responsibility, answering the sins of the people upon our own heads if we did not teach them the word of God with all diligence... their blood might not come upon our garments.” The faithful shepherd answers to God for failing to bring the lambs. The gatekeeper of s17 answers to God for keeping them from the Shepherd who was already moving toward them. The weight of accountability runs in both directions. 3 Nephi 18:32 grounds the community’s opposite vocation: “ye shall not cast him out from among you, but ye shall minister unto him and shall pray for him unto the Father, in my name.” Not obstruction but ministration; not standing between but bringing before the Father in Christ’s name.

biblical.text: I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep. But he that is an hireling, and not the shepherd, whose own the sheep are not, seeth the wolf coming, and leaveth the sheep, and fleeth: and the wolf catcheth them, and scattereth the sheep. The hireling fleeth, because he is an hireling, and careth not for the sheep. I am the good shepherd, and know my sheep, and am known of mine. As the Father knoweth me, even so know I the Father: and I lay down my life for the sheep.
biblical.comment: The Good Shepherd teaching that gives s17 its Christological ground. The gatekeeper of ¶2 occupies a third position beyond the shepherd/hireling contrast — she has not abandoned the sheep but has positioned herself as the obstructing door. “Do not stand between” is the spatial naming of this third position. First-time cluster deployment.

biblical.text: Thus saith the Lord GOD; Behold, I am against the shepherds; and I will require my flock at their hand, and cause them to cease from feeding the flock; neither shall the shepherds feed themselves any more; for I will deliver my flock from their mouth, that they may not be meat for them.
biblical.comment: “I will deliver my flock from their mouth” — God’s categorical response to those positioned between Him and His sheep. Not a warning but a declaration: He will deliver them. First-time cluster deployment.

restoration.text: And we did magnify our office unto the Lord, taking upon us the responsibility, answering the sins of the people upon our own heads if we did not teach them the word of God with all diligence; wherefore, by laboring with our might their blood might not come upon our garments; otherwise their blood would come upon our garments, and we would not be found spotless at the last day.
restoration.comment: The faithful shepherd’s accountability inverted: Jacob takes responsibility for failing to bring the people to God; the gatekeeper of s17 takes responsibility for keeping them from the Shepherd who was moving toward them. First-time cluster deployment.

restoration.text: Nevertheless, ye shall not cast him out from among you, but ye shall minister unto him and shall pray for him unto the Father, in my name; and if it so be that he repenteth and is baptized in my name, then shall ye receive him, and shall minister unto him of my flesh and blood.
restoration.comment: The community’s opposite vocation — not to stand between but to minister, not obstruction but bringing before the Father in Christ’s name. The calling is the exact inversion of the gatekeeping ¶2 rebukes. First-time cluster deployment.

s18.text: We exhort all souls in the name of Jesus Christ
s18.panel_comment: The span anchors the authority frame that governs all of ¶2’s exhortation — “in the name of Jesus Christ” is not incidental phrasing but the claim that the paragraph’s prophetic address is itself a Christological act. The exhortation that follows at s12 (“do not dare to condemn anyone over differences in doctrine or theology”) is issued in Christ’s name; the authority behind ¶2’s sharp language is Christ’s own. Acts 2:38, 40 provides the NT paradigm: Peter exhorts “in the name of Jesus Christ” as the authoritative form of apostolic witness, and “with many other words did he testify and exhort them” — the “in the name of” frame names the source of the address, not merely its subject. Colossians 3:17 grounds the principle universally: “whatsoever ye do in word or deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus” — the name of Christ is the governing frame for all speech-acts of the Christian disciple, not only formal proclamation. Moroni 10:4 carries the Restoration’s own exhortation-in-Christ’s-name pattern: “I would exhort you that ye would ask God, the Eternal Father, in the name of Christ” — Moroni addresses “all” who read and grounds the exhortation in Christ’s name as the proper address. 3 Nephi 27:5–7 grounds the “in my name” frame as Christ’s own definitive teaching: “ye must take upon you the name of Christ... whatsoever ye shall do, ye shall do it in my name.” All action taken in His name participates in the authority He extends; the exhortation of ¶2 operates within this authority, not apart from it.

biblical.text: Then Peter said unto them, Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost... And with many other words did he testify and exhort them, saying, Save yourselves from this untoward generation.
biblical.comment: The NT paradigm of exhortation in the name of Jesus Christ. Peter’s “in the name of Jesus Christ” names the authority frame; “many other words... testify and exhort” names the exhortatory act within that frame. Closest biblical parallel to the source span. First-time cluster deployment.

biblical.text: And whatsoever ye do in word or deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God and the Father by him.
biblical.comment: The universal principle: the name of Christ is the governing frame for all word and deed, not only formal proclamation. Grounds “in the name of Jesus Christ” as the comprehensive authority claim beneath ¶2’s exhortation. First-time cluster deployment.

restoration.text: And when ye shall receive these things, I would exhort you that ye would ask God, the Eternal Father, in the name of Christ, if these things are not true; and if ye shall ask with a sincere heart, with real intent, having faith in Christ, he will manifest the truth of it unto you, by the power of the Holy Ghost.
restoration.comment: The Restoration’s own exhortation-in-Christ’s-name pattern. Moroni addresses all souls who read and grounds his exhortation in Christ’s name as the proper frame — the same pattern the source span employs. First-time cluster deployment.

restoration.text: Have they not read the scriptures, which say ye must take upon you the name of Christ, which is my name? For by this name shall ye be called at the last day; And whoso taketh upon him my name, and endureth to the end, the same shall be saved at the last day. Therefore, whatsoever ye shall do, ye shall do it in my name; therefore ye shall call the church in my name; and ye shall call upon the Father in my name that he will bless the church for my sake.
restoration.comment: Christ’s own definitive teaching on acting in His name as the governing frame: “whatsoever ye shall do, ye shall do it in my name.” The authority the source span claims — exhorting in Christ’s name — is the direct application of Christ’s own command. First-time cluster deployment.

s19.text: Christ expressed His fierce protective nature over all who seek Him
s19.panel_comment: The span is the interpretive key to the millstone warning at s14 — before Christ’s words are quoted, their emotional and theological character is named: “fierce protective nature.” The source paragraph’s choice of “fierce” refuses the sentimentalization of Christ’s love; what follows (the millstone warning) is not a lapse into severity but the natural expression of the same love that makes every seeking soul precious at s13. Exodus 34:14 grounds “fierce protective nature” at the level of divine character: “the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God.” The Hebrew qanna names not petulant possessiveness but the intensity of covenantal love — God’s fierceness is what fierce love looks like when what is precious is threatened. “Whose name is Jealous” makes the fierceness definitional, not incidental; the source span names Christ’s protective fierceness as a nature, not a mood. John 2:17 grounds the pattern in Christ’s own mortal action: “The zeal of thine house hath eaten me up.” The disciples remembered this verse after the temple-cleansing — Christ’s fierce action was recognized as the expression of consuming zeal for what is sacred. The millstone warning is the same zeal expressed in speech: what He weeps over (3 Nephi 17:21–22 at s14), He also speaks fiercely for. D&C 122:4 carries the Restoration’s own fierce-protection idiom: “thy voice shall be more terrible in the midst of thine enemies than the fierce lion, because of thy righteousness; and thy God shall stand by thee forever and ever.” The compound claim — terrible voice + God standing by — grounds both the fierceness (more terrible than a lion) and the standing-by (the protective presence) that the source span names in compound form.

biblical.text: For thou shalt worship no other god: for the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God:
biblical.comment: “Whose name is Jealous” — the fierceness of divine protective love named at the level of divine character, not temperament. The qanna nature is covenantal: God’s fierceness is proportional to the preciousness of what He protects. Grounds “fierce protective nature” as a characterological claim. First-time cluster deployment.

biblical.text: And his disciples remembered that it was written, The zeal of thine house hath eaten me up.
biblical.comment: The Christological pattern of fierce-protective expression: consuming zeal for the sacred enacted as physical and verbal action. The millstone warning is the same zeal expressed in speech; what eats Him up does not become mild when articulated. First-time cluster deployment.

restoration.text: And thy voice shall be more terrible in the midst of thine enemies than the fierce lion, because of thy righteousness; and thy God shall stand by thee forever and ever.
restoration.comment: The Restoration’s own fierce-protection language: “more terrible than the fierce lion” for the righteous, and “thy God shall stand by thee.” The compound claim grounds the source span’s compound noun — fierceness (the voice) and protection (the standing-by) together. First-time cluster deployment.

s20.text: If any part of this warning offends you in the least degree, good! It was intended as a call to Christlike love, a call to repentance from contentions and judgments — a call that would not offend the pure in heart.
s20.panel_comment: The span is ¶2’s hermeneutic turn — the paragraph’s own instruction on how to read the millstone warning. “Good!” is the sharpest monosyllable in the article: a rhetorical pivot that transforms potential offense into confirmation of the warning’s intent. The logic is parabolic: those offended by a call to Christlike love reveal by their offense what the warning was addressed to. “A call that would not offend the pure in heart” closes ¶2 with a Beatitude allusion that frames the entire paragraph within the Sermon on the Mount’s register — the warning is not beside the Beatitudes but within them. Matthew 5:8’s “Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God” grounds the “pure in heart” closing allusion as a direct Beatitude citation. The pure in heart receive the warning rightly because they are the ones the warning calls toward, not away from. First-time cluster deployment. Proverbs 27:5’s “Open rebuke is better than secret love” grounds the “good!” pivot in the wisdom tradition’s own logic: the sharp warning is the merciful act, preferable to silence that permits harm to continue. Open rebuke is not the opposite of love; it is love’s frank expression. First-time cluster deployment. Jacob 3:2–3 carries the Restoration’s most direct articulation of the pure-in-heart / warning binary: “O all ye that are pure in heart, lift up your heads and receive the pleasing word of God... But, wo, wo, unto you that are not pure in heart, that are filthy this day before God.” Jacob’s own preaching maps exactly onto s20’s logic — the same words of warning are pleasing to the pure in heart and convicting to the impure. First-time cluster deployment. D&C 121:43 grounds the warning-as-love logic institutionally: “Reproving betimes with sharpness, when moved upon by the Holy Ghost; and then showing forth afterwards an increase of love toward him whom thou hast reproved.” The pattern names the sharp warning not as the opposite of love but as love’s operative form in a specific moment. “Moved upon by the Holy Ghost” grounds the reproof’s authority — the same authority s18 names as “in the name of Jesus Christ.” First-time cluster deployment. 3 Nephi 11:28–30 carries the theological ground for what the warning calls the reader to repent from: contention itself is “of the devil,” and the call to repentance from “contentions and judgments” is the call away from what Christ explicitly prohibited. (Reasserted from Article 1 Span 18, Article 8 Span 6, and Article 8 Span 10 in different rhetorical direction. At A1 s18 the passage anchored fellowship-without-doctrinal-credential; at A8 s6 it anchored the corporate confession of historical contention; at A8 s10 it anchored the disciple’s active refusal to perpetuate contention. Here at A10 s20 the passage anchors the meta-interpretive claim that a warning against contention is itself the call to Christlike love — the reader offended by the anti-contention warning is resisting what Christ Himself prohibited. The direction is hermeneutic: the passage explains why the warning “would not offend the pure in heart.”)

biblical.text: Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God.
biblical.comment: The Beatitude allusion that closes ¶2 within the Sermon on the Mount’s own framework. The pure in heart receive the warning rightly — not because they are above rebuke but because they are the ones the warning calls toward. First-time cluster deployment.

biblical.text: Open rebuke is better than secret love.
biblical.comment: The wisdom ground for the “good!” pivot: the sharp warning is the merciful act. Open rebuke is not the opposite of love but its frank expression, preferable to the silence that allows harm to continue. First-time cluster deployment.

restoration.text: O all ye that are pure in heart, lift up your heads and receive the pleasing word of God, and feast upon his love; for ye may, if your minds are firm, forever. But, wo, wo, unto you that are not pure in heart, that are filthy this day before God; for except ye repent the land is cursed for your sakes;
restoration.comment: The Restoration’s own pure-in-heart / warning binary: the same words are pleasing to the pure and convicting to the impure. Jacob’s preaching pattern maps exactly onto s20’s logic — the warning that offends the impure is the very word the pure receive with joy. First-time cluster deployment.

restoration.comment: The warning-as-love logic grounded institutionally: reproof moved upon by the Holy Ghost, followed by an increase of love. The sharp warning IS love’s operative form in this moment. “Moved upon by the Holy Ghost” grounds the authority — the same authority s18 names as “in the name of Jesus Christ.” First-time cluster deployment.

The direction is hermeneutic: the passage explains why the warning “would not offend the pure in heart.”)

s1.text: We are children of God by birth
s1.panel_comment: The article opens with its governing antithesis: "children by birth / disciples by covenant." The first clause establishes the unconditional ground; the second names what is done with it. Both Paul's address to Athens (Acts 17:28–29) and the Restoration's D&C 76:24 reach the same conclusion by different paths — divine parentage is universal, not covenantally achieved. The article's entire arc rests on this prior relationship: we do not covenant our way into being God's children; we are already His children, and covenant is how we become His disciples. Hebrews 12:9, reasserted from A2 s1 and A3 s2 in different rhetorical direction, here establishes the pre-covenantal relationship that the article presupposes throughout — not the Father-attribute doctrine (A2 s1) or the creation-sequence ground (A3 s2), but the prior and unconditional condition from which covenantal discipleship launches.

biblical.text: For in him we live, and move, and have our being...
biblical.comment: Paul's Athens address, universal divine parentage; interfaith register of "his offspring" as a universal claim rather than a covenantal achievement.

biblical.text: ...shall we not much rather be in subjection unto the Father of spirits, and live?
biblical.comment: Reasserted from A2 s1 and A3 s2 in different rhetorical direction. Here: grounds the prior and unconditional relationship that covenant presupposes — "children by birth" as the baseline identity from which covenantal discipleship launches.

restoration.text: For I, the Lord God, created all things...spiritually, before they were naturally...
restoration.comment: spiritual creation precedes physical birth; "by birth" carries double register, mortal birth and prior spiritual birth.

restoration.text: ...the inhabitants thereof are begotten sons and daughters unto God.
restoration.comment: universal divine sonship and daughterhood as cosmic fact preceding any human choice.

s2.text: We become disciples of Christ by covenant
s2.panel_comment: The article's governing antithesis turns on this clause. The declaration does not say that all who are born of God are therefore disciples — it distinguishes the unconditional (birth) from the covenantal (discipleship). Discipleship requires a covenant: a volitional act of entering, witnessed in ordinance, written on the heart. Hebrews 8:10–12 frames the covenant's interior character — not law imposed from without but desire sealed from within, God's initiative to write His laws on the heart and mind of His people. The Great Commission (Matthew 28:19) supplies the dominical link between making disciples and baptism. Mosiah 18:8–10 names the covenant's content — bearing burdens, mourning, comforting, witnessing — and makes baptism the visible expression of an interior covenant already forming in the heart. 2 Nephi 31:17 names the gate: repentance and baptism by water.

biblical.text: ...I will put my laws into their mind, and write them in their hearts...
biblical.comment: new covenant's interior character; grounds "disciples by covenant" as a relational-interior event.

biblical.text: Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them...
biblical.comment: apostolic commission linking "making disciples" directly to the baptismal act.

restoration.text: ...if this be the desire of your hearts, what have you against being baptized...that ye have entered into a covenant with him...
restoration.comment: most complete Restoration text of covenantal entrance.

restoration.text: ...the gate by which ye should enter is repentance and baptism by water...
restoration.comment: the gate; threshold of the disciple's path.

crossref.label: s5
crossref.title: baptism and ordinances as the covenantal acts by which s2 is enacted

s3.text: We surrender our will into His and then we live it. Not merely profess it. Not merely believe it. Live it — in the body, in the home, in the world, every day of the week, as reality.
s3.panel_comment: The article's most rhetorically compressed span — five sentences compressed into a single act. "We surrender our will" names the interior movement; "then we live it" names the embodied consequence. The triple refusal ("Not merely profess it. Not merely believe it.") stages the claim by elimination. Matthew 16:24–25 supplies the dominical architecture — deny self, take up cross, follow — as the source of the will-surrender claim. The paradox at verse 25 (losing life to find it) grounds the "reality" register. Romans 12:1–2 supplies the bodily, in-the-world, every-day register — "present your bodies," "be not conformed to this world." D&C 64:34 carries the Restoration's interior-surrender claim: the Lord requires the heart and the willing mind.

biblical.text: ...let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me...
biblical.comment: dominical will-surrender; paradox grounds "reality" register.

biblical.text: ...present your bodies a living sacrifice...be not conformed to this world...
biblical.comment: bodily, in-the-world, every-day covenant-living.

restoration.text: Behold, the Lord requireth the heart and a willing mind...
restoration.comment: heart and willing mind as the dual interior surrender that embodied discipleship expresses outwardly.

s4.text: We embrace His name as our central identity, staking our lives on Him
s4.panel_comment: The name-taking is the article's identity-formation claim — distinct from A6's soteriological name-uses and A4's hermeneutical name-uses. Here the function is personal and structural: taking His name as "central identity" means Christ is not one commitment among many but the organizing reference of the self. Isaiah 44:5 grounds this in the OT prophetic tradition — "shall surname himself by the name of Israel" is the verbal act of a new identity. D&C 20:37 makes it explicit in the baptismal covenant formula. 3 Nephi 27:5–6 supplies the structural principle: the name by which you shall be called at the last day is the name you take now — identity as eschatological fact. "Staking our lives on Him" echoes Matthew 10:38–39 directly.

biblical.text: And he that taketh not his cross...is not worthy of me. He that findeth his life shall lose it...
biblical.comment: "staking our lives on Him" in its dominical form.

biblical.text: ...another shall subscribe with his hand unto the LORD, and surname himself by the name of Israel.
biblical.comment: prophetic vision of name-taking as identity claim.

restoration.text: ...willing to take upon them the name of Jesus Christ, having a determination to serve him to the end.
restoration.comment: baptismal covenant formula; name-taking as the covenant's identity dimension.

restoration.text: ...by this name shall ye be called at the last day.
restoration.comment: identity as eschatological fact.

crossref.label: s2
crossref.title: covenant as the act of becoming a disciple; s4 names what the covenanted disciple carries

s5.text: We accept that He was baptized to fulfill all righteousness, and instituted ordinances to remember Him
s5.panel_comment: The paragraph closes by grounding covenant-discipleship in Christ's own acts. He did not merely command baptism; He submitted to it. Two claims anchored. First, "baptized to fulfill all righteousness" paraphrases Matthew 3:15 directly. 2 Nephi 31:5–9 draws the canonical Restoration inference: if He being holy had need of baptism, how much more do we? Second, "ordinances to remember Him" paraphrases Luke 22:19 — "this do in remembrance of me"; D&C 20:77 names the content of the sacrament prayer.

biblical.text: ...thus it becometh us to fulfil all righteousness...
biblical.comment: Christ's own rationale for His baptism; grounds the disciple's baptism as following Christ not merely in form but in meaning.

biblical.text: ...This is my body which is given for you: this do in remembrance of me.
biblical.comment: institution of the Lord's Supper; explicit purpose of the ordinance Christ established.

restoration.text: ...if the Lamb of God, he being holy, should have need to be baptized...how much more need have we...
restoration.comment: argument from the greater to the lesser.

restoration.text: ...eat in remembrance of the body of thy Son...willing to take upon them the name of thy Son, and always remember him...
restoration.comment: memorial purpose stated in covenantal language.

crossref.label: s2
crossref.title: Christ's own rationale for the ordinance s2 names as the gate

s6.text: His apostles were sent into the world and taught, “Be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only.”
s6.panel_comment: The paragraph opens by grounding its entire practical register in apostolic commission and apostolic teaching. "His apostles were sent into the world" names the divine origin of what follows — the doers-of-the-word command is not the article's own exhortation but the apostles' received teaching, authorized from above. John 20:21 grounds the sending in Christ's own commission. D&C 107:23 supplies the Restoration's standing definition of the Twelve as special witnesses in all the world. James 1:22 is the direct-quote anchor. This imperative is the practical hinge of the article — hearing alone is the failed option; doing is what the covenant demands. The span sets the keynote that s3's "live it" established from Christ's side and that s8's plain answer will enact from the apostolic side.

biblical.text: But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.
biblical.comment: the direct-quote anchor; "hearers only" names the anti-type of covenant discipleship.

biblical.text: ...as my Father hath sent me, even so send I you.
biblical.comment: Christ's commissioning language; grounds "His apostles were sent" as a continuation of the divine mission.

restoration.text: The twelve traveling councilors are called to be the Twelve Apostles, or special witnesses of the name of Christ in all the world...
restoration.comment: Restoration definition of apostolic office.

restoration.text: And the voice of warning shall be unto all people, by the mouths of my disciples, whom I have chosen in these last days.
restoration.comment: apostolic voice as universal warning.

crossref.label: s3
crossref.title: live it in the body; s6 names the scriptural imperative behind s3's embodied-reality claim

s7.text: Those who feel the Spirit of Truth in their teachings and begin to believe in Christ always ask, “What shall we do?”
s7.panel_comment: The conversion question "What shall we do?" (Acts 2:37) is the article's first quotation with an answer attached — the sequence mirrors Pentecost exactly: Spirit moves, conviction follows, the question arises, the plain answer awaits. "Those who feel the Spirit of Truth in their teachings" anchors the Spirit's operation as what precedes and produces the question. 1 Thessalonians 1:5 supplies the Pauline mechanism: the gospel comes not in word only but in power and in the Holy Ghost. 2 Nephi 33:1 carries the Restoration's most precise statement of the same mechanism — the Holy Ghost carries words into the hearts of the children of men. D&C 50:21–22 adds the symmetry: Spirit-preached and Spirit-received words edify together.

biblical.text: Now when they heard this, they were pricked in their heart, and said unto Peter...what shall we do?
biblical.comment: the direct-quote anchor; universal response of all who genuinely receive the Spirit's conviction.

biblical.text: For our gospel came not unto you in word only, but also in power, and in the Holy Ghost...
biblical.comment: Spirit-carried preaching; grounds "feel the Spirit of Truth in their teachings."

restoration.text: ...when a man speaketh by the power of the Holy Ghost the power of the Holy Ghost carrieth it unto the hearts of the children of men.
restoration.comment: most precise Restoration statement of Spirit-carrying mechanism.

restoration.text: ...he that preacheth and he that receiveth, understand one another, and both are edified and rejoice together.
restoration.comment: Spirit-teacher and Spirit-receiver symmetry.

s8.text: The answer was as plain then as it is now: “Repent and be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins.”
s8.panel_comment: The direct quotation of Acts 2:38 is the article's most load-bearing moment — the apostolic answer to the conversion question, stated in its plainest form without softening or paraphrase. "The answer was as plain then as it is now" is the article's own interpretive gloss: the passage of time does not complexify the plain answer. Acts 2:38 supplies the complete apostolic formula — repent, be baptized in His name, receive remission, receive the Holy Ghost. Luke 24:47 places the proclamation in its universal scope. 3 Nephi 27:20 provides the Restoration's own "repent and be baptized" commandment from Christ's own voice. Moroni 6:2–3 names the enacted form: broken heart, contrite spirit, demonstrated repentance, the name of Christ.

biblical.text: Then Peter said unto them, Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost.
biblical.comment: primary direct-quote anchor; the plain apostolic answer.

biblical.text: And that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name among all nations...
biblical.comment: universal scope of the plain answer.

restoration.text: Now this is the commandment: Repent, all ye ends of the earth, and come unto me and be baptized in my name...
restoration.comment: plain answer from Christ's own voice in the New World record.

restoration.text: ...save they came forth with a broken heart and a contrite spirit...took upon them the name of Christ, having a determination to serve him to the end.
restoration.comment: enacted form of the plain answer in the Restoration community.

crossref.title: the conversion question; s8 supplies the plain answer s7 awaits

s9.text: Each disciple must feel after God’s Spirit for what it means to be “born of the water and the Spirit” and how to enter into covenants with Christ.
s9.panel_comment: The paragraph closes by opening space rather than closing it. Having named the plain answer (s8), the article does not press it as a formula — it names the individual disciple's responsibility: to feel after God's Spirit for what covenant-entering means. "Feel after" echoes Acts 17:27's Pauline language directly. "Born of the water and the Spirit" paraphrases John 3:5 — the new birth's dual register. Mosiah 5:7 supplies the covenant-birth in its Restoration form: Benjamin's people who covenant become "spiritually begotten" children of Christ — connecting s9 back to s1's "children by birth" as the article's internal inclusio. The natural-born child of God (s1) who enters covenant discipleship (s2) becomes also a spiritually begotten child of Christ (s9): two births, one belonging. 2 Nephi 31:12 carries the sequential promise.

biblical.text: ...Except a man be born of water and of the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God.
biblical.comment: primary anchor; dominical statement of the new birth's dual register.

biblical.text: That they should seek the Lord, if haply they might feel after him, and find him...
biblical.comment: "feel after" language drawn directly from Paul's Athens address.

restoration.text: ...ye shall be called the children of Christ...for behold, this day he hath spiritually begotten you...
restoration.comment: covenant-birth as spiritual begetting; completes inclusio with s1. Two births, one belonging.

restoration.text: ...He that is baptized in my name, to him will the Father give the Holy Ghost, like unto me...
restoration.comment: sequential promise following the new birth.
