s10.text: We walk the path Christ set before us — Himself being the way, the truth, and the life.
s10.panel_comment: The paragraph's opening motion belongs to the disciple — "we walk." The path is Christ's to set; the walking is the disciple's to do. "Himself being the way, the truth, and the life" paraphrases John 14:6 in its fifth cluster deployment, here in its path-companionship register. The four prior deployments carried distinct functions — measurement-reference (A5 s16), salvation-way (A6 s8), verbatim self-claim (A9 s2), navigational integration (A9 s20). Here the "way" is the road Christ walked before us and set before the disciple — the pioneer and precursor dimension. 1 Peter 2:21 grounds this: He left an example that ye should follow his steps. D&C 19:23 names the mode — walk in the meekness of my Spirit, which yields peace. 2 Nephi 31:16 names the stakes — unless a man endure to the end in following the example of the Son, he cannot be saved.

biblical.text: Jesus saith unto him, I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.
biblical.comment: Reasserted from A5 s16, A6 s8, A9 s2, A9 s20 in different rhetorical direction. Here: path-companionship / pioneer-precursor dimension. Distinct from measurement, salvation, verbatim claim, and navigational integration.

biblical.text: ...Christ also suffered for us, leaving us an example, that ye should follow his steps.
biblical.comment: step-following ground; the path-walking is a personal following after Him.

restoration.text: Learn of me, and listen to my words; walk in the meekness of my Spirit, and you shall have peace in me.
restoration.comment: operative mode of covenant discipleship on the path Christ set; promise of peace.

restoration.text: ...unless a man shall endure to the end, in following the example of the Son of the living God, he cannot be saved.
restoration.comment: stakes of walking the path; links s10 to s12's endurance arc.

crossref.label: s3
crossref.title: live it in reality; s10 names the Christological ground of s3's embodied-walking claim

s11.panel_comment: The three-word span — "pray always" and "faint not" — is the article's most compressed commitment statement. Both phrases have deep scriptural roots. Luke 18:1 introduces the parable of the importunate widow with the explicit purpose "that men ought always to pray, and not to faint" — the exact compound the article claims. D&C 10:5 gives the Restoration's own "Pray always, that you faint not" as a commandment alongside the promise of overcoming. D&C 88:126 closes a long passage of covenant disciplines with the same phrase. The span is not a general piety note — it is the disciple's sustained orientation through all that s12 names: endurance through joy and trials, over a lifetime. 1 Thessalonians 5:17's three-word "pray without ceasing" is the Pauline parallel.

biblical.text: And he spake a parable unto them to this end, that men ought always to pray, and not to faint.
biblical.comment: primary biblical source for the paired command; parable told to this end.

biblical.text: Pray without ceasing.
biblical.comment: Pauline parallel; brevity is the point; unceasing prayer as ambient orientation.

restoration.text: Pray always, that you faint not; and that you overcome Satan...
restoration.comment: nearest Restoration parallel to the article's exact phrasing, with promise of overcoming.

restoration.text: ...Pray always, that ye faint not.
restoration.comment: closes a passage of covenant disciplines with the same paired phrase; confirms as standing Restoration formulation.

crossref.label: s12
crossref.title: endurance over a lifetime; s11's prayer sustains what s12 names as the full arc

s12.text: We endure in faith through joy and trials as God refines this new identity into mature discipleship over a lifetime of spiritual sanctification by the power of His Spirit.
s12.panel_comment: The article's broadest span — the definition of the lifetime of covenant discipleship. Three elements anchored. First, "endure in faith through joy and trials" — the discipline holds in both registers. Hebrews 12:1's "run with patience the race that is set before us" grounds endurance as the governing frame. Philippians 1:6 grounds the lifetime dimension specifically — "he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ" — God is the refiner, and the refining takes a lifetime. Second, "God refines this new identity into mature discipleship" — the agent is God; the disciple endures, but God does the refining work. Third, "spiritual sanctification by the power of His Spirit" — D&C 20:31 grounds sanctification through grace. D&C 121:45–46 names the Holy Ghost as the constant companion — the mechanism of the lifetime refining.

biblical.text: ...let us run with patience the race that is set before us.
biblical.comment: endurance as the race set before us; governing frame for persisting through joy and trials.

biblical.text: ...he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ.
biblical.comment: God will perform to completion; grounds lifetime dimension and assurance.

restoration.text: ...sanctification through the grace of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ is just and true, to all those who love and serve God with all their mights, minds, and strength.
restoration.comment: doctrinal ground for lifetime sanctification.

restoration.text: Let virtue garnish thy thoughts unceasingly...The Holy Ghost shall be thy constant companion...
restoration.comment: Spirit's ongoing presence as the mechanism of the lifetime refining process.

crossref.label: s11
crossref.title: pray always and faint not; s11 sustains what s12 names as the full arc

s13.text: We seek to enter into God’s Kingdom, which is at hand — now, in this moment — for those who have eyes to see, ears to hear, and willing hearts.
s13.panel_comment: The article closes with its most luminous sentence — not a command but an orientation. "We seek to enter into God's Kingdom" echoes 3 Nephi 13:33's "seek ye first the kingdom of God." The Kingdom is named as present — "at hand — now, in this moment" — cross-referencing A7's primary kingdom-at-hand architecture (A7 s2) without repeating its anchors. Luke 17:21 supplies the now-in-this-moment register directly — "the kingdom of God is within you." The eyes/ears/willing-hearts triad names the three receptive faculties required for present kingdom-perception — the same threefold faculty A7 s3 established. Matthew 13:16 grounds the blessed eyes and ears. D&C 136:32 supplies the Restoration's own "eyes may be opened...ears opened." The triad of eyes, ears, and willing hearts mirrors the article's opening triad — children by birth, covenant discipleship, lived reality — now transformed into a triad of receptive postures toward the Kingdom already present.

biblical.text: ...behold, the kingdom of God is within you.
biblical.comment: the now-in-this-moment register; grounds insistence that the Kingdom is present, not deferred.

biblical.text: But blessed are your eyes, for they see: and your ears, for they hear.
biblical.comment: blessed eyes and ears; Christ's own pronouncement of receptivity as already gifted.

restoration.text: But seek ye first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added unto you.
restoration.comment: seeking-posture as the article's closing orientation.

restoration.text: ...that his eyes may be opened that he may see, and his ears opened that he may hear.
restoration.comment: Restoration's eyes-and-ears invocation; capacities the Lord opens in the seeking disciple.

crossref.label: See Article 7
crossref.title: A7 s2 is the cluster primary kingdom-at-hand span; s13 names the disciple seeking-to-enter posture as the article close

s1.text: this life is not all there is. The grave is not the end.
s1.panel_comment: The article opens with its two-sided immortality affirmation — positive and negative — before naming Christ as the ground of the claim. "This life is not all there is" reaches beyond the mortal horizon; "The grave is not the end" refuses mortal finality. The two sentences are not redundant: the first names a more-than, the second refuses a full-stop. Together they are the article's epistemological premise — everything that follows rests here. They arrive before the Christological anchor at s2, which means the hope is asserted first, then evidenced. The sequence is deliberate.

biblical.text: For I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth: And though after my skin worms destroy this body, yet in my flesh shall I see God: Whom I shall see for myself, and mine eyes shall behold, and not another; though my reins be consumed within me.
biblical.comment: The OT anchor for both directions: Redeemer lives (the more-than), in my flesh shall I see God (the grave is not the end). Job's confession is the cluster's oldest voice for this claim and its most personal form. First-time cluster deployment.

biblical.text: If in this life only we have hope in Christ, we are of all men most miserable. But now is Christ risen from the dead, and become the firstfruits of them that slept.
biblical.comment: Paul names exactly the alternative the source paragraph refuses. The "But now" reversal is the biblical form of "The grave is not the end." First-time cluster deployment.

restoration.text: For as death hath passed upon all men, to fulfil the merciful plan of the great Creator, there must needs be a power of resurrection, and the resurrection must needs come unto man by reason of the fall; and the fall came by reason of transgression; and because man became fallen they were cut off from the presence of the Lord. Wherefore, the first judgment which came upon man must needs have remained to an endless duration. And if so, this flesh must have laid down to rot and to crumble to its mother earth, to rise no more.
restoration.comment: Jacob names the alternative — endless death, flesh rising no more — as what the Atonement and resurrection refuse. The negative form carries double weight: Jacob names what was at stake if the grave were the end. First-time cluster deployment.

crossref.label: Within this article
crossref.title: Span 2: Christ's resurrection is the promise and the proof (the Christological ground for s1's assertion)

s2.text: Christ's resurrection is the promise and the proof.
s2.panel_comment: The two nouns carry distinct weight. As promise, the Resurrection declares what awaits every soul — the firstfruits precedent s3 develops. As proof, it establishes that the declaration is not wishful eschatology but witnessed fact. The Resurrection is not one piece of evidence for a general resurrection theory; it is the event that established the category. Proof without promise yields only a Christological datum; promise without proof yields only hope. Together they name the Resurrection as the article's epistemological and eschatological ground simultaneously.

biblical.text: But now is Christ risen from the dead, and become the firstfruits of them that slept. For since by man came death, by man came also the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive. But every man in his own order: Christ the firstfruits; afterward they that are Christ's at his coming.
biblical.comment: Primary anchor for both directions. "Firstfruits" grounds the promise direction; the Adam/Christ parallel grounds the proof direction — if death entered by man, its reversal came by Man, and the logic is universal. First-time cluster deployment.

biblical.text: But if the Spirit of him that raised up Jesus from the dead dwell in you, he that raised up Christ from the dead shall also quicken your mortal bodies by his Spirit that dwelleth in you.
biblical.comment: The promise direction in its most direct personal address: the same power that raised Christ will raise you. First-time cluster deployment.

restoration.text: And now, after the many testimonies which have been given of him, this is the testimony, last of all, which we give of him: That he lives! For we saw him, even on the right hand of God; and we heard the voice bearing record that he is the Only Begotten of the Father— That by him, and through him, and of him, the worlds are and were created, and the inhabitants thereof are begotten sons and daughters unto God.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's own eyewitness testimony that Christ lives — the "proof" direction in its most immediate apostolic form. First-time cluster deployment.

crossref.label: Within this article
crossref.title: Span 1: this life is not all there is (s2 grounds s1's assertion Christologically)

crossref.label: Within this article
crossref.title: Span 3: what was sown in sorrow will be raised in glory (develops the promise direction)

s3.text: What was sown in sorrow will be raised in glory
s3.panel_comment: A paraphrase of 1 Corinthians 15:43's "it is sown in dishonour; it is raised in glory," with "sorrow" substituting Paul's "dishonour." The substitution reaches forward to s6's "every tear and smile will be accounted for" and into the tears-register of the eschatological literature. The "what was" construction carries theological weight: not that a better thing replaces the sorrowed thing — the sorrowed thing itself is raised. The mortal experience is not discarded but transformed.

biblical.text: So also is the resurrection of the dead. It is sown in corruption; it is raised in incorruption: It is sown in dishonour; it is raised in glory: it is sown in weakness; it is raised in power: It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. There is a natural body, and there is a spiritual body.
biblical.comment: Primary source. "Sown in dishonour; it is raised in glory" is the direct paraphrase anchor; the full four-beat sequence adds context: corruption → incorruption, dishonour → glory, weakness → power, natural → spiritual. First-time cluster deployment.

biblical.text: They that sow in tears shall reap in joy. He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him.
biblical.comment: The OT sowing-and-reaping grammar that Paul's metaphor inhabits and that the source paragraph's "sorrow" substitution deliberately echoes. The Psalmist names tears and joy; the span names sorrow and glory — the same arc in different vocabularies. First-time cluster deployment.

restoration.text: Ye cannot behold with your natural eyes, for the present time, the design of your God concerning those things which shall come hereafter, and the glory which shall follow after much tribulation. For after much tribulation come the blessings. Wherefore the day cometh that ye shall be crowned with much glory; the hour is not yet, but is nigh at hand.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's own sown-in-tribulation → raised-in-glory grammar. "The glory which shall follow" grounds the transformation; "the hour is not yet, but is nigh at hand" supplies the temporal patience register without which the claim becomes cheap. First-time cluster deployment.

crossref.label: Within this article
crossref.title: Span 2: Christ's resurrection is the promise (s3 develops the promise direction)

crossref.label: Within this article
crossref.title: Span 6: every tear and smile will be accounted for (sorrow motif continues)

s4.text: what is given to Him is not lost
s4.panel_comment: Where s3 names transformation, s4 names security: the redeemed are held. "What is given to Him" is a deliberate passive — not "who gives themselves to Him" but what the Father has given. The keeping is Christ's responsibility to the Father's gift. This is the Johannine shepherding claim in its resurrection register: not merely that Christ cares for the living flock but that death does not break the Shepherd's hold. The pastoral weight is direct: the span is addressed to those whose loved ones have died in Christ, or who wonder whether death undoes what was committed to Him. The answer is categorical: not lost. John 10:27–28 appeared at A9 s22 in the navigational-perseverance register — remaining in Christ's voice as the living disciple's navigational anchor. Here the function is distinct: not the living disciple's ongoing perseverance but the eschatological security of what Christ holds through death itself. (Reasserted from Article 9 Span 22 in different rhetorical direction. At A9 s22 the verse grounds the living disciple's navigational perseverance in Christ's voice — hearing and following; here at A12 s4 the same verse grounds the eschatological security of what Christ holds through death — neither the sheep's dying nor any other force can pluck them from His hand.)

biblical.text: And this is the Father's will which hath sent me, that of all which he hath given me I should lose nothing, but should raise it up again at the last day.
biblical.comment: Primary anchor. Christ's own words: the Father has given souls to Him; His declared responsibility is to lose none and raise them at the last day. Both the Father's will and Christ's responsibility are named. First-time cluster deployment.

biblical.text: My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me: And I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand.
biblical.comment: (Reasserted from Article 9 Span 22 in different rhetorical direction. At A9 s22 the verse grounds the living disciple's navigational perseverance in Christ's voice; here at A12 s4 the same verse grounds the eschatological security of what Christ holds through death — "they shall never perish" and "neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand" in their resurrection register.)

biblical.text: Which hope we have as an anchor of the soul, both sure and stedfast, and which entereth into that within the veil; Whither the forerunner is for us entered, even Jesus, who is made an high priest for ever after the order of Melchisedec.
biblical.comment: Hope as anchor of the soul — sure and steadfast. Christ as the forerunner who has entered beyond the veil confirms that what follows is held secure. First-time cluster deployment.

restoration.text: Wherefore, whoso believeth in God might with surety hope for a better world, yea, even a place at the right hand of God, which hope cometh of faith, maketh an anchor to the souls of men, which would make them sure and steadfast, always abounding in good works, being led to glorify God.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's anchor-to-the-soul idiom, grounding the sure and steadfast security of what hope in Christ holds. Flag: if a more direct Restoration "not lost" anchor exists, it would strengthen s4's Restoration column.

crossref.label: Within this article
crossref.title: Span 3: sown in sorrow, raised in glory (s4 adds the security dimension: what is given and transformed is also held)

crossref.label: Within this article
crossref.title: Span 5: every soul will be raised (the universal resurrection toward which s4's security points)

s5.text: Every soul will be raised to stand before God in naked honesty
s5.panel_comment: Two claims operate in tandem. "Every soul will be raised" is the universal resurrection affirmation — no partial resurrection, no selective raising. "To stand before God in naked honesty" is the judgment characterization: not naked shame, not naked condemnation, but naked honesty — truthful reckoning rather than adversarial verdict. The editorial choice of "naked honesty" over the conventional 2 Corinthians 5:10 "works" idiom is deliberate (April 25 editorial note): the encounter is named as honest before the One who already knows it entirely. The soul is not shielded and not accused — it stands in what it actually is. "Naked honesty" also rhymes structurally with the cluster's epistemological honesty register (A1's merognosis): the same souls who confess partial knowing in this life stand in full transparency before God at the last.

biblical.text: And I saw the dead, small and great, stand before God; and the books were opened: and another book was opened, which is the book of life: and the dead were judged out of those things which were written in the books, according to their works. And the sea gave up the dead which were in it; and death and hell delivered up the dead which were in them: and they were judged every man according to their works.
biblical.comment: "Every soul" in its most expansive form: small and great, sea and death and hell delivering up their dead. The opened books ground the "naked honesty" register — nothing concealed, all written. First-time cluster deployment.

biblical.text: For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ; that every one may receive the things done in his body, according to that he hath done, whether it be good or bad.
biblical.comment: "We must all appear" grounds universality; the judgment-seat register supports the standing-before. The span's phrasing declines this verse's "works" idiom while the verse properly anchors the event. First-time cluster deployment.

restoration.text: For our words will condemn us, yea, all our works will condemn us; we shall not be found spotless; and our thoughts will also condemn us; and in this awful state we shall not dare to look up to our God; and we would fain be glad if we could command the rocks and the mountains to fall upon us to hide us from his presence.
restoration.comment: Alma grounds the "naked" register in its most searching form: words, works, thoughts — the full human interior made visible. Nothing hidden; the soul stands in what it actually is. First-time cluster deployment.

crossref.label: Within this article
crossref.title: Span 6: every tear and smile will be accounted for (the positive content of what the accounting includes)

crossref.label: Within this article
crossref.title: Span 7: what form that accounting will take, we leave to God (s5 names the fact; s7 restrains the form)

s6.text: every tear and smile will be accounted for
s6.panel_comment: The pairing of "tear and smile" is the span's load-bearing decision: it refuses the reduction of eschatological accounting to suffering only. Both registers count — grief and joy, trial and ordinary delight, wound and laughter. "Accounted for" is deliberate: not "accounted against" but accounted for in the sense of received, held, remembered. The tear is not forgotten. The smile is not trivial. Both matter to the God who keeps the full record. This double-sided accounting pairs with s7's restraint: we name that everything is held (s6) while refusing to name the form of the accounting (s7).

biblical.text: Thou tellest my wanderings: put thou my tears into thy bottle: are they not in thy book?
biblical.comment: God keeps the tears; they are counted and bottled, written in His book. The Psalmist's image grounds "every tear will be accounted for" in its most intimate biblical form. First-time cluster deployment.

biblical.text: And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away.
biblical.comment: Where Psalm 56:8 grounds God's keeping of tears, Revelation 21:4 names their eschatological resolution: wiped away. The two anchors trace the tear's full arc — held through the journey, resolved at the destination. First-time cluster deployment.

restoration.text: For I, the Lord, will judge all men according to their works, according to the desire of their hearts.
restoration.comment: "The desire of their hearts" grounds the "smile" direction: God's accounting reaches interior motivations and desires, not only external acts. The person whose desire was good even when circumstances limited their acts is known by God in that dimension. First-time cluster deployment.

crossref.label: Within this article
crossref.title: Span 5: stand before God in naked honesty (s6 names the particular content of what is accounted)

crossref.label: Within this article
crossref.title: Span 7: what form that accounting will take, we leave to God (s6 names what is accounted; s7 restrains the form)

s7.text: What form that accounting will take, and what glories await, we leave to God
s7.panel_comment: The article's merognosis-in-eschatological-register move — structurally identical to the restraint pattern first established at A1 s1 and carried across the cluster, here applied to the last things themselves. The cluster has deployed this restraint in the epistemological register (A1), in the doctrine of God (A2 s7–s10), in soteriology (A6 s6), and in doctrinal disputes (A3 s6, A8 s8). Here the same restraint reaches the eschatological consummation: we name the fact of resurrection and accounting (s5–s6) and of fellowship with God (s9), but we do not claim to name the form of the accounting or the specific architecture of the glories. The "we leave to God" construction names active trust, not agnosticism. "Glories" (plural) is the article's restrained form — naming multiplicity without specifying the three-glory taxonomy of D&C 76; the container word remains wide enough for each tradition. Deuteronomy 29:29 reaches its seventh cluster deployment in its eschatological application: the secret things of the accounting's form and the glories' specific content are left with the LORD who keeps them. (Reasserted from Article 1 Spans 1, 4, 5; Article 2 Spans 7, 9; Article 3 Span 6; Article 6 Span 6. All prior deployments in epistemological or doctrinal-restraint registers. Here at A12 s7 the same anchor grounds eschatological restraint specifically — the form of the accounting and the content of the glories are the secret things this article leaves to God.) 1 Corinthians 13:9–12 reaches its fourth cluster deployment in a new eschatological direction. (Reasserted from Article 1 Span 1, Article 1 Span 7, and Article 6 Span 6 in different rhetorical direction. At A1 s1 and s7 the verse grounds the universal merognostic posture; at A6 s6 it grounds merognostic restraint on the soteriological mechanism. Here at A12 s7 the verse grounds eschatological restraint specifically — we know in part and prophesy in part; the form of the accounting and the content of the glories is not yet ours to name. The "face to face" and "fully known" of verse 12 names the direction of what awaits without naming its form.)

biblical.text: But as it is written, Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which God hath prepared for them that love him.
biblical.comment: The strongest fresh anchor for "what glories await, we leave to God": the glories exceed all human imagining, which is precisely why they are left to God. The restraint is honest recognition of the imagination's limit, not failure of vision. First-time cluster deployment.

biblical.text: For now we know in part, and we prophesy in part. But when that which is perfect is come, then that which is in part shall be done away. When I was a child, I spake as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child: but when I became a man, I put away childish things. For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known.
biblical.comment: (Reasserted from Article 1 Span 1, Article 1 Span 7, and Article 6 Span 6 in different rhetorical direction. At A1 s1 and s7 the verse grounds the universal merognostic posture; at A6 s6 it grounds merognostic restraint on the soteriological mechanism. Here at A12 s7 the verse grounds eschatological restraint specifically — the form of the accounting and the content of the glories are not yet ours to name. The "face to face" and "fully known" of verse 12 names the direction of what awaits without naming its form.)

biblical.text: The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever, that we may do all the words of this law.
biblical.comment: (Reasserted from Article 1 Spans 1, 4, 5; Article 2 Spans 7, 9; Article 3 Span 6; Article 6 Span 6 in different rhetorical direction. All prior deployments in epistemological or doctrinal-restraint registers. Here at A12 s7 the same anchor grounds eschatological restraint specifically — the form of the accounting and the content of the glories are the secret things this article leaves with the LORD.)

restoration.text: For by my Spirit will I enlighten them, and by my power will I make known unto them the secrets of my will—yea, even those things which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor yet entered into the heart of man.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's own parallel to 1 Corinthians 2:9: the glories are real but reserved for disclosure by the Spirit, not by human speculation. Grounds the eschatological restraint of s7 from the Restoration's own epistemology of glory. First-time cluster deployment.

crossref.label: Within this article
crossref.title: Span 8: who is faithful and who keeps His promises (the ground for s7's eschatological trust)

crossref.label: See Article 1, Span 1
crossref.title: Merognosis-restraint pattern established (s7 is its eschatological application)

s8.text: who is faithful and who keeps His promises
s8.panel_comment: The relative clause modifies God — "we leave to God, who is faithful and who keeps His promises." The theological function is to give the restraint at s7 its ground: we leave the eschatological glories to God not from resignation but from trust in who God is. The two nouns work in different registers: "faithful" names the character attribute; "keeps His promises" names the track record. Together they name both what God is and what God does. Eschatological humility and eschatological confidence are not in tension — they rest on the same ground. The "keeps His promises" direction is new to the cluster: faithfulness has been implied across many articles but not named as the explicit ground for leaving last things to God.

biblical.text: Let us hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering; (for he is faithful that promised;)
biblical.comment: The apostolic assurance that grounds the holding-fast: "he is faithful that promised" is the entire reason for eschatological confidence. The parenthetical form is itself the argument — the faithfulness is so well-established it needs only assertion. First-time cluster deployment.

biblical.text: It is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness.
biblical.comment: The covenant lament tradition's declaration of faithfulness as survival's ground. "Great is thy faithfulness" — not merely adequate, but great. First-time cluster deployment.

restoration.text: The works, and the designs, and the purposes of God cannot be frustrated, neither can they come to naught. For God doth not walk in crooked paths, neither doth he turn to the right hand nor to the left, neither doth he vary from that which he hath said, therefore his paths are straight, and his course is one eternal round.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's most direct anchor for "keeps His promises": God does not vary from what He has said; His course is one eternal round. First-time cluster deployment.

crossref.label: Within this article
crossref.title: Span 7: what glories await, we leave to God (s8 is the ground for s7's eschatological trust)

crossref.label: Within this article
crossref.title: Span 9: we were made to fellowship with Him in His glory (the promise s8 names as kept)

s9.text: we were made to fellowship with Him in His glory
s9.panel_comment: The article's eschatological telos claim — not only what happens after death but what mortality was always for. "Made to fellowship with Him" names the purpose of creaturely existence as relational and eschatological; "in His glory" names the register of that fellowship as not merely intimate but glorified. The article uses "fellowship" rather than "exaltation" — honoring the Restoration's disclosure without requiring all readers to receive its full theological content. The container word is wide enough for each tradition to fill from within its own frame while deep enough for the Restoration reader to recognize what is being named. The span lives in the John 17 orbit. John 17:22–24 — Christ's own eschatological prayer for the disciples to "be with me where I am" and "behold my glory" — supplies the most direct Christological anchor. John 17:3 reaches its third cluster deployment in the eschatological-destination register. (Reasserted from Article 7 Span 6 and Article 9 Span 7 in different rhetorical direction. At A7 s6 the verse grounded the kingdom-life-now claim — eternal life as knowing God in the present moment; at A9 s7 it grounded the relational priority over propositional accuracy. Here at A12 s9 the same verse grounds the eschatological destination — the knowing of God consummated as fellowship with Him in His glory, the telos toward which all mortal knowing has been moving.) Moses 1:39 reaches its third cluster deployment — and its most direct possible application — in the article whose title names the verse's own content. (Reasserted from Article 2 Span 12 and Article 7 Span 13 in different rhetorical direction. At A2 s12 the verse anchored God's benevolent intent; at A7 s13 it anchored the Father's will-claim for abundant living. Here at A12 s9 the verse anchors the eschatological purpose-claim itself — "immortality and eternal life" as God's work and glory, in the article that names those exact words as its subject. "We were made" names the telos Moses 1:39 declares as God's work.)

biblical.text: And the glory which thou gavest me I have given them; that they may be one, even as we are one: I in them, and thou in me, that they may be made perfect in one; and that the world may know that thou hast sent me, and hast loved them, as thou hast loved me. Father, I will that they also, whom thou hast given me, be with me where I am; that they may behold my glory, which thou hast given me: for thou lovedst me before the foundation of the world.
biblical.comment: Christ's own eschatological prayer: "be with me where I am" and "behold my glory." Fellowship-in-His-glory in its most direct Christological form. First-time cluster deployment.

biblical.text: And this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent.
biblical.comment: (Reasserted from Article 7 Span 6 and Article 9 Span 7 in different rhetorical direction. At A7 s6 the verse grounded eternal-life-as-knowing-God-now — the kingdom-life-now claim; at A9 s7 it grounded the relational priority over propositional accuracy. Here at A12 s9 the same verse grounds the eschatological destination — the knowing consummated as fellowship with God in His glory.)

restoration.text: For behold, this is my work and my glory—to bring to pass the immortality and eternal life of man.
restoration.comment: (Reasserted from Article 2 Span 12 and Article 7 Span 13 in different rhetorical direction. At A2 s12 the verse anchored God's benevolent intent; at A7 s13 it anchored the Father's will-claim for abundant living. Here at A12 s9 the verse anchors the eschatological purpose-claim itself — "immortality and eternal life" as God's work and glory, in the article that names those exact words as its subject.)

crossref.label: Within this article
crossref.title: Span 8: who is faithful and who keeps His promises (the promise s9 names as kept)

crossref.label: See Article 7, Span 6
crossref.title: A7 s6: eternal-life-as-knowing-God-now (s9 is the eschatological consummation of that arc)

s10.text: Christ has spoken. Christ is trustworthy. This is enough for us.
s10.panel_comment: The article's three-sentence close operates in the epistemic-sufficiency register that A1's opening established — where A1 named the ground of intellectual humility, A12 names the ground of eschatological confidence. The logic escalates: word → character → sufficiency. "Christ has spoken" names the disclosure — not a specific utterance but the full body of Christ's word across both canonical registers. "Christ is trustworthy" makes the speaker the authority: the claim rests not on the comprehensiveness of the disclosure but on the character of the one who spoke. "This is enough for us" closes the article — and the cluster's penultimate article — with an act of eschatological rest. The "for us" is corporate: the community together rests in this word. The three sentences form the eschatological preparation for A13's opening — "We proclaim that Christ is enough" — creating the cluster's closing sufficiency arc: A12 names it eschatologically, A13 names it in the present tense, two registers of the same confession.

biblical.text: God is not a man, that he should lie; neither the son of man, that he should repent: hath he said, and shall he not do it? or hath he spoken, and shall he not make it good?
biblical.comment: The OT ground for "Christ is trustworthy" in its most direct form: what God has spoken He will make good. The rhetorical question makes non-trustworthiness unthinkable. First-time cluster deployment.

biblical.text: For all the promises of God in him are yea, and in him Amen, unto the glory of God by us.
biblical.comment: All promises are Yes in Christ and Amen by us — the community's corporate ratification of the sufficiency claim. "By us" is the same corporate form as the source span's "for us." First-time cluster deployment.

restoration.text: Search these commandments, for they are true and faithful, and the prophecies and promises which are in them shall all be fulfilled. What I the Lord have spoken, I have spoken, and I excuse not myself; and though the heavens and the earth pass away, my word shall not pass away, but shall all be fulfilled, whether by mine own voice or by the voice of my servants, it is the same.
restoration.comment: "My word shall not pass away" grounds "Christ has spoken" as sufficient ground; "shall all be fulfilled" grounds "Christ is trustworthy." The Restoration's own claim that the spoken word stands — the theological basis for "This is enough for us." First-time cluster deployment.

crossref.label: See Article 1, Span 1
crossref.title: Epistemic-sufficiency register established (s10 is the eschatological form of that posture)

crossref.label: See Article 13
crossref.title: "We proclaim that Christ is enough" (adjacent declaration forming the cluster's closing sufficiency arc)

s1.text: We proclaim that Christ is enough.
s1.panel_comment: The cluster's closing sufficiency proclamation. The opening verb "We proclaim" signals A13's register as declaratory—not reflective like A12 s10's "This is enough for us" (eschatological trust across death), but present-tense and confessional. The two articles form the cluster's sufficiency arc: A12 closes with trust in what Christ has promised through death; A13 opens with the proclamation that He is sufficient now. 2 Cor 12:9 grounds sufficiency in the Pauline witness of weakness met by grace—the experiential registration of the claim. Heb 7:25 grounds it in Christ's intercessory office (to the uttermost), naming its scope as unconditional. Isa 45:22 provides the prophetic universal form (all the ends of the earth), preparing s3's invitation. D&C 45:3–5 provides the Restoration mechanism: Christ as Advocate, pleading his own sufferings as the defense before the Father—the doctrinal ground for why Christ is enough holds.

biblical.text: And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me.
biblical.comment: The Pauline witness that divine sufficiency meets human inadequacy—the experiential ground for the proclamation.

biblical.text: Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them.
biblical.comment: The scope of sufficiency—to the uttermost is unconditional, not partial or provisional.

biblical.text: Look unto me, and be ye saved, all the ends of the earth: for I am God, and there is none else.
biblical.comment: The prophetic universal form of the sufficiency claim. Prepares the scope of s3's invitation.

restoration.text: Listen to him who is the advocate with the Father, who is pleading your cause before him— Saying: Father, behold the sufferings and death of him who did no sin, in whom thou wast well pleased; behold the blood of thy Son which was shed, the blood of him whom thou gavest that thyself might be glorified; Wherefore, Father, spare these my brethren that believe on my name, that they may come unto me and have everlasting life.
restoration.comment: Christ as Advocate, presenting his own sufferings as the ground of the Father's mercy—the Restoration's doctrinal mechanism for why Christ is enough holds.

crossref.label: See Article 12
crossref.title: Span s10: This is enough for us — eschatological register of the sufficiency arc

s2.text: His gospel is for the flawed, the weary, the wounded, and the searching.
s2.panel_comment: The fourfold pastoral address names every category of spiritual condition the Declaration is written to meet. The four terms are not synonyms: flawed (moral condition), weary (exhaustion), wounded (injury), searching (epistemic condition)—ensuring no reader is unnamed. Isa 61:1–2 is the messianic commission Christ read from in the Nazareth synagogue (Luke 4:18–21) and claimed as His own; grounding A13 s2 in that commission anchors the claim in the mission Jesus Himself defined. Bind up the brokenhearted, proclaim liberty to the captives maps directly onto the wounded and weary. Isa 57:15 provides the theological ground beneath the pastoral claim: God has chosen to dwell with those of contrite and humble spirit—the weary and flawed are exactly the ones with whom He has made His home. 3 Ne 9:22 provides the Restoration's post-Resurrection voice of Christ extending the same welcome: for of such I have laid down my life. The searching and humbled condition is not an obstacle but a qualification.

biblical.text: The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me; because the Lord hath anointed me to preach good tidings unto the meek; he hath sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to them that are bound; To proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord, and the day of vengeance of our God; to comfort all that mourn;
biblical.comment: Christ's own mission charter claimed at Nazareth. The brokenhearted, captive, and bound map directly onto the wounded, weary, and flawed.

biblical.text: For thus saith the high and lofty One that inhabiteth eternity, whose name is Holy; I dwell in the high and holy place, with him also that is of a contrite and humble spirit, to revive the spirit of the humble, and to revive the heart of the contrite ones.
biblical.comment: The theological ground—God has chosen to dwell with exactly those the gospel is for.

restoration.text: Therefore, whoso repenteth and cometh unto me as a little child, him will I receive, for of such is the kingdom of God. Behold, for such I have laid down my life, and have taken it up again; therefore repent, and come unto me ye ends of the earth, and be saved.
restoration.comment: The resurrected Christ's voice extending the same welcome. For of such I have laid down my life—the atonement was wrought for precisely those named in A13 s2. The humbled condition is the entry posture, not the disqualifier.

s3.text: His invitation is to every tribe, in every tongue, and across every tradition.
s3.panel_comment: The Declaration's universal-scope claim—the invitation extending beyond Christendom to every human tradition. The three-part enumeration (tribe, tongue, tradition) echoes the Rev 7:9 vision of the multitude before the throne: all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues—grounding A13's invitation in the eschatological fulfillment John foresaw. Isa 49:6 provides the prophetic commission preceding the fulfillment: the Servant given for a light to the Gentiles so that God's salvation reaches the end of the earth. D&C 1:2 provides the Restoration's opening declaration that the voice of the Lord is unto all men without exception—there is no eye that shall not see, neither ear that shall not hear. The three anchors hold together commission, vision, and declaration across the canon.

biblical.text: After this I beheld, and, lo, a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues, stood before the throne, and before the Lamb, clothed with white robes, and palms in their hands;
biblical.comment: The eschatological vision of universal reception before the Lamb—the Declaration's universal invitation grounded in its prophetic fulfillment.

biblical.text: And he said, It is a light thing that thou shouldest be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give thee for a light to the Gentiles, that thou mayest be my salvation unto the end of the earth.
biblical.comment: The Servant's commission to bring salvation to the ends of the earth—the prophetic mandate underlying the universal invitation.

restoration.text: For verily the voice of the Lord is unto all men, and there is none to escape; and there is no eye that shall not see, neither ear that shall not hear, neither heart that shall not be penetrated.
restoration.comment: The Doctrine and Covenants' opening declaration of universal address—the Restoration's own statement that the Lord's voice reaches all men, without restriction or exception.

s4.text: He receives all who confess His name.
s4.panel_comment: The receptive act of Christ—naming not merely the invitation's scope (s3) but its outcome: He receives. John 6:37 is Christ's own direct promise of non-rejection (him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out)—the strongest possible anchor, in Christ's own words. Acts 10:34–35 is Peter's breakthrough confession that God is no respecter of persons—grounding universal reception in the apostolic witness that was itself a conversion from exclusivism. The confession carries extra pastoral weight because it came from a man who had to learn it. Alma 5:33 provides the Restoration's most direct statement of Christ's receptive posture: the arms of mercy are extended towards them, and he saith: Repent, and I will receive you. The arms-of-mercy image makes reception an active posture, not a passive permission.

biblical.text: All that the Father giveth me shall come to me; and him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.
biblical.comment: Christ's own direct promise of non-rejection—the verbatim ground for the Declaration's reception claim.

biblical.text: Then Peter opened his mouth, and said, Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons: But in every nation he that feareth him, and worketh righteousness, is accepted with him.
biblical.comment: The apostolic breakthrough—universal acceptability confirmed through prophetic experience. The weight increases because Peter had to be taught this.

restoration.text: Behold, he sendeth an invitation unto all men, for the arms of mercy are extended towards them, and he saith: Repent, and I will receive you.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's most direct statement of Christ's receptive posture—active embrace, not passive permission. The arms-of-mercy image is the visual ground for the Declaration's claim.

s5.panel_comment: The Declaration's most affective sentence—five words naming the experiential ground of everything proclaimed before it. Gal 2:20 is Paul's personal witness in its most concentrated form (Christ liveth in me)—testimonial ground. Col 1:27 names the theological mystery and the hope (Christ in you, the hope of glory)—doctrinal ground. The two biblical anchors frame the claim from two directions: the first is testimonial, the second is doctrinal. Alma 5:14 provides the Restoration's diagnostic question—Have ye received his image in your countenances?—whose answer A13 s5 is. The Declaration does not ask whether He is in our hearts. It declares that He is. The panel_comment closes here, matching the sentence's own restraint.

biblical.text: I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me: and the life which I now live in the flesh I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself for me.
biblical.comment: The Pauline personal witness of Christ's interior presence—testimonial ground.

biblical.text: To whom God would make known what is the riches of the glory of this mystery among the Gentiles; which is Christ in you, the hope of glory:
biblical.comment: The doctrinal ground—Christ's indwelling is not sentiment but revealed mystery and anchored hope.

restoration.text: And now behold, I ask of you, my brethren of the church, have ye spiritually been born of God? Have ye received his image in your countenances? Have ye experienced this mighty change in your hearts?
restoration.comment: Alma's diagnostic question whose answer A13 s5 is. Question and declaration form a call-and-response across the canon.

s6.text: We have accepted Him as our divine Savior with or without perfect doctrinal understanding.
s6.panel_comment: The closing confessional echo of the cluster's opening merognostic posture (A1 s1). At A1, merognostic restraint governed epistemology—the foundational acknowledgment of partial knowing. Here at A13, the same restraint appears in confessional register: the act of accepting Christ does not require doctrinal completion before it is valid. Divine Savior is a container word—each tradition's Christological register fills it from within, without requiring convergence as a precondition. Acts 16:31 is the Philippian jailer's salvation in its simplest form: Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved—no catechism required. Rom 10:9 grounds the confessional act itself (confess with thy mouth) as the operative instrument. Matt 18:3–4 provides the child-faith premise: humility, not doctrinal precision, is the credential. Ether 12:27 provides the Restoration's direct answer to the without perfect doctrinal understanding clause: grace sufficient for all who humble themselves closes the merognostic arc that A1 opened. This span is the Declaration's answer to the question the cluster has held since A1: what is enough to stand with Christ? This is enough.

biblical.text: And they said, Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved, and thy house.
biblical.comment: The minimal confessional statement—faith in Christ as the sufficient act of acceptance, without doctrinal elaboration.

biblical.text: That if thou shalt confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus, and shalt believe in thine heart that God hath raised him from the dead, thou shalt be saved.
biblical.comment: The confessional act as the operative instrument—naming the Lord Jesus and believing in the resurrection is the mechanism of acceptance.

biblical.text: And said, Verily I say unto you, Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven. Whosoever therefore shall humble himself as this little child, the same is greatest in the kingdom of heaven.
biblical.comment: The child-faith premise—humility, not doctrinal precision, is the credential for entry.

restoration.text: And if men come unto me I will show unto them their weakness. I give unto men weakness that they may be humble; and my grace is sufficient for all men that humble themselves before me; for if they humble themselves before me, and have faith in me, then will I make weak things become strong unto them.
restoration.comment: Grace sufficient for all who humble themselves—the Restoration's direct answer to the without perfect doctrinal understanding clause. The merognostic arc that A1 opened closes here.

crossref.label: See Article 1
crossref.title: Span s1: merognostic restraint in epistemological register; A13 s6 is its confessional echo

s7.text: We follow Him with or without the permission or approval of others.
s7.panel_comment: Paragraph 1's closing claim—discipleship as a covenant between the disciple and Christ, prior to any human institutional authorization. The three anchors work sequentially: the principle stated (Acts 5:29), the personal consequence named (Gal 1:10), the ground for confidence affirmed (D&C 122:9). Acts 5:29 is the apostolic declaration at its most direct: We ought to obey God rather than men. Gal 1:10 is Paul's personal framing that seeking human approval and serving Christ are mutually exclusive vocations. D&C 122:9 provides the Restoration confidence clause: fear not what man can do, for God shall be with you forever and ever. The cluster does not read this as defiance—s8 immediately opens in welcome—but as the prior claim that following Christ belongs to the disciple and to Christ before it belongs to any institution or tradition.

biblical.text: Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
biblical.comment: The apostolic statement of the principle—obedience to God as categorically prior to human authorization.

biblical.text: For do I now persuade men, or God? or do I seek to please men? for if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ.
biblical.comment: The personal consequence—seeking human approval and serving Christ occupy the same space and cannot both hold it.

restoration.text: Thy days are known, and thy years shall not be numbered less; therefore, fear not what man can do, for God shall be with you forever and ever.
restoration.comment: The confidence clause—the disciple who follows regardless of human permission does not do so alone. The fear-not structure is the ground for the Declaration's unconditional following.

s8.panel_comment: The ministry's declaration of discipleship loyalty—standing with Christ as the covenantal posture that defines everything the Declaration says next. John 15:4–5 provides the relational ground in Christ's own words: abiding in Him as branches in the vine, the mutual indwelling that makes standing with Him more than assent. Matt 10:32 provides the public covenantal dimension: confessing Christ before others draws His reciprocal acknowledgment before the Father—the exchange of standing. Mosiah 5:7–8 provides the Restoration's covenantal grounding: those who take upon them His name are called the children of Christ, His sons and daughters—standing with Him means entering the relationship He offers and bearing His name.

biblical.text: Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, except it abide in the vine; no more can ye, except ye abide in me. I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing.
biblical.comment: The relational posture of standing with Christ—mutual abiding as the ground of discipleship loyalty, in Christ's own words.

biblical.text: Whosoever therefore shall confess me before men, him will I confess also before my Father which is in heaven.
biblical.comment: The public covenantal dimension—confessing Christ draws His reciprocal standing with us before the Father.

restoration.text: And now, because of the covenant which ye have made ye shall be called the children of Christ, his sons, and his daughters; for behold, this day he hath spiritually begotten you; for ye say that your hearts are changed through faith on his name; therefore, ye are born of him and have become his sons and daughters. And under this head ye are made free, and there is no other head whereby ye can be made free. There is no other name given whereby salvation cometh; therefore, I would that ye should take upon you the name of Christ, all you that have entered into the covenant with God that ye should be obedient unto the end of your lives.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's covenantal ground—taking His name, being called His children. Standing with Christ is entering the relationship He offers.

s9.text: we welcome all who seek to understand, whether or not they share the same belief in God, or don't yet know what they believe, or even if they hold to creeds that differ from the basic foundations professed within these articles.
s9.panel_comment: A13 s9 extends the hospitality architecture of A8 beyond fellow believers to the furthest edge of the human community—those without settled belief, those who may hold no belief in God, and those whose creeds differ from the Declaration's own foundations. A8 welcomed believers across traditions; A13 welcomes whoever seeks to understand, regardless of what they currently hold. Luke 15:1–2 provides the canonical scene: tax collectors and sinners drew near to Jesus and He received them—the Pharisees' complaint (This man receiveth sinners) is exactly the hospitality the Declaration claims. Romans 15:7 provides the imperative ground: receive one another as Christ received us—the manner of His reception as the model. 2 Nephi 26:33 is reasserted from Article 1 Span 12 and Article 8 Spans 1–2 in different rhetorical direction. At A1 s12 the verse grounded the soteriological negation against gatekeeping; at A8 s1 and s2 it grounded universal ecclesial reception. Here at A13 s9 the verse grounds the Declaration's active welcome of all seekers including non-believers—he remembereth the heathen; and all are alike unto God. 3 Nephi 18:32 provides Christ's direct instruction not to cast out those who differ or falter: ye know not but what they will return. D&C 18:10–11 grounds the entire welcome in the worth of souls—the welcome is commensurate with what He suffered for each one.

biblical.text: Then drew near unto him all the publicans and sinners for to hear him. And the Pharisees and scribes murmured, saying, This man receiveth sinners, and eateth with them.
biblical.comment: The canonical scene of welcome—Jesus receiving those the self-righteous excluded. The Pharisees' complaint is the Declaration's claim.

biblical.text: Wherefore receive ye one another, as Christ also received us to the glory of God.
biblical.comment: The imperative ground—Christ's own manner of reception as the model for the Declaration's welcome.

restoration.text: For none of these iniquities come of the Lord; for he doeth that which is good among the children of men; and he doeth nothing save it be plain unto the children of men; and he inviteth them all to come unto him and partake of his goodness; and he denieth none that come unto him, black and white, bond and free, male and female; and he remembereth the heathen; and all are alike unto God, both Jew and Gentile.
restoration.comment: Reasserted from Article 1 Span 12 and Article 8 Spans 1–2 in different rhetorical direction. Prior deployments in soteriological and ecclesial registers; here the verse grounds the Declaration's active welcome of all seekers including non-believers—he remembereth the heathen.

restoration.text: Nevertheless, ye shall not cast him out of your synagogues, or your places of worship, for unto such shall ye continue to minister; for ye know not but what they will return and repent, and come unto me with full purpose of heart, and I shall heal them; and I, the Lord, will have mercy upon them.
restoration.comment: Christ's direct instruction not to exclude those who differ or falter—the Restoration's ground for continuing hospitality to seekers who may not yet believe.

restoration.text: Remember the worth of souls is great in the sight of God; For, behold, the Lord your Redeemer suffered death in the flesh; wherefore he suffered the pain of all men, that all men might repent and come unto him.
restoration.comment: The worth of every soul—the welcome is commensurate with what Christ suffered for each one sought.

crossref.label: See Article 8
crossref.title: Fellow Believers — hospitality architecture A13 s9 extends to the furthest edge of unbelief

s10.text: In the spirit of peace, we build on those beliefs we hold in common, and exercise careful restraint and Christ-like patience regarding things that might divide us.
s10.panel_comment: The Declaration's ecumenical discipline—two clauses naming the positive strategy (build on common ground) and the restrained posture (patience toward division). Eph 4:3 grounds the peace-orientation: endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace—the active work of maintaining unity, not assuming it. Endeavouring names the labor required. 2 Tim 2:24 grounds the patience clause: the servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men, patient—the Pastoral Epistle's naming of the disposition that makes theological difference bearable without pretending it does not exist. Moroni 7:3–4 provides the Restoration's naming of this posture: the peaceable followers of Christ who walk peaceably with the children of men—the peaceable walk as a posture grounded in the hope of what Christ has secured, not in the absence of disagreement. D&C 64:10 grounds the patience clause from the forgiveness side: of you it is required to forgive all men—the forgiveness imperative as the operational discipline behind Christ-like patience when division is real and difference is not resolved. The cluster throughout has named what divides; A13 s9 names the posture that makes the Declaration possible across all of it.

biblical.text: Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.
biblical.comment: The active work of peace-maintenance—deliberate effort, not passive tolerance. Endeavouring names the labor the common-ground strategy requires.

biblical.text: And the servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient,
biblical.comment: The Pastoral Epistle's disposition clause—no striving, but gentleness and patience with all, including those who differ.

restoration.text: Wherefore, I would speak unto you that are of the church, that are the peaceable followers of Christ, and that have obtained a sufficient hope by which ye can enter into the rest of the Lord, from this time henceforth until ye shall rest with him in heaven. And now I judge these things of you because of your peaceable walk with the children of men.
restoration.comment: Mormon's naming of the peaceable followers of Christ whose walk with the children of men reflects their sufficient hope. The peaceable walk is not acquiescence but a posture grounded in what Christ has secured.

restoration.text: I, the Lord, will forgive whom I will forgive, but of you it is required to forgive all men.
restoration.comment: The forgiveness imperative as the operational discipline behind Christ-like patience—the ground on which careful restraint is sustained when division is real and difference is not resolved.

s11.panel_comment: The Declaration's final sentence. Universal filiation as the closing word of the cluster—the ground beneath everything the thirteen articles have said. Psalm 82:6 provides the prophetic floor: Ye are gods; and all of you are children of the most High—the direct OT assertion of universal divine filiation, and the verse Jesus cites in John 10:34 when defending His own claim to divine sonship. Acts 17:28–29 is Paul's witness to the Athenians, addressed to non-believers in their own cultural register, that all people are God's offspring—the broadest possible audience for the broadest possible claim. Mal 2:10 provides the prophetic question whose answer the Declaration is: Have we not all one father? hath not one God created us? Malachi's rhetorical force turns filiation into a moral claim—if we share one Father, the division that follows becomes the thing the Declaration refuses. D&C 76:24 provides the Restoration's cosmological ground: the inhabitants of all worlds are begotten sons and daughters unto God—the filiation claim extended to every world Christ has made, not only this one. The panel_comment closes here. The Declaration ends with the simplest possible truth.

biblical.text: I have said, Ye are gods; and all of you are children of the most High.
biblical.comment: The OT prophetic floor for universal filiation—and the verse Christ cites in John 10:34 when the crowd accuses Him of claiming divine sonship.

biblical.text: For in him we live, and move, and have our being; as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring. Forasmuch then as we are the offspring of God, we ought not to think that the Godhead is like unto gold, or silver, or stone, graven by art and man's device.
biblical.comment: Paul's witness to non-believers in their own cultural register—the filiation claim addressed to the widest possible audience, in the broadest apostolic setting.

biblical.text: Have we not all one father? hath not one God created us? why do we deal treacherously every man against his brother, by profaning the covenant of our fathers?
biblical.comment: The prophetic question whose answer the Declaration is. Universal filiation as moral ground—if we share one Father, division becomes the thing refused.

restoration.text: That by him, and through him, and of him, the worlds are and were created, and the inhabitants thereof are begotten sons and daughters unto God.
restoration.comment: The Restoration's cosmological ground for universal filiation—all inhabitants of all worlds are begotten sons and daughters unto God. The scope matches and exceeds the Declaration's already-universal frame.
